# Glossary of Linguistics Terms

Phoneme: the smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning (e.g., /p/ vs. /b/ in English "pat" vs. "bat").
Allophone: a variant pronunciation of a phoneme that does not change word meaning (e.g., aspirated [pʰ] and unaspirated [p] in English).
Phone: any distinct speech sound, whether or not it is phonemically contrastive in a given language.
Morpheme: the smallest meaningful unit of language (e.g., the plural "-s" in "cats").
Morphology: the branch of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
Allomorph: a variant form of a morpheme (e.g., "un-", "in-", "im-" are allomorphs of the morpheme meaning "not").
Root: the core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning and cannot be further decomposed.
Stem: a morpheme or combination of morphemes to which inflectional affixes can be attached.
Affix: a morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Prefix: an affix attached before a root or stem (e.g., "un-" in "undo").
Suffix: an affix attached after a root or stem (e.g., "-ness" in "happiness").
Infix: a morpheme inserted within a root or stem (e.g., "-il-" in Cebuano "tum-ilog" from "log").
Circumfix: a bound morpheme that surrounds a root or stem (e.g., German "be-...-en" in "begehen").
Derivational morpheme: a morpheme that creates a new word or changes the grammatical category of a word.
Inflectional morpheme: a morpheme that modifies a word for grammatical purposes without changing its core meaning or category.
Zero morpheme: a morpheme that has no phonological content but is inferred from context (e.g., the absence of a plural marker in English "sheep").
Compounding: a morphological process that combines two or more free morphemes to form a new word.
Conversion: a morphological process that changes a word's grammatical category without adding an affix (e.g., "to google").
Portmanteau: a blend of two morphemes where a single affix serves multiple grammatical functions (e.g., French "j'" combining subject and article).
Agglutinative: a language type in which morphemes are typically concatenated in a one-to-one correspondence with grammatical meanings (e.g., Turkish, Finnish).
Fusional: a language type in which a single morpheme can express multiple grammatical features simultaneously (e.g., Latin, Arabic).
Isolating: a language type in which morphemes correspond to single words and there is little inflection (e.g., Mandarin Chinese).
Polysynthetic: a language type in which words can be extremely long, incorporating what would be entire clauses in other languages (e.g., Mohawk).
Paradigm: the complete set of inflected forms of a word (e.g., the conjugation table of a verb).
Lexeme: an abstract unit representing a set of related word forms (e.g., "run," "runs," "running" belong to the lexeme RUN).
Lemma: the citation form of a word, typically the base or uninflected form (e.g., "go" is the lemma for "goes," "going," "gone").
Homophone: words that are pronounced the same but differ in meaning and/or spelling (e.g., "flower" and "flour").
Homograph: words that are spelled the same but differ in meaning and/or pronunciation (e.g., "lead" the metal and "lead" to guide).
Homonym: words that share both form and pronunciation but have different meanings.
Heteronym: words that share spelling but differ in pronunciation (e.g., "read" present vs. past).
Polysemy: the phenomenon of a single word having multiple related senses (e.g., "head" as body part, top, leader).
Synonym: words that have the same or very similar meanings (e.g., "big" and "large").
Antonym: words with opposite meanings (e.g., "hot" and "cold").
Hyponym: a word whose meaning is a subset of another word's meaning (e.g., "sparrow" is a hyponym of "bird").
Hypernym: a word with a broader meaning that encompasses a set of more specific words (e.g., "animal" is a hypernym of "dog").
Meronym: a word denoting a part of a whole (e.g., "finger" is a meronym of "hand").
Holonym: a word denoting a whole composed of parts (e.g., "hand" is a holonym of "finger").
Syllable: a unit of organization in speech, typically consisting of a vowel (nucleus) optionally flanked by consonants.
Nucleus: the vowel or syllabic sonorant at the center of a syllable.
Onset: the consonant or consonant cluster at the beginning of a syllable, before the nucleus.
Coda: the consonant or consonant cluster at the end of a syllable, after the nucleus.
Rhyme: the portion of a syllable from the vowel (nucleus) through the coda.
Syllable weight: the classification of syllables as light or heavy based on their segmental content, often relevant to stress patterns.
Stress: the relative prominence of a syllable in a word or phrase, typically realized through pitch, duration, or loudness.
Tone: the use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning at the syllable level (e.g., in Mandarin Chinese).
Tone language: a language in which lexical distinctions are made through differences in pitch contour.
Prosody: the suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, rhythm, intonation, and tone, that pattern beyond individual segments.
Suprasegmental: a phonological feature that extends over more than one segment (e.g., stress, tone, intonation).
Segmental: a phonological feature associated with individual consonants or vowels.
Consonant: a speech sound produced with a constriction in the vocal tract that partially or completely obstructs airflow.
Vowel: a speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction.
Plosive (stop): a consonant produced by completely blocking airflow and then releasing it (e.g., /p/, /t/, /k/).
Fricative: a consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract to create turbulent airflow (e.g., /s/, /ʃ/).
Affricate: a consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative (e.g., /tʃ/ in "church").
Nasal: a consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nose (e.g., /m/, /n/, /ŋ/).
Lateral: a consonant in which airflow is directed around the sides of the tongue (e.g., /l/).
Rhotic: a consonant involving the tongue tip or blade making contact with or near the alveolar ridge (e.g., /r/, /ɹ/).
Trill: a rhotic produced by several rapid contacts of the tongue (e.g., Spanish /r/).
Tap (flap): a rhotic produced by a single brief contact of the tongue (e.g., American English /ɾ/ in "butter").
Glide: a consonant produced by a gradual change in articulatory position (e.g., /w/, /j/).
Place of articulation: the location in the vocal tract where a consonant's primary constriction occurs.
Manner of articulation: the type of constriction and airflow mechanism used to produce a consonant.
Voicing: the vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a speech sound.
Aspiration: a burst of breath accompanying the release of a voiceless stop.
Palatalization: a secondary articulation in which the body of the tongue approaches the hard palate.
Velarization: a secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue approaches the soft palate.
Labialization: a secondary articulation in which the lips are rounded during the production of a sound.
Bilabial: a place of articulation involving both lips (e.g., /p/, /b/, /m/).
Labiodental: a place of articulation involving the lower lip and upper teeth (e.g., /f/, /v/).
Dental: a place of articulation involving the tongue tip and upper teeth (e.g., Thai /θ/, /ð/).
Alveolar: a place of articulation involving the tongue tip and the alveolar ridge (e.g., English /t/, /d/, /n/, /l/, /s/, /z/).
Postalveolar: a place of articulation just behind the alveolar ridge (e.g., English /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/).
Palatal: a place of articulation involving the tongue body and the hard palate (e.g., /j/, /ɕ/).
Velar: a place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the soft palate (e.g., /k/, /g/, /ŋ/, /x/).
Uvular: a place of articulation involving the back of the tongue and the uvula (e.g., /q/, /ʁ/, /ʕ/).
Pharyngeal: a place of articulation involving the pharyngeal wall (e.g., Arabic /ħ/, /ʕ/).
Glottal: a place of articulation at the glottis (e.g., /h/, /ʔ/).
Diphthong: a vowel sound in which the pronunciation glides from one vowel quality to another (e.g., /aɪ/ in "my").
Monophthong: a pure vowel sound maintained at a single articulatory position throughout its duration.
Vowel harmony: a phonological rule requiring vowels within a word or phrase to share a particular feature (e.g., frontness, backness, or rounding).
Assimilation: a sound change in which one sound becomes more like a neighboring sound (e.g., "inpossible" → "impossible").
Dissimilation: a sound change in which two similar sounds become less alike (e.g., "spermatozoon" → "spermatozoon" in some languages).
Elision: the omission of a sound or syllable, often in fast speech (e.g., "gonna" from "going to").
Epenthesis: the insertion of an extra sound within or between words (e.g., the /t/ in "water" for some English speakers).
Metathesis: the transposition of sounds within a word (e.g., "ask" from Old English "æscian").
Lenition: a diachronic or stylistic process in which a consonant becomes phonetically weaker (e.g., /p/ → /f/).
Fortition: the strengthening of a consonant over time (e.g., /z/ → /s/ in some dialects).
Debuccalization: the weakening of a consonant to a glottal sound or its complete loss (e.g., /t/ → /ʔ/).
Vowel shift: a systematic change in the quality or position of vowels in a language over time (e.g., the Great Vowel Shift in English).
Phonotactics: the constraints on permissible sound combinations in a language (e.g., English cannot begin with /ŋ/).
Maximal onset principle: a syllabification rule that assigns as many consonants as possible to the onset of a syllable.
Schwa: the mid-central, unstressed vowel /ə/, the most common vowel in many languages.
Glottal stop: a plosive produced at the glottis, represented as /ʔ/ (e.g., in "uh-oh").
Creaky voice: a phonation type characterized by irregular, low-frequency vibration of the vocal folds (also called vocal fry).
F0 (fundamental frequency): the primary frequency of a voiced sound, perceived as pitch.
Formant: a resonant frequency of the vocal tract that characterizes vowel quality.
Spectrogram: a visual representation of the frequency content of a speech signal over time.
Articulatory phonetics: the study of how speech sounds are produced by the organs of the vocal tract.
Acoustic phonetics: the study of the physical properties of speech sounds as sound waves.
Auditory phonetics: the study of how speech sounds are perceived by the listener.
Minimal pair: a pair of words that differ in only one sound and have different meanings, demonstrating that the sound is a phoneme.
Complementary distribution: a situation in which two allophones never occur in the same phonetic environment.
Contrastive distribution: a situation in which two sounds can occur in the same environment and distinguish meaning.
Neutralization: a phonological process in which a contrast between two phonemes is eliminated in a particular environment.
Apophony: a system of vowel alternation within a paradigm (e.g., Latin "canto, canere, cecinī").
Ablaut: a type of apophony involving systematic vowel alternation (e.g., English "sing, sang, sung").
Umlaut: a type of vowel harmony or vowel change triggered by a following high vowel, often historical (e.g., German "Maus" → "Mäuse").
Phonological rule: a formal statement describing a systematic sound alternation in a language.
Distinctive features: binary or multi-valued properties (e.g., [+voice], [+nasal]) used to characterize and contrast speech sounds.
Feature geometry: a hierarchical model organizing phonological features into tiers to explain natural classes and patterns.
Natural class: a set of segments that share one or more distinctive features and behave similarly in phonological rules.
Archiphoneme: an abstract phoneme created when two or more phonemes are neutralized in a given environment.
Tense: a grammatical category that locates a situation in time relative to the moment of speech.
Aspect: a grammatical category that describes the temporal structure of a situation (e.g., progressive, perfective, imperfective).
Mood: a grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the content of a sentence (e.g., indicative, subjunctive, imperative).
Voice: a grammatical category relating the subject of a clause to the action (e.g., active, passive).
Evidentiality: a grammatical system marking the source or type of information for a statement (e.g., witnessed, inferred, reported).
Valency: the number of arguments a verb requires or allows.
Argument: a syntactic element (typically a noun phrase) that is required or permitted by a predicate.
Adjunct: an optional syntactic modifier that adds information but is not required by the predicate.
Complement: an obligatory syntactic element required to complete the meaning of a head.
Specifier: the element at the top of a phrase that typically determines its category (e.g., the determiner in a DP).
Head: the central, categorizing element of a phrase that determines its syntactic type.
Modifier: a syntactic element that modifies the meaning of another element.
Noun phrase (NP/DP): a syntactic constituent headed by a noun or determiner.
Verb phrase (VP): a syntactic constituent headed by a verb, including its complements and adjuncts.
Prepositional phrase (PP): a syntactic constituent headed by a preposition, typically followed by its complement.
Subordinate clause: a clause that functions as a constituent within a larger clause (e.g., "that he left").
Coordinate clause: a clause of equal rank joined by a coordinating conjunction (e.g., "and," "but").
Relative clause: a clause that modifies a noun and is typically introduced by a relative pronoun (e.g., "the man who called").
Complementizer: a word that introduces a complement clause (e.g., "that," "if," "whether").
Conjunction: a word that connects words, phrases, or clauses (e.g., "and," "or," "but").
Determiner: a word that precedes and modifies a noun, often specifying definiteness or quantity (e.g., "the," "a," "this").
Article: a type of determiner marking definiteness or indefiniteness (e.g., "the," "a/an").
Pronoun: a word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase (e.g., "he," "it," "they").
Demonstrative: a determiner or pronoun pointing to a specific entity (e.g., "this," "that").
Quantifier: a word or phrase expressing amount or number (e.g., "all," "some," "three").
Negation: a grammatical operation that reverses the truth value of a proposition (e.g., "not," "no," "never").
Scope: the domain over which a semantic or pragmatic operator (e.g., negation, quantifier) applies.
Binding: the syntactic and semantic relationship between a pronoun or variable and its antecedent.
Antecedent: the noun phrase to which a pronoun or anaphoric element refers.
Anaphora: a linguistic expression (e.g., pronoun) whose referent is determined by another expression in the discourse.
Exophora: reference to an entity outside the immediate discourse context (e.g., pointing at something).
Endophora: reference to an entity already mentioned in the discourse.
Cataphora: reference forward to an entity yet to be mentioned in the discourse.
Binding Theory: a set of principles in syntax (Principles A, B, C) governing the distribution of pronouns and anaphors.
Binding Principle A: an anaphor must be bound in its local domain (e.g., "Himself" must refer to a local antecedent).
Binding Principle B: a pronoun must be free in its local domain.
Binding Principle C: a referential expression must be free everywhere (e.g., "John" cannot be bound by a pronoun).
Ergative: a case marking or alignment system in which the agent of a transitive verb is marked differently from the sole argument of an intransitive verb and the patient of a transitive verb.
Absolutive: a case that marks the patient of a transitive verb and the sole argument of an intransitive verb, forming the other side of an ergative alignment.
Nominative-accusative alignment: a case system where the sole argument of an intransitive verb (S) is marked like the agent of a transitive verb (A), distinct from the patient (P).
Ergative-absolutive alignment: a case system where the patient of a transitive verb (P) is marked like the sole argument of an intransitive verb (S), distinct from the agent (A).
Split ergativity: a language pattern in which ergative and accusative alignments are used in different grammatical contexts (e.g., based on tense).
Nominative: a grammatical case marking the subject of an intransitive verb or the agent of a transitive verb in nominative-accusative languages.
Accusative: a grammatical case marking the patient or direct object of a transitive verb.
Dative: a grammatical case marking the indirect object or recipient.
Genitive: a grammatical case marking possession, origin, or other associative relations.
Vocative: a grammatical case used to address or call out to someone.
Instrumental: a grammatical case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Ablative: a grammatical case marking separation, source, or "from."
Allative: a grammatical case marking direction toward or "to."
Locative: a grammatical case marking location or position.
Evidential: a grammatical marker indicating the source of the speaker's knowledge (e.g., direct perception, inference, hearsay).
Illocutionary act: the intended communicative function of an utterance (e.g., promising, requesting, warning), a concept from speech act theory.
Perlocutionary act: the effect an utterance has on the listener (e.g., persuading, alarming, entertaining).
Propositional content: the descriptive or truth-conditional content of an utterance, independent of its force.
Speech act: a unit of communication that performs an action (e.g., ordering, promising) in addition to conveying a proposition.
Direct speech act: an utterance whose form directly matches its illocutionary force (e.g., "I promise" to promise).
Indirect speech act: an utterance whose surface form does not directly match its illocutionary force (e.g., "Can you pass the salt?" as a request).
Grice's Maxims: four conversational principles (Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner) proposed by Paul Grice to explain cooperative communication.
Implicature: an inferred meaning that goes beyond the literal content of an utterance, derived from conversational principles.
Conversational implicature: an inferred meaning arising from the assumption that a speaker is following the conversational maxims.
Conventional implicature: a meaning attached to a word or expression by convention, independent of context (e.g., "but" implies contrast).
Presupposition: background information assumed to be true for an utterance to be meaningful (e.g., "The king of France" presupposes a king exists).
Accommodation: the process by which a listener adjusts their contextual assumptions to make an utterance interpretable.
Deixis: the linguistic anchoring of expressions to the context of utterance (e.g., "here," "now," "I").
Anaphoric: relating to a word or expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity.
Cataphoric: relating to a word or expression that refers forward to an entity mentioned later.
Referent: the entity in the world to which a linguistic expression points.
Reference: the relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity it denotes in the world.
Denotation: the set of entities to which a word or expression applies (e.g., the denotation of "dog" is the set of all dogs).
Connotation: the set of associations, emotions, or implied meanings a word carries beyond its denotation.
Prototype: the most typical or central member of a category around which the category is organized (e.g., a robin as a prototype bird).
Prototype theory: the theory that categories are organized around central, typical members rather than defined by necessary and sufficient conditions.
Mental lexicon: the hypothesized repository in the mind where lexical items are stored and organized.
Semantic field: a set of words related by a common conceptual domain (e.g., words for colors).
Semantic role (theta role): the semantic relationship between an argument and the predicate (e.g., Agent, Patient, Goal, Experiencer).
Agent: the thematic role of a voluntary, sentient causer of an action.
Patient: the thematic role of an entity affected or changed by an action.
Experiencer: the thematic role of a sentient being that experiences a state or event.
Goal: the thematic role of an endpoint toward which motion or transfer is directed.
Source: the thematic role of an origin from which motion or transfer begins.
Location: the thematic role of the spatial or temporal setting of an event.
Instrument: the thematic role of the means or tool used to perform an action.
Beneficiary: the thematic role of an entity for whose benefit an action is performed.
Telicity: the property of a predicate denoting a bounded, goal-oriented event with a natural endpoint.
Atelicity: the property of a predicate denoting an unbounded, non-goal-oriented event with no natural endpoint.
Aktivity: an atelic, durative predicate denoting a continuous activity (e.g., "run").
Accomplishment: a telic, durative predicate denoting a bounded process (e.g., "build a house").
Achievement: a telic, punctual predicate denoting an instantaneous change of state (e.g., "recognize," "arrive").
State: an atelic, durative predicate denoting a static condition (e.g., "know," "be tall").
Aspectual class: the categorization of predicates intoAktivity, accomplishment, achievement, and state based on their temporal and boundedness properties.
Lexical aspect (Aktivity profile): the inherent temporal structure of a verb or event denoted by a predicate.
Grammatical aspect: the morphosyntactic encoding of aspectual information (e.g., progressive, perfective markers).
Perfective: an aspect indicating that an event is viewed as a completed whole.
Imperfective: an aspect indicating that an event is viewed as ongoing, habitual, or internally.
Progressive: an aspect indicating that an event is in progress at a reference time (e.g., "I was running").
Perfect: an aspect indicating a present relevance of a past event or a state resulting from a past event.
Passive: a voice construction in which the patient of an active clause becomes the grammatical subject.
Active: a voice construction in which the agent is the grammatical subject and the patient is the object.
Middle voice: a verbal category in which the subject is both affected by and involved in the action.
Antipassive: a voice construction that demotes the patient of a transitive verb, often making the verb intransitive.
Nominalization: the process of deriving a noun from a verb or other non-nominal category (e.g., "the destruction of the city" from "destroy").
Verbalization: the process of deriving a verb from a noun or other non-verbal category (e.g., "to desk" from "desk").
Inchoative: a verbal category or construction expressing the beginning of a state or change (e.g., "The door opened" in its inchoative sense).
Causative: a verbal category or construction expressing the causing of an event or state (e.g., "She broke the glass").
Reciprocal: a verbal category expressing a mutual or mutual action among participants (e.g., "They met").
Reflexive: a verbal construction in which the subject is also the object (e.g., "He hurt himself").
Iterative: a verbal aspect or morpheme indicating repeated or repeated action.
Diminutive: a morpheme indicating smallness or endearment (e.g., Spanish "-ito" in "gatito").
Augmentative: a morpheme indicating largeness or emphasis (e.g., Spanish "-ón" in "perro grande").
Pejorative: a morpheme or expression that conveys a negative or contemptuous evaluation.
Reduplication: a morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to express grammatical meaning (e.g., iterativity, plurality).
Portmanteau morpheme: a single morpheme that encodes multiple grammatical or semantic features (e.g., French "j'" = "je" + vowel elision).
Suppletion: the irregular use of an entirely different root to express a grammatical contrast (e.g., English "go" → "went").
Morphological productivity: the degree to which a morphological process can be freely applied to new or existing bases.
Morphological opacity: the degree to which the form of a word does not transparently reflect its underlying morphemes.
Morphological transparency: the degree to which the form of a word clearly reflects its component morphemes.
Morphotactics: the set of rules governing the order and combination of morphemes within a word.
Non-concatenative morphology: a morphological process that involves internal modification (e.g., vowel changes) rather than affixation (common in Semitic languages).
Non-linear morphology: the theoretical framework for describing morphological processes that rearrange or interleave segments rather than simply concatenating them.
Root and pattern (template) morphology: a system in which a consonantal root is interleaved with a fixed vocalic template to produce word forms (e.g., Arabic, Hebrew).
Broken plurals: irregular plural forms in Semitic languages created by changing the internal vowel pattern of a root rather than adding a suffix.
Sociolinguistics: the study of the relationship between language and society, including dialect, register, and language variation.
Dialect: a variety of a language associated with a particular geographic region or social group.
Register: a variety of language associated with a particular communicative context or purpose (e.g., legal, academic, casual).
Social dialect: a variety of language associated with a particular social class, group, or community.
Cocktail party effect: the ability to focus on a single conversation in a noisy environment.
Code-switching: the alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: the blending of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance.
Bilingualism: the ability to use two or more languages, either simultaneously or sequentially.
Multilingualism: the ability to use more than two languages.
Diglossia: a stable sociolinguistic situation in which two varieties of a language serve different social functions (e.g., "high" and "low" varieties).
Language death: the process by which a language loses its last native speakers and is no longer spoken.
Language revitalization: efforts to reverse language death and reestablish a language as a living, spoken language.
Language endangerment: a condition in which a language is at risk of losing its last speakers.
Ethnolinguistics: the study of the relationship between language and culture, identity, and ethnic groups.
Language policy: the set of governmental or institutional decisions regarding the use, status, and promotion of languages.
Language planning: the deliberate effort to influence the structure or function of a language (e.g., standardization, reform).
Pidgin: a simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language, typically with no native speakers.
Creole: a natural, fully developed language that arises from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Singlish, Konglish, etc.: examples of language contact varieties (terms for specific national pidgin/creole varieties).
Linguistic relativity: the hypothesis that the structure of a language influences or determines the ways in which its speakers perceive and think about the world (Sapir-Whorf hypothesis).
Strong Whorfianism (linguistic determinism): the strong version of linguistic relativity claiming that language determines thought.
Weak Whorfianism (linguistic relativity): the weak version claiming that language influences but does not determine thought.
Universal Grammar (UG): the theoretical framework in generative linguistics proposing that humans are born with an innate set of grammatical principles.
Innateness hypothesis: the claim that the ability to acquire language is biologically innate and not solely learned.
Language acquisition device (LAD): a hypothetical innate mechanism proposed by Chomsky for facilitating language acquisition.
Critical period hypothesis: the claim that there is a biologically determined window during which language acquisition is most effective.
Language acquisition: the process by which humans, especially children, learn a language.
First language acquisition (L1): the process of acquiring one's native or first language.
Second language acquisition (L2): the process of learning a language other than one's native language.
Interlanguage: the evolving linguistic system a second language learner develops between the target language and their native language.
Comprehensible input: language input that is slightly beyond the learner's current level but understandable, a key concept in Krashen's theory.
Input: the linguistic material a learner is exposed to.
Output: the linguistic material a learner produces.
Feedback: the response a learner receives that informs them about the acceptability of their utterances.
Transfer: the influence of one's first language on second language learning.
Positive transfer: when L1 structures facilitate L2 learning.
Negative transfer: when L1 structures interfere with L2 learning.
Interference: the influence of one language on another, particularly in the context of bilingualism or L2 learning.
Calque: a loan translation in which a word or expression is translated word-for-word from another language (e.g., "skyscraper" from German "Wolkenkratzer").
Loanword: a word borrowed from one language and integrated into another.
Borrowing: the process by which a language adopts words, structures, or sounds from another language.
Language contact: the interaction between speakers of different languages that leads to mutual influence.
Language convergence: the process by which two or more languages in contact become more similar.
Language divergence: the process by which two or more languages become more different over time.
Substrate: the influence of a previously spoken language on a newly dominant language in a region.
Superstrate: the influence of a dominant language on a previously spoken local language.
Adstrate: the influence between languages in geographic contact that are neither dominant nor subordinate.
Areale: a geographic region characterized by a set of shared linguistic features due to contact, regardless of genetic relation.
Sprachbund: a group of geographically proximate languages that share features due to prolonged contact (e.g., the Balkan Sprachbund).
Historical linguistics: the study of how languages change over time and how languages are related through common ancestry.
Comparative method: a methodology for reconstructing proto-languages and establishing genetic relationships by systematically comparing cognate words.
Cognate: words in different languages that are derived from a common ancestral word (e.g., English "father" and Latin "pater").
Etymology: the study of the origin and historical development of words.
Proto-language: a hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of related languages is reconstructed (e.g., Proto-Indo-European).
Language family: a group of languages descended from a common ancestral proto-language (e.g., Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan).
Language isolate: a language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other known language (e.g., Basque).
Language stock: a hypothetical grouping of language families that may share a common ancestor (e.g., the proposed Nostratic stock).
Glottalization: the production of a glottal stop or creaky voice as a phonological feature.
Verner's Law: a sound law in Proto-Germanic explaining the voicing of certain consonants after unstressed syllables.
Grimm's Law: a sound law describing the systematic shift of Proto-Indo-European stops in Proto-Germanic (e.g., /p/ → /f/).
Grimm's Law and Verner's Law together: foundational sound laws in the reconstruction of the Proto-Germanic language.
Laryngeal theory: the hypothesis that Proto-Indo-European contained one or more laryngeal consonants, proposed to explain irregularities in vowel patterns.
Reconstruction: the process of formulating a hypothetical proto-language based on systematic correspondences among descendant languages.
Sound change: a systematic phonological change that affects all applicable instances in a language over time.
Analogical change: a change in which a form is modified to follow a more common or regular pattern.
Morphological leveling: the process by which irregular alternations are reduced in favor of regular patterns.
Dialect leveling: the reduction of dialectal differences through social and geographic contact.
Creolization: the process by which a pidgin becomes a fully grammaticalized creole language.
Pidginization: the process by which a language simplifies into a pidgin.
Koiné: a common variety of a language that develops to facilitate communication among speakers of different dialects.
Hypercorrection: an excessive or incorrect application of a standard or prestige form, often by speakers trying to appear more formal.
Hypostandard variety: a non-standard variety of a language that is stigmatized but linguistically complete.
Prestige variety: the variety of a language considered socially most desirable or authoritative.
Stigmatized variety: a variety of a language that is socially devalued or looked down upon.
Linguistic prescriptivism: the practice of enforcing rules about what is considered "correct" or "proper" language use.
Linguistic descriptivism: the practice of documenting and analyzing language as it is actually used by its speakers.
Linguistic competence: a speaker's internalized knowledge of the grammatical, phonological, and semantic rules of their language (Chomsky's term).
Linguistic performance: the actual production and comprehension of language, which may be affected by memory, attention, and other factors.
I-language: the internal, abstract linguistic system of an individual speaker (Chomsky's term).
E-language: the external, observable linguistic system shared by a community of speakers (Chomsky's term).
I-language vs. E-language: the distinction between an individual's internal grammar and the external language of a community.
Chomskyan hierarchy: the distinction between deep structure (underlying syntax) and surface structure (actual word order) in early generative grammar.
Government and Binding (GB) theory: a framework in generative syntax that analyzes syntactic structures using principles and parameters.
Principles and parameters: the theoretical approach that all languages share a set of universal syntactic principles, varying only in the setting of specific parameters.
X-bar theory: a component of generative grammar proposing a uniform structural schema for phrases (XP → Specifier-X-Complement).
Merge: the fundamental operation in minimalist syntax that combines two syntactic objects to form a new structure.
Move: the operation in minimalist syntax that copies an element from one position and inserts it in another (e.g., wh-movement).
Copy theory of movement: the proposal that movement creates a copy of an element rather than simply relocating it.
Feature checking: the process in minimalist syntax in which syntactic features are matched and valued through syntactic operations.
Agree: the minimalist operation by which a head (e.g., a verb) probes its domain and values the features of a goal (e.g., a noun).
Phase: a unit of derivation in phase theory (Minimalist Program), typically a CP or vP, within which syntactic operations are applied before the next phase begins.
Phase Impenetrability Condition (PIC): the constraint that elements in the complement of a phase head are inaccessible to operations in a later phase.
Minimalist Program (MP): the most recent framework in Chomskyan generative linguistics, seeking to derive grammar with minimal computational operations.
Derivation: the step-by-step construction of a syntactic structure from the lexicon to the final representation.
Spell-out: the process of converting a syntactic structure into a phonological (PF) and semantic (LF) representation.
Phonological Form (PF): the level of representation concerned with the phonological output of a sentence.
Logical Form (LF): the level of representation concerned with the semantic and interpretive content of a sentence.
Deep structure: the underlying syntactic representation of a sentence before movement or other transformations (a concept from early Transformational Grammar).
Surface structure: the final syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied.
Transformational grammar: the framework in generative linguistics (1957–1965) in which deep structures are transformed into surface structures.
Generative grammar: the overarching theoretical framework in linguistics that aims to describe the set of grammatical sentences of a language using a finite set of rules.
Universal Grammar: see Universal Grammar (UG) above.
Parameter setting: the process by which a learner sets the language-specific options in Universal Grammar based on the input language.
Optionality: the property of a linguistic element that may or may not be present.
Obligatory: a linguistic element that must be present in a given construction.
Subcategorization: the property of a lexical item that specifies the type and number of arguments it requires or selects.
Selection: the property of a predicate that specifies the semantic or syntactic type of its arguments.
Government: a syntactic relationship in which one head (e.g., a verb or preposition) controls the structure of another element in its domain.
Binding: see Binding above.
Control: a syntactic relationship in which an overt element (the controller) determines the reference of a covert PRO element in an embedded clause.
PRO: a null (unpronounced) subject of a non-finite embedded clause in control constructions (e.g., "John tried [PRO to leave]").
Trace: a silent copy left behind when an element moves in syntax (e.g., the empty subject position in "Who [t] left?").
Empty category: a position in the syntactic structure that lacks overt phonological content (e.g., PRO, trace, variable).
Variable: a position in the syntactic structure that is bound by a wh-phrase or quantifier (e.g., "Which book did you read [t]?").
Wh-movement: the syntactic movement of a wh-word from its thematic position to the clause-initial position (e.g., "What did you buy?").
Operator movement: the movement of an operator (e.g., a wh-word or negative quantifier) to a clause edge for scope interpretation.
Focus: the informational element in an utterance that is contrastive or new, often marked by prosody or syntax.
Information structure: the organization of discourse into given and new information, and the marking of focus and topic.
Topic: the element in an utterance about which something is being said, typically the starting point of a discourse.
Given: information that is already established in the discourse.
New: information that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse.
Contrast: the marking of one element as different from an alternative set (e.g., "It was JOHN who called," contrasting with other possible callers).
Information packaging: the arrangement of discourse elements according to their informational status (topic, focus, given, new).
Word order: the linear arrangement of syntactic constituents in a language (e.g., SVO, SOV, VSO).
Subject-Verb-Object (SVO): a word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object (e.g., English, Mandarin).
Subject-Object-Verb (SOV): a word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb (e.g., Japanese, Turkish).
Verb-Subject-Object (VSO): a word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object (e.g., Classical Arabic, Irish).
Free word order: a language in which constituent order is relatively unconstrained, often due to rich case marking.
Fixed word order: a language in which constituent order is rigid and cannot be freely permuted.
Pro-drop: the omission of pronouns when the referent is recoverable from context or verbal morphology (e.g., Spanish, Italian).
Null subject: a syntactically required subject position that is not phonologically realized (as in pro-drop languages).
Null object: an object position that is not phonologically realized.
Pro (null pronoun): an unpronounced pronoun that is syntactically present in pro-drop languages.
Clitic: a morpheme that is syntactically independent but phonologically dependent on a host word (e.g., French "le" in "je le vois").
Enclitic: a clitic that attaches to the end of a host word.
Proclitic: a clitic that attaches to the beginning of a host word.
Cliticization: the process by which a clitic attaches to a host word, often with reduced phonological form.
Clitic climbing: the phenomenon in which a clitic "climbs" out of an embedded clause to attach to a higher verb (e.g., Italian).
Clitic cluster: a sequence of multiple clitics attached to a single host word (common in Slavic languages).
Enclitic cluster: a sequence of enclitics following a host word.
Proclitic cluster: a sequence of proclitics preceding a host word.
Noun incorporation: a process in which a noun is morphologically incorporated into a verb to form a single complex verb (common in polysynthetic languages).
Incorporation: the morphological process of combining a noun stem with a verb stem to form a single word.
Incorporate: the operation of combining a nominal element with a verbal element in a single morphological word.
Verbal noun: a noun derived from a verb, often retaining some verbal properties (e.g., "the running of the race").
Gerund: a verbal noun form, typically the -ing form in English (e.g., "Running is fun").
Infinitive: the base form of a verb, often marked by "to" in English (e.g., "to run").
Participle: a non-finite verb form used in participial phrases or as an adjective (e.g., "broken," "running").
Gerundive: a verbal adjective expressing necessity or obligation (e.g., Latin "legendus" = "to be read").
Nominal: relating to or having the function of a noun.
Verbal: relating to or having the function of a verb.
Adjectival: relating to or having the function of an adjective.
Adverbial: relating to or having the function of an adverb.
Prepositional: relating to or having the function of a preposition.
Postpositional: relating to or having the function of a postposition.
Preposition: a word that typically precedes a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or semantic relationship (e.g., "in," "on," "with").
Postposition: a word that follows a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or semantic relationship (e.g., Japanese "ni," Turkish "de").
Circumposition: a preposition-like element that consists of two parts, one before and one after the noun phrase (e.g., German "von...bis").
Case: a grammatical category marking the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase.
Case marking: the morphological or syntactic marking of the grammatical role of a noun phrase.
Noun class: a system of categorizing nouns into classes, often marked by agreement (e.g., Bantu noun classes, gender in many European languages).
Gender: a grammatical categorization of nouns (e.g., masculine, feminine, neuter) that typically triggers agreement.
Number: a grammatical category distinguishing singular, dual, trial, plural, or other quantity values.
Dual: a grammatical number for exactly two.
Trial: a grammatical number for exactly three.
Plural: a grammatical number for more than one.
Collective: a grammatical number referring to a group as a single unit.
Distributive: a grammatical number referring to members of a group individually.
Augmentative: see Augmentative above.
Diminutive: see Diminutive above.
Vocative: see Vocative above.
Instrumental: see Instrumental above.
Ablative: see Ablative above.
Allative: see Allative above.
Locative: see Locative above.
Dative: see Dative above.
Genitive: see Genitive above.
Nominative: see Nominative above.
Accusative: see Accusative above.
Ergative: see Ergative above.
Absolutive: see Absolutive above.
Evidential: see Evidential above.
Illocutionary: see Illocutionary act above.
Perlocutionary: see Perlocutionary act above.
Deictic: see Deixis above.
Anaphoric: see Anaphora above.
Cataphoric: see Cataphora above.
