Complementizer: A word introducing a subordinate clause, such as "that" or "if."
Head: The central or governing word of a phrase.
Head noun: The main noun in a noun phrase.
Head verb: The main verb in a verb phrase.
Argument: A participant in an event or state required by a predicate.
Predicate: The part of a sentence that says something about the subject.
Subject: The argument that typically controls agreement with the verb.
Object: The argument that receives the action of the verb.
Direct object: The primary object of a transitive verb.
Indirect object: The secondary object of a ditransitive verb.
Dative: The grammatical case marking the recipient of an action.
Genitive: The grammatical case marking possession or association.
Ablative: The grammatical case marking separation or source.
Locative: The grammatical case marking location.
Allative: The grammatical case marking direction toward a location.
Instrumental: The grammatical case marking the means or instrument.
Vocative: The grammatical case used for direct address.
Ergative: A transitive argument that performs the action.
Absolutive: An intransitive subject or transitive object in an ergative language.
Nominative: The case marking the subject of a transitive verb in a nominative language.
Accusative: The case marking the direct object in a nominative language.
Transitive alignment: A case-marking pattern based on transitivity.
Ergative alignment: A case-marking pattern grouping intransitive subjects with transitive objects.
Split ergativity: A system where ergative and nominative patterns coexist in different contexts.
Word order: The typical sequence of constituents in a sentence.
SOV: Subject-Object-Verb word order.
SVO: Subject-Verb-Object word order.
VSO: Verb-Subject-Object word order.
VOS: Verb-Object-Subject word order.
OVS: Object-Verb-Subject word order.
OSV: Object-Subject-Verb word order.
Scrambling: The ability to reorder sentence constituents.
Constituent: A syntactic unit within a sentence.
Constituency test: A method for determining the boundaries of a syntactic phrase.
C-command: A structural relationship in which one node dominates a sister node.
Dominance: A structural relationship in which one node is a parent of another.
Adjacency: The property of two elements being next to each other in a structure.
Recursion: The ability to embed structures within structures of the same type.
Embedding: The inclusion of one clause within another.
Coordination: The joining of two or more syntactic elements of the same type.
Subordination: The joining of a main clause with a dependent clause.
Conjunction: A word that links elements of the same syntactic rank.
Complement clause: A clause that functions as the complement of a verb.
Adverbial clause: A clause that modifies the main clause.
Relative clause: A clause that modifies a noun.
Noun clause: A clause that functions as a noun.
Adjective clause: A clause that functions as an adjective.
Interrogative: A clause or sentence that asks a question.
Declarative: A clause or sentence that makes a statement.
Imperative: A clause or sentence that gives a command.
Exclamative: A clause or sentence that expresses strong emotion.
Finite: A verb form that is inflected for person, number, and tense.
Non-finite: A verb form not inflected for tense, person, or number.
Infinitive: The base form of a verb.
Participle: A verb form used to form perfect tenses or adjectives.
Gerund: A verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun.
Aspect: The grammatical representation of how an action unfolds over time.
Tense: The grammatical representation of the time of an action.
Mood: The grammatical expression of the speaker's attitude toward the action.
Indicative: The mood expressing factual statements or questions.
Subjunctive: The mood expressing hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations.
Imperative mood: The mood expressing commands or requests.
Optative: The mood expressing wishes or desires.
Perfective: An aspect indicating a completed action.
Imperfective: An aspect indicating an ongoing or habitual action.
Progressive: An aspect indicating an action in progress.
Perfect: A tense-aspect combination indicating a past action with present relevance.
Pluperfect: A tense-aspect combination indicating a past action before another past action.
Future: A tense indicating an action that has not yet occurred.
Present: A tense indicating an action occurring now.
Past: A tense indicating an action that occurred before now.
Agreement: The matching of grammatical features between a head and its dependent.
Government: The requirement that a head controls the case or form of a dependent.
Case marking: The use of inflection to indicate grammatical role.
Pro-drop: The omission of a pronoun when it is recoverable from context.
Null subject: The absence of an overt subject in a clause.
Null object: The absence of an overt object in a clause.
Pro: A theoretical null pronoun in generative grammar.
Trace: A theoretical element left behind by movement.
Move: A syntactic operation that displaces an element from one position to another.
Merge: A syntactic operation that combines two elements into a phrase.
XP: A phrase with head X.
X-bar: A theoretical framework for describing phrase structure.
Specified head: A head with overt morphological content.
Empty category: A theoretical element with no phonetic content.
Binding theory: A component of syntax governing the distribution of pronouns and anaphors.
Reflexive pronoun: A pronoun referring back to the subject.
Reciprocal pronoun: A pronoun expressing mutual action between two or more participants.
Anaphor: A word that must have an antecedent within a local domain.
Bounded: A pronoun that must have an antecedent.
Bare: A pronoun without a determiner.
Referent: The entity in the world that a noun phrase refers to.
Antecedent: The noun phrase that a pronoun or anaphor refers back to.
Cleft: A syntactic construction that emphasizes a particular constituent.
Pseudo-cleft: A cleft construction with "what" as the wh-element.
Wh-question: A question involving a wh-word such as "what," "who," or "where."
Yes-no question: A question that can be answered with "yes" or "no."
Tag question: A short question appended to a statement.
Focus: The information in a sentence that is new or emphasized.
Topic: The information in a sentence that is already known or given.
Information structure: The organization of information in an utterance.
Given: Information already established in the discourse.
New: Information not previously established in the discourse.

Semantics & Pragmatics:
Semantics: The study of meaning in language.
Pragmatics: The study of how context contributes to meaning.
Meaning: The interpretation of linguistic expressions.
Signifier: The form of a linguistic sign.
Signified: The concept or meaning of a linguistic sign.
Referent: The entity in the world referred to by a linguistic expression.
Denotation: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word.
Connotation: The associated or implied meaning of a word.
Polysemy: The phenomenon of a word having multiple related meanings.
Homonymy: The phenomenon of two or more unrelated words sharing the same form.
Synonymy: The relationship between words with the same or very similar meanings.
Antonymy: The relationship between words with opposite meanings.
Hyponym: A word whose meaning is included in the meaning of another word.
Hypernym: A word whose meaning includes the meanings of more specific words.
Meronym: A word whose meaning is a part of the meaning of another word.
Holonym: A word whose meaning is a whole composed of the meaning of a part.
Tautology: A statement that is true by its form or by the meanings of its words.
Contradiction: A statement that is false by its form or by the meanings of its words.
Entailment: A relationship where the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another.
Presupposition: Background information assumed to be true for an utterance to make sense.
Implicature: A meaning inferred from context beyond the literal content.
Conversational implicature: An implicature arising from the conversational maxims.
Gricean maxims: The principles of quantity, quality, relation, and manner in conversation.
Speech act: An action performed through the use of language.
Locution: The literal content of an utterance.
Illocution: The intended force or function of an utterance.
Perlocution: The effect of an utterance on the listener.
Performative: A statement that performs an action by being uttered.
Deixis: The dependence of an expression's meaning on the context of utterance.
Anaphora: A linguistic element that refers back to a previously mentioned element.
Cataphora: A linguistic element that refers forward to a subsequently mentioned element.
Co-reference: The relationship between two expressions that refer to the same entity.
Ellipsis: The omission of words that are recoverable from context.
Metaphor: A figure of speech that compares two things based on shared features.
Metonymy: A figure of speech that substitutes a related term for the intended referent.
Litotes: A form of understatement using a double negative.
Hyperbole: An exaggerated statement for emphasis.
Irony: The expression of a meaning opposite to the literal one.
Sarcasm: A form of verbal irony that is mocking or cutting.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect substitute for a harsh or blunt term.
Dysphemism: A harsh or unpleasant term used in place of a neutral one.
Hedge: A linguistic element that softens or qualifies a statement.
Mood: (already listed under syntax)
Illocutionary force: The communicative function of an utterance.
Perlocutionary effect: The impact an utterance has on the hearer.
Act: A linguistic action performed through speech.
Searle: (not a term per se, but a theorist - skip)
Conversational context: The situational background that informs interpretation.
Shared knowledge: Information mutually known by the participants in a conversation.
Common ground: The set of assumptions and beliefs shared by conversation participants.
Relevance: The relationship between an utterance and its context that makes it interpretable.
Salience: The degree to which a concept is easily accessible in memory.
Conceptualization: The process of forming a mental representation.
Framing: The way a topic is presented, influencing its interpretation.
Prototype: A central or typical member of a category.
Radial category: A category organized around a central prototype with extensions.
Fuzziness: The lack of sharp boundaries in certain semantic categories.
Scalar: A linguistic element that implies a particular point on a scale.
Scale: An ordered set of semantic alternatives.
Focus particle: A word that marks or reinforces focus, such as "only" or "even."
Scope: The domain over which an operator applies.
Negation: The expression of falsity or absence.
Polarity: The grammatical expression of positive or negative meaning.
Polarity item: A word whose distribution is restricted by polarity context.
Negative polarity item: A word that can only appear in negative contexts, such as "any."
Positive polarity item: A word that can only appear in positive contexts, such as "some."
Free choice item: A word expressing that a choice is unrestricted, such as "any" in a positive context.

Sociolinguistics & Dialectology:
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region or social group.
Accent: The pronunciation characteristics of a speaker.
Register: A variety of language associated with a particular context or function.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties in a single conversation.
Code-mixing: The combination of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker.
Language revitalization: Efforts to restore a moribund or dormant language to active use.
Endangerment: The risk that a language will lose all its native speakers.
Bilingualism: The ability to use two languages.
Multilingualism: The ability to use more than two languages.
L1: The first language or native language.
L2: A second language acquired after the first.
Native speaker: A person who acquired a language as their first language.
Non-native speaker: A person who acquired a language after their first language.
Accented speech: Speech with pronunciation features of a non-native or different dialect.
Sociolect: A dialect associated with a particular social group.
Jargon: The specialized vocabulary of a particular profession or group.
Slang: Informal vocabulary associated with a particular group or subculture.
Argot: A secret or specialized language used by a particular group.
Lingua franca: A language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different languages.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with different languages.
Creole: A fully developed language that evolved from a pidgin.
Patois: A colloquial or non-standard variety of a language.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker.
Ethnolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and culture.
Linguistic anthropology: The study of language in its cultural and social context.
Linguistic relativity: The hypothesis that language influences or determines thought.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: The hypothesis that the structure of a language affects its speakers' worldview.
Strong version: The hypothesis that language determines thought.
Weak version: The hypothesis that language influences but does not determine thought.
Language ideology: Beliefs and attitudes held about language and language varieties.
Language policy: The official regulations and decisions about language use.
Language planning: The deliberate effort to influence the structure or use of a language.
Standardization: The process of establishing a standard form of a language.
Prestige: The social value associated with a particular language variety.
Stigma: The negative social value associated with a particular language variety.
Language attitudes: Beliefs and feelings people hold about language varieties.
Diglossia: The coexistence of two varieties of a language in a community with distinct functions.
High variety: The prestige variety used in formal contexts.
Low variety: The non-prestige variety used in informal contexts.
Multilingualism: (already listed)
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages.
Borrowing: The adoption of words or structures from one language into another.
Calque: A loan translation in which a word or phrase is translated element by element.
Loanword: A word borrowed from another language.
Loan translation: The translation of a word from one language into another.
Interference: The influence of one language on another in a bilingual speaker.
Substratum: The influence of a previously dominant language on a newly dominant one.
Superstratum: The influence of a newly dominant language on a previously dominant one.
Adstratum: The influence of a neighboring language of equal status.
Areal feature: A linguistic feature shared by languages in a geographic region.
Sprachbund: A group of languages that share features due to prolonged contact.
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or construction becomes a single word.
Semantic shift: A change in the meaning of a word over time.
Pejoration: A shift in meaning toward a negative connotation.
Amelioration: A shift in meaning toward a positive connotation.
Broadening: A shift in which a word's meaning becomes more general.
Narrowing: A shift in which a word's meaning becomes more specific.
Metaphorical extension: A semantic shift based on perceived similarity.
Metonymic extension: A semantic shift based on contiguity or association.
Taboo: A word or expression avoided due to social or cultural sensitivity.
Euphemistic replacement: The substitution of a less offensive term for a taboo one.
Hypocorism: A shortened or affectionate form of a word or name.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression.
Archaism: A word or expression that is no longer in current use.
Dead language: A language with no native speakers.
Living language: A language with native speakers who use it as their primary means of communication.
Extinct language: A language with no remaining speakers.
Sleeping language: A language that is not currently in active use but could be revived.
Oral tradition: The transmission of knowledge through spoken word.
Literacy: The ability to read and write.
Standard language: The variety of a language used in formal and educational contexts.
Non-standard variety: A language variety that deviates from the standard.
Prestige dialect: A dialect that carries social prestige.
Regional dialect: A variety of language associated with a particular geographic area.
Social dialect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group.
Ethnic dialect: A variety of language associated with a particular ethnic group.
Gender dialect: Differences in language use associated with gender.
Age dialect: Differences in language use associated with age.
Occupational dialect: Differences in language use associated with profession.

Historical & Comparative Linguistics:
Historical linguistics: The study of the development of languages over time.
Comparative linguistics: The study of the relationships between languages.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which related languages descend.
Language family: A group of languages descended from a common ancestor.
Language stock: A grouping of language families or isolates.
Language isolate: A language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other language.
Cognate: A word in one language that is related to a word in another language through a common ancestor.
Cognate set: A set of cognate words across related languages.
Sound law: A regular correspondence in sound changes between related languages.
Grimm's Law: The set of sound changes from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic.
Verner's Law: An exception to Grimm's Law involving voicing.
Swadesh list: A list of basic vocabulary items used for lexical comparison.
Levenshtein distance: A measure of the similarity between two strings.
Divergence: The process by which related languages become increasingly different.
Convergence: The process by which different languages become more similar.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary marking a difference in a linguistic feature.
Linguistic map: A map showing the distribution of linguistic features.
Glottolog: A reference work cataloging the world's languages.
Ethnologue: A reference work cataloging the languages of the world.
Reconstruction: The process of inferring the features of a proto-language.
Internal reconstruction: The process of inferring earlier forms using evidence within a single language.
Comparative method: The method of identifying regular sound correspondences between related languages.
Proto-Indo-European: The hypothetical ancestor of the Indo-European language family.
Proto-Afroasiatic: The hypothetical ancestor of the Afroasiatic language family.
Proto-Austronesian: The hypothetical ancestor of the Austronesian language family.
Proto-Niger-Congo: The hypothetical ancestor of the Niger-Congo language family.
Proto-Sino-Tibetan: The hypothetical ancestor of the Sino-Tibetan language family.
Proto-Dravidian: The hypothetical ancestor of the Dravidian language family.
Uralic: A language family including Finnish, Hungarian, and Estonian.
Indo-European: A large language family including English, Hindi, Spanish, and many others.
Afroasiatic: A language family including Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic, and Berber.
Sino-Tibetan: A language family including Chinese, Burmese, and Tibetan.
Niger-Congo: A large language family in Africa including Swahili and Yoruba.
Austronesian: A language family spread across the Pacific and Southeast Asia.
Dravidian: A language family in South India.
Uto-Aztecan: A language family in the American Southwest and Mexico.
Quechuan: A language family in South America.
Tupian: A language family in South America.
Trans-New Guinea: A proposed large language family in New Guinea.
Pama-Nyungan: A language family in Australia.
Na-Dene: A proposed language family in North America.
Eskimo-Aleut: A language family in the Arctic region.
Kartvelian: A language family in the Caucasus region.
Paleosiberian: A grouping of language families in northeastern Siberia.
Isolate: A language with no known relatives.
Borrowing: (already listed)
Substrate: (already listed)
Superstrate: (already listed)
Adstrate: (already listed)
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects where neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible.
Mutual intelligibility: The ability of speakers of different varieties to understand each other.
Language shift: The process by which a community abandons its native language for another.
Language maintenance: Efforts to preserve a language and its use in the community.
Immersion: A method of language learning through full exposure to the target language.
Contact language: A language that has developed through prolonged contact between different languages.
Mixed language: A language with substantial lexical and grammatical contributions from two or more source languages.
Lexical borrowing: The adoption of words from one language into another.
Grammatical borrowing: The adoption of grammatical structures from one language into another.
Phonological borrowing: The adoption of sound patterns from one language into another.
Calque: (already listed)
Loan blend: A word that combines elements from two languages.
Doublet: Two words in the same language that have different forms but the same etymology.
Etymology: The study of the origin and development of words.
Etymon: The earliest form of a word or the source word in a borrowing.
Derivative: A word formed from another word by adding an affix or changing form.
Compound: A word formed from two or more free morphemes.
Portmanteau: (already listed)
Phraseme: A fixed or semi-fixed expression.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from its individual words.
Collocation: A habitual combination of words.
Binomial: A fixed pair of words, such as "salt and pepper."
Formulaic language: Pre-constructed sequences of language.
Proverb: A short, well-known saying expressing a general truth.
Motto: A short phrase expressing a guiding principle.
Catchphrase: A distinctive phrase repeatedly used by a particular person or group.
Slogan: A short, memorable phrase used in advertising or political campaigns.

Psycholinguistics & Language Acquisition:
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurobiological processes underlying language.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn language.
Critical period: The hypothesized window during which language acquisition occurs most easily.
Sensitivity period: An alternative term for the critical period.
First language acquisition: The process by which children acquire their native language.
Second language acquisition: The process by which adults or children learn a language other than their first.
Universal Grammar: The hypothesized innate set of principles underlying all human languages.
Language faculty: The innate cognitive capacity for language.
Innateness: The hypothesis that certain aspects of language are genetically determined.
Language universal: A feature shared by all human languages.
Absolute universal: A feature present in every known human language.
Tendency universal: A feature present in most but not all known human languages.
Exception universal: A feature present in many but not all known human languages.
Language organ: The proposed specialized neural mechanism for language.
Broca's area: A region of the brain associated with speech production and language processing.
Wernicke's area: A region of the brain associated with language comprehension.
Aphasia: The impairment or loss of language ability due to brain damage.
Broca's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by non-fluent speech.
Wernicke's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by fluent but nonsensical speech.
Global aphasia: A severe form of aphasia affecting both production and comprehension.
Conduction aphasia: A type of aphasia affecting the ability to repeat words.
Anomic aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by difficulty finding the right word.
Apraxia: The inability to produce speech despite intact motor function.
Dyslexia: A learning disorder affecting reading ability.
Dysgraphia: A disorder affecting the ability to write.
Dysarthria: A motor speech disorder affecting articulation.
Stuttering: A speech fluency disorder involving repetitions or prolongations.
Language development: The progression of a child's language abilities over time.
Babbling: The stage of vocal play in early language development.
One-word stage: The stage in which a child uses single words to communicate.
Two-word stage: The stage in which a child combines two words.
Telegraphic speech: The stage in which a child uses minimal phrases.
Overregularization: The application of a regular rule to irregular forms.
Overgeneralization: The overextension of a grammatical rule.
Undergeneralization: The failure to extend a grammatical rule to appropriate contexts.
Language delay: A significant lag in the development of language skills.
Language disorder: A clinical condition affecting language ability.
Specific language impairment: A language disorder not attributable to hearing loss or general cognitive impairment.
Dysphasia: Another term for aphasia.
Neurolinguistics: The study of the neural basis of language.
Cognitive neuroscience: The study of the brain mechanisms underlying cognition.
Functional MRI: A neuroimaging technique measuring brain activity.
EEG: Electroencephalography, a technique measuring brain electrical activity.
ERP: Event-related potential, a measure of brain response to stimuli.
TMS: Transcranial magnetic stimulation, a technique for modulating brain activity.
Language processing: The cognitive processes involved in understanding and producing language.
Parsing: The process of structuring a sentence as it is being understood.
Garden-path sentence: A sentence that leads the reader down an initially incorrect parse.
Ambiguity: The property of a linguistic expression having multiple interpretations.
Structural ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from multiple possible syntactic structures.
Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having multiple meanings.
Scope ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from the different ways an operator can be interpreted.
Pragmatic ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from context-dependent interpretation.
Pragmatic inference: The process of deriving meaning beyond the literal content.
Common ground: (already listed)
Shared intentionality: The mutual understanding between communication partners.
Theory of mind: The ability to attribute mental states to oneself and others.
Pragmatic development: The acquisition of pragmatic skills in language development.
Pragmatic deficit: A difficulty with pragmatic language skills.
Language and thought: The relationship between linguistic structures and cognitive processes.
Mental lexicon: The mental representation of vocabulary.
Mental grammar: The mental representation of grammatical rules.
Mental model: A cognitive representation of a situation described by language.
Conceptual metaphor: A mapping from one conceptual domain to another.
Image schema: A basic mental structure organizing experiential knowledge.
Cognitive grammar: A linguistic framework emphasizing the cognitive basis of language.
Construction grammar: A linguistic framework organizing language in terms of form-meaning pairings.
Construction: A pairing of linguistic form with meaning, grammar, or function.
Usage-based model: A theoretical model emphasizing frequency and usage in language learning.
Implicit learning: The unconscious acquisition of patterns.
Explicit learning: The conscious learning of rules and patterns.
Declarative memory: Memory for facts and events.
Procedural memory: Memory for skills and routines.
Working memory: The system for holding and manipulating information in the present.
Episodic memory: Memory for specific events and experiences.
Semantic memory: Memory for general knowledge and concepts.
Lexical access: The process of retrieving a word from the mental lexicon.
Lexical retrieval: The process of finding the right word to express a concept.
Tip of the tongue: The experience of knowing a word is on the tip of one's tongue.
Word-finding difficulty: The inability to produce a word despite knowing its meaning.
Naming latency: The time it takes to name a visual stimulus.
Lexical-semantic network: A model of the organization of word meanings in the mind.
Semantic priming: The facilitation of word processing by a related word presented earlier.
Semantic satiation: The temporary loss of a word's meaning through repeated exposure.
Lexicalization: (already listed)
Morphological processing: The cognitive process of decomposing words into morphemes.
Syntactic processing: The cognitive process of building sentence structure.
Discourse processing: The cognitive process of integrating information across sentences.
Pragmatic processing: The cognitive process of interpreting meaning beyond the literal content.

Computational & Formal Linguistics:
Computational linguistics: The application of computational methods to the study of language.
Natural language processing: The use of computer programs to process and analyze human language.
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts for linguistic analysis.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large corpora.
Corpus-based method: A research method that uses corpus data.
Computational model: A formal representation of a linguistic phenomenon implemented in a computer program.
Formal grammar: A mathematical description of the syntax of a language.
Context-free grammar: A type of formal grammar that generates context-free languages.
Chomsky hierarchy: A classification of formal grammars by generative power.
Type 0 grammar: An unrestricted grammar, the most general type in the Chomsky hierarchy.
Type 1 grammar: A context-sensitive grammar.
Type 2 grammar: A context-free grammar.
Type 3 grammar: A regular grammar.
Regular language: A language that can be described by a regular grammar or finite automaton.
Context-free language: A language that can be described by a context-free grammar.
Pushdown automaton: A finite automaton with a stack, recognizing context-free languages.
Finite automaton: A computational model recognizing regular languages.
Turing machine: A theoretical model of computation that can recognize recursively enumerable languages.
Decidability: The property of a problem having an algorithm that always gives a correct answer.
Undecidability: The property of a problem for which no algorithm can always give a correct answer.
Grammar: (already listed)
Production rule: A rule in a formal grammar that rewrites one string into another.
Terminal: A symbol in a formal grammar that appears in the generated strings.
Non-terminal: A symbol in a formal grammar that can be further rewritten.
Start symbol: The initial non-terminal from which a formal grammar begins.
Derivation: A sequence of production rule applications in a formal grammar.
Sentential form: An intermediate string in a derivation.
Yield: The set of terminal strings generated by a grammar.
Ambiguous grammar: A grammar that generates the same string with multiple parse trees.
Unambiguous grammar: A grammar in which each string has exactly one parse tree.
Parsing: (already listed)
Top-down parsing: A parsing strategy that starts from the start symbol and works toward the input.
Bottom-up parsing: A parsing strategy that starts from the input and works toward the start symbol.
Shift-reduce parsing: A bottom-up parsing strategy.
Recursive descent parsing: A top-down parsing strategy.
Chart parsing: A parsing strategy that avoids redundant work.
Stochastic parsing: A parsing strategy that assigns probabilities to parse trees.
Probabilistic grammar: A grammar that assigns probabilities to production rules.
Bayesian model: A probabilistic model based on Bayes' theorem.
Hidden Markov model: A statistical model used in speech recognition and part-of-speech tagging.
Part-of-speech tagging: The assignment of grammatical categories to words.
Parsing: (already listed)
Dependency parsing: A parsing strategy that identifies the relationships between words.
Constituency parsing: A parsing strategy that identifies the phrase structure of a sentence.
Syntactic chunking: The grouping of words into phrases.
Named entity recognition: The identification of proper nouns and other entities in text.
Sentiment analysis: The computational identification of emotional expression in text.
Machine translation: The automatic translation of text from one language to another.
Statistical machine translation: A machine translation approach based on statistical models.
Neural machine translation: A machine translation approach based on neural networks.
Speech recognition: The automatic conversion of spoken language to text.
Automatic speech recognition: (same as above)
Speech synthesis: The automatic generation of spoken language from text.
Text-to-speech: Another term for speech synthesis.
Natural language understanding: The computational interpretation of natural language text.
Natural language generation: The computational production of natural language text.
Semantic parsing: The conversion of natural language to a formal semantic representation.
Information extraction: The process of extracting structured information from unstructured text.
Question answering: The computational process of answering questions from a text or knowledge base.
Dialogue system: A computational system that engages in conversational interaction.
Chatbot: A program that simulates conversation with a human user.
Language model: A statistical model of the probability of word sequences.
N-gram: A sequence of N words used in statistical language modeling.
Perplexity: A measure of how well a language model predicts a sample.
BLEU: A metric for evaluating machine translation quality.
ROUGE: A metric for evaluating text summarization quality.
Token: The basic unit of text in computational linguistics.
Tokenization: The process of splitting text into tokens.
Lemmatization: (already listed)
Stemming: The process of reducing a word to its root form.
POS: Part of speech, the grammatical category of a word.
Parse tree: A tree representation of the syntactic structure of a sentence.
Dependency tree: A tree representation of the dependency relationships in a sentence.
Corpus annotation: The addition of linguistic information to a corpus.
Annotation: The labeling of linguistic data with categories.
Tagset: A set of tags used to annotate a corpus.
