Relexification: A language contact process in which the lexicon of one language is replaced by that of another while retaining the grammatical structure of the first.
Substratum: The influence of a previously spoken language on the grammar or phonology of a later language in the same region.
Superstratum: The influence of a later-arriving, socially dominant language on the grammar or phonology of a previously established language.
Adstratum: The mutual influence between languages of roughly equal prestige in a bilingual community.
Areal feature: A linguistic feature shared by languages in a geographical region due to contact rather than common descent.
Sprachbund: A group of languages that have developed shared features through prolonged contact, regardless of genetic relationship.
Linguistic area: A geographical region in which languages share a set of areal features.
Creole: A natural language that develops from pidgin when it becomes the native language of a new community.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language.
Creolization: The process by which a pidgin develops into a full creole with complex grammar.
De-creolization: The process by which a creole loses features and converges toward its lexifier language.
Lexifier: The language that contributes most of the vocabulary to a creole or pidgin.
Substrate: The language that contributes most of the grammatical influence to a creole or pidgin.
Plantation creole: A creole that developed in plantation or colonial contexts, often in the Caribbean or Pacific.
Coastal creole: A creole that developed in coastal trade or port contexts.
Domestic creole: A creole that developed in domestic or household settings.
Trade pidgin: A pidgin that developed for commercial or trade purposes.
Lingua franca: A language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Prestige language: A language that is considered socially elevated and is the model for other varieties.
Stigmatized variety: A dialect or language variety that is subject to negative social evaluation.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region, social group, or community.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker.
Register: A variety of language associated with a particular situation, purpose, or audience.
Jargon: The specialized vocabulary of a particular profession or activity.
Jargon (informal): Informal or slang vocabulary used by a particular group.
Slang: Informal, often short-lived vocabulary used by a particular social group.
Argot: A specialized vocabulary used by a particular group, often to exclude outsiders.
Cant: A secret or coded vocabulary used by a particular group, historically associated with thieves or other subcultures.
Pidgin grammar: The simplified grammatical system of a pidgin language.
Creole syntax: The grammatical system of a creole language.
Lexicon (historical): The vocabulary of a language at a particular period in its history.
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts used for linguistic analysis and research.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large electronic collections of real-world text data.
Frequency analysis: The statistical examination of how often particular words, phrases, or patterns occur in a corpus.
Collocation: The tendency of certain words to appear together more often than would be expected by chance.
Collocate: A word that frequently co-occurs with a given word.
N-gram: A sequence of N adjacent words in a text, such as a bigram (two words) or trigram (three words).
Co-occurrence: The simultaneous presence of two or more linguistic elements in the same text or discourse.
Discourse: Language used in extended communication, such as conversation, writing, or argumentation.
Discourse analysis: The study of language in use, focusing on how meaning is constructed in extended texts and conversations.
Text linguistics: The study of the structure and organization of extended texts.
Cohesion: The linguistic ties that connect elements within a text, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical ties.
Coherence: The logical and meaningful connection between elements in a text, ensuring that the text makes sense as a whole.
Reference: The use of linguistic elements to identify entities in the discourse, such as through pronouns or definite descriptions.
Anaphoric reference: The use of a pronoun or noun phrase to refer back to a previously mentioned entity.
Cataphoric reference: The use of a pronoun or noun phrase to refer forward to a later-mentioned entity.
Exophoric reference: Reference to an entity in the physical or extralinguistic context rather than in the discourse.
Coreference: The relation between two or more linguistic expressions that refer to the same entity.
Deictic expression: A linguistic expression whose referent depends on the context of utterance, such as "here," "now," or "I."
Spatio-temporal deixis: Deictic expressions that refer to location or time, such as "here," "there," "now," or "then."
Person deixis: Deictic expressions that refer to participants in the discourse, such as first, second, and third person pronouns.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes or comments on the flow of discourse, such as "well," "so," or "however."
Turn-taking: The system by which speakers alternate in conversation, governed by social and linguistic conventions.
Interruption: A conversational event in which one speaker begins speaking before the current speaker has completed their turn.
Repair: A conversational process in which a speaker corrects or clarifies a problem in the current or prior talk.
Self-repair: A repair in which the speaker corrects their own utterance.
Other-repair: A repair in which a listener corrects the speaker's utterance.
Adjacency pair: A pair of conversational turns in which the second turn is a response to the first, such as question-answer or greeting-greeting.
Backchannel: A brief utterance or sound by a listener that signals attention or encouragement, such as "mm" or "yeah."
Repair sequence: The set of conversational moves involved in identifying and resolving a problem in communication.
Turn completion: The point in a turn at which the speaker signals that their contribution is finished.
Transition relevance place: A point in a turn at which a change of speaker is anticipated.
Talk: The general term for spoken language in conversation, used in conversation analysis.
Conversation analysis: The study of the organization and structure of naturally occurring conversation.
Sequential organization: The study of how conversational turns are ordered and related to each other.
Preference organization: The study of how speakers structure responses to show agreement or disagreement, favoring agreement.
Repair (discourse): The process of identifying and correcting misunderstandings or errors in discourse.
Topic shift: A change in the topic of a conversation or discourse.
Topic continuation: The continuation of the current topic in a conversation or discourse.
Topic reversion: The return to a previously abandoned topic in a conversation or discourse.
Narrative: A discourse structure in which events are presented in temporal sequence.
Frame (narrative): The introductory section of a narrative that provides background information.
Orientation: The part of a narrative that provides context for the events to be described.
Complication: The main event sequence of a narrative.
Resolution: The part of a narrative that provides the outcome of the complication.
Coda: The concluding part of a narrative that comments on or evaluates the events.
Evaluation: The part of a narrative in which the speaker comments on the significance of the events.
Summary: A brief restatement of the main points of a discourse.
Abstract: A condensed summary of a longer text, often used in academic writing.
Thematic progression: The pattern by which themes (given information) are introduced and advanced in a text.
Zigzag: A thematic pattern in which a new theme is introduced in each sentence while also maintaining continuity.
Constant theme: A thematic pattern in which the same theme is maintained across a series of sentences.
Linear progression: A thematic pattern in which the rheme of one sentence becomes the theme of the next.
Given: Information in a sentence that is already known or established in the discourse.
New: Information in a sentence that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse.
Rheme: The information in a clause that is new or not yet established, typically appearing at the end of the clause.
Theme: The information in a clause that is given or already established, typically appearing at the beginning of the clause.
End focus: The tendency in English and other languages to place new or important information at the end of a clause.
Left-dislocation: The placement of a noun phrase at the beginning of a clause, followed by a resumptive pronoun, such as "John, I like him."
Right-dislocation: The placement of a tag-like phrase at the end of a clause, such as "It's raining, isn't it, John?"
Resumptive pronoun: A pronoun that appears in a position where a gap is expected, often in complex or informal syntax.
Gap: An empty position in a syntactic structure where a moved element is understood, such as in wh-questions.
Trace: A theoretical representation of the original position of a moved constituent in a syntactic derivation.
Movement (syntax): The syntactic operation that displaces a constituent from one position to another.
Base generation: The process by which a constituent is generated directly in its surface position rather than being moved.
Subjacency: A condition on movement in syntax that limits the number of boundaries a constituent can cross in a single step.
Minimal Link Condition: A constraint in the Minimalist Program that requires the closest available element to be moved.
Proper Binding: A condition in syntax requiring that certain empty categories be bound within a specific domain.
EPP (Extended Projection Principle): A principle in generative grammar requiring that every clause have a subject.
Case filter: A condition in generative grammar requiring that every overt noun phrase receive case.
Theta criterion: A condition in generative grammar requiring that each argument receive exactly one theta role.
Subcategorization: The specification of the types of complements that a verb or other head requires or permits.
Selectional restriction: A constraint on the semantic type of an argument or complement, such as "eat" requiring an edible theme.
Government: A syntactic relation in which a head selects and governs its complements.
C-command: A structural relation in which one node dominates a node and all its siblings.
D-structure: The underlying representation in early generative grammar showing the base position of all constituents.
S-structure: The surface representation in early generative grammar after movement operations have been applied.
Logical form (syntax): The level of representation in generative grammar that encodes the logical or semantic properties of a sentence.
Phonological form: The level of representation in generative grammar that encodes the phonetic properties of a sentence.
Minimalist Program: The current generative framework for syntax that seeks to explain grammatical operations in terms of computational efficiency.
Merge: The operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects into a larger structure.
Agree: The operation in the Minimalist Program that establishes a feature-sharing relationship between two syntactic objects.
Phase: A unit of computation in the Minimalist Program, such as a VP or CP, after which intermediate structures are sent to the interfaces.
Phase Impenetrability Condition: A condition in the Minimalist Program that restricts access to material within a completed phase.
Vocabulary insertion: The process in the Minimalist Program by which morphemes are inserted into the syntactic structure to satisfy phonological and semantic requirements.
Spell-out: The process by which the syntactic structure is converted into a phonological representation.
Interfaces: The connection points in the Minimalist Program between syntax and the phonological and conceptual (semantic) interfaces.
Extended Projection Principle: The requirement that every clause must have a subject, stated as a principle of UG.
Binding theory (pronouns): The set of principles governing the distribution of pronouns, anaphors, and referential expressions in syntax.
Anaphor: A linguistic expression that must be bound within a local domain, such as a reflexive pronoun like "himself."
R-expression: A referential expression that must not be bound, such as a proper name like "John."
Local domain: The syntactic domain within which certain binding conditions must be satisfied, such as a clause or phrase.
Government (binding): A relation in which one element c-commands another and there is no intervening clause boundary.
Subject Condition: A binding condition stating that an anaphor cannot be bound by a subject in a certain configuration.
Condition A: The binding principle stating that an anaphor must be bound in its local domain.
Condition B: The binding principle stating that a pronoun must be free in its local domain.
Condition C: The binding principle stating that an R-expression must be free everywhere.
Bare NP: A noun phrase that appears without a determiner, such as "water" or "information."
Bare plural: A plural noun phrase that appears without a determiner, such as "dogs" in "Dogs are animals."
Existential "there": A dummy element that introduces an existential construction, as in "There is a cat."
Dummy subject: A syntactic subject that does not refer to an entity, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Expletive: A linguistic element that has no semantic content but fulfills a syntactic requirement, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Placeholder: A syntactic element that occupies a position for structural purposes without contributing meaning.
Pro: A theoretical empty category in generative grammar representing a null pronoun.
Pro (null subject): The empty subject in languages that allow subject omission, such as Italian or Spanish.
Pro-drop: A parametric feature of a language that allows the omission of subjects and objects when they are recoverable from context.
Null subject: A subject that is not phonologically realized but is understood from context.
Null object: An object that is not phonologically realized but is understood from context.
Proper name: A noun that refers to a unique individual, such as "John" or "Paris."
Proper noun: A noun that names a specific individual or entity and is typically capitalized in English.
Common noun: A noun that refers to a general class of entities, such as "dog" or "city."
Count noun: A noun that refers to entities that can be individually counted, such as "book" or "apple."
Mass noun: A noun that refers to substances or collections that cannot be individually counted, such as "water" or "rice."
Uncountable noun: A noun that cannot be used in the plural or with indefinite articles, similar to a mass noun.
Numeral: A word or expression that specifies a quantity, such as "three" or "several."
Cardinal number: A numeral that indicates an exact quantity, such as "one," "two," or "three."
Ordinal number: A numeral that indicates a position in a sequence, such as "first," "second," or "third."
Fractional number: A numeral that indicates a part of a whole, such as "half" or "third."
Quantificational: A property of expressions that specify quantity, such as "every," "some," or "three."
Maximality: The property of a quantifier or expression that refers to the maximum or entire set.
Existential quantifier: A logical quantifier that asserts the existence of at least one entity with a given property.
Universal quantifier: A logical quantifier that asserts that all entities in a domain have a given property.
Negation: A grammatical operation that inverts the truth value of a proposition.
Negative polarity item: A word or expression that is grammatical only in the scope of negation or other downward-entailing contexts, such as "any" or "ever."
Downward entailment: A logical property of a context in which a statement about the whole implies a statement about a part, such as under "not" or "few."
Anti-entailment: A logical property of a context that does not support downward entailment, such as under "exactly."
Scalar: A linguistic expression that can be placed on a scale of intensity, such as "tall," "bigger," or "very."
Scalar implicature: An inference drawn from the use of a weaker scalar term, such as inferring "not all" from "some."
Entailment: A logical relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another.
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be true for a sentence to be felicitously used.
Trigger: A linguistic element that carries or projects a presupposition, such as a factive verb like "know."
Accommodation: The process by which a listener accepts a presupposition as true to make sense of an utterance.
Factivity: A property of certain verbs and constructions that presuppose the truth of their complements, such as "regret" or "realize."
Factive verb: A verb that presupposes the truth of its clausal complement, such as "know," "realize," or "regret."
Non-factive verb: A verb that does not presuppose the truth of its clausal complement, such as "think" or "believe."
Hedge: A linguistic expression that reduces the strength or commitment of a claim, such as "I think," "perhaps," or "sort of."
Hedging: The use of linguistic expressions to qualify or soften a statement.
Mitigation: The process of reducing the force or bluntness of an utterance.
Politeness: The social strategies and linguistic devices used to maintain or enhance positive and negative face.
Face: A concept in pragmatics referring to the public self-image that a speaker wants to maintain.
Positive face: The desire to be liked, approved of, and included by others.
Negative face: The desire to be unimpeded in one's actions and to have autonomy.
Face-threatening act: An utterance that threatens the positive or negative face of the hearer.
Indirect speech act: An utterance whose primary communicative purpose is not what its literal form suggests, such as "Can you pass the salt?" meaning "Please pass the salt."
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action beyond merely conveying information, such as promising, ordering, or apologizing.
Locutionary act: The act of saying something, the basic act of producing an utterance.
Illocutionary act: The act performed in saying something, such as asking, promising, or warning.
Perlocutionary act: The effect of an utterance on the listener, such as persuading, alarming, or amusing.
Declarative: A speech act that brings about a change in the world simply by being uttered, such as "I now pronounce you husband and wife."
Directive: A speech act that attempts to get the listener to do something, such as a request or command.
Commissive: A speech act that commits the speaker to a future action, such as a promise or threat.
Expressive: A speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state, such as thanking, apologizing, or congratulating.
Representative: A speech act that states or asserts a proposition, such as a statement or description.
Performative: An utterance that performs the action it describes, such as "I promise" or "I declare."
Illocutionary force: The intended action or purpose of a speech act.
Illocutionary point: The aspect of a speech act that defines its type, such as the direction of fit.
Felicity conditions: The conditions that must be met for a speech act to be successfully performed.
Searle's classification: The classification of speech acts into representative, directive, commissive, expressive, and declarative categories.
Austin's distinction: The distinction between the locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts of an utterance, introduced by J.L. Austin.
Conversational maxims: The principles of cooperation in conversation, as proposed by Paul Grice, including quantity, quality, relation, and manner.
Cooperative principle: The general principle in conversation that participants make contributions appropriate to the purpose of the exchange.
Maxim of quantity: The conversational maxim to be as informative as required and no more.
Maxim of quality: The conversational maxim to be truthful and do not assert what one lacks evidence for.
Maxim of relation: The conversational maxim to be relevant.
Maxim of manner: The conversational maxim to be clear, brief, and orderly in expression.
Implicature: A meaning that is implied but not explicitly stated, derived from the conversational context.
Conversational implicature: A meaning derived from the application of conversational maxims in a specific context.
Conventional implicature: A meaning that is part of the conventional meaning of a word or expression, independent of context.
Cancelability: The property of conversational implicatures that they can be explicitly denied without contradiction.
Calculability: The property of conversational implicatures that they can be derived through reasoning from the context.
Non-detachability: The property of conventional implicatures that they cannot be removed by changing the sentence structure.
Non-conventionality: The property of conversational implicatures that they depend on context rather than fixed meaning.
Gricean reasoning: The process of deriving conversational implicatures by assuming the speaker is following the maxims.
Context (pragmatics): The set of assumptions, knowledge, and situational factors that influence the interpretation of an utterance.
Situational context: The physical and social setting in which an utterance is produced.
Linguistic context: The surrounding linguistic material, such as the preceding and following discourse.
Pragmatic inference: The process of deriving meaning beyond the literal content of an utterance based on context.
Satoshi: A term sometimes used in linguistics to refer to a unit of pragmatic meaning, though this is not standard.
Speech: The act of producing and perceiving spoken language.
Hearing: The sensory process of receiving sound waves, relevant to phonetics and the physiology of speech perception.
Voicing (production): The physiological process of vocal fold vibration during speech production.
Resonance: The amplification and shaping of sound waves by the vocal tract cavities.
Formant: A peak in the frequency spectrum of a vowel sound, determined by the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract.
F0: The fundamental frequency of a sound, corresponding to the rate of vocal fold vibration and perceived as pitch.
Pitch: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, corresponding to frequency.
Loudness: The perceived intensity of a sound, related to amplitude.
Duration: The length of time a sound or speech segment lasts.
Amplitude: The magnitude of the pressure variation in a sound wave.
Waveform: A graphical representation of the pressure variation in a sound wave over time.
Spectrogram: A visual representation of the frequency content of a sound over time.
Harmonic: A frequency that is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.
Noise: A non-periodic, aperiodic component in a sound, produced by turbulent airflow.
Periodic: A sound wave that repeats in a regular pattern, characteristic of voiced sounds.
Aperiodic: A sound wave that does not repeat in a regular pattern, characteristic of voiceless sounds.
Vocal fold: The pair of tissue folds in the larynx that vibrate to produce voiced sounds.
Larynx: The part of the vocal tract that contains the vocal folds and is involved in phonation.
Pharynx: The part of the vocal tract behind the mouth and nasal cavities, involved in the production of pharyngeal sounds.
Uvula: The fleshy tissue hanging at the back of the soft palate, involved in the production of uvular sounds.
Alveolar ridge: The bony ridge behind the upper teeth, the place of articulation for alveolar sounds.
Hard palate: The bony roof of the mouth, the place of articulation for palatal sounds.
Soft palate: The muscular back part of the roof of the mouth, also called the velum.
Velum: The soft palate, which can be raised or lowered to control the nasal cavity's involvement in sound production.
Tongue tip: The anterior end of the tongue, involved in the production of dental, alveolar, and retroflex sounds.
Tongue blade: The flat portion of the tongue just behind the tip, involved in the production of some retroflex and palatal sounds.
Tongue body: The main, central portion of the tongue, involved in the production of palatal, velar, and back vowels.
Tongue root: The posterior portion of the tongue, involved in the production of pharyngeal and uvular sounds.
Lips: The muscular structures at the front of the mouth, involved in the production of labial and labiodental sounds.
Teeth: The hard structures at the front of the mouth, involved in the production of dental and labiodental sounds.
Gums: The tissue surrounding the teeth, involved in the production of some dental sounds.
Lower lip: The bottom lip, involved in the production of bilabial and labiodental sounds.
Upper lip: The top lip, involved in the production of bilabial and labiodental sounds.
Mandible: The lower jawbone, which moves to open and close the mouth during speech.
Maxilla: The upper jawbone, which is fixed and provides the upper boundary of the oral cavity.
Oral cavity: The space inside the mouth, through which air passes during the production of oral sounds.
Nasal cavity: The space inside the nose, through which air passes during the production of nasal sounds.
Laryngeal cavity: The space in the larynx, involved in the production of laryngeal sounds.
Vocal tract: The entire passage from the larynx through the pharynx, oral cavity, and nasal cavity.
Articulator: A part of the vocal tract that moves to modify the airflow, such as the tongue, lips, or velum.
Passive articulator: A fixed part of the vocal tract against which an active articulator is brought, such as the alveolar ridge.
Active articulator: A moving part of the vocal tract that approaches a passive articulator, such as the tongue tip.
Approximation: The closest approach of an articulator to a passive articulator without complete closure.
Closure: The complete contact between articulators that stops the airflow, as in a plosive.
Narrowing: The partial closure that creates a constriction for fricatives and approximants.
Manner of articulation (fricative): The production of a continuous stream of turbulent airflow through a narrow constriction.
Manner of articulation (stop): The production of a complete closure followed by a sudden release of airflow.
Manner of articulation (nasal): The production of a complete oral closure with the velum lowered, allowing nasal airflow.
Manner of articulation (lateral): The production of a closure with the sides of the tongue open, directing airflow laterally.
Manner of articulation (trill): The production of a sound by rapid vibration of an articulator, as in the Spanish /r/.
Manner of articulation (tap): The production of a sound by a single, rapid contact of an articulator, as in the American English /ɾ/.
Manner of articulation (flap): Another term for a tap, a single rapid contact.
Manner of articulation (ejective): The production of a plosive by closing the glottis and raising the larynx, creating a burst of air.
Manner of articulation (implosive): The production of a plosive by lowering the larynx, creating a lowering in air pressure.
Manner of articulation (click): The production of a sound by creating two closures in the mouth and releasing one to create a suction.
Manner of articulation (voiced): A sound produced with the vocal folds vibrating.
Manner of articulation (voiceless): A sound produced with the vocal folds apart and not vibrating.
Manner of articulation (breathy): A sound produced with the vocal folds in a wide, relaxed configuration, allowing turbulent airflow through the glottis.
Manner of articulation (creaky): A sound produced with the vocal folds in a tight, narrow configuration, producing a creaky voice quality.
Manner of articulation (whispered): A sound produced with the vocal folds slightly apart and the larynx raised, creating a whispered voice quality.
Phonation: The production of sound by the vibration of the vocal folds.
Aspiration (phonetics): A strong burst of air that follows the release of a voiceless plosive.
Deaspiration (phonetics): The absence of a strong burst of air following the release of a plosive.
Release: The moment at which the articulators part after a closure, allowing airflow to resume.
Aspiration (release): The duration of the voiceless interval between the release of a plosive and the onset of voicing for the following vowel.
VOT: Voice Onset Time, the interval between the release of a stop and the onset of voicing.
Pre-voicing: The production of voicing before the release of a stop.
Post-voicing: The production of voicing after the release of a stop.
Stop gap: The silent interval between the release of one consonant and the onset of the next.
Coarticulation: The overlapping of articulatory gestures so that the production of one sound influences the articulation of adjacent sounds.
Anticipatory coarticulation: The influence of a following sound on the articulation of a preceding sound.
Perceptual coarticulation: The influence of a preceding sound on the perception of a following sound.
Gestural overlap: The simultaneous production of multiple articulatory gestures in the vocal tract.
Motor program: A planned sequence of articulatory movements for producing speech.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of the physical movements of the vocal tract organs during speech production.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of the physical properties of the sound waves produced during speech.
Perceptual phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived and processed by the listener.
Auditory phonetics: The study of the auditory system's role in speech perception.
Speech perception: The process by which listeners identify and interpret speech sounds.
Speech production: The process by which speakers plan, produce, and articulate speech sounds.
Articulatory kinematics: The study of the movement of articulators during speech production.
Electromagnetic articulography: A technique for measuring the position and movement of articulators during speech.
X-ray articulation: A technique for visualizing the internal structure and movement of the vocal tract during speech.
Magnetic resonance imaging: A technique for visualizing soft tissue structures, including the vocal tract, during speech.
Electroglottography: A technique for measuring the vibration of the vocal folds.
Ultrasound: A technique for imaging the internal structure and movement of the vocal tract in real time.
Palatography: The technique of recording the contact patterns of the tongue against the palate during speech.
Phonatory transcription: The representation of the phonatory state (voiced, voiceless, etc.) in phonetic transcription.
IPA: International Phonetic Alphabet, the standard system for transcribing the sounds of all languages.
Broad transcription: A phonetic transcription that captures only the phonemic level of detail.
Narrow transcription: A phonetic transcription that captures all phonetic details, including allophonic variation.
Diagonal transcription: A method of transcribing both broad and narrow phonetic detail in a single system.
IPA brackets: Square brackets [ ] used to enclose narrow phonetic transcriptions.
IPA slashes: Forward slashes / / used to enclose phonemic or abstract phonological transcriptions.
Suprasegmental transcription: The representation of features such as stress, tone, and intonation in phonetic or phonological transcription.
Moraic transcription: A method of transcribing moraic structure, the units of phonological timing.
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized in a hierarchical structure.
Distinctive feature: A binary property of a sound that distinguishes it from other sounds, such as [+voice] or [+nasal].
Feature matrix: A table listing the distinctive feature values for a set of sounds.
Feature coarticulation: The spread of distinctive features across multiple segments in the phonological representation.
Feature geometry (hierarchical): The hierarchical organization of distinctive features in phonological theory.
Phonological rule: A rule that specifies a phonological change, stated in terms of distinctive features.
Rule ordering: The sequence in which phonological rules are applied in a derivation.
Natural class: A set of sounds that are defined by a common feature or set of features.
Naturalness: The phonetic or articulatory basis for a phonological process, making it easier to explain or predict.
OCP: Obligatory Contour Principle, a constraint in phonology that prohibits certain types of tonal or feature repetition.
No-Wrap Constraint: A constraint in feature geometry that prohibits a feature from dominating multiple segments.
Identical: A constraint in phonology that requires two elements to be identical in their feature specification.
Dissimilatory: A phonological process in which similar sounds become less similar.
Assimilatory: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound.
Progressive assimilation: Assimilation in which a sound influences a following sound.
Regressive assimilation: Assimilation in which a sound is influenced by a following sound, also called anticipatory assimilation.
Metathesis (phonology): The reversal of the order of two or more sounds in a word.
Deletion: The omission of a sound in a particular phonological environment.
Insertion: The addition of a sound in a particular phonological environment.
Substitution: The replacement of one sound with another in a particular phonological environment.
Epenthetic: A sound that is inserted to facilitate pronunciation, such as the /j/ in "beautiful."
Schwa: The mid-central vowel /ə/, often the reduced vowel in unstressed syllables.
Reduced vowel: A vowel that is shortened or centralized in unstressed positions.
Vowel reduction: The process by which vowels are shortened or centralized in unstressed syllables.
Strong form: The full, unreduced form of a function word used in stressed positions.
Weak form: The reduced form of a function word used in unstressed positions.
Stress (word): The relative prominence of a syllable within a word.
Stress (sentence): The relative prominence of a word or phrase within a sentence.
Primary stress: The most prominent stress in a word or sentence.
Secondary stress: A stress that is less prominent than primary stress but more prominent than no stress.
Stress pattern: The distribution of stressed and unstressed syllables in a word or language.
Tonal language: A language in which pitch distinctions on syllables distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning.
Tone language: Another term for a tonal language.
Tone contour: The pattern of pitch movement on a syllable or word in a tonal language.
Tone sandhi: A tonal change that occurs when tones interact across syllable or word boundaries.
Tone spreading: The extension of a tone to adjacent syllables.
Tone association: The assignment of tones to syllables or moras in a tonal language.
Tone bearing unit: The unit to which a tone is assigned, such as a syllable or mora.
Register (tone): A high or low range of fundamental frequency in a tonal language, as in the tonal registers of some West African languages.
Tone (lexical): A tone that distinguishes one word from another, as in the four tones of Mandarin Chinese.
Tone (grammatical): A tone that marks a grammatical function, such as a plural or aspect marker.
Pitch accent: A tonal system in which a single pitch contrast on a mora or syllable distinguishes words, as in Japanese.
Accent (prosodic): A pattern of pitch, stress, or duration that distinguishes words or phrases.
Intonational phrase: A stretch of speech with a single intonation contour.
Prosodic word: A unit of prosody that corresponds roughly to a lexical word or affix.
Prosodic structure: The hierarchical organization of prosodic units, from segments to intonational phrases.
Intonational contour: The pattern of pitch movement over an intonational phrase.
Boundary tone: A pitch feature associated with the edges of prosodic or syntactic domains.
Pitch range: The total range of fundamental frequency values used in speech.
F0 range: The range of fundamental frequency values in a speech sample.
F0 mean: The average fundamental frequency in a speech sample.
F0 contour: The pattern of fundamental frequency variation over time.
Pitch track: A sequence of fundamental frequency values extracted from a speech signal.
Pitch reset: The phenomenon in which F0 returns to a baseline at the beginning of a new phrase or sentence.
Pitch declination: The general downward trend in F0 over the course of a phrase or sentence.
Pitch prominence: A peak or salient point in the F0 contour, often associated with stress or focus.
Nuclear stress: The primary stress or pitch prominence in a sentence, typically on the last content word.
Sentence stress: The pattern of stress distribution in a sentence.
Phrase stress: The pattern of stress distribution within a phrase.
Word stress: The pattern of stress distribution within a word.
Syllable stress: The pattern of stress distribution across syllables.
Moraic stress: A stress pattern based on the moraic structure of syllables.
Quantitative stress: A stress pattern based on the length of vowels or syllables.
Dynamic stress: A stress pattern based on the force or amplitude of articulation.
Pitch stress: A stress pattern based on pitch prominence.
Durational stress: A stress pattern based on the length of the stressed syllable.
Intensive stress: A stress pattern based on the increased articulatory effort on the stressed syllable.

Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated, often to express plurality, intensity, or iterativity.
Portmanteau: A word or morpheme that simultaneously encodes two or more grammatical distinctions, as in Latin verb endings.
Agglutination: A morphological typology in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each typically expressing a single grammatical category.
Fusional morphology: A morphological typology in which a single affix may encode multiple grammatical distinctions simultaneously.
Isolating morphology: A morphological typology in which words typically consist of a single morpheme and grammatical relationships are expressed through word order or particles.
Polysynthetic morphology: A morphological typology in which words can be extremely long, incorporating many morphemes that in other languages would be separate words.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages based on their predominant morphological strategies (isolating, agglutinative, fusional, polysynthetic).
Word: A free morpheme or a complex form that functions as a single unit in speech, typically separated by pauses or boundaries.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and fixed expressions in a language.
Lexical entry: The complete set of information associated with a word in a lexicon, including form, meaning, grammatical category, and distribution.
Lemma: The canonical or dictionary form of a word under which its inflected forms are listed, such as "run" for "runs," "running," "ran."
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or construction becomes a single lexical item in the vocabulary of a language.
Folk etymology: A popular but incorrect explanation of a word's origin, sometimes leading to changes in the word's form.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words.
Onomatopoeia: The formation of words that phonetically imitate or suggest the sound they represent, such as "buzz" or "splash."
Sememe: The smallest unit of lexical meaning, analogous to a phoneme in phonology.
Word sense: A particular meaning of a word, as distinguished from other meanings of the same word.
Sense relation: The semantic relationship between different meanings of the same word or between different words.
Semantic field: A set of words related by a common concept or domain, such as words related to "color" or "kinship."
Semantic component analysis: A method of analyzing word meanings by breaking them down into a set of binary semantic features or components.
Radial category: A lexical category organized around a central prototypical member with extensions along various dimensions.
Lexical gap: The absence of a word in a language to express a particular concept that is expressed by a single word in another language.
Lexical entry: The set of information about a word stored in a speaker's mental lexicon.
Colloquialism: A word or expression characteristic of informal, spoken language.
Archaism: A word or expression that is no longer in common use but is still understood, such as "thou" or "whilst."
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression, often entering the language through popular culture, technology, or academic use.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a blunter or more direct one, such as "passed away" for "died."
Dysphemism: A deliberately harsh, offensive, or unflattering word or expression, the opposite of a euphemism.
Slang: Informal, often nonstandard vocabulary used by particular social groups, frequently marked by novelty and exclusivity.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used within a particular profession, trade, or group.
Loanword: A word borrowed from one language and incorporated into another, often with some phonological or semantic adaptation.
Calque: A word or expression formed in one language by translating a foreign word or phrase component by component, such as "skyscraper" for French "gratte-ciel."
Doublet: Two or more words in a language that have different forms but share a common etymological origin, often from different borrowing waves, such as "king" and "royal."
Cognate: Words in different languages that share a common etymological origin from a shared ancestral language, such as English "father" and German "Vater."
Fals friend: A pair of words in different languages that look or sound similar but have different meanings, such as English "polish" (clean) and Spanish "polish" (to be polite).
Borrowing: The process by which a language adopts a word, expression, or grammatical feature from another language.
Code-switching: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or dialects within a conversation or even a single sentence.
Code-mixing: The blending of elements from two languages within a single utterance, as opposed to alternating between complete code-switches.
Bilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use two languages, either simultaneously or sequentially.
Multilingualism: The use of more than two languages by an individual or within a community.
Diglossia: A situation in which two distinct varieties of the same language (or two different languages) are used for different social functions, such as High and Low varieties.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops between groups with no common language, lacking native speakers.
Creole: A fully developed language that evolves from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a speech community.
Sesquipedalian: Pertaining to words with many syllables; a term sometimes used to describe overly long or complex words.
Anglicism: A word or expression borrowed from English into another language.
Galloicism: A word or expression borrowed from French into another language.
Hellenism: A word or expression borrowed from Greek into another language.
Latinism: A word or expression borrowed from Latin into another language.
Semantic shift: A change in the meaning of a word over time, encompassing broadening, narrowing, amelioration, and pejoration.
Semantic broadening: A type of semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more general, such as "bird" once meaning "young bird."
Semantic narrowing: A type of semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more specific, such as "meat" once meaning all food.
Amelioration: A semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more positive or favorable over time.
Pejoration: A semantic shift in which a word's meaning becomes more negative or derogatory over time.
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one thing is described in terms of another based on perceived similarity, such as "time is money."
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a thing is referred to by something closely associated with it, such as "the White House announced" for the administration.
Synecdoche: A type of metonymy in which a part is used to represent the whole or vice versa, such as "all hands on deck."
Pleonasm: The use of more words than necessary, often for emphasis or stylistic effect, such as "free gift" or "ATM machine."
Tautology: Redundant repetition of meaning in different words, such as "return back" or "advance forward."
Hypernym: A word whose meaning encompasses the meanings of more specific words, such as "animal" as a hypernym of "dog" and "cat."
Hyponym: A word whose meaning is included within a more general word, such as "dog" as a hyponym of "animal."
Coordinate terms: Hyponyms at the same level of a semantic hierarchy, such as "dog" and "cat" as coordinates under "animal."
Antonym types: Categories of antonymy including gradable (hot/cold), complementary (dead/alive), and converse (buy/sell).
Gradable antonym: An antonym pair on a scale with intermediate values, such as "hot" and "cold" with "warm" in between.
Complementary antonym: An antonym pair with no intermediate values, where if one is true, the other is false, such as "alive" and "dead."
Converse antonym: An antonym pair that expresses a reciprocal relationship from different perspectives, such as "husband" and "wife" or "buy" and "sell."
Scare quote: Quotation marks used to indicate skepticism, irony, or that the term is being used in a nonstandard or disputed sense.
Oxymoron: A figure of speech combining contradictory terms, such as "bittersweet," "deafening silence," or "living death."
Tropism: A directional tendency or association in language, such as a preference for a particular word order.
Zeugma: The use of a single word to govern or modify two or more other words in different senses, such as "He took his hat and his leave."
Synecdoche: A figure of speech using a part to represent the whole or the whole to represent a part.
Litotes: A form of understatement using a double negative to express a positive, such as "not bad" meaning "good."
Person: A grammatical category distinguishing the speaker (first person), the addressee (second person), and others (third person).
Number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular, plural, and sometimes dual or trial forms of nouns, pronouns, and verbs.
Gender: A grammatical category that classifies nouns into sets (masculine, feminine, neuter, or other), often not correlating with biological sex.
Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic or semantic role of a noun or pronoun in a sentence.
Declension: The paradigm of case endings for nouns, adjectives, and pronouns in inflectional languages.
Conjugation: The paradigm of verb forms showing changes in person, number, tense, mood, and aspect.
Infinitive: The non-finite form of a verb that typically has no subject, such as "to walk" or "go."
Participle: A non-finite verb form that can function as an adjective or form perfect tenses, such as "walking" or "broken."
Gerund: A verb form ending in "-ing" in English that functions as a noun, such as "Swimming is fun."
Infinitive: The base form of a verb that does not show person or number, often preceded by "to" in English.
Subjunctive: A mood expressing hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations, such as "I wish he were here."
Indicative: The mood used for statements of fact or straightforward questions.
Imperative: The mood used to give commands or make requests, such as "Close the door!"
Conditional: A mood or construction expressing a hypothetical situation dependent on a condition, such as "If I were rich, I would travel."
Perfect: A grammatical category expressing a completed action with present relevance, such as "I have eaten."
Pluperfect: A grammatical category expressing an action completed before another past action, such as "I had eaten before she arrived."
Future: A grammatical category expressing an action that will occur after the time of speaking.
Progressive: An aspect marking an action as ongoing or in progress, such as "I am eating."
Habitual: An aspect marking a repeated or customary action, such as "I always drink coffee in the morning."
Perfective: An aspect marking an action as a complete whole, without reference to internal structure.
Imperfective: An aspect marking an action as ongoing, habitual, or internally structured, as opposed to perfective.
Frequentative: An aspect or derivational process indicating repeated or habitual action.
Inchoative: A grammatical or semantic category indicating the beginning of a state or action.
Completive: An aspect indicating the completion of an action.
Durative: An aspect indicating that an action or state continues over a period of time.
Stative: A verb or predicate describing a state rather than an action, such as "know," "love," or "be."
Dynamic: A verb or predicate describing an action or process, as opposed to a state.
Punctual: An aspect or event type that is conceived as having no duration, occurring at a single point in time.
Iterative: A grammatical or derivational process indicating repeated action.
Singular: The grammatical number form referring to one entity.
Plural: The grammatical number form referring to more than one entity.
Dual: The grammatical number form referring to exactly two entities, found in some languages like Arabic and some Slavic languages.
Trials: The grammatical number form referring to exactly three entities, found in some languages like Tariana.
Paucal: The grammatical number form referring to a small, unspecified number greater than one, found in some Australian and Papuan languages.
Collective: A grammatical number form referring to a group of entities as a single unit.
Singularia tantum: Nouns that exist only in the singular form, such as "information" or "furniture" in English.
Pluralia tantum: Nouns that exist only in the plural form, such as "scissors" or "trousers" in English.
Heteronome plural: A plural form that is not formed by regular suffixation but by a wholly different root, such as "man/men."
Suppletive plural: A plural form derived from an entirely different etymological root, such as "goose/geese" or "ox/oxen."
Irregular plural: A plural form that does not follow the most common plural formation pattern in a language.
Regular plural: A plural form created by applying the most common plural morpheme, such as adding "-s" in English.
Gender agreement: The requirement that certain words (adjectives, articles, verbs) match the grammatical gender of a noun they modify or govern.
Neuter: A grammatical gender category not specifically associated with male or female, common in German, Scandinavian, and Slavic languages.
Masculine: A grammatical gender category that may or may not correlate with biological sex.
Feminine: A grammatical gender category that may or may not correlate with biological sex.
Common gender: A grammatical gender category that does not distinguish between masculine and feminine, as in modern English.
Animate gender: A grammatical gender category grouping nouns referring to living beings.
Inanimate gender: A grammatical gender category grouping nouns referring to non-living things.
Feminization: A linguistic or social process in which women are assigned a feminine grammatical form, as in feminine agent nouns.
Morphological markedness: The tendency for the less expected or less frequent form to carry an overt morphological marker, as in masculine being unmarked in many gender systems.
Syntactic gender: Gender assigned based on syntactic properties such as number or animacy rather than semantic class.
Lexical gender: Gender assigned to individual nouns based on convention or historical origin.
Natural gender: The biological sex of the referent of a noun.
Grammatical gender: A system of noun classification based on conventional rather than semantic or biological criteria.
Person marking: The morphological or syntactic encoding of grammatical person in verbs or pronouns.
Clusivity: The distinction between inclusive and exclusive first-person plural pronouns, found in many Pacific and Amazonian languages.
Inclusive: A first-person plural that includes both the speaker and the addressee ("we" including you).
Exclusive: A first-person plural that includes the speaker but not the addressee ("we" excluding you).
Deictic: Relating to words or expressions that refer to elements in the situational context, such as "I," "here," "now."
Anaphoric: Relating to expressions that refer back to a previously mentioned element in the discourse.
Cataphoric: Relating to expressions that refer forward to an element not yet mentioned in the discourse.
Referential: Describing an expression that points to a specific entity in the world.
Non-referential: Describing an expression that does not point to a specific entity, such as the subject of "It is raining."
Expletive: A syntactically required but semantically empty element, such as the "it" in "It is raining" or "there" in "There are three books."
Dummy subject: A non-referential subject used to satisfy a language's requirement for a subject in certain constructions.
Dummy object: A non-referential object used to satisfy a language's requirement for an object, as in "I find it hard to believe."
Null subject: A subject position that is syntactically present but phonologically empty, as in pro-drop languages like Italian or Spanish.
Pro-drop: The grammatical licensing of null (unexpressed) subjects, as in Italian "Parlo italiano" (I speak Italian, with "I" unexpressed).
Null object: A grammatically licensed null object position in a language.
Overt: A linguistic element that is explicitly pronounced or written, as opposed to null or zero.
Covert: A linguistic element that is not explicitly pronounced or written but is understood from context.
Zero anaphora: The use of a null (unexpressed) pronoun that is interpreted from context, common in Chinese and Japanese.
Discourse: The study of language use in extended stretches of text or conversation beyond the sentence level.
Text: A sequence of sentences or utterances that form a coherent whole.
Cohesion: The set of linguistic devices that link elements within a text, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical ties.
Coherence: The overall logical and meaningful connection between ideas in a text, beyond surface-level linguistic links.
Topic: The entity or subject about which a sentence or discourse is predicated.
Focus: The element in a sentence that carries new or contrastive information.
Information structure: The organization of a sentence into given and new information, or old and new, guiding the hearer's processing.
Given information: Information that is already known or accessible to the hearer.
New information: Information that is not yet known or accessible to the hearer.
Contrast: A prosodic or syntactic marking that signals an element is being set against an alternative.
Presupposition projection: The way presuppositions in embedded clauses propagate to the matrix clause.
Factivity: The property of a verb or adjective that presupposes the truth of its complement, as in "regret" or "know."
Non-factivity: The property of a verb or adjective that does not presuppose the truth of its complement, as in "think" or "claim."
Veridical: A verb or context that presupposes or entails the truth of a proposition.
Non-veridical: A verb or context that does not presuppose or entail the truth of a proposition.
Scalar: Relating to a scale of ordered alternatives, as in scalar implicatures with "some," "only," or "even."
Even: A scalar particle that signals that a proposition is true of all more or equally likely alternatives.
Only: A scalar particle that signals that a proposition is true of no other alternatives.
Focus-sensitive: A linguistic expression whose interpretation changes depending on which element bears focus.
Hedging: The use of linguistic expressions to soften or qualify a statement, such as "perhaps," "I think," or "sort of."
Vagueness: A property of expressions that lack precise boundaries, such as "tall," "old," or "a lot."
Fuzziness: The property of category boundaries that are indeterminate, studied in fuzzy logic and linguistic typology.
Prototype: A best example or central member of a category around which other members are organized.
Fuzzy logic: A mathematical framework for dealing with partial truth values, applied to linguistic categories with imprecise boundaries.
Categorical: Having clear, sharp boundaries, as opposed to fuzzy or graded.
Graded: Having a continuum of degrees rather than sharp boundaries, such as color terms.
Boundary: The limit of a category's extension, which may be sharp or fuzzy.
Extension: The set of real-world entities to which a term applies.
Intension: The set of properties or conditions that define the extension of a term.
Sense: The cognitive content or meaning of a linguistic expression.
Reference: The entity or state of affairs in the world that a linguistic expression points to.
Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to semantics that defines the meaning of a sentence in terms of the conditions under which it is true.
Model-theoretic semantics: A formal approach to semantics that defines meaning in terms of mathematical structures (models) and satisfaction relations.
Mereological semantics: The semantic treatment of part-whole relationships.
Temporal semantics: The formal semantic treatment of time, tense, and aspect.
Modal semantics: The formal semantic treatment of modality, including possibility, necessity, and various modalities.
Quantificational semantics: The formal semantic treatment of quantifiers such as "all," "some," "no," and "every."
Scope: The domain over which a quantifier or operator has effect, which can vary in ambiguous sentences.
Wide scope: A quantifier taking effect over a larger domain, as in "Every student read every book."
Narrow scope: A quantifier taking effect over a smaller domain, as in "Every book was read by every student."
Ambiguous scope: A sentence in which two quantifiers can take either scope, yielding different interpretations.
Lift: In formal semantics, the operation of raising the type of a denotation, such as from a truth value to a set of possible worlds.
Intension: The function from possible worlds to extensions, used in intensional semantics.
Extension: The actual set of entities a term refers to in a given world.
Possible world: A complete and consistent way the world might be, used as a parameter in intensional semantics.
Intensional context: A linguistic context in which the extension of an expression depends on the possible world, such as "believes that."
Extensional context: A linguistic context in which the extension of an expression is independent of the possible world.
De dicto: An interpretation in which the modal or attitude operator has scope over the embedded proposition.
De re: An interpretation in which a quantified noun phrase has scope over the modal or attitude operator.
Opacity: A property of certain contexts in which substituting a co-referential expression changes the truth value, as in belief contexts.
Transparency: A property of contexts in which substituting a co-referential expression does not change the truth value.
Proposition: The truth-apt content expressed by a declarative sentence.
Propositional attitude: A mental relation between a person and a proposition, such as belief, desire, or knowledge.
Entailment: A semantic relation in which the truth of one proposition necessitates the truth of another.
Presupposition: A background assumption that is taken for granted in an utterance.
Contradiction: A pair of propositions that cannot both be true.
Subcontradiction: A pair of propositions that cannot both be false but can both be true.
Subalternation: A relation in which the truth of a more general proposition implies the truth of a more specific one.
Contrariety: A relation in which two propositions cannot both be true but can both be false.
Square of opposition: A traditional diagram showing the logical relations between categorical propositions (A, E, I, O).
Modal verb: A verb that expresses modality, such as "can," "must," "should," or "may."
Alethic modality: Modality relating to truth and falsity, including necessity and possibility.
Deontic modality: Modality relating to obligation, permission, and prohibition.
Epistemic modality: Modality relating to knowledge and belief, including certainty and probability.
Boulomaic modality: Modality relating to desire and volition.
Dynamic modality: Modality relating to ability, permission, or compulsion from an external source.
Root modality: Modal expressions used in non-declarative sentences (imperatives, conditionals, questions).
Modal auxiliary: A verb expressing modality that is used with another verb, such as "can," "must," "may."
Modality: A grammatical or semantic category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, including necessity, possibility, obligation, or permission.
Complement clause: A clause that serves as a complement to a verb, adjective, or noun, such as "that he is here" in "I know that he is here."
Finite clause: A clause whose verb is inflected for tense and person, as opposed to a non-finite clause.
Non-finite clause: A clause whose verb is in a non-finite form, such as an infinitive or participle clause.
Finite: A verb form that is inflected for tense, person, and number.
Non-finite: A verb form that is not inflected for tense, person, and number, such as an infinitive or participle.
Embedded clause: A clause that is syntactically contained within another clause.
Matrix clause: The main or outer clause in a sentence containing an embedded clause.
Subordinate clause: A clause that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence and depends on a main clause.
Adverbial clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adverbial modifier, such as "after she left" or "although it rained."
Adjectival clause: A subordinate clause that functions as an adjective, modifying a noun, such as a relative clause.
Nominal clause: A subordinate clause that functions as a noun phrase, such as the subject or object of a verb.
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, typically introduced by a relative pronoun, such as "the book that I read."
Appositive: A noun or noun phrase that renames or further identifies another noun or noun phrase immediately adjacent to it.
Free relative: A relative clause that functions as a noun phrase without a head noun, such as "whatever you want."
Restrictive relative: A relative clause that is essential to identifying the referent of its head noun.
Non-restrictive relative: A relative clause that provides additional information and is not essential to identifying the referent.
Reduced relative: A relative clause in which the relative pronoun and copula are omitted, such as "the man standing there."
Cleft sentence: A sentence constructed to place emphasis on a particular element, such as "It was John who did it."
Pseudo-cleft: A cleft construction in which the focus is in the wh-clause, such as "What I want is a cup of tea."
Extraposition: The movement of a constituent to a position after the main clause, often replacing it with a placeholder, such as "It is likely that he will come."
Left dislocation: A construction in which a constituent is placed before the main clause, with a pronoun referring to it in the main clause, such as "John, he is here."
Right dislocation: A construction in which a constituent is placed after the main clause, with a pronoun in the main clause, such as "He is here, John."
Topicalization: The movement of a constituent to the beginning of a sentence to mark it as the topic.
Fronting: The placement of a constituent at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis or topicalization.
Inversion: A syntactic construction in which the normal subject-verb order is reversed, as in questions or after certain adverbials.
Subject-auxiliary inversion: The reversal of subject and auxiliary verb, as in "Did you go?" versus "You did go."
Expletive inversion: A construction in which an expletive subject precedes an inverted verb phrase, such as "There are many reasons."
Causative: A construction in which a subject causes an event, as in "She made him leave."
Passive: A construction in which the theme or patient becomes the subject.
Antipassive: A construction in which the transitivity of a verb is reduced, typically demoting the object.
Middle voice: A verbal construction that indicates the subject is the affected participant of an action, intermediate between active and passive.
Refl
exive: A construction in which the subject and object are the same entity.
Reciprocal construction: A construction expressing a mutual action between two or more participants.
Valency: The number of arguments (participants) a predicate requires or can take.
Transitivity: A property of verbs and clauses related to the number and type of arguments, often contrasting agentive actions with patient undergoers.
De
transitivization: A process that reduces the valency of a verb, such as through passivization or antipassivization.
Transitivization: A process that increases the valency of a verb, such as through causativization.
Causativization: A morphological or syntactic process that adds a causer argument to a verb, such as "break" → "break (causative)."
Applicative: A morphological or syntactic process that adds an additional argument to a verb, often promoting a peripheral role to core argument status.
Locative applicative: An applicative construction that adds a location argument to a verb.
Benefactive applicative: An applicative construction that adds a beneficiary argument to a verb.
Instrumental applicative: An applicative construction that adds an instrument argument to a verb.
Comitative: A grammatical relation or marker indicating accompaniment, such as "together with."
Allative: A grammatical relation or marker indicating direction toward a location.
Ablative: A grammatical relation or marker indicating direction away from a location.
Elative: A grammatical relation or marker indicating emergence from a location.
Illative: A grammatical relation or marker indicating entry into a location.
Allative: A grammatical relation or marker indicating direction toward a location.
Lative: A general term for case relations indicating direction or location.
Spatiotemporal: Relating to the combination of spatial and temporal dimensions in language.
Deictic center: The point of reference (typically the speaker's location and the time of utterance) from which spatial and temporal deictic expressions are anchored.
Temporal deixis: The use of words to refer to time relative to the utterance, such as "now," "yesterday," "tomorrow."
Spatial deixis: The use of words to refer to location relative to a deictic center, such as "here," "there," "above," "below."
Path: The route or trajectory of motion in a motion event.
Manner: The way in which motion is carried out.
Motive: The reason or cause of motion.
Motion verb: A verb that encodes the path of motion, as in many European languages.
Manner verb: A verb that encodes the manner of motion, as in many Asian and American Indian languages.
SAT (Satellite-framed): A typological classification for languages in which path is encoded in a satellite element (adverb, particle) and manner in the verb.
VFR (Verb-Frame): A typological classification for languages in which path is encoded in the verb frame and manner in the satellite.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages by their morphological structure.
Syntactic typology: The classification of languages by their syntactic structures and word order patterns.
Phonological typology: The classification of languages by their sound systems.
Semantic typology: The classification of languages by their semantic systems.
Pragmatic typology: The classification of languages by their pragmatic features.
Universals: Generalizations or constraints that hold across all or most human languages.
Absolute universal: A linguistic generalization that holds without exception in all known languages.
Tendential universal: A linguistic generalization that holds in the majority of languages but with exceptions.
Implicational universal: A universal that states if a language has property A, it also has property B.
Typology: The comparative study of the structural features of languages to identify patterns, universals, and parameters.
Parameter: A setting in a language that can vary across languages, such as head-initial vs. head-final word order.
Head: The main word in a phrase or clause that determines its type.
Dependent: A word or phrase that modifies or is governed by a head.
Head-initial: A structure in which the head precedes its dependents, as in English noun phrases ("big house").
Head-final: A structure in which the head follows its dependents, as in Japanese noun phrases ("big house").
SOV: A basic word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb, as in Japanese and Turkish.
SVO: A basic word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object, as in English and French.
VSO: A basic word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object, as in Arabic and classical Celtic languages.
VOS: A basic word order in which the verb precedes the object, which precedes the subject.
OSV: A basic word order in which the object precedes the subject, which precedes the verb, as in some Mayan languages.
OVS: A basic word order in which the object precedes the verb, which precedes the subject, as in some Australian and Amazonian languages.
Word order: The relative arrangement of syntactic elements (subject, object, verb, etc.) in a clause.
Free word order: A property of a language that allows significant variation in constituent order.
Flexible word order: A property of a language that allows some variation in constituent order but with constraints.
Strict word order: A property of a language that requires a fixed constituent order.
Topic-prominent: A typological classification for languages that organize discourse around topics rather than grammatical subjects.
Subject-prominent: A typological classification for languages that organize discourse around grammatical subjects.
Split-S: A language with different subject marking for transitive and intransitive clauses, as in some Australian languages.
Split-A: A language with different marking for the agent of a transitive verb depending on certain conditions.
Ergative-absolutive: A case alignment system in which the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb share the same case.
Nominative-accusative: A case alignment system in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs shares the same case.
Tripartite: A case alignment system in which the subject of a transitive verb, the subject of an intransitive verb, and the object of a transitive verb are all marked differently.
Active-stative: A case alignment system in which arguments are marked based on their semantic role (agent vs. patient) rather than syntactic position.
Case alignment: The system by which languages mark the grammatical relations of arguments.
Person hierarchy: The ranking of first person > second person > third person in many languages' pronoun and verb agreement systems.
Animacy hierarchy: A ranking of nouns by animacy (human > animal > inanimate) that affects case marking and agreement in many languages.
Inalienable: A noun that refers to something inherently possessed or a body part, often marked differently from alienable nouns in some languages.
Alienable: A noun that refers to something that can be possessed or transferred, as opposed to inalienable nouns.
Inalienable possession: A grammatical system in which body parts, kinship terms, and other inherently possessed items are marked differently from other nouns.
Intransitive alignment: A system in which the subject of an intransitive verb is treated differently from subjects and objects of transitive verbs.
Transitive alignment: A system in which the agent of a transitive verb is treated differently from the patient, the intransitive subject, and the transitive object.
Nominal: A word or phrase that functions as a noun, including nouns, pronouns, and noun phrases.
Verbal: A word or phrase that functions as a verb, including verbs, verb phrases, and non-finite verb forms.
Adverbial: A word or phrase that functions as an adverb, modifying a verb, adjective, or clause.
