Nasal: a consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity
Lateral: a consonant produced with the tongue tip making contact while air flows around the sides of the tongue
Rhotic: a consonant, typically an r-sound, produced with the tongue tip or body near the alveolar ridge
Approximant: a consonant produced with a partial constriction that does not create turbulent airflow
Glide: a consonant that functions as a transitional or semivowel sound
Place of articulation: the location in the vocal tract at which a consonantal constriction is made
Manner of articulation: the manner in which the airstream is obstructed or modified to produce a consonant
Voicing: the vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a speech sound
Aspiration: a burst of turbulent airflow accompanying the release of a voiceless stop
Nasalization: the lowering of the velum during the production of a sound, allowing nasal airflow
Palatalization: the secondary articulation in which the tongue body approaches the hard palate
Labialization: the secondary articulation in which the lips are rounded during the production of a sound
Phonemic: pertaining to or constituting a phoneme or the system of phonemes in a language
Morphophonemic: pertaining to the systematic interaction between morphological and phonological processes
Syllable: the basic unit of phonological organization, typically containing a vowel as its nucleus
Onset: the consonant or consonant cluster preceding the vowel nucleus in a syllable
Nucleus: the peak of sonority in a syllable, typically a vowel
Coda: the consonant or consonant cluster following the vowel nucleus in a syllable
Rhyme: the stressed vowel and any following consonants within a syllable
Stress: the relative prominence of a syllable, often marked by higher pitch, greater loudness, or longer duration
Intonation: the melodic contour of pitch variation across an utterance
Pitch: the perceptual correlate of frequency, determining how high or low a sound is perceived
Duration: the temporal length of a speech segment, syllable, or utterance
Amplitude: the magnitude of the pressure variation in a sound wave, perceived as loudness
Tone: a lexical or grammatical use of pitch contour to distinguish meaning, as in tonal languages
Mora: a unit of syllable weight used in phonological analysis, roughly corresponding to a short vowel or a single consonant
Phonotactics: the rules governing which sequences and combinations of sounds are permissible in a given language
Feature geometry: a model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized in a hierarchical structure
Distinctive feature: a binary phonological property, such as [voice] or [nasal], used to characterize and contrast phonemes
Neutralization: a phonological context in which a contrast between two phonemes is suspended
Archiphoneme: an abstract phonological entity representing a set of phonemes that are neutralized in a given context
Complementary distribution: a relationship between two variants that never occur in the same phonological environment
Minimal pair: a pair of words in a language that differ in only one phoneme and have different meanings
Allophonic variation: non-contrastive phonetic variation in which different surface forms correspond to the same underlying phoneme
Phoneme inventory: the complete set of phonemes used in a particular language
Word: a free morpheme or a morphologically bound string of morphemes that functions as an independent unit
Lexical entry: a representation of a word or fixed expression stored in the mental lexicon
Paradigm: a set of related inflected or derived forms of a word
Inflectional paradigm: the full set of inflected forms a word takes to mark tense, case, number, or person
Agglutination: a morphological strategy in which each morpheme typically carries a single grammatical meaning with clear boundaries
Fusional morphology: a morphological strategy in which a single affix may encode multiple grammatical features simultaneously
Isolating morphology: a morphological strategy in which words are predominantly single morphemes with minimal inflection
Polysynthesis: a typological classification in which words routinely incorporate multiple morphemes, often expressing clause-like meaning
Bound morpheme: a morpheme that cannot stand independently as a free word
Free morpheme: a morpheme that can function as an independent word
Infix: a morpheme inserted within the stem of a word rather than at its edges
Circumfix: a pair of affixes that must appear together on opposite sides of a root to form a single morphological unit
Suppletion: an irregular morphological alternation in which the forms of a paradigm are historically unrelated
Reduplication: the morphological process of repeating all or part of a word or morpheme to express a grammatical or lexical meaning
Zero morpheme: a morpheme that has no overt phonetic realization but is inferred from its morphological function
Productive morpheme: a morpheme that is actively used in the formation of new words in a language
Unproductive morpheme: a morpheme that survives in existing words but is no longer used to form new ones
Word order: the syntactic arrangement of major constituents in a clause, such as Subject-Verb-Object
Constituent: a syntactic unit that functions as a single element within a larger structure
Phrase: a syntactic unit headed by a single word and containing zero or more modifiers
Clause: a syntactic unit containing at minimum a subject and a predicate
Sentence: a maximal syntactic projection that expresses a complete propositional or illocutionary unit
Noun phrase: a phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, potentially modified by determiners and adjectives
Verb phrase: a phrase headed by a verb, including its arguments and modifiers
Adjective phrase: a phrase headed by an adjective, potentially modified by adverbs
Adverb phrase: a phrase headed by an adverb, potentially modified by other adverbs
Prepositional phrase: a phrase headed by a preposition, followed by its complement
Determiner: a word that precedes a noun to specify its reference, such as a, the, or this
Noun: a lexical category denoting entities, qualities, or abstractions
Verb: a lexical category denoting actions, states, processes, or events
Adjective: a lexical category that modifies or characterizes nouns
Adverb: a lexical category that modifies verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs
Preposition: a word that introduces a phrase and expresses a spatial, temporal, or abstract relation
Postposition: a word that follows a noun or phrase and expresses a grammatical or spatial relation
Conjunction: a word that links words, phrases, or clauses of equal or unequal status
Interjection: an expletive or exclamatory word expressing spontaneous emotion
Article: a determiner that marks definiteness or indefiniteness, as in "the" or "a"
Pronoun: a word that functions in place of a noun phrase, referring to an entity already in discourse
Subject: the syntactic argument that typically agrees with the verb and performs or undergoes the action
Object: the syntactic argument that receives the action or is affected by the predicate
Predicate: the part of a clause that contains the verb and expresses what is asserted about the subject
Complement: a required argument of a predicate that completes its valency
Adjunct: an optional syntactic constituent that modifies a phrase or clause
Specifier: the constituent occupying the position immediately below the head in a phrase structure
Head: the central lexical or functional element that determines the category of a phrase
Projection: the syntactic structure generated by a head, extending through its specifier and complement positions
X-bar theory: a generalization in syntax stating that phrases have a uniform three-part structure: specifier, head, and complement
Phrase structure grammar: a model of syntax that generates sentences using a set of rewrite rules for nonterminal symbols
Transformational grammar: a syntactic framework that derives surface structures from deep structures through transformations
Generative grammar: the overarching theoretical framework for describing the rules that generate all grammatical sentences of a language
Government and Binding: a syntactic theory within the generative framework that organizes structure through principles and parameters
Minimalist Program: the contemporary syntactic framework seeking to account for grammar with the most economical set of operations
Dependency grammar: a syntactic model in which structure is represented as a set of asymmetric head-to-dependent relations
Tree diagram: a graphical representation of hierarchical syntactic structure using branching nodes
Structural ambiguity: ambiguity arising from the possibility of multiple syntactic parses for the same surface string
Lexical ambiguity: ambiguity arising from the multiple meanings of a single word or expression
Cleft sentence: a construction that highlights a specific constituent, as in "It was John who left"
Passive voice: a voice construction in which the patient or object is promoted to subject position
Active voice: a voice construction in which the agent or subject is in the canonical subject position
Topicalization: the syntactic process of moving a topic to the front of a clause
Focus: the discourse-prominent element of an utterance, receiving special prosodic and syntactic marking
Negation: the grammatical device for expressing the falsity, absence, or denial of a proposition
Question: an interrogative construction that requests information
Imperative: a clause type expressing a command, request, or instruction
Declarative: a clause type that states a proposition as fact
Interrogative: a clause type that asks a question, marked by question intonation or inversion
Exclamative: a clause type expressing strong emotion or emphasis
Coordinate structure: a syntactic construction in which two or more constituents of the same category are joined by a conjunction
Subordinate structure: a syntactic construction in which a clause is embedded within a larger clause as a constituent
Relative clause: a subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or complementizer
Noun clause: a subordinate clause that functions syntactically as a noun phrase
Adverbial clause: a subordinate clause that functions syntactically as an adverb, modifying the main clause
Subordinator: a word or morpheme that introduces a subordinate clause
Correlative: a pair of structurally dependent words, such as "both...and" or "neither...nor"
Agreement: a grammatical requirement that certain features, such as number, gender, or person, match between related constituents
Concord: the specific agreement between a subject and its verb in number and person
Case: a grammatical category that marks the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase in a clause
Nominative case: the case marking the subject of a finite clause
Accusative case: the case marking the direct object of a transitive verb
Genitive case: the case marking possession, origin, or other attributive relations
Dative case: the case marking the indirect object or recipient of a transitive action
Vocative case: the case marking a form of direct address
Ablative case: the case marking source, separation, or the means by which something is done
Locative case: the case marking the location or position of an entity
Instrumental case: the case marking the tool or means used in an action
Ergative: a case alignment system in which the agent of a transitive verb is marked differently from the intransitive subject
Absolutive: a case alignment system in which the intransitive subject and the patient of a transitive verb share the same case
Split-ergativity: a case alignment pattern in which ergative and accusative marking co-occur, often conditioned by tense or aspect
Transitivity: the property of a verb that takes a direct object argument
Intransitivity: the property of a verb that does not take a direct object argument
Valency: the number and type of arguments that a predicate requires or may take
Argument structure: the set of semantic and syntactic arguments associated with a predicate
Theta role: the semantic role, such as agent or patient, that a predicate assigns to each of its arguments
Agent: the theta role of the volitional initiator of an action
Patient: the theta role of the entity that undergoes or is affected by an action
Theme: the theta role of the entity that undergoes a change of state or location
Experiencer: the theta role of the entity that feels an emotion or perceives a sensation
Goal: the theta role of the endpoint toward which an entity or entity moves
Source: the theta role of the starting point from which an entity or entity moves
Location: the theta role of the spatial position at which an event occurs
Instrument: the theta role of the tool or means by which an action is carried out
Recipient: the theta role of the entity that receives a transferred entity
Benefactive: the theta role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed
Aspect: the grammatical category that encodes the internal temporal structure of an event
Tense: the grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speech
Mood: the grammatical category that encodes the speaker's attitude toward the propositional content
Indicative mood: the mood used for statements of fact or reality
Subjunctive mood: the mood used for hypothetical, counterfactual, or desired situations
Imperative mood: the mood used for commands or requests
Optative mood: the mood used to express wishes or hopes
Perfective aspect: the aspectual viewpoint that presents an event as a complete, bounded whole
Imperfective aspect: the aspectual viewpoint that presents an event as ongoing, habitual, or unbounded
Progressive aspect: the aspect marking that an action is in progress at a given time
Habitual aspect: the aspect marking that an action occurs repeatedly or as a general pattern
Aorist aspect: the aspect that presents an event as a simple, unmarked occurrence without emphasis on completion
Evidentiality: the grammatical encoding of the source or type of evidence for a proposition
Evidential: a grammatical marker that indicates whether information is witnessed, reported, inferred, or assumed
Subordination: the syntactic relationship in which one clause is embedded within another as a constituent
Coordination: the syntactic relationship in which two or more clauses of equal status are joined
Morphophonemics: the study of systematic sound changes that are triggered by morphological processes
Phonological rule: a formal statement describing a systematic sound change in a particular phonological environment
Syllabification: the process of assigning segments to syllabic positions in a phonological representation
Suprasegmental: a feature of speech, such as stress or tone, that is not restricted to a single segment
Minimal contrast: the smallest phonological difference that distinguishes meaning between two words
Phonological process: a rule or constraint governing the behavior of sounds in a language
Sound law: a regular historical change in the pronunciation of a sound in a particular environment
Analogical change: a type of language change in which irregular forms are regularized on the model of existing patterns
Morphological alternation: a change in the form of a morpheme depending on its morphological or phonological environment
Morpheme boundary: the point at which one morpheme ends and the next begins within a word
Word formation: the process by which new words are created from existing linguistic material
Compounds: words formed by the combination of two or more free morphemes
Portmanteau: a word formed by blending the sounds and meanings of two or more words
Acronym: a word formed from the initial letters of a multi-word name
Neologism: a newly coined or recently adopted word in a language
Semantic shift: a change in the meaning of a word over the course of a language's history
Broadening: a semantic change in which a word's meaning expands to cover a wider range of referents
Narrowing: a semantic change in which a word's meaning contracts to cover a narrower range of referents
Pejoration: a semantic change in which a word acquires a negative or derogatory connotation
Amelioration: a semantic change in which a word acquires a positive or more respectful connotation
Metonymy: a figure of speech in which a related concept is used to refer to the intended referent
Synecdoche: a figure of speech in which a part is used to represent the whole or vice versa
Metaphor: a figure of speech that maps the structure of one domain onto another based on perceived similarity
Litotes: a form of understatement in which a positive is expressed by negating its opposite
Hyperbole: a figure of speech involving deliberate exaggeration for effect
Tautology: the use of more words than necessary to convey the same meaning, often for emphasis
Antanagogy: a rhetorical device in which a fault is offset by a corresponding virtue
Aposiopesis: a rhetorical device in which a sentence is deliberately left unfinished
Anaphora: a figure of speech in which the same word or phrase is repeated at the beginning of successive clauses
Epistrophe: a figure of speech in which the same word or phrase is repeated at the end of successive clauses
Chiasmus: a rhetorical structure in which two or more clauses are balanced by reversing their order
Zeugma: a figure of speech in which a single word governs or is connected to two or more others
Syllepsis: a figure of speech in which one word is used in two different senses simultaneously
Asyndeton: the omission of conjunctions between coordinate elements
Polysyndeton: the use of repeated conjunctions between coordinate elements
Rhetorical question: a question posed for effect rather than to elicit an answer
Irony: the expression of meaning through language that directly contradicts or is incongruous with the intended meaning
Sarcasm: a form of irony in which the intent is to mock or convey contempt
Understatement: a figure of speech that deliberately presents something as less significant than it is
Personification: a figure of speech that attributes human qualities to nonhuman entities
Alliteration: the occurrence of the same initial consonant sound in a sequence of adjacent words
Assonance: the repetition of vowel sounds in nearby stressed syllables
Consonance: the repetition of consonant sounds within or at the ends of nearby words
Alliteration: the repetition of initial consonant sounds in closely associated words
Phonemic contrast: a pairing of two phonemes that distinguishes meaning in a language
Vowel harmony: a phonological constraint in which the vowels within a word share a common phonetic feature
Consonant harmony: a phonological constraint in which consonants within a word share a common feature
Tone sandhi: a phonological process in which the tone of a syllable changes in response to adjacent tones
Syllable weight: the phonological property of a syllable determined by the number and type of its segments
Maximally filled syllable: a syllable containing the maximum number of segments permitted by a language's phonotactics
Open syllable: a syllable that ends in a vowel with no coda consonant
Closed syllable: a syllable that ends in a consonant, with a coda
Plosive release: the moment of articulatory release in the production of a stop consonant
Pre-voicing: the voicing of a consonant in the closure phase before its release
Coarticulation: the overlapping and mutual influence of adjacent articulatory gestures in speech
Liaison: the linking of a normally silent final consonant to the initial vowel of a following word
Elision: the omission of a sound or syllable in connected speech
Epenthesis: the insertion of a sound or syllable between two consonants or vowels in a word
Assimilation: a phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound
Dissimilation: a phonological process in which similar sounds become less similar
Metathesis: a phonological or historical process in which the order of two sounds is reversed
Lenition: a process of consonant weakening in a particular phonological environment
Fortition: a process of consonant strengthening in a particular phonological environment
Degemination: the reduction of a geminate or long consonant to a single short consonant
Gemination: the lengthening or doubling of a consonant in a particular phonological context
Vocalization: the process by which a consonant becomes a vowel
Consonant cluster: a sequence of two or more consonants without an intervening vowel
Plosive: a consonant produced by a complete stoppage and subsequent release of the airstream
Labial-velar: a consonant produced simultaneously at the lips and the velum, such as the /w/ sound
Trill: a consonant produced by the vibration of the tongue tip or uvula
Tap: a consonant produced by a brief single contact of the tongue tip with the alveolar ridge
Click: a consonant produced by creating a vacuum in the mouth and releasing it explosively
Ejective: a consonant produced by a glottalic egressive airstream mechanism
Ingressive: a consonant produced by an implosive or ingressive airstream mechanism
Voiceless: a consonant produced without vibration of the vocal folds
Voiced: a consonant produced with vibration of the vocal folds
Fortis: a consonant produced with greater articulatory tension
Lenis: a consonant produced with less articulatory tension
Aspirated: a consonant released with a strong burst of air
Deaspirated: a consonant released without a significant burst of air
Laryngealized: a consonant produced with a secondary laryngeal constriction
Pharyngealized: a consonant produced with a secondary constriction in the pharynx
Phonemic nasal: a nasal phoneme that contrasts with its oral counterpart in a language
Contrastive length: a phonological distinction based on the duration of a vowel or consonant
Prosodic word: a phonological unit that corresponds roughly to a linguistic word and bears stress
Phonological phrase: a domain of phonological organization larger than the phonological word
Intonational phrase: a domain of intonational structure, typically corresponding to a major pause or clause boundary
Utterance: a complete stretch of speech or writing produced by a single speaker
Prosodic structure: the hierarchical organization of prosodic units such as syllables, feet, and phrases
Stress timing: a rhythmic pattern in which stressed syllables occur at roughly regular intervals
Syllable timing: a rhythmic pattern in which syllables tend to occupy roughly equal time intervals
Iamb: a metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable
Trochee: a metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable
Spondee: a metrical foot consisting of two consecutive stressed syllables
Anapest: a metrical foot consisting of two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed syllable
Dactyl: a metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables
Prominence: the relative acoustic salience of a syllable or segment within an utterance
Pitch accent: a prosodic feature that marks a syllable with a distinctive pitch movement
Tone accent: a tonal feature that distinguishes lexical items in a language
Accent: a distinctive pronunciation pattern associated with a particular region or social group
Diacritics: symbols added to a letter to indicate a special phonetic quality or to distinguish homographs
Morphosyntax: the interaction between morphological and syntactic processes
Nominalization: the process of deriving a noun from a verb or adjective
Verbalization: the process of deriving a verb from a noun or adjective
Adverbialization: the process of deriving an adverb from an adjective or noun
Deverbal: a word derived from a verb
Denominal: a word derived from a noun
Deadjectival: a word derived from an adjective
Parasitic: a word or morpheme that is dependent on another for its grammatical function
Clitic: a morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically independent
Enclitic: a clitic that attaches to the end of a host word
Proclitic: a clitic that attaches to the beginning of a host word
Inclitic: a clitic that attaches to the middle of a host word
Proform: a word that stands in for another word or expression of the same category
Expletive: a syntactic element that occupies a position in the structure but carries no semantic content
Dummy subject: a proform such as "it" or "there" used to satisfy a syntactic subject requirement
Copula: a verb, such as "be," that links a subject to its predicate nominal
Light verb: a verb that carries little lexical meaning and depends on a complement for its full interpretation
Auxiliary: a verb that combines with a main verb to form a compound predicate, expressing tense, aspect, or modality
Modal verb: an auxiliary verb expressing modality, such as possibility, necessity, or permission
Aspectual marker: a morphological element that encodes the aspectual properties of an event
Tense marker: a morphological element that encodes the temporal location of an event
Morphological case: a case expressed by a bound morpheme or affix on the noun
Syntactic case: a case expressed by the positional arrangement of noun phrases in a clause
Obligatory: a grammatical requirement that must be satisfied for an utterance to be well-formed
Optional: a grammatical element that may or may not be present without rendering the utterance ungrammatical
Default: a morphological form used in the absence of specific agreement or inflectional marking
Unmarked: the more basic or neutral member of a grammatical contrast
Marked: the more specific or deviant member of a grammatical contrast
Gender: a grammatical classification of nouns into categories such as masculine, feminine, or neuter
Number: a grammatical category distinguishing singular, dual, and plural
Person: a grammatical category distinguishing first, second, and third person
Clusivity: a grammatical distinction between first-person inclusive and first-person exclusive
Animacy: a semantic or grammatical distinction between animate and inanimate entities
Definiteness: a grammatical property indicating whether a noun phrase refers to a specific, identifiable entity
Specificity: a semantic property indicating whether the referent of a noun phrase is known to the speaker
Quantification: the expression of quantity, such as count or mass, through grammatical means
Mass noun: a noun that refers to substances or concepts not naturally divided into discrete units
Count noun: a noun that refers to entities that can be counted as discrete units
Partitive: a grammatical construction expressing a part or portion of a whole
Genitive: a construction expressing possession, origin, or other attributive relationships
Possessive: a grammatical or syntactic construction expressing ownership or association
Possessor: the entity that owns or is associated with a possessed entity in a possessive construction
Possessee: the entity that is owned or associated with a possessor in a possessive construction
Demonstrative: a determiner that points to a specific entity, such as "this" or "that"
Indefinite pronoun: a pronoun that refers to a non-specific or unknown entity
Reciprocal: a pronoun or expression indicating a mutual action between two or more participants
Reflexive: a pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause
Intensive: a pronoun that emphasizes or adds emphasis to the subject, as in "I myself"
Interrogative pronoun: a pronoun used to ask a question, such as "who," "what," or "which"
Relative pronoun: a pronoun that introduces a relative clause and refers back to an antecedent noun
Pronominal: relating to or of the nature of a pronoun
Pronominalization: the process of replacing a noun phrase with a pronoun
Anaphoric: relating to or functioning as an anaphora
Cataphoric: relating to or functioning as a cataphora
Deictic: relating to or functioning as a deictic expression
Indexical: a word or expression whose reference depends on the context of utterance
Demonstrative deixis: the use of words like "this" and "that" to point to entities in space or discourse
Personal deixis: the use of person markers such as "I," "you," and "he" to identify participants
Spatial deixis: the use of words like "here," "there," and "over there" to indicate location
Temporal deixis: the use of words like "now," "then," "yesterday," and "tomorrow" to indicate time
Social deixis: the use of language to encode social relationships, such as honorifics or forms of address
Discourse marker: a word or phrase that organizes or signals a transition in discourse
Hedge: a linguistic device that softens or qualifies a statement to reduce commitment
Mitigator: a word or expression that reduces the force or directness of an utterance
Emphatic: a device that adds force or emphasis to a statement
Cleft: a syntactic construction that places special focus on a particular constituent

Topic-comment structure: a discourse structure in which a topic is presented and then commented upon
Given-new structure: a discourse strategy in which information is organized from old to new
Information structure: the organization of an utterance according to given and new information
Topic: the entity or subject about which an utterance is directed
Comment: the new information or assertion made about the topic
Focus: the element of an utterance that is being highlighted or contrasted
Contrastive focus: a focus that contrasts with a previously mentioned or implied alternative
Presupposition trigger: a word or expression that introduces a presupposition, such as "know" or "stop"
Conversational implicature: a meaning inferred from the context and the cooperative principles governing conversation
Gricean maxims: the four maxims of quality, quantity, relation, and manner proposed by H. P. Grice
Scoop: a conversational repair where a speaker corrects their own utterance
Self-repair: a conversational repair initiated by the speaker who made the error
Other-repair: a conversational repair initiated by a listener
Mitigated disagreement: a softened form of expressing disagreement in conversation
Backchannel: a minimal response, such as "mm-hm" or "uh-huh," that signals the listener is attending
Turn-initial: occurring at the beginning of a conversational turn
Turn-medial: occurring in the middle of a conversational turn
Turn-final: occurring at the end of a conversational turn
Completion point: a position in an utterance where a speaker is expected to yield the floor
Transition relevance place: a point in a turn where a change of speaker is possible
Overlap: the simultaneous production of speech by two or more participants in conversation
Pause: a silence during conversation that may or may not mark a turn transition
Truncation: the abrupt ending of a turn before its expected completion
Interruption: the unsolicited takeover of the floor by a second speaker
Floor: the right or opportunity to speak in a conversational setting

Floor-taking: the assumption of the speaking turn by a participant
Back-channeling: the use of minimal responses to signal continued listening without taking the floor
Garden path: a syntactic structure that leads the listener to an initially incorrect interpretation
Garden path effect: the cognitive phenomenon in which a reader or listener is led to a false parsing
Lexical ambiguity resolution: the process of selecting the correct meaning of a polysemous word in context
Syntactic parsing: the process of determining the syntactic structure of a sentence
Garden-path sentence: a sentence whose initial partial structure leads to a misparse that is later corrected
Center embedding: the embedding of a clause within another clause in a way that creates processing difficulty
Garden-path: a sentence that initially leads the parser to an incorrect structure
Syntactic ambiguity: ambiguity that arises from the potential for multiple syntactic structures
Satz: a complete grammatical sentence
Vocative: a form of direct address, often marked by a special case or intonation
Interjection: an exclamation expressing a spontaneous emotional reaction
Expletive: a profane or emphatic expression used for emphasis or emotional expression
Cursing: the use of taboo or obscene words, often for emphasis or emotional expression
Taboo: a social prohibition against the use of certain words or expressions
Politeness: the social practice of showing respect and consideration in language use
Face: the public self-image that a speaker wishes to maintain in interaction
Positive face: the desire to be approved of, liked, and accepted by others
Negative face: the desire to be unimpeded and not imposed upon by others
Face-threatening act: a communicative act that endangers the positive or negative face of a participant
Politeness strategy: a linguistic strategy used to mitigate the face-threatening potential of an utterance
Redress: the linguistic means used to repair a perceived face threat
Impoliteness: the deliberate or inadvertent violation of social norms of linguistic respect
Mating: a social interaction in which two or more speakers negotiate a communicative goal
Discourse analysis: the study of language as it is used in extended texts or conversations
Text linguistics: the study of the properties of coherent and cohesive texts
Cohesion: the set of linguistic devices that link elements within a text
Coherence: the logical and meaningful connectedness of a text
Reference: the use of pronouns, nouns, or other expressions to point to entities in a text
Substitution: the replacement of a word or phrase with another, such as a pronoun
Ellipsis: the omission of words that are recoverable from context
Conjunction: the use of connective words or phrases to link clauses or sentences
Lexical cohesion: the use of repetition, synonyms, and related vocabulary to create textual unity
Information structure: the organization of a text into given and new information
Theme: the topic or starting point of a clause or text
Rheme: the new or focal information in a clause or text
Satellite: a discourse element that provides background, context, or supplementary information

Micro-structure: the local organization of a text at the level of sentences and clauses
Superstructure: the overall organizational pattern of a text, such as chronological or problem-solution

Narrator: the voice or perspective that tells a story
Narratee: the intended or actual audience of a narrative
Focalization: the perspective from which a narrative is presented
Focalizer: the character or entity whose perspective determines the presentation of a narrative
Unreliable narrator: a narrator whose account is inconsistent with the facts or other characters' accounts
Genre conventions: the shared structural and stylistic expectations for a particular genre
Register analysis: the study of how language varies according to the communicative situation
