Phoneme: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language whose substitution can change the meaning of a word.
Allophone: A variant form of a phoneme that occurs in a specific phonetic environment without changing word meaning.
Phone: Any distinct speech sound considered as a concrete segment, regardless of its functional role in a language.
Phonology: The study of the systematic organization of sounds in a particular language or across languages.
Phonetics: The study of the physical production, transmission, and perception of speech sounds.
Segment: A discrete unit of speech that can be identified within a continuous sound stream, such as a vowel or consonant.
Suprasegment: A phonological feature that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Stress: The relative prominence given to a syllable in a word or utterance, typically marked by greater loudness, pitch, or duration.
Tone: The use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning in a language, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Intonation: The variation of pitch across a phrase or sentence that conveys attitudes, questions, or discourse functions.
Prosody: The study of rhythmic and pitch patterns in speech, including stress, tone, intonation, and rhythm.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, allowing air to flow freely without significant obstruction.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a partial or complete obstruction of airflow in the vocal tract.
Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel created by the proximity of two articulators.
Plosive: A consonant produced by completely blocking airflow and then releasing it in a burst, also called a stop.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the center of the tongue raised while air flows over the sides of the tongue.
Rhotic: A consonant or consonantal feature associated with the letter R, including trills, taps, and fricatives.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative at the same place of articulation.
Glide: A vowel-like consonant, also called a semivowel, such as /w/ or /j/, that serves as a syllable onset.
Place of articulation: The position in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The way airflow is obstructed or modified in producing a consonant, such as stop, fricative, or nasal.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during speech, distinguishing voiced sounds from voiceless ones.
Aspiration: A burst of air accompanying the release of a voiceless stop, as in the contrast between /p/ in "pat" and /pʰ/ in English.
Uvular: Pertaining to articulation at the uvula, the fleshy projection at the back of the soft palate.
Velar: Pertaining to articulation at the soft palate (velum), as in /k/ or /g/.
Palatal: Pertaining to articulation at the hard palate, as in the /j/ of English "yes."
Alveolar: Pertaining to articulation at the alveolar ridge, just behind the upper front teeth.
Dental: Pertaining to articulation involving the tongue against the upper teeth, as in English /θ/ and /ð/.
Bilabial: Pertaining to articulation involving both lips, as in /p/, /b/, and /m/.
Labiodental: Pertaining to articulation involving the lower lip against the upper teeth, as in /f/ and /v/.
Glottal: Pertaining to articulation at the glottis, the space between the vocal folds, as in the English /h/ or the glottal stop.
Epiglottal: Pertaining to articulation at the epiglottis, the flap of tissue at the entrance to the larynx.
Pharyngeal: Pertaining to articulation in the pharynx, the cavity between the nasal and oral cavities and the larynx.
Tense vowel: A vowel produced with relatively greater muscular tension and usually longer duration.
Lax vowel: A vowel produced with relatively less muscular tension and usually shorter duration.
Front vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body positioned toward the front of the mouth.
Back vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body positioned toward the back of the mouth.
Central vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body in a mid-position, neither front nor back.
High vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body raised toward the roof of the mouth.
Low vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body lowered in the mouth.
Mid vowel: A vowel produced with the tongue body at an intermediate height between high and low.
Rounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips rounded or protruded.
Unrounded vowel: A vowel produced with the lips spread or neutral, not rounded.
Diphthong: A vowel that glides from one position to another within a single syllable, such as /aɪ/ in "my."
Monophthong: A pure vowel sound with a relatively fixed tongue position throughout its duration.
Triphthong: A vowel sequence involving a transition through three distinct vowel positions within a single syllable.
Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which the vowels in a word must share a particular feature, such as frontness or backness.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound, as in "input" pronounced with a bilabial /m/ before /b/.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which sounds that were originally identical or similar become different to reduce redundancy.
Metathesis: A phonological process in which two sounds swap positions, as in the historical development from "ask" to "aks" in some dialects.
Deletion: A phonological process in which a sound is removed from a form, as in the loss of /t/ in "water" pronounced as "wader."
Epenthesis: A phonological process in which a sound is inserted into a word, often to break up difficult consonant clusters.
Elision: The omission of a sound or syllable in casual or rapid speech, such as "going to" becoming "gonna."
Coalescence: A phonological process in which two adjacent sounds merge into a single sound, as in "doing" pronounced with a /dʒ/ sound.
Distinctive feature: A binary or scalar phonological property, such as [+voice] or [-nasal], used to characterize and contrast sounds.
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation that organizes distinctive features into hierarchical tiers.
Neutralization: A phonological context in which a contrast between two or more phonemes is eliminated, as in English final devoicing of /b/ to [p].
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phonological element and have different meanings, such as "pat" and "bat."
Complementary distribution: The situation in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones of one phoneme.
Free variation: The ability to use two different sounds in the same environment without changing meaning, as in the /l/ and /r/ in some dialects.
Archiphoneme: An abstract phoneme representing a set of phonemes that are neutralized in a particular environment.
Phonotactics: The rules governing which sound sequences are permissible in a language.
Syllable: A unit of organization in speech consisting of a peak vowel surrounded by optional consonants.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the nucleus of a syllable.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any following coda, also called the rime.
Nucleus: The central, most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel or syllabic consonant.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the nucleus of a syllable.
Mora: A unit of syllable weight used in prosodic analysis, typically corresponding to a long vowel or a vowel plus coda consonant.
Moraic: Describing a segment that contributes a mora to the syllable, such as a long vowel or a sonorant in the coda.
Light syllable: A syllable with a short vowel and no coda consonant, containing one mora.
Heavy syllable: A syllable with a long vowel, diphthong, or coda consonant, containing two or more moras.
Prosodic hierarchy: The abstract hierarchy of prosodic constituents, including syllable, foot, prosodic word, phonological phrase, and intonational phrase.
Foot: A prosodic unit consisting of one stressed syllable (the head) and any associated unstressed syllables.
H-dominance: A principle in prosodic phonology stating that in a constituent, the most prominent element is the one closest to the right edge.
L-dominance: A principle in prosodic phonology stating that in a constituent, the most prominent element is the one closest to the left edge.
Boundary: A prosodic or syntactic edge that separates one constituent from another, marked phonologically by features like lengthening or pitch accents.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language that cannot be further divided without loss of meaning.
Morphology: The study of the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
Allomorph: A variant phonological form of a morpheme, such as /tʃ/ and /ʃ/ in English "church" and "teach" for the past-tense morpheme.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries its primary lexical meaning and to which affixes can be attached.
Affix: A morpheme that is attached to a root or stem to form a new word or modify meaning.
Prefix: An affix that is attached before the root of a word, as in "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: An affix that is attached after the root of a word, as in "-ed" in "walked."
Infix: An affix that is inserted within the root of a word, as in the Indonesian -in- in "ma-in-kan."
Circumfix: A derivational morpheme that consists of two or more parts surrounding the root, such as German ge-...-t in "gesagt."
Interfix: A connecting morpheme used in compounds to link elements, such as the "o" in "armchair" (historical) or "o" in "bikini" (modern coinages).
Derivational morphology: The part of morphology concerned with the formation of new words or word forms with potentially different grammatical categories.
Inflectional morphology: The part of morphology concerned with the modification of words to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, or case.
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more free morphemes (lexemes) are combined to create a new word, as in "blackboard."
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a longer word is shortened, often losing the beginning, end, or both, as in "phone" from "telephone."
Blending: A word-formation process in which parts of two words are combined to create a new word, as in "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Portmanteau: A word formed by blending the sound and meaning of two or more words, such as "smog" from "smoke" and "fog."
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, as in "editor" from "edit."
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes its grammatical category without any morphological change, as in "to butter" from "butter."
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that is expressed with no overt phonological material, as in the plural of "sheep" or the past tense of "cut."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to another morpheme.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word, such as "cat" or "run."
Agglutinative: A language type in which morphemes are strung together in a transparent, one-to-one manner, each expressing a single grammatical category, as in Turkish.
Fusional: A language type in which a single affix can express multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin or Russian.
Isolating: A language type in which words tend to be monomorphemic and grammatical relations are expressed by word order and particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A language type in which complex words can be formed by combining many morphemes, often encoding an entire clause's worth of information, as in Inuit languages.
Inflection: The modification of a word form to express grammatical categories without creating a new lexeme, such as adding -s for plural.
Derivation: The process of forming a new word or lexeme by adding affixes to a root, potentially changing the grammatical category.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word, such as all tenses of a verb or all cases of a noun.
Conjugation: The systematic pattern of verb inflection in a language.
Declension: The systematic pattern of noun, adjective, or pronoun inflection in a language.
Suppletion: A morphological process in which the forms of a paradigm are derived from unrelated etymological roots, as in "go" / "went."
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of related word forms, such as the lexeme WRITE encompassing "write," "writes," "wrote," "written."
Lemma: The dictionary headword or canonical form of a lexeme, typically the base or citation form.
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase, idiom, or construction becomes a fixed lexical item in the vocabulary of a language.
Agreement: A syntactic or morphological process in which a word changes its form to match another word in features such as number, gender, or person.
Concord: A synonym for agreement in morphology, particularly in older or British linguistic literature.
Subject: The noun phrase that typically controls verb agreement and is the primary argument of a clause.
Object: A noun phrase that serves as the target or recipient of an action expressed by the verb.
External argument: The argument, usually the subject, that is not thematically assigned by the verb itself but is merged outside the verb phrase.
Internal argument: An argument, such as the object, that is thematically assigned within the verb phrase.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to arguments by a verb, such as Agent, Patient, Theme, Goal, Source, or Experiencer.
Theta theory: A component of syntactic theory that governs the assignment of semantic roles (theta roles) to arguments.
Case: A grammatical category expressed by inflection or word order that indicates the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase.
Case marking: The morphological expression of case on nouns, pronouns, or adjectives through inflectional affixes or clitics.
Case government: The process by which a verb, preposition, or other element assigns a specific case to its argument.
Nominative case: The case typically marking the subject of a transitive clause and the sole argument of an intransitive clause in nominative-accusative languages.
Accusative case: The case typically marking the direct object in nominative-accusative languages.
Ergative case: The case marking the sole argument of an intransitive verb and the agent of a transitive verb in ergative-absolutive languages.
Absolutive case: The case marking the patient of a transitive verb and the sole argument of an intransitive verb in ergative-absolutive languages.
Ergative-absolutive: A case alignment system in which intransitive subjects are marked the same as transitive objects (absolutive) and differ from transitive subjects (ergative).
Nominative-accusative: A case alignment system in which intransitive subjects are marked the same as transitive subjects (nominative) and differ from transitive objects (accusative).
Tripartite alignment: A case alignment system in which intransitive subjects, transitive agents, and transitive patients each receive distinct case marking.
Split-S alignment: A case alignment system in which intransitive subjects are marked differently depending on the verb class, aligning with either agent or patient.
Valency: The number of arguments a verb requires or can take.
Devaluation: The reduction of a verb's valency, as in passive or antipassive constructions that remove one argument.
Causativization: A verbal process that adds an external cause argument to a verb, increasing its valency by one.
Passivization: A syntactic or morphological process that promotes the object to subject position and demotes or removes the agent.
Antipassive: A construction in ergative-absolutive languages that demotes the transitive object and promotes the agent to intransitive subject.
Reciprocal: A verbal construction expressing a mutual or bidirectional relationship between participants, as in "they met each other."
Reflexive: A verbal construction in which the subject and object are co-referential, as in "She sees herself."
Middle voice: A verbal voice in which the subject is both the agent and the affected entity, as in "The book reads easily."
Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal flow or internal temporal structure of an event, such as perfective vs. imperfective.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of utterance, such as past, present, or future.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the reality or likelihood of an event, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source of the speaker's information, such as direct observation, hearsay, or inference.
Evidential: A morpheme, particle, or construction that explicitly marks the source or basis of the speaker's knowledge.
Irrealis: A grammatical mood or category marking events that are not realized, such as hypothetical, future, or desired events.
Realis: A grammatical mood or category marking events that are actual, factual, or realized.
Subjunctive: A verbal mood expressing wishes, doubts, conditions, or non-factual situations.
Optative: A verbal mood expressing wishes or desires, as in the English "May he live long."
Imperative: A verbal mood used to issue commands or requests, as in "Go!"
Indicative: The default verbal mood expressing statements of fact or certainty.
Conditional: A verbal mood or construction expressing a hypothetical situation dependent on a condition.
Perfective aspect: An aspect marking an event as a completed whole, without reference to its internal structure.
Imperfective aspect: An aspect marking an event as ongoing, habitual, or internally structured, without focusing on completion.
Progressive aspect: An aspect marking an event as in progress at a particular point in time, as in "is running."
Habitual aspect: An aspect marking an event as a regular or repeated occurrence, as in "She always sings."
Stative: Describing a verb or predicate that denotes a state rather than an event or activity, such as "know" or "love."
Aorist: A verbal aspect or tense in some languages, particularly Greek, that presents an action as a simple, undifferentiated event.
Light verb: A verb with minimal semantic content that combines with a nominal element to express the full predicate, such as "give" in "give a kiss."
Heavy verb: A verb that carries substantial semantic content on its own without requiring a nominal complement.
Productive morpheme: A morpheme that can be freely applied to new or existing bases to form new words.
Unproductive morpheme: A morpheme that is no longer used to form new words but remains in existing vocabulary, such as the -en in "wooden."
Word formation: The set of processes by which new words are created in a language, including compounding, derivation, blending, and borrowing.
Neologism: A newly coined or newly attested word or expression entering the vocabulary of a language.
Morphological markedness: The principle that certain morphological forms are less common, more restricted, or more complex than their unmarked counterparts.
Unmarked form: The default, less restricted, or more frequent form in a morphological pair, such as the singular in English.
Marked form: The less frequent, more restricted, or more complex form in a morphological contrast, such as the plural.
Morphological alternation: A phonological or morphological change that occurs in the stem when a particular affix is added, as in "man/men."
Suppletion: A morphological process in which a paradigm contains forms that are not phonologically related, as in "go/went/gone" or "good/better/best."
Stem: The core part of a word to which inflectional and derivational affixes are attached, which may include the root plus derivational morphology.
Theme: A derivational affix or element that connects a root to inflectional morphology, common in Slavic and Baltic linguistics.
Morpheme boundary: An abstract or phonologically marked point indicating the division between morphemes within a word.
Morphological alignment: The system of case or agreement marking in a language with respect to transitivity.
Morphological case: The grammatical case expressed through inflectional morphology on nouns, adjectives, or pronouns.
Morphological number: The grammatical category expressed morphologically to indicate the quantity of entities, such as singular, dual, or plural.
Morphological gender: The grammatical classification of nouns into categories (masculine, feminine, neuter, etc.) that affects agreement.
Morphological person: The grammatical category expressed morphologically to distinguish first, second, and third person.
Morphological voice: The expression of voice (active, passive, middle, etc.) through morphological means on the verb.
Syntax: The study of the rules and principles by which words are combined to form phrases, clauses, and sentences.
Phrase structure grammar: A type of grammar that uses phrase structure rules to describe the hierarchical organization of sentences.
Generative grammar: A framework in linguistic theory that aims to describe the full set of grammatical sentences of a language using a finite set of rules.
Transformational grammar: A model of syntax in which deep structures are transformed into surface structures through a set of transformational rules.
Deep structure: The abstract underlying syntactic representation of a sentence before transformational rules are applied.
Surface structure: The final, observable syntactic representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied.
X-bar theory: A generalization in phrase structure stating that phrases consist of a specifier, a head, and a complement (XP → Specifier + X' → X + Complement).
Constituency: The property of a string of words forming a single syntactic unit that can be moved, replaced, or tested as a whole.
Immediate constituent: A direct component of a larger constituent in a hierarchical syntactic structure.
Binary branching: The principle in tree diagramming that each node dominates exactly two daughter nodes.
Unbounded dependency: A syntactic relationship between two elements that are separated by any number of intervening material, such as subject-verb agreement or relative clauses.
Movement: A syntactic operation in which an element is displaced from one position to another in the structure.
Trace: An empty element left in the original position of a moved constituent, marking the site from which the element was extracted.
Copy theory: An analysis of movement in which the moved element is copied in the higher position, leaving the original copy in place.
A-movement: Movement to a grammatical (theta-role-assigning or case-assigning) position, such as subject raising.
A-bar movement: Movement to a non-grammatical (non-theta-assigning) position, such as wh-movement or topicalization.
Raising: A syntactic process in which an element is moved to a higher subject position, as in "John seems to be happy."
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is typically introduced by a relative pronoun or relative marker.
Embedded clause: A clause that is syntactically contained within another clause, serving as a complement or modifier.
Main clause: The highest-level clause in a sentence, which can stand alone and is not embedded within another clause.
Subordinate clause: A clause that is syntactically dependent on a main clause and cannot stand alone.
Coordinate clause: Two or more clauses of equal syntactic status joined by a coordinating conjunction, such as "and" or "but."
Noun phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a noun or determiner, encompassing modifiers and complements.
Verb phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a verb, including its complements and adjuncts.
Complement: A constituent that completes the meaning of a head, such as the object of a transitive verb or the clause introduced by a complementizer.
Specifier: The constituent that occupies the highest position in a phrase, preceding the head, such as the determiner in a DP.
Complementizer: A word or morpheme that introduces a complement clause, such as "that," "if," or "whether."
Auxiliary: A verb that combines with a main verb to express tense, aspect, mood, or voice, such as "be," "have," or "will."
Modal: A type of auxiliary verb that expresses modality, such as ability, permission, or obligation, including "can," "must," and "should."
Copula: A linking verb that connects a subject to a predicate nominal, such as "be" in "She is a doctor."
Head: The central or most important element of a syntactic constituent, determining its category and core meaning.
Modifier: A constituent that provides additional descriptive or restrictive information about a head or another constituent.
c-command: A structural relation in which a node A c-commands a node B if the first branching node dominating A also dominates B, and A does not dominate B.
Binding: A component of syntactic theory governing the reference of pronouns, anaphors, and names within a sentence.
Principle A: A binding principle stating that an anaphor (such as "himself") must be bound within its local domain.
Principle B: A binding principle stating that a pronoun must be free (unbound) in its local domain.
Principle C: A binding principle stating that an R-expression (such as a proper name) must be free everywhere in the sentence.
Anaphor: A reflexive or reciprocal element, such as "himself" or "each other," that must find its antecedent in a local domain.
R-expression: A referential expression, such as a proper name or definite description, that is not subject to binding.
Coreference: The relationship between two expressions that refer to the same entity, as in "John said he was tired."
Antecedent: The expression that a pronoun, anaphor, or other referring expression refers back to.
Expletive: A syntactic element with no semantic content, used to satisfy grammatical requirements, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Dummy subject: An expletive noun phrase that occupies the subject position to satisfy syntactic requirements, as in "It is raining."
Dummy object: An expletive element in object position used to satisfy valency requirements, as in "consider it done."
Expletive subject: A subject that is purely syntactic and has no referential content, such as "there" in "There are three cats."
Pro-drop: The ability of a language to omit overt pronouns when the referent is recoverable from context or verbal morphology, as in Spanish or Italian.
Null subject: An unpronounced subject position that is grammatically licensed, common in pro-drop languages.
Null operator: An unpronounced operator, such as a wh-operator, assumed to exist in the syntax of certain constructions like object relative clauses.
Empty category: A syntactic position that is phonologically silent but structurally present, such as a trace or pro.
Government: A structural relation in which a head (such as a verb or preposition) syntactically controls a complement or specifier.
Case government: The assignment of a grammatical case to a noun phrase by a governing head, such as a verb assigning accusative case to its object.
Transitivity: A property of a verb or clause involving both an agent and a patient argument, such as "She killed the snake."
Intransitivity: A property of a verb or clause involving only one argument, the subject, such as "The snake died."
Ambitransitive: A verb that can be used both transitively and intransitively, such as "The glass broke" vs. "She broke the glass."
Anticausative: A construction in which a transitive verb is used intransitively, with the patient promoted to subject and the agent removed, as in "The window broke."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes two internal arguments, typically a theme and a goal, as in "She gave him the book."
Logophoric: An anaphoric pronoun or noun phrase that refers to the protagonist or main participant of a discourse.
Semantics: The study of meaning in language, including the meaning of words, sentences, and how they combine.
Lexical semantics: The study of word meaning, including semantic relations such as synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy, and polysemy.
Sentence semantics: The study of how the meaning of a sentence is composed from the meanings of its parts.
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined.
Synonymy: The relationship between words or expressions that have the same or very similar meaning, such as "big" and "large."
Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold" or "buy" and "sell."
Hyponymy: A semantic relationship in which the meaning of one term is included within the meaning of another, as "rose" is a hyponym of "flower."
Hypernymy: The inverse of hyponymy; a more general term that encompasses a more specific term, as "flower" is a hypernym of "rose."
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word or expression has multiple related meanings, such as "head" (body part, leader, top).
Homonymy: The relationship between words that have identical form but unrelated meanings, such as "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Sense: A distinct meaning of a polysemous or ambiguous word or expression.
Prototype: A central or typical example of a category used in prototype theory to explain how category membership is graded.
Prototype theory: A cognitive semantic theory holding that categories are organized around central, typical members rather than strict necessary and sufficient conditions.
Frame semantics: A semantic approach that analyzes word meaning in terms of the broader situational contexts or frames in which they are used.
Cognitive semantics: A school of linguistics that emphasizes the role of cognition, embodied experience, and conceptual structure in shaping linguistic meaning.
Metaphor: A linguistic device in which meaning is extended from a source domain to a target domain based on perceived similarity, as in "time is money."
Metonymy: A figurative device in which a related concept is used to refer to another, as in "The White House announced" for "the administration."
Gricean maxims: A set of four conversational principles (Quality, Quantity, Relation, Manner) proposed by Paul Grice to explain how meaning is inferred in conversation.
Implicature: An inferred meaning in conversation that is not explicitly stated but is derived from the application of conversational principles.
Conventional implicature: A speaker's meaning that is attached to the literal content of an utterance and is not cancelable, often triggered by specific words.
Scalar implicature: An inferred meaning based on a semantic scale, such as interpreting "some" as "not all" in many contexts.
Speech act: An utterance understood in terms of its communicative function, such as asserting, requesting, promising, or commanding.
Illocutionary act: The intended function of an utterance, such as a request, promise, or warning, performed by speaking.
Perlocutionary act: The effect or consequence of an utterance on the listener, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Propositional content: The truth-conditional content of a sentence, the state of affairs it describes or asserts.
Deixis: The linguistic expression of reference that depends on the context of the utterance, such as "here," "now," "I," and "you."
Anaphoric reference: The use of a pronoun or other expression to refer back to a previously mentioned entity.
Cataphoric reference: The use of a pronoun or other expression to refer forward to an entity that will be mentioned later.
Indexical: A linguistic expression whose referent is determined by the context of utterance, such as "I," "here," or "now."
Presupposition: A background assumption or piece of information that is taken for granted in an utterance and is not cancelled by negation.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one sentence guarantees the truth of another, as "She is a bachelor" entails "She is a man."
Inference: A reasoning process by which a listener derives additional meaning from an utterance that is not explicitly stated.
Satisfaction: A pragmatic or semantic relationship in which one expression fulfills the requirements of another, such as an answer satisfying a question.
Contradiction: A semantic relationship in which two sentences cannot both be true at the same time.
Pragmatics: The study of how context, speaker intent, and world knowledge contribute to the interpretation of utterances.
Speech situation: The full context in which an utterance is produced, including participants, setting, purpose, and shared knowledge.
Shared knowledge: Information that is assumed to be common to all participants in a conversation and need not be explicitly stated.
Relevance: In relevance theory, the cognitive effect an utterance is expected to produce relative to the effort required to process it.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic theory by Sperber and Wilson proposing that human cognition is geared toward maximizing the relevance of incoming stimuli.
Face: In politeness theory, a person's public self-image, including positive face (desire to be approved of) and negative face (desire for autonomy).
Face-threatening act: An utterance that threatens the positive or negative face of a participant, such as a request, criticism, or apology.
Politeness strategy: A linguistic device used to mitigate the face-threatening effects of an utterance, such as indirectness or hedging.
Indirect speech act: An utterance whose literal form differs from its intended illocutionary force, as in "Could you pass the salt?" meaning "Please pass the salt."
Deixis: The linguistic mechanism by which reference is anchored to the context of the utterance, including spatial, temporal, and personal deixis.
Spatial deixis: The use of deictic expressions to refer to locations relative to the speaker, such as "here," "there," "this," and "that."
Temporal deixis: The use of deictic expressions to refer to times relative to the moment of utterance, such as "now," "then," "today," and "tomorrow."
Personal deixis: The use of pronouns and other expressions to refer to participants in the speech event, such as "I," "you," "we," and "they."
Discourse: Language use extended beyond the sentence, involving coherent sequences of utterances in conversation or text.
Discourse analysis: The study of language in extended use, focusing on how meaning is constructed across sentences and in social context.
Text: A coherent sequence of sentences or utterances forming a meaningful whole, whether spoken or written.
Cohesion: The system of linguistic devices that create surface-level connections between sentences, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical repetition.
Coherence: The underlying logical and thematic connectedness of a text that allows it to be interpreted as a meaningful whole.
Information structure: The organization of an utterance into given (old) information and new (focus) information.
Topic: The entity about which a clause or discourse segment is predicated, typically the starting point of a proposition.
Comment: The information stated about the topic, expressing something new or relevant.
Focus: The element in an utterance that is presented as new, contrastive, or most relevant information.
Contrastive focus: A type of focus that presents an element as being different from alternatives, as in "I want the RED one" (not the blue one).
Information focus: A type of focus that introduces entirely new information into the discourse, as in "I bought a CAR."
Given-new principle: The heuristic that the topic or subject of a sentence tends to refer to given information, while the predicate introduces new information.
Thematic progression: The pattern by which the end of one sentence (rhematic) becomes the beginning (thematic) of the next in a text.
Rheme: The new or non-given information in a sentence, typically expressed in the predicate or at the end of the clause.
Given: Information that is already established or inferable in the discourse context.
New information: Information that is not yet established in the discourse and is being introduced for the first time.
Definiteness: A grammatical category distinguishing between known or unique referents (definite) and unknown or non-unique referents (indefinite).
Specificity: A semantic property of noun phrases indicating whether the speaker has a particular entity in mind, regardless of definiteness.
Referentiality: The property of a linguistic expression of being used to identify a particular entity in the world or discourse.
Discourse referent: An entity in the discourse model to which noun phrases are linked for tracking purposes.
Discourse representation theory: A semantic framework by Kamp that models the construction of a discourse model through the introduction and linking of referents.
File change semantics: A semantic framework by Heim that tracks the update of discourse files as new information is introduced in conversation.
Dynamic semantics: An approach to semantics that treats meaning as a function that updates the discourse context rather than a static truth condition.
Context: The situational and linguistic environment in which an utterance is interpreted, including prior discourse, shared knowledge, and physical setting.
Context set: The set of possible worlds or situations compatible with the discourse context up to a given point.
Contextualism: The view that the meaning of an utterance or expression depends significantly on the context of its use.
Anti-realist: A position in philosophy of language and semantics denying that meaning or reference is fixed independently of use or context.
Use theory: The philosophical view that the meaning of a word is determined by its use in a language rather than by reference or truth conditions.
Convention: A socially established regularity in language use that is not natural or logical but is maintained by mutual agreement.
Language community: A group of speakers who share a common language or dialect and participate in a shared system of communication.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and the social functions of language.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region, social group, or community of speakers.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social class, profession, or group.
Ethniclect: A variety of language associated with a particular ethnic group.
Register: A variety of language adapted to a particular communicative situation, such as formal, informal, technical, or legal.
Jargon: The specialized vocabulary of a particular profession, group, or activity.
Slang: Informal, often playful or transient vocabulary used within a particular social group or community.
Argot: A specialized vocabulary used by a particular group, sometimes to exclude outsiders, as in criminal or trade argot.
Prestige: The social value or status associated with a particular linguistic variety or feature.
Stigmatized: Describing a linguistic variety or feature that is negatively evaluated by the dominant speech community.
Accent: The phonological or prosodic features of a speaker's language that indicate regional or social origin.
Dialectal variation: Differences in language that are geographically or socially conditioned, encompassing phonology, grammar, and vocabulary.
Language variation: The existence of multiple forms or varieties within a speech community for the same communicative function.
Language change: The process by which a language's phonology, morphology, syntax, or vocabulary evolves over time.
Language contact: The influence that occurs when speakers of different languages interact, leading to borrowing, interference, or pidginization.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word or expression from one language into another, as in English "ballet" from French.
Code-switching: The alternating use of two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The mixing of elements from two or more languages within a single clause or sentence.
Pig Latin: A playful "secret" language game in which the initial consonant or consonant cluster of a word is moved to the end and "ay" is added.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops between groups with no common language, typically without native speakers.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that evolves from a pidgin and becomes the native language of a community.
Lingua franca: A language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be used as a means of communication.
Language revival: Efforts to re-establish a language that has fallen out of use or is in severe decline.
Endangerment: The state of a language whose number of speakers is declining or whose intergenerational transmission has been interrupted.
Vitality: The degree to which a language is actively used across domains and generations, indicating its likelihood of continued use.
Diglossia: A sociolinguistic situation in which two distinct varieties of a language or two different languages are used for different social functions.
High variety: The prestige, formal variety of a language used in education, government, and literature in a diglossic situation.
Low variety: The informal, vernacular variety of a language used in everyday conversation in a diglossic situation.
Linguistic imperialism: The process by which a dominant language or language group exerts cultural and political influence over other languages.
Linguistic rights: The rights of individuals and communities to use, maintain, and develop their own language(s).
Language policy: The set of governmental or institutional decisions and actions concerning the status, use, and planning of languages.
Language planning: Deliberate efforts to influence the structure, use, or attitude toward a language, including codification, standardization, and promotion.
Standardization: The process of establishing a norm for a language variety, often for use in education, media, and government.
Codification: The process of documenting and establishing the rules of a language through dictionaries, grammars, and style guides.
Normalization: The sociolinguistic process by which a variety becomes the accepted standard for a community.
Purism: The ideology or practice of resisting foreign influence on a language and promoting the use of native or archaic forms.
Revitalization: A broader effort to strengthen and re-energize a language community, going beyond mere speaker increase to include cultural identity.
Interlanguage: The developmental language system constructed by a second-language learner between the native language and the target language.
Transfer: The influence of a learner's first language on their acquisition or use of a second language, positive or negative.
Interference: The negative influence of one language on the production or perception of another, such as pronunciation errors due to L1 habits.
Foreign accent: The phonological features of a speaker's L1 that affect the pronunciation of L2 words, making them sound non-native.
Error: A deviation from the norms of the target language in second-language acquisition, which may reflect developmental stages or transfer.
Deviance: A non-normative linguistic production in first-language use that may reflect dialectal, social, or developmental variation.
Fossilization: The stabilization of a non-native linguistic feature at an intermediate level, preventing further progress toward native-like competence.
Input: The language data that a learner is exposed to in the process of language acquisition.
Comprehensible input: Language input that is slightly beyond the learner's current level but still understandable, as proposed by Krashen.
Output: The language a learner produces in speech or writing, which may serve to test hypotheses about the target language.
Negotiation of meaning: The interactive process by which conversation participants resolve misunderstandings and clarify meaning.
Recast: A reformulation of a learner's utterance that corrects an error while maintaining the learner's intended meaning.
Correction: An explicit indication by a teacher or interlocutor that a learner's production is inappropriate.
Complement: A linguistic element that completes the meaning of another element and is typically required by its governor.
Adjunct: A linguistic element that provides optional additional information, such as a time or place expression.
Modality: A linguistic category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, including epistemic (knowledge) and deontic (obligation) modality.
Epistemic modality: A type of modality expressing the speaker's degree of certainty or commitment to the truth of a proposition, such as "probably" or "must be."
Deontic modality: A type of modality expressing permission, obligation, or necessity, such as "must," "should," and "may."
Negation: A linguistic operation that reverses the truth value of a proposition, expressed by particles, affixes, or intonation.
Polarity: The property of an utterance or expression being affirmative or negative, and the rules governing the distribution of negative and non-standard forms.
Negative polarity item: An expression that is grammatical only in negative or downward-entailing contexts, such as "any" in English "I don't have any."
Downward entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of a statement in a set implies the truth of statements in subsets, such as under "not" or "no."
Upward entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of a statement in a subset implies the truth in the superset.
Entailment: A semantic relationship where the truth of the antecedent guarantees the truth of the consequent.
Presupposition projection: The rules governing how presuppositions from embedded sentences are maintained or cancelled in larger sentences.
Accommodating: The pragmatic process by which a listener adjusts their background knowledge to make an utterance comprehensible or felicitous.
Common ground: The shared knowledge, assumptions, and goals that participants in a conversation mutually recognize and use as a basis for communication.
Relevance: The balance between the cognitive effects an utterance produces and the processing effort required to achieve them.
Optimal relevance: The principle in relevance theory that utterances are interpreted as being optimally relevant, offering sufficient effects for the effort expended.
Explanandum: The phenomenon or problem that a theory or account is designed to explain.
Explanans: The explanation or set of premises offered to account for the explanandum.
Hypothesis: A proposed explanation or account that can be tested against data.
Paradigmatic relation: A relationship between linguistic elements that can occupy the same structural position and are in a relation of selection.
Syntagmatic relation: A relationship between linguistic elements that occur in combination in a linear sequence, such as the relation between a noun and its determiner.
Saussurean axis: The conceptual framework distinguishing between the horizontal (syntagmatic) and vertical (paradigmatic) dimensions of language.
Synchronic: The study of a language at a particular point in time, as opposed to its historical development.
Diachronic: The study of a language's historical development and change over time.
Comparative method: A historical linguistics technique for reconstructing proto-languages by comparing related daughter languages.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a group of related daughter languages is descended.
Sound law: A regular and systematic change in the phonological system of a language over time, such as Grimm's Law.
Regular correspondence: A consistent, predictable mapping between sounds in related languages that is evidence of common descent.
Cognate: A word in one language that is etymologically related to a word in another language through common descent.
Loanword: A word borrowed from another language and integrated into the borrowing language's vocabulary.
Calque: A translation-based borrowing in which the structure of a phrase is replicated using native words, as in "skyscraper" calqued in French as "gratte-ciel."
Morphological change: The process by which the morphological structure of a language shifts over time, such as the loss of case endings in English.
Syntactic change: The process by which the syntactic structure of a language changes over time, such as the rise of the periphrastic passive in English.
Semantic change: The process by which the meaning of a word shifts over time, including broadening, narrowing, pejoration, and amelioration.
Semantic broadening: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning expands to cover a wider range of referents, as with "bird" from "young bird" to "any bird."
Semantic narrowing: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more restricted, as with "meat" from "food" to "flesh of animals."
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more negative or derogatory over time, as with "silly" from "happy" to "foolish."
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more positive or elevated over time, as with "nice" from "ignorant" to "agreeable."
Taboo: A social prohibition against the use of certain words, often related to death, disease, or sexuality, leading to euphemism.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression substituted for a blunt, offensive, or taboo term, as in "passed away" for "died."
Metathesis: A sound change in which two adjacent segments reverse their order, as in the historical shift from /sk/ to /ks/ in English "ask."
Lenition: A type of sound change in which a consonant becomes weaker or less obstruent over time, such as /p/ becoming /f/ or /w/.
Strengthening: A sound change in which a consonant becomes stronger or more obstruent over time, the reverse of lenition.
Anaptyxis: A sound change in which a vowel is inserted between consonants, as in the development of "island" from Old English "iland."
Syncope: A sound change in which a vowel is deleted from the interior of a word, as in the historical loss of a vowel in "advice" from "advis."
Apheresis: The loss of the initial sound or syllable of a word over time, as in "answer" from "sweanswer."
Apostrophe: The loss of the final sound or syllable of a word, as in "chocolate" from "chocolatte."
Elision: The deletion of a sound or syllable in a particular phonological context, especially in connected speech.
Assimilation: A phonological or historical sound change in which a sound becomes more like an adjacent sound.
Dissimilation: A phonological or historical sound change in which two similar sounds become more different.
Metathesis: A sound change involving the transposition of two adjacent segments.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a segment between two others, either synchronically or historically.
Coalescence: The merger of two adjacent sounds into a single sound.
Deletion: The loss of a sound from a word or utterance.
Palatalization: A sound change in which a consonant becomes palatal, often due to the influence of a following front vowel.
Uvularization: A sound change in which a consonant's place of articulation shifts to the uvula.
Retroflexion: A sound change or articulatory feature in which the tip of the tongue curls back toward the hard palate.
Lateralization: A phonological process in which a segment acquires a lateral feature.
Nasalization: A phonological process or sound change in which a segment acquires a nasal feature.
Voicing: A phonological feature or sound change involving the vibration of the vocal folds.
Devoicing: A phonological process or sound change in which a voiced segment becomes voiceless.
Aspiration: A phonological feature involving a burst of air following the release of a stop consonant.
Depharyngealization: A sound change in which a pharyngealized segment loses its pharyngealization.
Delabialization: A sound change in which a labialized segment loses its labialization.
Dentalization: A sound change in which a consonant's place of articulation shifts to the dental region.
Alveolarization: A sound change in which a consonant's place of articulation shifts to the alveolar ridge.
Velarization: A sound change in which a consonant acquires a secondary velar articulation.
Fronting: A vowel change in which the tongue position shifts forward.
Backing: A vowel change in which the tongue position shifts backward.
Raising: A vowel change in which the tongue position shifts upward.
Lowering: A vowel change in which the tongue position shifts downward.
Rounding: A vowel change in which the lips become rounded.
Unrounding: A vowel change in which the lips become unrounded.
Monophthongization: A vowel change in which a diphthong becomes a simple vowel.
Diphthongization: A vowel change in which a simple vowel becomes a diphthong.
Truncation: The historical loss of word-final syllables or sounds.
Extension: The historical addition of syllables or sounds to a word.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated, used to express plurality, intensity, or other meanings.
Partial reduplication: A type of reduplication in which only a portion of the base is copied, as in Tagalog "kanta-kanta" for "sing-sing."
Full reduplication: A type of reduplication in which the entire base is copied.
Iterative: A grammatical meaning expressed by reduplication indicating repeated or continuous action.
Distributive: A grammatical meaning expressed by reduplication indicating action applied to multiple entities individually.
Intensive: A grammatical meaning expressed by reduplication indicating an increase in degree or intensity.
Plural: A grammatical number indicating more than one entity.
Dual: A grammatical number indicating exactly two entities.
Trials: A grammatical number indicating exactly three entities.
Augmentative: A derivational process or affix that increases the perceived size or importance of a referent.
Diminutive: A derivational process or affix that decreases the perceived size, importance, or intensity of a referent.
Pejorative: A derivational process or affix that adds a derogatory or contemptuous connotation.
Augmentative: A derivational process or affix that adds a sense of increased size, quantity, or intensity.
Derivational: Pertaining to the formation of new lexemes through the addition of affixes or other morphological processes.
Inflectional: Pertaining to the modification of word forms to express grammatical relationships without creating new lexemes.
Morphophonology: The interface between morphology and phonology, dealing with how morphemes interact with phonological rules.
Morpho-phonemic: Relating to the interaction between morphological and phonemic systems.
Productivity: The degree to which a morphological process or pattern is used to form new words in a language.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its components, such as "kick the bucket."
Idiomatic: Pertaining to or characterized by the use of fixed expressions with non-compositional meanings.
Collocation: A habitual or predictable combination of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Collocational: Pertaining to the tendency of certain words to co-occur in predictable patterns.
Phraseological: Pertaining to the study of fixed or semi-fixed multi-word expressions.
Idiomatization: The process by which a compositional phrase acquires a non-compositional, fixed meaning.
Lexical entry: The representation of a word or expression in the mental lexicon, including its phonological, semantic, and syntactic properties.
Mental lexicon: The cognitive store of vocabulary and its associated representations in a speaker's mind.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected or derived forms of a word.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and fixed expressions in a language or in a speaker's mind.
Vocabulary: The set of words known and used by an individual or community.
Word: A free linguistic unit that can stand alone and be separated by spaces in writing.
Morph: The smallest unit of a word that has a recognizable form, whether or not it corresponds to a morpheme.
Morphology: The study of the structure and formation of words.
Morphological analysis: The process of decomposing a word into its constituent morphemes.
Morphological parsing: The computational or linguistic process of identifying the morpheme boundaries and identities within a word.
Stemming: The process of reducing an inflected or derived word to its base or root form.
Lemmatization: The process of reducing an inflected or derived word to its dictionary headword (lemma) form.
Morphological ambiguity: The situation in which a word form can be parsed into different morpheme sequences, as in "tear-tear" (rip vs. cry).
Morphological opacity: The degree to which the morphological structure of a form is not transparently recoverable from its surface form.
Productivity: The extent to which a word-formation process can be applied to generate new, acceptable words.
Dead morpheme: A morpheme that is no longer productive and appears only in a limited set of inherited words.
Live morpheme: A morpheme that is still actively used to form new words.
Native: Describing a word or morpheme that belongs to the core, inherited vocabulary of a language.
Foreign: Describing a word or morpheme borrowed from another language.
Loan translation: The calquing of a foreign phrase or expression using native words.
Phonological borrowing: The adoption of a word from another language with minimal or no semantic change.
Semantic borrowing: The adoption of a new meaning for an existing native word under the influence of a foreign cognate.
Grammatical borrowing: The adoption of grammatical structures, patterns, or constructions from another language.
Morphological borrowing: The adoption of a specific affix or morphological pattern from another language.
Syntactic borrowing: The adoption of a particular syntactic construction or word order from another language.
Pragmatic borrowing: The adoption of speech act patterns or discourse strategies from another language.
Interlanguage: The developmental language system of a second-language learner.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that arises for communication between groups without a shared language.
Creole: A natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the primary language of a community.
Patois: A colloquial variety of a language, often associated with rural or informal speech, or a creole.
Contact language: A language that arises from prolonged contact between speakers of different languages.
Esperanto: A constructed international auxiliary language designed to facilitate communication between people of different native languages.
Conlang: A constructed language created for artistic, literary, or experimental purposes, as opposed to a natural language.
Vulgar Latin: The colloquial spoken form of Latin from which the modern Romance languages developed.
Anglo-Saxon: Another name for Old English, the earliest attested form of the English language.
Middle English: The stage of the English language from roughly 1100 to 1500, following the Norman Conquest.
Early Modern English: The stage of English from roughly 1500 to 1700, including the period of Shakespeare.
Late Modern English: The stage of English from roughly 1700 to the present, marked by the Industrial Revolution and global expansion.
Old English: The earliest stage of the English language, from roughly 450 to 1150, characterized by complex inflectional morphology.
Norman French: The variety of Old French spoken in northern France, which had a major influence on English vocabulary after the 1066 Conquest.
Middle French: The stage of French from roughly 1100 to 1500, transitioning from Old to Modern French.
Old French: The earliest attested stage of French, from roughly 842 to 1100.
Middle English: The stage of English from approximately 1100 to 1500, marked by the transition from Old to Modern English.
Great Vowel Shift: A series of systematic vowel changes in English between the 15th and 18th centuries that dramatically altered the pronunciation of long vowels.
Grimm's Law: A regular sound change describing the shift of Proto-Indo-European stops to Germanic sounds, such as /p/ to /f/.
Verner's Law: A phonological rule describing the voicing of certain fricatives in Germanic, complementary to Grimm's Law.
High German consonant shift: A major series of consonant changes distinguishing High German from Low German and other West Germanic languages.
First Consonant Shift: The Germanic consonant shift (Grimm's Law) that distinguishes Germanic from other Indo-European languages.
Second Consonant Shift: The High German consonant shift that distinguishes High German from other West Germanic languages.
Sound change: A regular, systematic shift in the phonological system of a language over time.
Chain shift: A series of interconnected sound changes in which the shift of one segment triggers shifts in others, as in the Great Vowel Shift.
Drift: The cumulative, directional change in a language's phonological system over a long period.
Analogy: A linguistic process in which a regular pattern in one set of forms is extended to an irregular form, as in "mouses" for "mice."
Leveling: A process in which variations within a paradigm are reduced, making the paradigm more regular.
Reconstruction: The method of inferring the properties of a proto-language from its attested daughter languages.
Glottal stop: A consonant produced by a complete closure of the glottis, as in the Hawaiian 'okina or the English "uh-oh."
Glottal fricative: A consonant produced with a turbulent airflow through a constricted glottis, as in English /h/ in "hi."
Uvular fricative: A consonant produced with friction at the uvula, as in the French /ʁ/ in "rouge."
Pharyngeal fricative: A consonant produced with friction in the pharynx, as in the Arabic /ħ/ and /ʕ/.
Epiglottal stop: A consonant produced by closing the epiglottis against the pharyngeal wall.
Click: A consonant produced by creating a suction or pressure burst in the mouth, found in several African language families.
Ejective: A consonant produced by a glottalic egressive airstream, involving a sharp closure and release of the glottis, common in Caucasian languages.
Implosive: A consonant produced by lowering the larynx during closure, creating an ingressive airstream, common in Dravidian and some African languages.
Flap: A consonant produced by a single rapid contact of the tongue with the alveolar ridge, as in the /ɾ/ in many varieties of Spanish.
Trill: A consonant produced by multiple rapid vibrations of a consonantal articulator, such as the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge.
Tapped: A consonant produced by a single quick tap of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, as in the American English /ɾ/ in "butter."
Lateral flap: A flap consonant with a lateral airstream, found in some languages of South America.
Velar nasal: A nasal consonant produced at the velum, as in the /ŋ/ in "sing" or the Portuguese "nh."
Palatal nasal: A nasal consonant produced at the palate, as in the /ɲ/ in Spanish "año."
Labial-velar: A consonant with simultaneous bilabial and velar articulation, as in the /kw/ in "queen."
Rhotic: A consonant or consonantal feature associated with the R sound, including trills, taps, fricatives, and approximants.
R-coloring: The influence of a preceding or following rhotic consonant on the quality of a vowel, as in the American English /ɚ/ in "bird."
Centing: A process in which the vowels of a language shift toward the center of the vowel space, as in some dialects of English.
Tensing: A process in which vowels become tenser, often involving lengthening and raising.
Laxing: A process in which vowels become la
