response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language that can change meaning, such as /p/ vs /b/ in "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A variant form of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word, such as the aspirated [pʰ] in "pin" vs the unaspirated [p] in "spin."
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language that cannot be further divided without loss or change of meaning.
Grapheme: The smallest visual unit in a writing system, typically corresponding to a single letter or character.
Phonotactics: The rules governing the permissible combinations of sounds within a syllable or word in a given language.
Aspiration: The burst of air accompanying the release of a voiceless stop consonant, as in the [pʰ] in English "pin."
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal cords during the production of a speech sound; vowels and some consonants are voiced, others are voiceless.
Place of articulation: The position in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced, such as bilabial, alveolar, velar, or glottal.
Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is obstructed or modified in the vocal tract, such as stop, fricative, nasal, or approximant.
Suprasegmental: A phonetic property that extends over more than one segment, including stress, tone, intonation, and length.
Tone: A use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in tonal languages like Mandarin Chinese.
Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a syllable within a word or phrase, affecting its pitch, loudness, or duration.
Intonation: The pattern of pitch variation over a phrase or sentence that conveys grammatical or attitudinal meaning.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a phonological system, typically consisting of an optional onset, a vowel nucleus, and an optional coda.
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, preceding the vowel nucleus.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus (vowel) and coda, as in the /aɪn/ in "rain."
Nucleus: The central vowel or vowel-like element of a syllable, which is typically the most sonorous part.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster at the end of a syllable, following the nucleus.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phoneme at the same position, demonstrating that the sounds are distinct phonemes.
Complementary distribution: A situation in which two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment, suggesting they are allophones of one phoneme.
Phonological rule: A statement describing a systematic sound change or correspondence within a language's phonological system.
Feature geometry: A theoretical model representing distinctive features in a hierarchical structure, organized into feature classes.
Natural class: A set of phonemes or morphemes that share one or more distinctive features and behave similarly in a rule.
Distinctive feature: A binary property of a speech sound (e.g., [+voice], [−nasal]) used to characterize and contrast phonemes.
Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which vowels in a word or phrase are adjusted to share a particular vowel feature, such as backness or rounding.
Palatalization: The modification of a consonant by raising or fronting the tongue body toward the hard palate, e.g., [k] → [c].
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more similar to a neighboring sound in some respect.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less similar to a neighboring sound, often to reduce redundancy.
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound, typically a vowel or consonant, into a word, as in "hamster" from "hamster."
Elision: The deletion of a sound or sounds from a word or phrase in normal speech, as in "gotten" from "got."
Metathesis: The transposition of sounds within a word, as in the historical shift from "ask" to "aks" in some English dialects.
Lenition: The weakening of a consonant over time or in a particular phonetic environment, such as /p/ → [β] in Irish.
Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant over time or in a particular environment, such as /ɣ/ → [g].
Uvularization: The articulation of a consonant with the back of the tongue raised toward the uvula.
Velarization: The articulation of a consonant with the body of the tongue raised toward the soft palate.
Labialization: The rounding of the lips during the production of a consonant, e.g., [w] or [kʷ].
Glottalization: The constriction or closure of the vocal cords during the production of a sound, e.g., [ʔ].
Creaky voice: A laryngeal voice quality produced by the adduction of the vocal folds, characterized by a creaky or rough quality.
Nasalization: The production of a sound with lowered velum, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity simultaneously with the oral cavity.
Advanced Tongue Root (ATR): A phonological feature describing the retraction or advancement of the tongue root, affecting vowel height and backness.
Backness: A vowel feature describing the degree of retraction of the tongue body toward the velum.
Height: A vowel feature describing the vertical position of the tongue, ranging from close/high to open/low.
Frontness: A vowel feature describing the degree of advancement of the tongue body toward the hard palate.
Roundness: A vowel feature describing the degree of lip rounding during vowel articulation.
Tense vowel: A vowel produced with greater muscular tension and typically a higher tongue position, as in English /iː/ vs /ɪ/.
Lax vowel: A vowel produced with less muscular tension and a lower or more central tongue position, as in English /ɪ/ vs /iː/.
Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel sound [ə], the most common vowel in many languages, including English.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins at one vowel quality and glides to another within a single syllable, e.g., /aɪ/ in "my."
Triphthong: A complex vowel sequence of three elements within a single syllable, e.g., /aɪə/ in some pronunciations of "fire."
Monophthong: A single, pure vowel sound without a glide, e.g., /ɑː/ in "father."
Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel to create turbulent noise, e.g., /f/, /s/, /ʃ/.
Plosive: A consonant produced by complete closure of the vocal tract followed by a sudden release of air, e.g., /p/, /t/, /k/.
Approximant: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract without creating turbulent noise, e.g., /w/, /l/, /j/.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue tip contacting the alveolar ridge while air flows around the sides of the tongue, e.g., /l/.
Trill: A consonant produced by rapid vibration of a articulator, typically the tongue tip (e.g., [r] in Spanish) or the uvula.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single rapid contact of the tongue tip with the alveolar ridge, as in the "tt" of American "butter."
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, directing airflow through the nasal cavity, e.g., /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative at the same place of articulation, e.g., /tʃ/ in "church."
Ejective: A consonant produced with a glottalic airstream mechanism, involving a closed glottis and a sharp release, common in African and Caucasian languages.
Implosive: A voiced plosive produced with a lowering of the larynx during closure, creating an inward airflow, e.g., [ɓ], [ɗ].
Click: A consonant produced by creating a suction in the mouth and releasing it, producing a sharp popping sound; common in Khoisan languages.
Inflection: A morphological process that modifies a word to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person without changing its basic lexical meaning.
Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word or changes the lexical meaning or part of speech of a word, e.g., "happy" → "unhappiness."
Agglutination: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each expressing a single grammatical meaning, as in Turkish or Japanese.
Fusion: A morphological type in which a single morpheme expresses multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in many Indo-European languages.
Isolation: A morphological type in which each word corresponds to a single morpheme and grammatical relations are expressed by word order and particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthesis: A morphological type in which words can be extremely long, combining what would be multiple words in other languages into a single complex word, as in many Native American languages.
Root: The base morpheme of a word that carries the core lexical meaning and cannot be further decomposed into smaller meaningful units.
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, consisting of the root plus any derivational morphemes.
Affix: A bound morpheme that is attached to a stem to form a word or to modify its meaning, including prefixes, suffixes, and infixes.
Prefix: An affix attached to the beginning of a stem, e.g., "un-" in "unhappy."
Suffix: An affix attached to the end of a stem, e.g., "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: An affix inserted within a stem rather than at its beginning or end, as in the Malay "um-" in "ta-um-akap" (to repeat).
Circumfix: A bound morpheme that surrounds a stem, consisting of a prefix and a suffix that must appear together, as in the German "ge-...-t" in "gesungen."
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically behaves as an independent word, e.g., the English "-n't" in "don't."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a free word and must be attached to another morpheme, e.g., "-ness," "un-," "-ed."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a complete word, e.g., "book," "run," "the."
Allomorph: One of two or more phonological variants of a single morpheme, e.g., the plural morpheme /s/ in "cats," /z/ in "dogs," and /ɪz/ in "boxes."
Zero morpheme: A morpheme with no phonetic content, inferred from the presence of a grammatical form, e.g., the regular past tense in English where the base form is used.
Portmanteau: A single morpheme that simultaneously expresses two or more grammatical categories, e.g., French "mes" combining first person and plural possessive.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to express a grammatical meaning such as plurality, intensity, or aspect.
Suppletion: A morphological process in which the forms of a paradigm are derived from unrelated roots, e.g., English "go" → "went."
Productivity: The degree to which a particular morphological rule or pattern can be applied to new or unfamiliar forms in a language.
Morphological alternation: A systematic change in the form of a stem or affix depending on the morphological or phonological context.
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to create a new word, e.g., "blackboard."
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes its part of speech without any change in form, e.g., the noun "butter" becoming the verb "to butter."
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an affix from an existing word, e.g., "editor" → "edit."
Morphological blend: A word formed by combining parts of two words, e.g., "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Derivational affix: An affix that creates a new lexical item or changes the part of speech of a word, e.g., "-ness," "un-," "ify."
Inflectional affix: An affix that marks grammatical relations such as tense, number, case, or person without changing the core lexical meaning, e.g., "-s," "-ed," "-ing."
Suprasegmental morpheme: A morpheme whose meaning is carried by a prosodic feature such as tone or stress rather than by segmental material.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of utterance, typically past, present, or future.
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the temporal structure or internal constitution of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, or progressive.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, imperative, or optative.
Voice: A grammatical category that describes the relationship between the verb and its arguments, typically active or passive.
Number: A grammatical category that categorizes nouns as singular, dual, or plural.
Case: A grammatical category that indicates the syntactic role or semantic relation of a noun phrase, such as nominative, accusative, dative, or genitive.
Gender: A grammatical classification of nouns, typically into categories such as masculine, feminine, and neuter, in many languages.
Person: A grammatical category that distinguishes the speaker (first), the addressee (second), and others (third).
Agreement: A syntactic or morphological process in which one element takes a form determined by the features of another, e.g., verb agreeing with its subject in person and number.
Phrase structure: The hierarchical organization of words into phrases and clauses according to the rules of a language's grammar.
Constituency: The property of a string of words forming a single syntactic unit that can be substituted, moved, or tested as a block.
Head: The central or primary word in a phrase that determines the category and core meaning of the phrase, e.g., the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: A constituent that is required by a head to complete its subcategorization frame, e.g., the direct object required by a transitive verb.
Specifier: The constituent that precedes the head in a phrase, often a determiner, quantifier, or subject, occupying the edge of the phrase.
Adjunct: An optional constituent that modifies a phrase or clause, adding descriptive information, such as an adverbial or prepositional phrase.
X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure in generative grammar that posits a uniform binary branching structure for all phrase types: XP, X', and X.
Immediate constituent: A direct component of a phrase that cannot be further subdivided within the context of the analysis.
Deep structure: The underlying abstract representation of a sentence in transformational grammar, before surface-level transformations are applied.
Surface structure: The final observable form of a sentence in transformational grammar, after all transformations have been applied.
Transformation: A rule in transformational grammar that maps a deep structure to a surface structure, such as passive voice or question formation.
Generative grammar: A theoretical framework for describing the syntax of natural languages, associated with Noam Chomsky, that uses rules to generate all and only grammatical sentences.
Government and binding: A sub-theory of generative grammar developed in the 1980s, organizing syntax into modules such as theta theory, binding theory, case theory, and the extended projection principle.
C-command: A structural relation in which a node dominates a sister node that contains another node, central to binding theory and scope interpretations.
Binding theory: A sub-theory of syntax that governs the distribution of pronouns, reflexives, and names in relation to their antecedents (Principles A, B, and C).
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Theme, Goal, or Experiencer.
Argument structure: The set of semantic roles that a predicate requires or allows its participants to fulfill.
Subcategorization: A property of a lexical item specifying the types and number of complements it requires, e.g., "believe" requires a subject and a clausal complement.
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object, e.g., "eat" in "She eats an apple."
Intransitive: A verb that does not take a direct object, e.g., "sleep" in "She sleeps."
Ditransitive: A verb that takes both a direct and an indirect object, e.g., "give" in "She gave him a book."
Valency: The number of arguments (including the subject) that a predicate requires to form a complete proposition.
Nominalization: A syntactic process in which a verb or adjective is converted into a noun, e.g., "decide" → "decision."
Relativization: The formation of a relative clause in which a modifier clause is attached to a noun, e.g., "the book [that I read]."
Cleft: A sentence structure that divides a clause into two parts for emphasis, e.g., "It was John who broke the window."
Topicalization: A syntactic process in which a constituent is moved to the front of the sentence to mark it as the topic, often accompanied by a resumptive pronoun or a marker.
Focus: The element of a sentence that is highlighted as new or contrastive information, often marked by stress or syntactic movement.
Scope: The range over which a quantifier or operator is interpreted in a sentence, determining the logical relationship between quantifiers.
Recursion: The ability of a grammatical rule to apply within its own output, allowing for potentially infinite sentence complexity, e.g., embedding clauses within clauses.
Embedded clause: A clause that functions as a constituent within a larger clause, e.g., the object clause in "I think [that she left]."
Matrix clause: The main or framing clause in a complex sentence that contains one or more embedded clauses.
Coordination: A syntactic process that joins two or more constituents of the same category with a coordinator, e.g., "and," "or," "but."
Subordination: A syntactic process in which one clause is dependent on another, typically introduced by a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun.
Relative clause: A clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or marker, e.g., "the woman [who lives next door]."
Noun phrase: A phrase whose head is a noun or pronoun, typically including determiners, adjectives, and other modifiers.
Verb phrase: A phrase whose head is a verb, typically including its arguments and adjuncts.
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition and its complement, e.g., "in the house."
Determiner: A word that specifies the reference of a noun, including articles, demonstratives, and quantifiers.
Quantifier: A word or expression that specifies quantity or scope, e.g., "every," "some," "many," "no."
Article: A determiner that specifies definiteness or indefiniteness, e.g., "the," "a," "an."
Demonstrative: A determiner or pronoun that points to a specific referent in the discourse or physical context, e.g., "this," "that."
Interrogative: A word or expression used to form questions, e.g., "what," "who," "where," "how."
Relative pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause and refers back to an antecedent noun, e.g., "who," "which," "that."
Personal pronoun: A pronoun that refers to participants in the discourse, categorized by person, number, and sometimes gender, e.g., "I," "you," "he," "they."
Reflexive pronoun: A pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, e.g., "myself," "himself," "themselves."
Reciprocal: A pronoun or expression that indicates a mutual relationship between two or more participants, e.g., "each other," "one another."
Possessive: A morphological or syntactic form indicating ownership or a relationship of possession, e.g., "John's book," "my."
Comparative: A form of an adjective or adverb expressing a higher degree of a property relative to a standard, e.g., "taller," "more quickly."
Superlative: A form of an adjective or adverb expressing the highest degree of a property within a set, e.g., "tallest," "most quickly."
Progressive aspect: An aspectual value indicating that an event is ongoing or in progress at a reference time, e.g., "is eating."
Perfective aspect: An aspectual value that presents an event as a complete whole, without internal temporal structure.
Imperfective aspect: An aspectual value that presents an event as ongoing, habitual, or unbounded in time.
Aorist: A verbal category that expresses simple past or unmarked past action without specifying aspect, as in many ancient and classical languages.
Pluperfect: A tense that describes an event completed before another past event or time reference, e.g., "I had left before she arrived."
Conditional: A mood or tense expressing a hypothetical or dependent situation, often in if-clauses, e.g., "If I had time, I would go."
Optative: A mood expressing a wish, hope, or command, found in languages such as Ancient Greek and Turkish.
Subjunctive: A mood used to express hypothetical, doubtful, or desired situations, as opposed to factual statements in the indicative.
Irrealis: A grammatical category marking events that are not presented as actual or factual, encompassing hypothetical, future, or non-asserted situations.
Realis: A grammatical category marking events as actual, factual, or asserted.
Lexical semantics: The study of the meaning of individual words and the relationships between their meanings.
Compositional semantics: The study of how the meanings of complex expressions are built up from the meanings of their parts and the rules of combination.
Sense: A particular meaning or interpretation of a lexical item, as distinguished from other possible meanings (senses) of the same word.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or situation in the world to which it points or refers.
Truth conditions: The set of circumstances under which a sentence would be true, used in formal semantics to define meaning.
Entailment: A semantic relation in which the truth of one sentence logically guarantees the truth of another, e.g., "She is a bachelor" entails "She is male" (though semantically odd).
Presupposition: Background information assumed to be true for a sentence to be felicitous, not directly asserted but taken for granted.
Implicature: A meaning that is conveyed by a speaker but is not part of the literal or conventional meaning of the utterance, often derived through pragmatic reasoning.
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which one entity is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it, e.g., "The White House issued a statement."
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one domain is described in terms of another based on perceived similarity, e.g., "Time is money."
Polysemy: The phenomenon of a single word having multiple related senses, e.g., "head" as body part, leader, or tip.
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two or more unrelated words share the same form, e.g., "bank" (financial) and "bank" (river).
Synonymy: The relationship between words that have the same or nearly the same meaning, e.g., "big" and "large."
Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite or contrasting meanings, e.g., "hot" and "cold."
Hyponymy: A semantic relation in which the meaning of one word (hyponym) is included within the meaning of another (hypernym), e.g., "robin" is a hyponym of "bird."
Meronimy: A semantic relation in which one entity is a part of another, e.g., "wheel" is a meronym of "car."
Hypernym: A word with a general meaning that encompasses the meanings of more specific words (hyponyms), e.g., "vehicle" for "car."
Lexical field: A set of words that are related by a common semantic domain or topic, e.g., words related to "agriculture."
Semantic role: The function a noun phrase plays in the meaning of a verb, such as Agent, Patient, Theme, Goal, Source, or Experiencer.
Agent: The semantic role of a voluntary initiator or doer of an action, typically the subject of an active transitive verb.
Patient: The semantic role of the entity that undergoes or is affected by the action of a verb, typically the direct object.
Theme: The semantic role of the entity that is moved or whose state changes, often overlapping with Patient.
Goal: The semantic role of the endpoint or target of a movement or directed action.
Source: The semantic role of the origin or starting point of a movement or directed action.
Experiencer: The semantic role of the entity that has a mental or emotional state, e.g., the subject of "fear" or "know."
Instrument: The semantic role of the entity used as a means to perform an action, e.g., "with a hammer."
Benefactive: The semantic role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed, e.g., the indirect object in "She made me a cake."
Causer: The semantic role of the entity that causes an event or state without directly performing the action.
Proposition: A statement or claim that can be either true or false, representing the content of a sentence independent of its form.
Predication: The relation between a predicate and its arguments, expressing a property or relation of entities.
Modality: A semantic or grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the truth or likelihood of a proposition, such as possibility, necessity, or obligation.
Scalar meaning: Meaning that can be arranged on an ordered scale, e.g., "few < some < many" or "cold < warm < hot."
Graded antonymy: A type of antonymy in which the two terms represent opposite ends of a scale, e.g., "hot" and "cold."
Complementary antonymy: A type of antonymy in which the two terms are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, e.g., "alive" and "dead."
Contrary: A pair of antonyms where both cannot be true at the same time but both can be false, e.g., "hot" and "cold" (something can be lukewarm).
Contradictory: A pair of antonyms where exactly one must be true and the other false, e.g., "mortal" and "immortal."
Vagueness: A property of a term whose boundaries of application are imprecise or gradual, e.g., "tall," "young."
Prototype: The most typical or central member of a category, around which other members are organized in fuzzy-boundary categories.
Family resemblance: A concept from Wittgenstein describing how members of a category share overlapping features without any single feature common to all members.
Conceptual metaphor: A metaphorical mapping from one conceptual domain to another that structures thought and language, e.g., "ARGUMENT IS WAR."
Frame semantics: A semantic theory in which word meanings are understood in terms of structured background knowledge (frames) that provide context for interpretation.
Lexical decomposition: The analysis of a word's meaning into a set of more primitive semantic components or features.
Collocation: A sequence of words or phrases that occur together with greater frequency than would be expected by chance, e.g., "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its individual words, e.g., "kick the bucket."
Connotation: The emotional, cultural, or associative meanings that a word carries in addition to its literal or dictionary meaning.
Denotation: The literal, dictionary-defined meaning of a word, independent of emotional or associative connotations.
Extension: The set of all entities or situations to which a term applies in the world.
Intension: The set of properties or conditions that define the meaning of a term, i.e., what it means rather than what it refers to.
Coreference: The relationship between two or more expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity.
Anaphora: A linguistic element that refers back to a previously mentioned (or about to be mentioned) entity in the discourse.
Cataphora: A linguistic element that refers forward to an entity that will be mentioned later in the discourse.
Deixis: The linguistic expression of reference relative to the context of the utterance, such as person, time, or space, e.g., "here," "now," "I."
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to conveying a propositional content, such as promising, ordering, or apologizing.
Locutionary act: The act of producing an utterance with a particular literal meaning, the basic act of saying something.
Illocutionary act: The act performed in saying something, such as asserting, questioning, commanding, or promising.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the listener, such as persuading, alarming, or entertaining.
Direct speech act: An utterance in which the illocutionary force matches the propositional content, e.g., "Close the door" (an imperative form for an ordering act).
Indirect speech act: An utterance in which the illocutionary force differs from the propositional content, e.g., "Could you pass the salt?" (an interrogative form used to request).
Gricean maxims: Four conversational principles (quality, quantity, relation, and manner) proposed by H.P. Grice that underlie cooperative communication.
Cooperative principle: Grice's overarching assumption that participants in a conversation generally cooperate by making their contributions appropriate to the purpose of the exchange.
Maxim of quality: The Gricean maxim that one should not say what one believes to be false or for which one lacks adequate evidence.
Maxim of quantity: The Gricean maxim that one should make one's contribution as informative as required and no more.
Maxim of relation: The Gricean maxim that one should be relevant to the ongoing conversational purpose.
Maxim of manner: The Gricean maxim that one should be clear, brief, and orderly in one's contribution.
Flouting: A deliberate, obvious violation of a Gricean maxim that generates a conversational implicature rather than breaking the cooperative principle.
Context: The linguistic, situational, social, and cultural circumstances surrounding an utterance that influence its interpretation.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular social situation, field, or communicative purpose, distinguished by vocabulary, grammar, and style.
Discourse: Language use that extends beyond the single sentence, encompassing connected text, conversation, and structured communication.
Cohesion: The linguistic devices that create surface-level connectedness in a text, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical repetition.
Coherence: The logical and meaningful connectedness of a text, going beyond surface forms to create a unified and interpretable whole.
Turn-taking: The system by which speakers alternate in conversation, governed by overlapping, gaps, and transition rules.
Repair: The process by which speakers identify and correct problems in communication, such as misunderstandings or production errors.
Adjacency pair: A two-part exchange in conversation in which the second part is a response to the first, e.g., question-answer, greeting-greeting.
Backchannel: A short response by a listener, such as "mm-hm" or "I see," that signals attentiveness without taking a full turn.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or dialects within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The combination of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance, often at the word or phrase level.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages that leads to mutual influence and borrowing.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word or phrase from one language into another, often with phonological adaptation.
Calque: A word or phrase formed by translating a foreign expression word for word, e.g., "skyscraper" in many languages.
Interlanguage: The evolving linguistic system of a second language learner that is neither the native language nor the target language.
Fossilization: The process in second language acquisition in which an incorrect form or feature becomes fixed and resistant to further correction.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language, typically with reduced grammar and vocabulary.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that emerges from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Bilingualism: The ability of an individual or community to use two languages, either simultaneously or sequentially.
Multilingualism: The use of three or more languages by an individual or community.
Diglossia: A situation in which two distinct varieties of a language (or two different languages) are used in complementary social domains, e.g., High and Low varieties.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and is no longer used as a primary means of communication.
Language endangerment: The state in which a language is at risk of losing its speaker community and ceasing to be transmitted to future generations.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually adopts another language, often leading to the abandonment of the original language.
Language revitalization: Efforts to reverse language decline and restore a language's vitality through education, media, and community use.
Language policy: The official decisions and regulations made by governments or institutions regarding the status, use, and teaching of languages.
Language planning: The deliberate effort to influence the development, use, and maintenance of a language or language variety.
Prestige: The positive social value assigned to a particular language variety, speaker, or linguistic feature within a community.
Stigma: The negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety, speaker, or linguistic feature.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular geographic region or social group, differing from other varieties in vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, distinguished by factors such as class, education, or profession.
Idiolect: The unique linguistic variety used by an individual speaker, reflecting personal habits and idiosyncrasies.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession, group, or community, often unfamiliar to outsiders.
Slang: Informal vocabulary or expressions associated with particular social groups, often transient and creative.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression used in place of one considered harsh, blunt, or offensive, e.g., "passed away" for "died."
Pejorative: A word or expression that conveys a negative or derogatory connotation, e.g., "boss" vs "chief" in some contexts.
Honorific: A linguistic form that expresses respect or deference toward the addressee, common in languages such as Japanese and Korean.
Phatic communication: Language use that serves to establish or maintain social contact rather than to convey specific information, e.g., greetings and small talk.
Formulaic language: Fixed or semi-fixed expressions that are used as whole units rather than being generated from smaller parts, e.g., "thank you very much."
Politeness strategy: Linguistic strategies used to mitigate face-threatening acts and maintain social harmony in communication.
Face: The public self-image or social identity that a person claims and expects others to respect in social interaction.
Face-threatening act: An utterance or action that has the potential to damage the positive or negative face of the speaker or hearer.
Audience design: The practice of adjusting one's linguistic output to suit the perceived characteristics or expectations of the audience.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic theory developed by Sperber and Wilson that explains communication in terms of the search for optimal relevance between cognitive effort and contextual effects.
Informativeness: The degree to which a proposition is logically strong and carries significant information relative to the hearer's expectations.
Contextual effect: The combination of a new belief or the strengthening or weakening of an existing belief that results from processing an utterance.
Optimal relevance: The principle in relevance theory that an utterance is relevant enough to be worth processing and better than any alternative available to the hearer.
Communicative intention: The intention to make the hearer's mutual knowledge of the speaker's informative intention explicit, as defined in relevance theory.
Speaker meaning: The intended message or interpretation that a speaker aims to convey, as distinct from the literal or encoded meaning of the utterance.
Sentence meaning: The conventional, compositional meaning of a sentence derived from the meanings of its parts and the rules of combination.
Propositional attitude: The psychological relation a person bears toward a proposition, such as believing, desiring, or fearing.
Sound change: A systematic alteration in the pronunciation of sounds over time within a language or dialect.
Regularity: The principle in historical linguistics that sound changes affect all applicable instances uniformly, forming the basis of the Neogrammarian school.
Analogy: A morphological process in which the form of a word is changed to conform to a more familiar or productive pattern, e.g., "oxen" → "oxes."
Innovation: A novel linguistic form or feature that arises within a language and may spread through the community.
Reconstruction: The process of hypothesizing the phonological, morphological, or lexical system of a proto-language using the comparative method.
Comparative method: A systematic procedure in historical linguistics for establishing genetic relationships between languages by comparing regular sound correspondences.
Correspondence: A systematic relationship between sounds or forms in related languages that reflects a common ancestral source.
Cognate: A word in two or more related languages that is derived from a common ancestral form, e.g., English "father" and German "Vater."
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of related languages is descended, e.g., Proto-Indo-European.
Language family: A group of languages that are descended from a common ancestral proto-language, e.g., the Indo-European family.
Sister language: Two languages that share an immediate common ancestor within a language family, e.g., English and German within West Germanic.
Substrate: The language of an earlier population that is replaced by a new language, influencing the new language's phonology, vocabulary, or syntax.
Superstrate: The language of a dominant or conquering group that replaces a local language, contributing loanwords and features to the recipient language.
Sprachbund: A group of languages in a geographic area that share structural features due to prolonged contact rather than common descent.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line on a map that separates areas where a particular linguistic feature is used from areas where it is not.
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible but the most distant varieties may not be.
Lexicostatistics: A quantitative method for estimating the time depth of language relationships by calculating the percentage of cognate vocabulary shared.
Glottochronology: A method for estimating the time since two related languages diverged based on the rate of vocabulary replacement, now largely discredited.
Genetic relationship: The relationship between languages that share a common ancestral proto-language, established through systematic correspondences.
Internal reconstruction: A method of historical linguistics that infers earlier stages of a single language by analyzing its internal alternations and paradigms.
Palaeo-linguistics: The study of ancient languages, often through inscriptions, manuscripts, and other historical sources.
Philology: The study of language in historical literature, involving textual criticism, editing, and the interpretation of ancient and medieval texts.
Onomastics: The study of proper names, including personal names, place names, and institutional names.
Toponymy: The branch of onomastics dealing with the origin and meaning of place names.
Anthroponymy: The branch of onomastics dealing with the origin and meaning of personal names.
Neologism: A newly coined or adopted word or expression in a language.
Archaism: A word or form that has fallen out of general use but may survive in specific registers, texts, or dialects.
Semantic narrowing: A type of semantic change in which the meaning of a word becomes more restricted or specific over time, e.g., "meat" from "food" to "flesh."
Semantic broadening: A type of semantic change in which the meaning of a word becomes more general or inclusive, e.g., "bird" from "young bird" to "any bird."
Semantic bleaching: The gradual loss of specific lexical meaning of a word as it becomes more grammatical or functional, e.g., "very" losing intensity.
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a negative or derogatory connotation over time, e.g., "silly" from "blessed" to "foolish."
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more positive or elevated meaning, e.g., "nice" from "foolish" to "pleasant."
Grammaticalization: The diachronic process by which lexical items or phrases develop into grammatical morphemes or structures, e.g., "going to" → "gonna."
Decategorization: The loss of category-specific properties of a lexical item as it becomes a grammatical element.
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or compound becomes fixed and treated as a single lexical item in the mental lexicon.
Reanalysis: A diachronic process in which speakers reinterpret the structural boundaries or grammatical relations within a form, often leading to grammatical change.
Analogical leveling: The diachronic process by which irregular or alternating forms are replaced by regular ones through analogy, e.g., "mice" → "mices" (hypothetical).
Diachronic linguistics: The study of language change and historical development over time.
Synchronic linguistics: The study of a language at a particular point in time, ignoring its historical development.
Speech production: The process by which a speaker transforms intended meanings into audible utterances, involving planning, phonological encoding, and motor execution.
Speech perception: The process by which a listener transforms auditory signals into linguistic representations, involving segmentation, recognition, and interpretation.
Lexical access: The cognitive process of retrieving word representations from the mental lexicon during speech production or comprehension.
Word recognition: The process of identifying a spoken or written word and accessing its meaning and other properties from the mental lexicon.
Aphasia: A language disorder caused by brain damage that affects one or more aspects of language production or comprehension.
