response.text:
Phoneme: the smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.
Morpheme: the smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or a grammatical function.
Allomorph: a variant form of a morpheme that occurs in different phonological contexts.
Allophone: a phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning.
Phonotactics: the set of rules governing which sequences of phonemes are permissible in a given language.
Syllable: a unit of organization for a sequence of speech sounds that typically contains one vowel as its nucleus.
Syllabification: the process of dividing a word or string of sounds into syllables.
Suprasegmental: a feature of speech that extends over more than one sound segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Prosody: the aspects of speech involving patterns of stress, rhythm, intonation, and timing.
Intonation: the variation in pitch over a stretch of speech that conveys grammatical or pragmatic meaning.
Stress: the relative emphasis placed on a particular syllable within a word or phrase.
Tone: the use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning in a tone language.
Segmental: relating to individual discrete units of sound (phonemes) as opposed to suprasegmental features.
Non-segmental: relating to features of speech that are not tied to individual segments, such as pitch, duration, and loudness.
Minimal pair: two words that differ in only one phoneme at the same position, demonstrating that the sounds are distinct phonemes.
Complementary distribution: the situation where two sounds never occur in the same phonological environment, suggesting they are allophones of one phoneme.
Free variation: the situation where two or more sounds can occur in the same environment without changing the meaning of a word.
Archiphoneme: an abstract phonological unit that represents two or more phonemes in a particular context where they merge.
Distinctive feature: a binary or multi-valued property used in feature theory to characterize and differentiate phonemes.
Feature geometry: a hierarchical model organizing distinctive features into structured tiers for phonological representation.
Autosegment: a phonological tier representing suprasegmental features (such as tone) that are associated to segmental tiers.
Tier: a level of phonological representation in multi-tiered models where different features are stored.
Association line: a line in autosegmental phonology linking a feature on a higher tier to a segment on a lower tier.
Contour: a melodic pattern in which two or more distinct pitch values are associated with a single segment.
Plateau: a stretch of two or more adjacent tones of the same pitch value.
Peak: a local maximum in pitch contour.
Valley: a local minimum in pitch contour.
Rising tone: a tone in which pitch moves from a lower to a higher level.
Falling tone: a tone in which pitch moves from a higher to a lower level.
Level tone: a tone in which pitch remains constant throughout the segment.
Tone sandhi: the alteration of a tone in certain phonological environments, especially in tonal languages.
Contour tone: a tone whose realization involves a change in pitch across the syllable.
Register: a secondary laryngeal setting that modifies the pitch range of tones, as in some tonal languages.
Phonological rule: a rule in phonology that describes the systematic transformation of underlying forms to surface forms.
Phonotactic constraint: a restriction on the permissible combinations of phonemes in a language.
Epenthesis: the insertion of an extra sound (vowel or consonant) into a word.
Elision: the omission of a sound or syllable in connected speech.
Metathesis: the transposition of two adjacent or nearby sounds within a word.
Assimilation: a phonological process in which one sound becomes more like a neighboring sound.
Dissimilation: a phonological process in which two similar sounds become less similar to each other.
Lenition: the weakening of a consonant's articulation over time or in a particular environment.
Fortition: the strengthening of a consonant's articulation over time or in a particular environment.
Devoicing: a phonological process in which a voiced sound becomes voiceless.
Voicing: a phonological feature in which the vocal folds vibrate during the production of a sound.
Aspiration: a strong burst of air that accompanies the release of certain stop consonants.
Nasalization: the production of a sound with simultaneous airflow through the nasal cavity.
Palatalization: a consonantal change in which a consonant is articulated with the tongue body raised toward the hard palate.
Velarization: a consonantal change in which a consonant is articulated with the back of the tongue raised toward the velum.
Uvularization: a consonantal change in which a consonant is articulated with the back of the tongue raised toward the uvula.
Labialization: a consonantal change in which a consonant is articulated with rounded lips.
Rounding: the protrusion of the lips during the articulation of a vowel or consonant.
Spreading: a phonological process in which a feature extends across a domain beyond its original location.
Vowel harmony: a phonological constraint requiring vowels within a word to share a particular feature such as backness or height.
Consonant harmony: a phonological constraint requiring consonants within a word to share a particular feature such as place of articulation.
Tone melody: the sequence of tone values across a phrase or word.
Lexical tone: a tone that is part of the lexical representation of a word and distinguishes one word from another.
Grammatical tone: a tone that encodes grammatical information such as tense, aspect, or mood.
Pitch accent: a prosodic system in which pitch is used to mark a single accented syllable, distinguishing word-level accents.
Accent: a prosodic prominence assigned to a particular syllable or word in a language.
Rhythm: the patterned alternation of strong and weak syllables or stressed and unstressed beats in speech.
Ictus: the stressed or prominent beat in a rhythmic pattern.
Mora: a unit of syllable weight used in rhythmic and phonological analysis, typically corresponding to a short vowel or a coda segment.
Syllable weight: the measure of a syllable's heaviness, often determined by the presence or absence of a coda or the length of the nucleus.
Onset: the initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable preceding the vowel.
Rhyme: the portion of a syllable from the vowel nucleus to the end, including the coda.
Nucleus: the most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel.
Coda: the final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable following the vowel.
Open syllable: a syllable that ends in a vowel, with no coda consonant.
Closed syllable: a syllable that ends in a consonant.
Maximal syllable: a syllable containing the greatest number of consonants permitted by the phonotactics of a language.
Monosyllable: a word consisting of a single syllable.
Disyllable: a word consisting of two syllables.
Polysyllable: a word consisting of more than two syllables.
Heterosyllabic: pertaining to elements that occur in different syllables.
Homosyllabic: pertaining to elements that occur within the same syllable.
Homonym: words that are identical in form (spelling or pronunciation) but differ in meaning.
Heteronym: words that differ in pronunciation but share the same spelling.
Homophone: words that are identical in pronunciation but differ in spelling or meaning.
Heterophone: words that are identical in spelling but differ in pronunciation.
Homograph: words that are identical in spelling but differ in pronunciation or meaning.
Heterograph: words that differ in spelling.
Synonym: words that share the same or very similar meanings.
Antonym: words that have opposite meanings.
Hypernym: a word with a broad meaning that subsumes the meanings of more specific words.
Hyponym: a word with a specific meaning that is subsumed by a broader hypernym.
Meronym: a word that denotes a part or component of the whole denoted by another word.
Holonym: a word that denotes a whole of which another word denotes a part.
Polysemy: the phenomenon of a single word or form having multiple related senses.
Monosemy: the property of a word having only one distinct sense.
Ambiguity: the property of a linguistic expression having more than one possible interpretation.
Entailment: a semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another.
Contradiction: a semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the falsity of another.
Presupposition: a proposition that is taken for granted as true for an utterance to be interpretable.
Implicature: a meaning that is conveyed by a speaker without being explicitly stated, derived from context and conversational principles.
Connotation: the associated or emotional meaning of a word beyond its literal definition.
Denotation: the literal or primary meaning of a word.
Sense: a particular meaning or interpretation of a linguistic expression.
Reference: the relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity in the world it denotes.
Referring expression: a linguistic expression that is used to identify or point to a particular entity.
Anaphora: a referring expression that points backward to a previously mentioned entity in the discourse.
Cataphora: a referring expression that points forward to an entity that will be mentioned later in the discourse.
Exophora: a referring expression that points to something in the physical or situational context rather than in the text.
Deixis: the linguistic expression of relations among the speaker, the addressee, the time of utterance, and the place of utterance.
Indexical: a word or expression whose referent depends on the context of the utterance, such as I, here, or now.
Demonstrative: a word that indicates a particular entity by means of spatial or contextual pointing, such as this, that, these, or those.
Personal pronoun: a pronoun that refers to the participants in the discourse, such as I, you, he, she, it, we, or they.
First person: the grammatical person referring to the speaker.
Second person: the grammatical person referring to the addressee.
Third person: the grammatical person referring to entities other than the speaker and addressee.
Speaker: the person who produces an utterance in a communicative act.
Addressee: the person to whom an utterance is directed.
Referent: the entity in the world to which a linguistic expression points.
Illocutionary act: the intended communicative function of an utterance, such as promising, requesting, or warning.
Perlocutionary act: the effect that an utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Locutionary act: the act of producing a meaningful utterance, consisting of the phonetic, phrastic, and illocutionary acts.
Speech act: an utterance that performs an action by virtue of being spoken, such as naming, ordering, or apologizing.
Performative: an utterance that performs the action it describes, typically introduced by a performative verb like "I promise" or "I name."
Constative: an utterance that describes or states a state of affairs, as opposed to a performative.
Directive: a speech act that attempts to get the hearer to do something, such as a command or request.
Commissive: a speech act in which the speaker commits to a future action, such as a promise or threat.
Declarative: a speech act that brings about the state of affairs it describes, such as a judge declaring "I sentence you to ten years."
Expressive: a speech act that expresses the speaker's psychological state, such as thanking, apologizing, or congratulating.
Assertive: a speech act that commits the speaker to the truth of a proposition, such as stating, reporting, or guessing.
Grice's maxims: four principles of cooperative communication (quantity, quality, relation, and manner) proposed by H.P. Grice.
Cooperative principle: the conversational assumption that participants in a conversation are generally cooperative and contribute meaningfully.
Quantity maxim: the maxim that one should make one's contribution as informative as required but not more informative than necessary.
Quality maxim: the maxim that one should not say what one believes to be false or for which one lacks adequate evidence.
Relation maxim: the maxim that one's contribution should be relevant to the ongoing conversation.
Manner maxim: the maxim that one should be clear, brief, and orderly in expression, avoiding obscurity and ambiguity.
Flouting: the deliberate open violation of a conversational maxim to generate an implicature.
Violation: the covert breaking of a conversational maxim that undermines the cooperative principle.
Inference: the process of deriving unstated meaning from an utterance based on context and pragmatic principles.
Conversational implicature: a meaning derived from the flouting or violation of Grice's maxims in a particular conversational context.
Particularized implicature: an implicature that is specific to a particular context and is not a general property of the expression.
Generalized implicature: an implicature that is attached to an expression regardless of the specific context in which it is used.
Context of utterance: the situation in which an utterance is produced, including the participants, time, place, and shared knowledge.
Context of situation: the physical and social environment surrounding an act of communication.
Text: a coherent sequence of sentences or utterances that form a meaningful whole.
Discourse: language use that extends beyond the sentence level, including conversation, narrative, and extended texts.
Cohesion: the set of linguistic relationships that link elements within a text, such as reference, conjunction, and lexical ties.
Coherence: the logical and semantic connectedness of a text that makes it meaningful and interpretable as a whole.
Referential cohesion: a cohesive device in which one element in a text refers back to or forward to another, such as through pronouns or definite descriptions.
Cohesive device: a linguistic means by which elements in a text are linked, including reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, and lexical items.
Definiteness: the grammatical marking that a referent is identifiable to the listener, often signaled by a definite article.
Indefiniteness: the grammatical marking that a referent is not yet identifiable to the listener, often signaled by an indefinite article.
Topicalization: the process of making a particular entity the topic of a discourse or utterance.
Givenness: the property of a discourse entity that has already been introduced or is assumed to be known to the interlocutor.
Newness: the property of a discourse entity that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse.
Information structure: the organization of an utterance or text into known (given) and new information for the addressee.
Theme: the given or starting point of a clause or sentence from which new information is communicated.
Rheme: the new or informative part of a clause or sentence that advances the discourse.
Focus: the element in an utterance that is emphasized to convey new or important information.
Contrastive focus: a type of focus that highlights an element by contrasting it with other possible alternatives.
Cleft sentence: a construction that divides a clause into two parts to place emphasis on a particular element, such as "It was John who called."
Pseudo-cleft: a type of cleft construction that begins with a wh-clause, such as "What I need is a break."
Extraposition: a syntactic process in which an element, often a clause, is moved to a position after the main clause, such as "It is likely that he will come."
Cleft: a syntactic construction that splits a single clause into two to foreground a particular constituent.
Fronting: a syntactic process in which a constituent is moved to the beginning of a clause.
Inversion: a syntactic process in which the normal order of subject and verb is reversed, as in questions or after certain adverbials.
Wh-cleft: a cleft construction introduced by a wh-word, such as "Who was it that you saw?"
It-cleft: a cleft construction introduced by "it," such as "It was Mary who broke the vase."
Do-cleft: a cleft construction introduced by "what," such as "What he did was leave early."
Left-dislocation: a construction in which a constituent is placed at the beginning of a clause and resumed by a pronoun, such as "John, he left early."
Right-dislocation: a construction in which a constituent is placed at the end of a clause after a resumptive pronoun, such as "He left early, John."
Focalization: the process of assigning focus to a particular element in a clause.
Focus marking: the linguistic means by which focus is indicated in a language, through intonation, particles, or word order.
Broad focus: a type of focus in which the entire proposition is new or important information.
Narrow focus: a type of focus in which only a specific constituent is new or important information.
Informational focus: a type of focus that marks information as new or not previously established in the discourse.
Accentual focus: a type of focus realized through prosodic stress or intonational prominence.
Logical focus: a type of focus that corresponds to a logically stressed constituent in the semantic representation.
Topic comment: a discourse structure in which a topic (given information) is followed by a comment (new information) about it.
Topic: the entity or subject matter about which a discourse is oriented.
Comment: the new information asserted about the topic in a discourse.
Constituent: a word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a clause or sentence structure.
Phrase: a group of words organized around a head that functions as a unit within a larger syntactic structure.
Clause: a syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be independent or dependent.
Sentence: the basic unit of syntactic analysis, typically consisting of a subject and a predicate.
Predicate: the part of a clause that contains the verb and its complements, expressing what is said about the subject.
Subject: the noun phrase or pronoun that a clause is about and that typically agrees with the verb.
Object: a noun phrase that functions as the recipient or target of the action expressed by the verb.
Complement: a word or phrase required by a verb, adjective, or noun to complete its meaning.
Adjunct: an optional modifier in a clause that adds supplementary information such as time, place, or manner.
Head: the central or most semantically significant word in a phrase to which other elements are attached.
Specifier: a constituent that precedes the head in certain phrase structures, such as a determiner in a noun phrase.
Modifier: a word or phrase that adds descriptive or limiting information to a head.
Determiner: a word that precedes a noun to specify its reference, such as a, the, this, or some.
Article: a determiner that indicates definiteness or indefiniteness, such as "the" or "a/an."
Pronoun: a word that stands in for a noun or noun phrase, such as he, she, it, or they.
Preposition: a word that expresses a spatial, temporal, or logical relationship between its complement and another element.
Postposition: a word that follows its complement to express a relationship, as in many agglutinative and polysynthetic languages.
Adjective: a word that modifies a noun by describing a property or quality.
Adverb: a word that modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb, often indicating manner, time, place, or degree.
Adposition: a general term for prepositions and postpositions.
Conjunction: a word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as and, but, or, or because.
Coordination: a syntactic process in which two or more elements of equal status are joined by a conjunction.
Subordination: a syntactic process in which a clause is dependent on and modifies another clause.
Complementizer: a word that introduces a subordinate clause, such as that, whether, or if.
Relative clause: a subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is typically introduced by a relative pronoun.
Adverbial clause: a subordinate clause that functions as an adverb, modifying the main clause.
Noun clause: a subordinate clause that functions as a noun within a larger clause.
Adjective clause: a subordinate clause that functions as an adjective, modifying a noun.
Participle: a non-finite verb form used to form progressive or passive constructions, such as "running" or "broken."
Infinitive: a non-finite verb form expressing the base form of a verb, such as "to go" or "go."
Gerund: a verbal noun formed from a present participle, as in "Swimming is fun."
Inflection: the modification of a word form to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, or case.
Derivation: a morphological process that creates a new word from an existing one, often changing the part of speech.
Affix: a morpheme that is attached to a base or root to form a new word, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: an affix that is attached before the base or root of a word.
Suffix: an affix that is attached after the base or root of a word.
Infix: an affix that is inserted within the root of a word.
Circumfix: an affix that surrounds the root of a word, consisting of both a prefix and a suffix.
Superfix: a prosodic or suprasegmental affix, such as stress or tone, that is added to a word.
Root: the core morpheme of a word to which affixes may be attached.
Stem: the part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, which may include derivational affixes.
Base: the form to which an affix is attached in a morphological operation.
Free morpheme: a morpheme that can stand alone as a word.
Bound morpheme: a morpheme that cannot stand alone and must be attached to another morpheme.
Clitic: a morpheme that is phonologically dependent on an adjacent word but syntactically independent, such as English "-n't" or "don't."
Parasite: a word or phrase inserted into an utterance without syntactic integration, such as "you know" or "I mean."
Reduplication: a morphological process in which part or all of a word is repeated to create a new form or meaning.
Portmanteau: a morpheme that simultaneously expresses two or more grammatical categories, such as the Latin "-runt" for third person plural past.
Polysynthesis: a morphological type in which a single word incorporates multiple morphemes representing what would be a full sentence in analytic languages.
Agglutination: a morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes each expressing a single grammatical category.
Fusion: a morphological type in which a single morpheme expresses multiple grammatical categories simultaneously.
Isolation: a morphological type in which each word is a single morpheme and grammatical relationships are expressed by word order.
Analytic: a language type in which grammatical relationships are primarily expressed by word order and function words rather than inflection.
Synthetic: a language type in which grammatical relationships are primarily expressed through affixation and inflection.
Morphological typology: the classification of languages based on their dominant morphological strategies.
Word order: the linear arrangement of syntactic constituents in a sentence.
SOV: a word order in which the subject precedes the object and the object precedes the verb.
SVO: a word order in which the subject precedes the verb and the verb precedes the object.
VSO: a word order in which the verb precedes the subject and the subject precedes the object.
VOS: a word order in which the verb precedes the object and the object precedes the subject.
Free word order: a property of a language in which constituents can appear in multiple orders without changing grammaticality.
Scrambling: a syntactic phenomenon in which constituents are rearranged in an order that is not canonical.
Constituency test: a diagnostic used to determine whether a string of words forms a constituent, such as substitution, movement, or clefting.
C-command: a structural relationship in which one node dominates another and the first branch point above the first also dominates the second.
Spec: the specifier position in a phrase structure, typically occupying the leftmost position.
Complementizer phrase: a clause-level projection introduced by a complementizer such as "that" or "whether."
Tense phrase: a projection above the verb phrase that encodes temporal information.
Aspect phrase: a projection that encodes aspectual information such as perfective or imperfective.
Mood phrase: a projection that encodes modal or modal-like information such as indicative or subjunctive.
Voice phrase: a projection that encodes voice distinctions such as active or passive.
Nominal phrase: a phrase whose head is a noun, noun phrase, or determiner.
Prepositional phrase: a phrase whose head is a preposition followed by its complement.
Adjectival phrase: a phrase whose head is an adjective.
Adverbial phrase: a phrase whose head is an adverb.
Verbal phrase: a phrase whose head is a verb.
VP shell: a theoretical construct in which the VP is separated from its verbal head to account for certain syntactic phenomena.
X-bar theory: a model of phrase structure in which every phrase consists of a specifier, a head, and a complement, with an intermediate X-bar projection.
Head complement: the constituent that immediately follows and is required by the head in a phrase.
Head specifier: the constituent that immediately precedes and modifies the head in a phrase.
Endocentric: a constituent in which the head is contained within the constituent itself.
Exocentric: a constituent in which no single element within it functions as the head.
Endocentric head: the head of an endocentric constituent.
Exocentric construction: a construction like a prepositional phrase in which no single element is the head.
Subcategorization: the specification of the types and number of arguments that a verb or other predicate requires or selects.
Selectional restriction: a constraint on the semantic type of arguments that a predicate can take.
Theta role: a semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Theme, or Goal.
Agent: the theta role of a voluntary or animate causer of an action.
Patient: the theta role of the entity most directly affected by an action.
Theme: the theta role of the entity that undergoes a change of state or location.
Goal: the theta role of the endpoint of a motion or the recipient of a transfer.
Experiencer: the theta role of the entity that undergoes a psychological or perceptual experience.
Source: the theta role of the origin of a motion or the donor in a transfer.
Locative: the theta role of the location where an event occurs.
Instrument: the theta role of the tool or means used to perform an action.
Reciprocal: a construction in which the subject and object are interchangeable, as in "The boys and girls helped each other."
Reflexive: a pronoun that refers back to the subject, as in "She saw herself."
Reflexivization: the process by which a reflexive pronoun replaces a coreferential argument.
Binding theory: a component of generative grammar that governs the distribution of anaphoric elements like pronouns and reflexives.
Anaphor: a linguistic expression that must be bound by an antecedent within a specific domain, such as a reflexive pronoun.
R-expression: a noun phrase that cannot be bound by a pronoun, such as a proper name.
Binding domain: the local domain within which an anaphor must find its antecedent.
Government: a structural relationship in which a head licenses a complement in certain syntactic configurations.
Trace: a theoretical element left behind in a syntactic derivation when a constituent has been moved.
Wh-movement: the syntactic process in which a wh-phrase moves to the specifier position of CP to form a question.
Passive: a voice construction in which the object of an active sentence becomes the subject.
Middle voice: a voice construction in which the agent is unexpressed and the subject is the patient, such as "The book reads well."
Causative: a construction in which an agent is added to a non-causative predicate.
Anticausative: a construction in which an agent is removed from a causative predicate.
Unaccusative: an intransitive verb whose sole argument is the theme or patient, such as "arrive" or "fall."
Unergative: an intransitive verb whose sole argument is the agent, such as "run" or "laugh."
Transitive: a verb that takes a direct object.
Intransitive: a verb that does not take a direct object.
Ditransitive: a verb that takes both a direct and an indirect object, such as "give" or "send."
Valency: the number of arguments a predicate requires or can take.
Argument: a required participant in an event as encoded by a predicate.
Non-argument: an optional participant or adjunct not required by the predicate.
Case: a grammatical category that marks the syntactic function of a noun phrase in a clause.
Nominative case: the case typically marking the subject of a clause.
Accusative case: the case typically marking the direct object of a clause.
Dative case: the case typically marking the indirect object or recipient of a clause.
Genitive case: the case typically marking possession or association.
Instrumental case: the case typically marking the instrument or means of an action.
Locative case: the case typically marking location or position.
Ablative case: the case typically marking separation or source.
Allative case: the case typically marking direction or goal.
Ergative: a grammatical relationship in which the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently from the subject of an intransitive verb.
Absolutive: the unmarked case in an ergative language, used for the object of transitive verbs and the subject of intransitive verbs.
Split ergativity: a system in which ergative-absolutive alignment applies in some clauses but accusative alignment in others, often conditioned by tense or aspect.
Nominative-accusative alignment: a system in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs is marked the same way, distinct from the object.
Ergative-absolutive alignment: a system in which the object of transitive verbs and the subject of intransitive verbs are marked the same way, distinct from the subject of transitive verbs.
Alignment: the system by which a language groups grammatical functions for case marking.
Core grammar: the component of grammar dealing with the structure of clauses and sentences.
Periphrasis: the use of a multi-word construction to express a meaning that could be expressed by a single word or inflection.
Periphrastic construction: a multi-word construction, such as "have been going" for the present perfect progressive.
Analytic construction: a construction that uses separate words rather than inflection to express grammatical meaning.
Periphrastic aspect: aspect expressed through auxiliary constructions rather than verbal inflection.
Periphrastic tense: tense expressed through auxiliary constructions rather than verbal inflection.
Tense: a grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the utterance time.
Present tense: the grammatical tense indicating an event simultaneous with the utterance time.
Past tense: the grammatical tense indicating an event prior to the utterance time.
Future tense: the grammatical tense indicating an event after the utterance time.
Remote past: a tense indicating an event at a considerable distance in the past.
Recent past: a tense indicating an event at a recent distance in the past.
Aspect: a grammatical category that describes the internal temporal structure of an event.
Perfective aspect: an aspect that presents an event as a complete whole.
Imperfective aspect: an aspect that presents an event as ongoing, habitual, or incomplete.
Progressive aspect: an aspect that presents an event as in progress at a particular time.
Habitual aspect: an aspect that presents an event as recurring or habitual.
Perfect aspect: an aspect that relates an event to a subsequent reference time.
Pluperfect: a tense-aspect combination indicating an event prior to another past event.
Future perfect: a tense-aspect combination indicating an event that will be completed before a future reference time.
Aspectual class: the inherent temporal properties of a verb, such as stative, activity, accomplishment, or achievement.
Stative: a verb describing a state or condition without inherent boundaries, such as "know" or "believe."
Activity: a verb describing an unbounded, durative event, such as "run" or "swim."
Accomplishment: a verb describing a bounded, durative event with an inherent endpoint, such as "build a house."
Achievement: a verb describing a punctual, instantaneous change of state, such as "arrive" or "recognize."
Semelfactive: a verb describing a single, punctual, bounded event, such as "knock" or "blink."
Durative: a verb or event that extends over a period of time.
Punctual: a verb or event that occurs at a single point in time.
Iterative: a verb or event that is repeated or recurring.
Frequentative: an aspect that indicates the repetition or frequency of an event.
Inchoative: a verb or construction that marks the beginning of a state or process.
Resultative: a verb or construction that marks the completion or result of a process.
Terminative: a verb or construction that marks the end of a process.
Mood: a grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the proposition.
Indicative mood: the mood used for statements of fact or reality.
Subjunctive mood: the mood used for hypothetical, desired, or uncertain situations.
Imperative mood: the mood used for commands or requests.
Optative mood: the mood used to express wishes or hopes.
Jussive mood: the mood used for commands or wishes, particularly in some Semitic languages.
Conditional: a mood or construction that expresses a hypothetical situation and its consequence.
Counterfactual: a proposition that describes a situation contrary to fact.
Modal: an adverb or auxiliary expressing the speaker's attitude such as necessity, possibility, or permission.
Epistemic modality: modality expressing the degree of certainty or knowledge about a proposition.
Deontic modality: modality expressing obligation, permission, or prohibition.
Dynamic modality: modality expressing ability, willingness, or capacity.
Quantifier: a word or expression that indicates the quantity or scope of a set, such as all, some, or no.
Universal quantifier: a quantifier that refers to all members of a set, such as "all" or "every."
Existential quantifier: a quantifier that asserts the existence of at least one member of a set, such as "some" or "there is."
Negative quantifier: a quantifier that denotes the absence of any members of a set, such as "no" or "none."
Distributive: a property of a quantifier that applies to each member of a set individually.
Collective: a property of a quantifier that applies to the set as a whole.
Scope: the range of elements over which a quantifier or operator exerts its force.
Quantifier scope: the domain over which a quantifier ranges, which can interact with other operators to create ambiguity.
Negation: the operation that reverses the truth value of a proposition.
Polarity: the grammatical distinction between positive and negative assertions.
Negative polarity item: an expression that is grammatical only in a negative or downward-entailing context, such as "any" or "ever."
Positive polarity item: an expression that is grammatical only in positive contexts, such as "some" or "at all" in certain uses.
Downward entailment: a semantic property of a context in which replacing a term with a more specific term preserves truth.
Upward entailment: a semantic property of a context in which replacing a term with a more general term preserves truth.
Antisymmetry: a semantic property in which both upward and downward entailment are licensed.
Presupposition trigger: a word or construction that introduces a presupposition, such as "again," "know," or "stop."
Accommodation: the process by which a listener updates their common ground to make a presupposed proposition true.
Common ground: the set of propositions that are mutually known or assumed by the participants in a conversation.
Relevance: a principle in relevance theory that explains how listeners interpret utterances by seeking the most cognitively accessible meaning.
Gricean implicature: an implicature derived from the flouting of Grice's conversational maxims.
Scalar implicature: an implicature derived from the use of a weaker term on a linguistic scale, such as using "some" to implicate "not all."
Free choice implicature: an implicature derived from the use of a free choice operator, such as "any" in a question.
Horn implicature: a type of scalar implicature based on the use of a weaker term on a scale.
Langford implicature: a type of implicature based on the failure of a presupposition.
Presupposition projection: the process by which a presupposition of a constituent is inherited by the larger clause or sentence.
Presupposition accommodation: the process by which a listener adds a presupposed proposition to the common ground.
Entailment: a logical relationship where the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another.
Paraphrase: a restatement of a sentence in different words that preserves its meaning.
Tautology: a proposition that is true by virtue of its logical form, such as "A or not A."
Contradiction: a proposition that is false by virtue of its logical form, such as "A and not A."
Modal logic: a branch of logic that deals with the modalities of necessity and possibility.
Intensional context: a context in which substituting co-referential expressions can change the truth value, such as belief contexts.
Extensional context: a context in which substituting co-referential expressions preserves the truth value.
Compositionality: the principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined.
Schematic meaning: the abstract, formulaic meaning of a word or expression.
Conceptual structure: the network of semantic features and relations that constitute the meaning of a lexical item.
Frame semantics: a model of meaning in which words are understood in terms of the conceptual frames or situations they evoke.
Proto-category: a category that has no sharp boundaries and is defined by a set of prototypical and peripheral members.
Prototype: the most central or typical member of a category.
Cognitive model: a mental representation of a domain of knowledge that structures meaning.
Image schema: a basic, pre-linguistic pattern of experience that structures meaning, such as container, path, or force.
Metaphor: a figurative expression in which one domain is understood in terms of another, as in "time is money."
Metonymy: a figurative expression in which one entity is referred to by another entity with which it is associated, as in "The White House announced."
Polysemy network: a structured representation of the various senses of a polysemous word and the relations between them.
Sense relation: the semantic relationship between different senses of a word, such as metaphorical extension or metonymic extension.
Lexical field: a set of related words that form a coherent semantic domain.
Semantic field: a group of words that share a common semantic domain or concept.
Collocation: a habitual or fixed combination of words that co-occur with higher-than-chance frequency.
Collocational restriction: a constraint on the words that can appear in a particular syntactic position.
Collocational preference: a statistical tendency for certain words to co-occur in particular positions.
Frame: a structured set of roles and relations that a lexical item evokes, such as the "Buy" frame with Buyer, Seller, Goods, and Money.
Frame element: a participant or role in a frame, such as Agent, Patient, or Instrument.
Valency frame: the set of required and optional arguments associated with a verb.
Lexical entry: the representation of a word in a lexicon, including its phonological, morphological, syntactic, and semantic properties.
Lexical gap: the absence of a word in a language for a concept that is expressed by a phrase or a loanword.
Basic level category: the most salient or prototypical level of categorization in a domain, such as "chair" as opposed to "furniture" or "rocking chair."
Taxonomy: a hierarchical classification of concepts from general to specific.
Meronymy: the part-whole relationship between concepts.
Holonymy: the whole-part relationship between concepts.
Tropism: the systematic relationship between the meanings of words in a language, such as metaphorical extensions.
Lexicalization: the process by which a multi-word expression or construction becomes a single lexical item.
Phraseologism: a fixed or semi-fixed multi-word expression, such as an idiom, phrase, or set expression.
Idiom: a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be predicted from the literal meanings of its components.
Idiomaticity: the degree to which an expression's meaning deviates from the literal composition of its parts.
Colloquialism: a word or expression characteristic of informal spoken language.
Neologism: a newly coined or recently adopted word or expression.
Archaism: a word or expression that is no longer in common use but appears in older texts.
Anglicism: a word or expression borrowed from English into another language.
Loanword: a word borrowed from one language and integrated into the vocabulary of another.
Code-switching: the practice of alternating between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation.
Code-mixing: the practice of combining elements from two or more languages within a single sentence.
Borrowing: the process by which a language adopts words or morphemes from another language.
Calque: a translation of a word or expression from one language into another by a word-for-word or structure-for-structure rendering.
Language contact: the interaction between speakers of different languages that leads to mutual influence.
Interference: the influence of a speaker's first language on their use of a second language.
Substrate: the influence of a previously spoken language on a subsequently adopted language in a region.
Superstrate: the influence of a socially dominant language on a previously spoken language in a region.
Adstrate: the influence of a neighboring language on a language in a region.
Areale feature: a linguistic feature shared by languages in a geographic area due to contact rather than common descent.
Sprachbund: a group of languages that share features due to prolonged contact and proximity.
Language family: a group of languages descended from a common proto-language.
Proto-language: the hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of languages is reconstructed.
Language death: the process by which a language loses its last native speaker.
Language shift: the process by which a community of speakers abandons one language for another.
Language revitalization: efforts to recover and promote the use of a language that is endangered or dormant.
Endangered language: a language at risk of losing its last native speaker.
Vulnerable language: a language whose use is decreasing but is still spoken by some children.
Extinct language: a language that no longer has any native speakers.
Revived language: a language that was revived as a spoken language after a period of dormancy.
Creole: a natural language that develops from the contact of two or more languages, typically in a pidgin context, and becomes the native language of a community.
Pidgin: a simplified language that develops for communication between groups with no common language and does not become anyone's native language.
Mixed language: a language that combines structural elements from two or more source languages in a non-standard way.
Contact language: a language that arises from sustained contact between different language communities.
Creolization: the process by which a pidgin develops into a full creole language.
Plantation Creole: a creole that developed on a plantation or in a colonial setting.
Urban Creole: a creole that developed in an urban setting.
Kreol: another term for creole.
Lingua franca: a language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Esperanto: a constructed international auxiliary language designed to facilitate communication between speakers of different languages.
Vernacular: the everyday language used by a community in ordinary conversation.
Standard language: a variety of a language that has been codified and is used in formal education, media, and government.
Dialect: a variety of a language associated with a particular geographic region or social group.
Idiolect: the unique variety of a language used by a particular individual.
Register: a variety of language associated with a particular communicative situation or domain.
Sociolect: a variety of language associated with a particular social group.
Ethnolect: a variety of language associated with a particular ethnic group.
Geographical dialect: a variety of language associated with a particular geographic region.
Urban dialect: a variety of language associated with a particular urban area.
Rural dialect: a variety of language associated with a particular rural area.
Regionalism: a word or expression specific to a particular geographic region.
Localism: a word or expression specific to a small or local community.
Dialectal: pertaining to or characteristic of a dialect.
Dialectology: the study of the geographic and social distribution of linguistic variation.
Isogloss: a geographic boundary that separates areas where a particular linguistic feature is used.
Linguistic map: a map showing the geographic distribution of linguistic features.
Dialect continuum: a chain of dialects in which adjacent varieties are mutually intelligible but distant varieties may not be.
Lingua: the general term for a natural human language.
Grammar: the system of rules, structures, and conventions that governs the use of a language.
Syntax: the branch of linguistics that studies the structure of sentences and the rules governing the arrangement of words.
Semantics: the branch of linguistics that studies meaning in language, particularly at the level of words, phrases, and sentences.
Pragmatics: the branch of linguistics that studies how context contributes to meaning in communication.
Phonology: the branch of linguistics that studies the systematic organization of sounds in a language.
Phonetics: the branch of linguistics that studies the physical properties of speech sounds and their perception.
Morphology: the branch of linguistics that studies the structure and formation of words.
Lexicography: the compilation and editing of dictionaries and the study of lexical entries.
Etymology: the study of the origin and historical development of words.
Historical linguistics: the study of language change and the reconstruction of ancestral languages.
Comparative method: a method of historical linguistics that reconstructs proto-languages by comparing related languages.
Sound law: a regular correspondence between sounds in related languages, as in Grimm's Law.
Grimm's Law: the sound change describing the shift of Proto-Indo-European stops into Proto-Germanic fricatives and stops.
Verner's Law: a sound change describing the voicing of certain fricatives in Germanic languages.
Reconstruction: the process of positing the forms and features of a proto-language based on comparative evidence.
Cognate: words in different languages that are derived from a common ancestral form.
Loan translation: the translation of a word or phrase from one language into another by a corresponding word or phrase.
Calque: a loan translation.
Fossil: a linguistic form that persists in a language long after it has lost its original productivity or meaning.
Archaism: a word or form that has fallen out of common use.
Obsolescence: the process by which a linguistic form falls out of use.
Innovation: the introduction of a new linguistic form or feature into a language.
Language change: the process by which languages evolve and develop over time.
Dialectal split: the divergence of a language into separate dialects that may eventually become distinct languages.
Language family tree: a diagram representing the genetic relationships among languages in a family.
Glottolog: a comprehensive catalog of the world's languages and their classifications.
Ethnologue: a reference work that catalogs and describes the world's languages.
Corpus linguistics: the study of language using large collections of real-world texts and recordings.
Corpus: a large, structured collection of texts or recordings used for linguistic analysis.
Concordance: a list of all occurrences of a word or pattern in a corpus with their surrounding context.
N-gram: a sequence of n items, such as words, that occur together in a text.
Collocational analysis: the study of the distributional patterns of words in a corpus.
Frequency analysis: the study of how often words or patterns occur in a text or corpus.
Distributional analysis: the study of the environments in which a linguistic item occurs.
Computational linguistics: the application of computer science and artificial intelligence to the study of language.
Natural language processing: the use of computers to process, understand, and generate human language.
Machine translation: the use of computers to translate text from one language to another.
Speech recognition: the use of computers to convert spoken language into text.
Speech synthesis: the use of computers to convert text into spoken language.
Stylometry: the study of stylistic features of writing using quantitative methods.
Forensic linguistics: the application of linguistic analysis to legal and investigative contexts.
Clinical linguistics: the application of linguistic analysis to the diagnosis and treatment of language disorders.
Applied linguistics: the application of linguistic theory and methods to practical problems, particularly language teaching and policy.
Language teaching: the practice of instructing learners in a language.
Second language acquisition: the study of how people learn a language other than their first.
First language acquisition: the study of how children acquire their native language.
Critical period: the proposed period in childhood during which language acquisition is most efficient.
Language universals: properties that are shared by all natural human languages.
Universal Grammar: Noam Chomsky's theory that posits an innate set of linguistic principles and parameters.
Parameter: a choice in a set of innate linguistic options that is set differently in different languages.
Principle: a universal constraint or rule in the theory of Universal Grammar.
Minimalist program: a version of generative grammar that seeks to derive syntactic structure with the most economical operations.
Merge: the operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects.
Phase: a unit of computation in the Minimalist Program, typically CP or vP.
Agree: the operation in the Minimalist Program by which a functional head establishes a relationship with a goal.
Move: the operation in the Minimalist Program by which a syntactic object is displaced to a new position.
Check: an operation in earlier generative grammar by which a feature is verified against a goal.
Feature checking: the process of verifying that a syntactic feature is satisfied in a derivation.
Case filter: a principle in generative grammar that requires every nominal to receive Case.
Theta criterion: a principle in generative grammar that requires each argument to receive exactly one theta role.
Subcategorization framework: a model of syntax that uses a lexicon of subcategorization frames to drive syntactic derivation.
Lexical-functional grammar: a model of syntax that separates grammatical functions from syntactic structure and lexical information.
Head-driven phrase structure grammar: a model of syntax that uses attribute value matrices to represent structural relationships.
Tree-adjoining grammar: a model of syntax that uses two types of operations, substitution and adjunction, to generate sentences.
Categorial grammar: a model of syntax in which each word is assigned a logical type and sentences are built by type composition.
Dependency grammar: a model of syntax in which words are connected by head-dependent relations rather than constituent structure.
Functional grammar: a model of syntax that focuses on the functional organization of clauses.
Cognitive grammar: a model of grammar that integrates form and meaning in a unified conceptual framework.
Construction grammar: a model of grammar in which constructions (form-meaning pairings) are the basic units of analysis.
Radical construction grammar: a model of construction grammar that focuses on the emergence of constructions from usage.
Usage-based model: a model of language that emphasizes frequency, analogy, and categorization over rule-based systems.
Embodied cognition: the theory that cognitive processes, including language, are rooted in the body's interactions with the world.
Neurolinguistics: the study of the neural basis of language, including brain structures and processes involved in language production and comprehension.
Broca's area: a region of the brain in the left frontal lobe associated with language production and syntactic processing.
Wernicke's area: a region of the brain in the left temporal lobe associated with language comprehension.
Aphasia: a language disorder resulting from brain damage that affects language production or comprehension.
Broca's aphasia: a form of aphasia characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
Wernicke's aphasia: a form of aphasia characterized by fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.
Conduction aphasia: a form of aphasia characterized by impaired repetition with relatively preserved production and comprehension.
Global aphasia: a severe form of aphasia affecting both production and comprehension.
Anomic aphasia: a form of aphasia characterized by word-finding difficulties with relatively preserved grammar.
Agrammatism: a deficit in grammatical processing, characterized by the omission of function words and morphemes.
Language processing: the cognitive operations involved in the production and comprehension of language.
Parsing: the process of assigning a syntactic structure to a sentence during comprehension.
Garden-path sentence: a sentence that leads the reader down an initially plausible but ultimately incorrect interpretation.
Garden-path effect: the difficulty experienced when encountering a sentence that requires reanalysis after an initial misparse.
Reanalysis: the process of revising an initial syntactic or semantic interpretation during comprehension.
Working memory: the cognitive system that holds and manipulates information temporarily, essential for language processing.
Short-term memory: the cognitive system that holds a limited amount of information for a brief period.
Long-term memory: the cognitive system that stores information over extended periods.
Semantic memory: the memory system that stores general knowledge about words and concepts.
Episodic memory: the memory system that stores specific events and experiences.
Procedural memory: the memory system that stores skills and habits, including aspects of grammatical knowledge.
Declarative memory: the memory system that stores facts and events, including aspects of lexical knowledge.
Implicit learning: the acquisition of knowledge without conscious awareness, as in the acquisition of grammatical patterns.
Explicit learning: the acquisition of knowledge through conscious instruction and awareness.
Implicit grammar: grammatical knowledge acquired implicitly through exposure to language.
Explicit grammar: grammatical knowledge acquired through conscious instruction.
Metalinguistic awareness: the ability to think about and reflect on language as an object of study.
Phonological awareness: the ability to recognize and manipulate the sound structure of language.
Morphological awareness: the ability to recognize and manipulate the morphological structure of words.
Syntactic awareness: the ability to recognize and manipulate the syntactic structure of sentences.
Pragmatic awareness: the ability to recognize and manipulate the pragmatic features of language.
Discourse analysis: the study of language use in extended texts and conversations.
Conversation analysis: the detailed study of the structure and organization of spoken conversation.
Turn-taking: the system by which speakers alternate in a conversation.
Adjacency pair: a pair of turns in conversation that are closely related, such as question-answer or greeting-greeting.
Repair: the process by which a speaker or listener addresses a problem in communication.
Self-repair: a repair initiated by the speaker who produced the problem.
Other-repair: a repair initiated by the listener in response to a problem.
Completion: the process by which a speaker finishes a turn or utterance.
Turn completion: the point at which a speaker's turn is understood as finished.
Transition relevance place: a point in a turn at which a speaker change is possible.
Overlap: the occurrence of simultaneous speech from two or more speakers.
Backchannel: a brief response, such as "mm-hm" or "uh-huh," that signals continued listening.
Repair sequence: a sequence of turns in which a problem is identified and resolved.
Preface: a preliminary element that introduces a potentially problematic utterance.
Mitigation: the use of linguistic strategies to soften the force of an utterance.
Hedging: the use of expressions that express uncertainty or reduce the commitment of a statement.
Mitigating device: a linguistic means used to reduce the force or directness of an utterance.
Face: a social concept referring to the public self-image that a person maintains in interaction.
Positive face: the desire to be approved of, liked, and admired by others.
Negative face: the desire to be free of imposition and to have one's autonomy respected.
Face-threatening act: an action that endangers the positive or negative face of a participant.
Politeness: the set of linguistic and behavioral strategies used to maintain face in social interaction.
Politeness strategy: a linguistic strategy used to mitigate the face-threatening potential of an utterance.
Indirect speech act: a speech act in which the intended illocutionary force is not directly encoded in the sentence structure.
Directive strategy: a politeness strategy that uses indirect language to make a request.
Bald on-record: a politeness strategy that makes the speech act explicit and direct without mitigation.
Positive politeness: a strategy that emphasizes in-group solidarity and shared identity.
Negative politeness: a strategy that emphasizes respect for the hearer's autonomy and freedom.
Off-record: a politeness strategy that uses ambiguous or indirect language to avoid direct imposition.
Brown and Levinson's theory: a theory of politeness that analyzes face-threatening acts and politeness strategies.
Speech act theory: a framework for analyzing the actions performed by utterances, developed by Austin and Searle.
Locution: the literal meaning of an utterance.
Illocution: the force or intent behind an utterance.
Perlocution: the effect of an utterance on the listener.
Austin's distinction: the distinction between the locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary aspects of an utterance.
Searle's taxonomy: the classification of speech acts into representatives, directives, commissives, expressives, and declarations.
Representative: a speech act that commits the speaker to the truth of a proposition.
Searle's classification: the categorization of speech acts by their illocutionary point.
Illocutionary point: the goal or purpose of an utterance in speech act theory.
Propositional content: the state of affairs described by an utterance.
Preparatory condition: a condition that must be met for a speech act to be performed felicitously.
Sincerity condition: a condition that the speaker must genuinely believe or intend for the speech act to be felicitous.
Essential condition: a condition that is necessary for the speech act to be performed at all.
Felicitous: a speech act that is performed successfully and meets all its conditions.
Infelicitous: a speech act that fails to meet one or more of its conditions.
Contextually appropriate: a speech act that is suitable and fitting for the given situation.
Gricean framework: the framework of conversational principles developed by H.P. Grice.
Conversational maxims: the set of four maxims (quantity, quality, relation, and manner) in Grice's framework.
Implicature cancellation: the ability to cancel or revoke a conversational implicature by adding explicit clarification.
Implicature detachment: the derivation of an implicature from a form whose literal meaning does not entail it.
Implicature reinforcement: the explicit addition of a statement that confirms an implicature.
Contextual implicature: an implicature that depends on a specific context for its derivation.
Lexical implicature: an implicature that is attached to a lexical item regardless of context.
Conversational inference: the derivation of meaning through reasoning about the speaker's intentions and the conversational context.
Relevance theory: a theory of communication developed by Sperber and Wilson that explains how listeners interpret utterances by seeking optimal relevance.
Optimal relevance: the balance between cognitive effects and processing effort in interpreting an utterance.
Cognitive effect: the impact of an utterance on the listener's beliefs or assumptions.
Processing effort: the mental effort required to interpret an utterance.
Communicative intention: the speaker's intention to make their assumptions manifest to the listener.
Manifestness: the degree to which a proposition is already in the listener's cognitive environment.
Cognitive environment: the set of assumptions and beliefs that a person has at a given time.
Communicative procedure: the process by which a speaker makes their assumptions manifest to a listener.
Inferential process: the process by which a listener derives the intended meaning of an utterance through reasoning.
Pragmatic enrichment: the addition of meaning to an expression through pragmatic reasoning.
Pragmatic restriction: the narrowing of the meaning of an expression through pragmatic reasoning.
Pragmatic strengthening: the addition of a stronger meaning to an expression through pragmatic reasoning.
Scalar reasoning: the use of linguistic scales to derive implicatures.
Lexical scale: a set of words or expressions ordered by strength, such as know > believe > guess.
Conversational scale: a scale of alternatives that are relevant in a given conversational context.
Horn scale: a scale of words ordered by strength where the weaker member is used to implicate the negation of the stronger member.
Langford scale: a scale of words ordered by strength where the stronger member is used to implicate the presence of the weaker member.
Natural deduction: a method of logical reasoning that is used in formal semantics to model entailment and inference.
Model-theoretic semantics: a formal approach to semantics that assigns truth conditions to linguistic expressions using mathematical models.
Possible worlds: a framework in which meaning is defined in terms of the set of possible states of affairs in which a proposition is true.
Intension: the set of possible worlds in which a proposition is true.
Extension: the set of actual entities in the world to which a term refers.
Truth-conditional semantics: an approach to semantics that defines meaning in terms of the conditions under which a sentence is true.
Truth value: the property of being true or false.
Proposition: the content or meaning expressed by a declarative sentence, which can be true or false.
Sense and reference: the distinction between the mode of presentation of a referent and the referent itself, as discussed by Frege.
Frege's puzzle: the problem of how two co-referential expressions can differ in cognitive significance.
Description theory: a theory of reference in which definite descriptions refer by satisfying a set of properties.
Russell's theory of descriptions: a theory in which definite descriptions are analyzed as quantified expressions.
Donnellan's distinction: the distinction between referential and attributive uses of definite descriptions.
Referential use: a use of a definite description in which the speaker has a particular individual in mind.
Attributive use: a use of a definite description in which the speaker intends to refer to whoever satisfies the description.
Kaplan's indexical theory: a theory of indexical meaning that distinguishes between character and content.
Character: the rule or function that determines the content of an expression in a context.
Content: the proposition or property expressed by an expression in a particular context.
Context-sensitivity: the property of an expression whose meaning varies with the context of use.
Radical context-dependence: the property of an expression whose meaning is entirely determined by the context.
Weak context-dependence: the property of an expression whose meaning is partly determined by the context and partly by its lexical content.
Indexical expression: a word or expression whose reference depends on the context of utterance.
Demonstrative expression: a word or expression that refers to an entity by means of a deictic gesture or pointing.
Pronominal reference: the use of a pronoun to refer to an entity mentioned in the discourse.
Anaphoric reference: the use of a pronoun or expression to refer to a previously mentioned entity.
Cataphoric reference: the use of a pronoun or expression to refer to an entity that will be mentioned later.
Deictic reference: the use of an expression to refer to an entity in the physical or situational context.
Self-reference: the use of an expression to refer to itself or the speaker.
Coreference: the relationship between two expressions that refer to the same entity.
Cofunction: a relationship in which two expressions share the same grammatical function.
Collocational frame: the set of words that typically co-occur with a particular word in a particular syntactic position.
Frame semantics: a model of lexical meaning that organizes words in terms of the conceptual frames they activate.
Frame evoking: the activation of a conceptual frame by a lexical item.
Frame filling: the assignment of thematic roles to arguments within a frame.
Frame shift: a change in the frame associated with a lexical item in a particular context.
Frame network: a network of related frames that are linked by various semantic relations.
Radical frame semantics: a model of frame semantics that emphasizes the role of frames in word learning and acquisition.
Proto-role: a central or prototypical role in a frame, as opposed to peripheral or optional roles.
Radical construction: a construction that is not derivable from other constructions and must be stored as a unit.
Construction: a form-meaning pair that is a unit of grammatical knowledge in construction grammar.
Construction schema: an abstract pattern that captures the common properties of a set of constructions.
Productive construction: a construction that can be used to generate new combinations.
Idiosyncratic construction: a construction that is stored as a fixed form with a specific meaning.
Schematization: the process of abstracting a general pattern from specific examples.
Categorization: the process of grouping items into categories based on shared features.
Analogy: the process of extending a pattern from one domain to another.
Frequency effect: the influence of the frequency of a form or pattern on its processing and acquisition.
Exemplar: a specific instance of a form or pattern that serves as a model for generalization.
Prototype effect: the tendency for central or typical members of a category to be processed more easily than peripheral members.
Radical category: a category that is defined by a single set of features rather than a prototype.
Family resemblance: a pattern of category membership in which members share overlapping but not identical features.
Fuzzy boundary: a boundary of a category that is not sharp or well-defined.
Graded category: a category whose membership is a matter of degree rather than an all-or-nothing property.
Cognitive category: a category that is defined by cognitive and perceptual properties rather than formal features.
Perceptual category: a category that is defined by the perceptual properties of its members.
Functional category: a category that is defined by the function or role of its members.
Ontological category: a category that is defined by the nature or essence of its members.
Radical category membership: the process of determining whether an item belongs to a category.
Radical prototype: the most central or typical member of a category.
Radical periphery: the most peripheral or atypical members of a category.
Radical extension: the process of extending a category to include new members.
Radical reduction: the process of narrowing a category to exclude certain members.
Radical shift: the process of a category changing its prototype or boundary over time.
Radical reorganization: the process of a category being restructured into a new form.
Radical restructuring: the process of a category being reorganized into a different structure.
Radical remapping: the process of a category being mapped onto a different conceptual domain.
Radical recategorization: the process of an item being moved from one category to another.
Radical reclassification: the process of a category being reclassified into a different system.
Radical redefinition: the process of a category being given a new definition.
Radical recontextualization: the process of a category being interpreted in a new context.
