response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language that can change the meaning of a word.
Allophone: A variant form of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight used to measure syllable structure, roughly equivalent to the length of a short vowel.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a sequence of speech, typically having a peak of sonority.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the vowel nucleus within a syllable.
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the vowel nucleus within a syllable.
Nucleus: The most sonorous segment of a syllable, typically a vowel.
Aspirated: A consonant pronounced with a noticeable burst of air following its release.
Voiced: A sound produced with the regular vibration of the vocal folds.
Voiceless: A sound produced without vibration of the vocal folds.
Dental: A place of articulation in which the tongue tip or blade touches the upper teeth.
Alveolar: A place of articulation in which the tongue tip touches the alveolar ridge behind the upper teeth.
Palatal: A place of articulation in which the body of the tongue approaches the hard palate.
Velar: A place of articulation in which the back of the tongue contacts the soft palate.
Uvular: A place of articulation in which the back of the tongue contacts the uvula.
Pharyngeal: A place of articulation in which the back of the tongue or epiglottis contacts the pharyngeal wall.
Glottal: A place of articulation involving the vocal folds at the glottis.
Labial: A place of articulation involving the lips, either bilabial or labiodental.
Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel, creating turbulent airflow.
Stop: A consonant produced by completely obstructing the airflow and then releasing it.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a stop and releases into a fricative at the same place of articulation.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing airflow through the nasal cavity.
Lateral: A consonant in which airflow is directed around the sides of the tongue.
Trill: A consonant produced by the vibration of an articulator, such as the tongue tip or vocal folds.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single brief contact of the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge.
Vowel: A speech sound produced without significant constriction in the vocal tract.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a constriction or complete closure in the vocal tract.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable.
Triphthong: A vowel sequence that glides through three vowel positions within a single syllable.
Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel sound, the most common vowel in many languages, represented as /ə/.
Creaky voice: A vocal fold configuration producing a low, rough, creaky quality in the voice, also called vocal fry.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing permissible sound sequences and combinations in a particular language.
Minimal pair: Two words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating that the phonemes are distinct.
Complementary distribution: A relationship in which two or more variants of a sound never occur in the same phonetic environment.
Free variation: A relationship in which two or more phonetic forms may be used interchangeably in the same environment without changing meaning.
Tone: A distinctive use of pitch on a syllable that serves to differentiate lexical items or grammatical categories.
Pitch accent: A system in which pitch is used on specific syllables within a word to distinguish meanings, rather than on every syllable.
Suprasegmental: Features of speech that extend over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, and intonation.
Stress: The relative prominence given to a syllable within a word or phrase, marked by increases in loudness, pitch, or duration.
Prosody: The rhythm, stress, and intonation patterns of spoken language.
Intonation: The variation of pitch across a phrase or sentence, used to convey attitude, question, or statement.
Phonological rule: A systematic pattern describing how phonemes alternate in specific phonetic contexts.
Phonemic: Pertaining to the study of phonemes and their distribution in a language.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or a grammatical function.
Allomorph: A variant phonetic form of a morpheme, such as the different sounds of the English plural morpheme /s/, /z/, /ɪz/.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries its primary lexical meaning and to which affixes can be attached.
Affix: A morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Prefix: An affix attached to the beginning of a word or stem.
Suffix: An affix attached to the end of a word or stem.
Infix: An affix inserted within the root or stem of a word.
Circumfix: A morpheme that surrounds a stem, consisting of both a prefix and a suffix.
Inflection: A morphological process that changes a word to express a grammatical category such as tense, number, or case.
Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word from an existing one, often changing the part of speech.
Agglutination: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes with relatively clear boundaries.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single affix can encode multiple grammatical categories simultaneously.
Isolating: A morphological type in which morphemes are typically one-to-one with words, with little or no affixation.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which words are formed by combining many morphemes into complex, often clause-sized units.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to another morpheme.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as a root.
Compounding: A morphological process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to form a new word.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a morpheme is repeated to express grammatical meaning.
Portmanteau: A single morpheme that simultaneously expresses multiple grammatical categories, such as the English ending "-ing."
Clipping: A word-formation process in which a longer word is shortened, such as "gym" from "gymnasium."
Blending: A word-formation process that combines parts of two words into one, such as "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch."
Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the rules and principles by which words are combined to form phrases and sentences.
Constituent: A word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a syntactic structure.
Head: The central element of a phrase that determines the phrase's category and core meaning.
Complement: A constituent required by a head to complete its meaning or grammatical structure.
Specifier: A constituent that appears before the head in a phrase and modifies or determines it.
Modifier: A constituent that adds descriptive information to a head without being required by it.
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, potentially including determiners, adjectives, and other modifiers.
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its complements and modifiers.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing a subject and a predicate (verb phrase), which may be independent or dependent.
Sentence: A syntactic unit that expresses a complete thought and can stand independently.
Subordinate clause: A clause that cannot stand alone as a complete sentence and depends on a main clause.
Main clause: An independent clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence.
Coordination: A syntactic process in which two or more elements of the same rank are joined, typically by a conjunction.
Subordination: A syntactic process in which one clause is embedded within another as a dependent element.
Embedding: The syntactic process of placing one clause or phrase inside another.
Recursion: The property of grammar that allows a structure to contain another instance of the same type of structure, enabling infinite sentence length.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence.
X-bar theory: A framework in generative syntax that describes the internal structure of phrases as having specifier, head, and complement positions.
Case: A grammatical category that marks the syntactic role of a noun or pronoun in a sentence, such as nominative, accusative, or genitive.
Agreement: A syntactic process in which one word changes form to match properties of another, such as subject-verb agreement.
Binding: A principle in syntax governing the relationship between an anaphoric expression and its antecedent.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument of a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, or Experiencer.
A-movement: A type of syntactic movement of arguments that preserves theta roles, such as passivization.
A-bar movement: A type of syntactic movement that bypasses normal argument positions, such as wh-movement in questions.
Trace: An invisible element left in a syntactic structure at the original position of a moved constituent.
Empty category: A theoretically posited silent element in a syntactic structure, such as PRO or a null subject.
PRO: A null pronoun that appears in the subject position of an infinitival clause, such as in "John seems to be smart."
Semantics: The branch of linguistics that studies meaning in language, including the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Lexical semantics: The study of meaning at the level of individual words and their relations to one another.
Sense: A distinct meaning or interpretation of a polysemous word.
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word or form has multiple related senses.
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two distinct words have the same form but unrelated meanings.
Synonymy: The relationship between words that have the same or very similar meanings.
Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite meanings.
Hypernym: A word whose meaning is broader and encompasses the meaning of another word, such as "animal" for "dog."
Hyponym: A word whose meaning is more specific and is encompassed by a broader word, such as "dog" under "animal."
Meronym: A word that denotes a part of a whole, such as "wheel" in relation to "car."
Holonym: A word that denotes a whole composed of parts, such as "car" in relation to "wheel."
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one statement guarantees the truth of another.
Contradiction: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one statement guarantees the falsity of another.
Presupposition: A proposition that is taken for granted or assumed to be true for a statement to be interpretable.
Connotation: The associated or implied meaning of a word beyond its literal or dictionary definition.
Denotation: The literal, primary, or dictionary meaning of a word.
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one thing is described in terms of another based on perceived similarity.
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a thing is referred to by something associated with it, such as "the White House" for the U.S. government.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics that studies how context contributes to the interpretation of meaning in communication.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action, such as promising, ordering, or requesting, in addition to conveying information.
Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful utterance with a specific propositional content.
Illocutionary act: The intended force or function of an utterance, such as a request, warning, or declaration.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the listener, such as persuading, shocking, or comforting.
Implicature: A meaning that is communicated indirectly, beyond the literal content of an utterance, inferred by the listener.
Gricean maxims: Four conversational principles proposed by H.P. Grice: Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner.
Cooperative principle: Grice's assumption that participants in a conversation generally aim to be cooperative and informative.
Deixis: Words or expressions whose interpretation depends on the context of the utterance, such as "here," "now," "I," and "this."
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity in discourse.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an entity that will be mentioned later in discourse.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity in the world or discourse it points to.
Coreference: The phenomenon in which two or more expressions in a text or discourse refer to the same entity.
Discourse: The study of language as it is used in extended communication beyond the individual sentence.
Topic: The entity or subject that a discourse is "about" or centered on.
Focus: The element in a sentence or discourse that carries new or contrastive information.
Information structure: The organization of a discourse or sentence into given (old) and new (focus) information.
Given-new: A principle of discourse organization stating that sentences typically begin with given information and end with new information.
Paradigm: A set of related word forms that exhibit a particular grammatical pattern, such as verb conjugations.
Morphology: The branch of linguistics that studies the structure, formation, and classification of words and morphemes.
Lexicon: The mental dictionary or inventory of words and their associated information in a speaker's mind.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of lexical meaning that encompasses all inflected forms of a particular word.
Lexical entry: The complete set of information stored in the mental lexicon for a particular word, including phonology, semantics, and syntax.
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, which may be a root or a derived form.
Inflectional class: A group of words that share the same set of inflectional endings or patterns.
Generative grammar: The theoretical framework, initiated by Noam Chomsky, that describes language in terms of finite rules generating an infinite set of sentences.
Transformational grammar: A model of syntax in which base structures are transformed by rules to derive surface forms of sentences.
Universal Grammar: The theory that all human languages share certain innate structural properties and principles.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans, particularly children, learn and internalize a language.
Critical period: The hypothesized window of time during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and completely.
Language death: The loss of a language when its last native speaker dies and it is no longer used.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually abandons one language in favor of another.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region, social group, or community of speakers.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, such as a class, profession, or age group.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language.
Creole: A natural, fully developed language that evolves from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular communicative situation or context, such as formal or informal.
Code-switching: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or language varieties within a single conversation.
Bilingualism: The ability to use two languages, either simultaneously or in alternation.
Multilingualism: The use or knowledge of more than two languages by an individual or community.
Diglossia: A situation in which two distinct varieties of a language are used in complementary social domains, often with different prestige levels.
Prestige: The perceived social value or high status associated with a particular language variety.
Stigma: Negative social evaluation or disapproval attached to a particular language variety or feature.
Isogloss: A geographical boundary line separating regions where different linguistic features are used.
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects across a region in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible but distant ones may not be.
Reconstruction: The process of hypothesizing the features of a proto-language by comparing its daughter languages.
Comparative method: The primary technique of historical linguistics for reconstructing proto-languages through systematic sound correspondences.
Sound change: A systematic shift in the phonetic realization of a sound over time within a language.
Regularity: The principle that sound changes apply systematically and consistently across all eligible words in a language.
Irregularity: A deviation from the expected regular pattern of sound change or morphological alternation in a language.
Fossilization: The preservation of an older linguistic form that no longer participates in the current productive grammar of a language.
Borrowing: The process by which a language adopts words or structures from another language.
Loanword: A word taken from one language and incorporated into the vocabulary of another.
Calque: A word or phrase that is a direct translation of a word or expression from another language, built with native morphemes.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words and their meanings.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of related languages is believed to have descended.
Cognitive linguistics: An approach to linguistics that emphasizes the role of general cognitive processes in language use and understanding.
Conceptual metaphor: A cognitive mapping from one domain of experience to another, such as "time is money."
Frame semantics: A theory of meaning that interprets word meanings in terms of structured situations or "frames" of knowledge.
Prototype: A central, most typical example of a category that serves as a reference point for membership judgments.
Cognitive grammar: A linguistic framework developed by Ronald Langacker that analyzes grammar in terms of conceptual structures.
Usage-based: An approach to linguistics that explains grammatical structure in terms of frequency, generalization, and exemplar-based processing.
Embodiment: The principle in cognitive linguistics that language and meaning are grounded in bodily experience and perception.
Grounding: The anchoring of linguistic meaning in physical, perceptual, and motor experience.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large collections of real-world texts, called corpora, often analyzed with computational tools.
Computational linguistics: The use of computational methods to model, process, and analyze natural language.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurobiological factors that enable humans to acquire, use, and understand language.
Neurolinguistics: The study of the neural mechanisms and brain structures underlying language processing and production.
Discourse analysis: The study of language in extended texts and conversations, focusing on coherence, structure, and social function.
Text linguistics: The study of the internal structure and organization of texts as units larger than the sentence.
Stylistics: The study of the properties and effects of language use in literary and other textual contexts.
Rhetoric: The art and study of persuasive and effective language use, particularly in public speaking and writing.
Onomastics: The study of proper names, their origins, meanings, and the conventions governing their use.
Lexicography: The practice and study of compiling dictionaries and organizing lexical information.
Morphophonemics: The study of the interaction between morphological structure and phonological form.
Prosody: The system of rhythmic, stress, and intonational patterns in a language that conveys meaning at the phrase and sentence level.
Allomorphy: The phenomenon in which a single morpheme has multiple phonetic realizations depending on context.
Morpho-phonology: The study of the interactions and mutual influence between morphological and phonological systems.
Agreement: The grammatical process by which one element changes form to correspond to features of another element, such as number or gender.
Case government: The process by which a verb, preposition, or other head determines the case marking of its arguments.
Valency: The number and type of arguments required or licensed by a predicate, such as the transitivity of a verb.
Subcategorization: The specification of the syntactic frames in which a particular word or expression can appear.
Government: A syntactic relationship in which one element licenses the presence and form of another in its structure.
Isomorphism: A one-to-one correspondence between the morphological structure of a word and its semantic content.
Parasynthesis: A type of borrowing in which a word is both borrowed and calqued simultaneously from the source language.
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix, such as "edit" from "editor."
Conversion: A word-formation process in which a word changes its part of speech without adding an affix, such as "to google."
Paraphrase: A restatement of a text or passage using different words while preserving the original meaning.
Collocation: A statistically significant co-occurrence of words or phrases, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Phraseme: A fixed or semi-fixed multi-word expression that functions as a single unit, such as "by and large."
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its individual components.
Tautology: The use of redundant words or phrases that say the same thing, such as "absolutely essential."
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsher, blunt, or offensive one.
Dysphemism: A deliberately harsh, negative, or unpleasant term used where a neutral or positive term would otherwise apply.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression, or a word given a new meaning.
Archaism: A word, phrase, or usage that is no longer in common use but may appear in historical or formal contexts.
Malapropism: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, often resulting in a humorous or absurd effect.
Syllepsis: The use of a word to apply to two or more other words in different senses, such as "I and my brother brought our cars and our pride."
Zeugma: A figure of speech in which one word is used to connect two or more elements that it governs in different ways.
Metathesis: A sound change or word-formation process in which the order of sounds is reversed, such as "ask" from an older "orsk."
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound or syllable in speech, such as "gonna" for "going to."
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which two similar sounds become less alike, often by separation or change.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound or letter within a word, such as the /t/ in "water" in some dialects.
Lenition: A historical or diachronic process of sound weakening, such as the softening of plosives into fricatives.
Fortition: A historical process of sound strengthening, the opposite of lenition.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound changes to become less similar to a nearby identical or similar sound.
Vowel harmony: A phonological pattern in which all vowels in a word share a particular feature, such as frontness or roundedness.
Tone sandhi: The phonological process in which the tone of a syllable changes due to the influence of neighboring tones.
Prosodic hierarchy: The nested structural organization of speech into levels: segment, syllable, prosodic word, phrase, and utterance.
Prosodic word: A level in the prosodic hierarchy that typically corresponds to a lexical word and its clitics.
Phrasal accent: A prosodic feature marking a phrase boundary or a group of words that form a prosodic unit.
Enclitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a following word but syntactically independent.
Proclitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a preceding word but syntactically independent.
Clitic: A morpheme that is syntactically free but phonologically bound to an adjacent word.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that is expressed by the absence of any overt form, such as the English past tense "-ed" in "go" to "went" (irregular) or the plural in some languages with no suffix.
Suppletion: The use of an entirely different root to express an inflectional or derivational relationship, such as "go" and "went."
Productivity: The degree to which a particular morphological or syntactic pattern is actively used to form new items in a language.
Obligation: A semantic or syntactic property requiring a certain element or feature to be present, such as a verb requiring a direct object.
Selectional restriction: A semantic constraint on the types of arguments a predicate can combine with, such as "drink" requiring a liquid.
Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal structure of an event, such as perfective, imperfective, or progressive.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speaking, such as past, present, or future.
Mood: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the event, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Voice: A grammatical category expressing the relationship between the verb's arguments, such as active, passive, or middle.
Determiner: A word that specifies the definiteness or quantity of a noun, such as "the," "a," or "some."
Article: A type of determiner indicating definiteness or indefiniteness, such as "the" and "a/an" in English.
Pronoun: A word that substitutes for a noun or noun phrase, such as "he," "it," or "they."
Pronominalization: The syntactic process of replacing a noun phrase with a pronoun.
Pronominal: Relating to or involving pronouns.
Coreference: The phenomenon in which two or more expressions in a discourse refer to the same entity.
Antecedent: The noun phrase or entity to which a pronoun or anaphoric expression refers.
Bound variable: A variable in formal semantics or syntax whose value is determined by a quantifier or operator in the structure.
Free variable: A variable not bound by any operator, whose value is determined by context or assignment.
Quantifier: An expression that specifies the quantity or scope of a set, such as "all," "some," "every," or "no."
Scope: The range over which a quantifier or other operator is interpreted in a sentence.
Ambiguity: A property of an utterance having two or more plausible interpretations.
Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a word having multiple senses.
Structural ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from the multiple syntactic structures an utterance can have.
Vagueness: A property of a word or expression lacking precise boundaries, such as "tall" or "old."
Presupposition: A background assumption that must be true for a sentence to be felicitous or interpretable.
Speech-act theory: A framework for analyzing language as a system of actions performed through utterances.
Conversational implicature: An indirect meaning inferred by a listener based on the assumption that the speaker is being cooperative.
Conventional implicature: A meaning contributed by a specific word or expression that is not part of its truth-conditional content.
Gricean maxims: The four conversational principles of Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner proposed by Paul Grice.
Maxim of quantity: The conversational principle of being as informative as required and not more than required.
Maxim of quality: The conversational principle of being truthful and not asserting what one lacks evidence for.
Maxim of relation: The conversational principle of being relevant to the ongoing topic of conversation.
Maxim of manner: The conversational principle of being clear, orderly, and avoiding ambiguity.
Deictic: Pertaining to expressions whose reference depends on the situational context of the utterance.
Indexical: A linguistic expression that points to or indicates something in the context of the utterance, such as a demonstrative.
Demonstrative: A word that points to a specific entity relative to the speaker, such as "this," "that," "these," or "those."
Interrogative: A word or construction used to form a question, such as "what," "where," "who," or "how."
Negation: The grammatical expression of the falsity or non-occurrence of a proposition, such as "not" or "no."
Double negation: The use of two negations in a sentence, which in standard logic cancels out but in some dialects reinforces a negative meaning.
Contrast: The highlighting of a difference between two or more elements in a discourse or sentence.
Topic-comment: A discourse structure in which a topic (old information) is presented followed by a comment (new information) about it.
Thematic: Relating to the topic of a discourse, the entity that the utterance is about.
Rhematic: Relating to the focus or comment in a sentence, the new information being asserted about the topic.
Cleft sentence: A sentence structure that emphasizes a particular constituent, such as "It was John who broke the vase."
Pseudo-cleft: A type of cleft construction beginning with "what," such as "What I need is coffee."
Extraposition: A syntactic process in which a clause or phrase is moved to the end of a sentence, such as "It is likely that he will come."
Expletive: A syntactically required but semantically empty element, such as "it" in "It is raining."
Light verb: A verb with little or no independent lexical meaning that relies on its complement for content, such as "give" in "give a sigh."
Lexical gap: A slot in a paradigm where a language lacks a form that other languages have, such as English lacking a future perfect passive progressive.
Morphological productivity: The tendency of a morphological pattern to be extended to new words in ongoing use.
Paradigmatic: Relating to the vertical axis of linguistic choice, where a speaker selects from a set of alternatives in a given slot.
Syntagmatic: Relating to the horizontal axis of linguistic combination, where elements are strung together in sequence.
Langue: In Saussurean linguistics, the abstract, systematic structure of a language shared by a speech community.
Parole: In Saussurean linguistics, the individual, concrete act of speaking by a particular speaker.
Sign: In Saussurean linguistics, the arbitrary union of a signifier (sound form) and a signified (concept).
Signifier: The physical form of a linguistic sign, such as the sound pattern or written form of a word.
Signified: The mental concept or meaning associated with a linguistic sign.
Arbitrariness: The principle that the relationship between a linguistic sign and its referent is conventional and not inherently motivated.
Distinctiveness: The property of a linguistic sign that makes it different from all other signs in the system.
System: The totality of interrelated elements in a language, where the value of each element is determined by its difference from others.
Value: In Saussurean linguistics, the precise meaning of a sign as determined by its relationship to other signs in the system.
Merism: A rhetorical device that refers to a whole by naming its parts, such as "hands and feet" for "body."
Chiasmus: A rhetorical structure in which the second half parallels the first in reverse order, such as "Never let a fool kiss me or a kiss fool me."
Anadiplosis: A rhetorical device in which the last word or phrase of one clause is repeated at the beginning of the next.
Epistrophe: A rhetorical device in which the same word or phrase is repeated at the end of successive clauses.
Anaphora (rhetorical): A rhetorical device in which the same word or phrase is repeated at the beginning of successive clauses.
Aporia: A rhetorical device in which a speaker expresses feigned uncertainty or doubt.
Litotes: A form of understatement in which an affirmative is expressed by negating its opposite, such as "not bad" for "good."
Hyperbole: A rhetorical device using deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect.
Synecdoche: A figure of speech in which a part is used to represent the whole or vice versa, such as "all hands on deck."
Metalepsis: A rhetorical or narrative device in which a shift occurs between different levels of representation or reality.
Pleonasm: The use of more words than necessary to express an idea, sometimes for emphasis.
Tmesis: The splitting of a compound word or phrase by the insertion of other words, such as "ab-so-lutely."
Apocope: The loss of a sound or letter at the end of a word, such as "ad" from "adverb."
Syncope: The loss of a sound or letter from the middle of a word, such as "mus" from "must."
Apheresis: The loss of a sound or letter at the beginning of a word, such as "egg" from an older "æg."
Diphthongization: A historical sound change in which a single vowel becomes a diphthong.
Monophthongization: A historical sound change in which a diphthong becomes a single vowel.
Palatalization: A sound change in which a consonant becomes more palatal in place of articulation, often due to the influence of a neighboring front vowel.
Umlaut: A type of vowel harmony or sound change in which a back vowel is fronted due to the influence of a following front vowel or consonant.
Vowel breaking: A historical sound change in Germanic languages in which a pure vowel became a diphthong under certain conditions.
Umlaut: A Germanic sound change in which a stem vowel was fronted by the presence of a palatal or fronting suffix.
Dialectology: The study of the geographical and social distribution of dialects and linguistic variation.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and language attitudes.
Ethnolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and culture, particularly in non-Western or indigenous communities.
Linguistic anthropology: The study of language in its cultural and social context, encompassing variation, change, and structure.
Typology: The comparative study of the structural features and typological patterns found across the world's languages.
Universal: A linguistic property or constraint that holds across all or nearly all natural languages.
Isolate: A language with no known genetic relationship to any other language.
Sprachbund: A group of geographically adjacent languages that share features due to prolonged contact rather than common descent.
Language family: A group of languages that descend from a common ancestral proto-language.
Language isolate: A language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other known language.
Genetic relationship: The historical relatedness of languages through descent from a common ancestor.
Are
al feature: A linguistic feature shared by languages in a geographical region due to contact rather than common descent.
Contact linguistics: The study of the effects of language contact on the structure and development of languages.
Substrate: The influence of a previously spoken language on a later, dominant language in the same region.
Superstrate: The influence of a newer, dominant language on a previously spoken language in the same region.
Adstrate: The influence of a neighboring, contemporaneous language on another through contact.
Language drift: The gradual, unconscious change in a language's features due to prolonged contact with another language.
Interference: The influence of one language on the speech of a bilingual speaker, often manifesting as errors or transfer.
Transfer: The application of rules or features from one language to another in bilingual speech.
Backsliding: The process by which a second language, once acquired, is lost or regressed due to reduced exposure.
Language revitalization: Efforts to increase the number of speakers and the vitality of a declining or endangered language.
Endangered language: A language at risk of falling out of use, often with few remaining speakers and limited intergenerational transmission.
Language documentation: The systematic recording and description of a language, particularly one at risk of being lost.
Fieldwork: The process of collecting linguistic data directly from speakers in the community, often for documentation purposes.
Elicitation: The method of drawing out linguistic data from speakers through questions, prompts, or structured tasks.
Introspection: The use of a linguist's own intuition and native-speaker knowledge to judge the grammaticality of sentences.
Grammaticality: The property of a sentence or expression of conforming to the grammatical rules of a language.
Acceptability: The judgment by a speaker of how natural or natural-sounding a sentence is, which may differ from strict grammaticality.
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts used for linguistic analysis and research.
Corpus tagging: The process of annotating corpus data with grammatical, semantic, or syntactic labels for computational analysis.
Token: A single instance of a word or linguistic form in a text or corpus.
Type: An abstract word form that subsumes all its individual instances (tokens) in a text or corpus.
Token-type ratio: The ratio of the number of unique words (types) to the total number of words (tokens) in a text, used as a measure of vocabulary richness.
Zipf's law: The empirical observation that the frequency of a word in a text is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency table.
Collocational analysis: The study of the statistical co-occurrence patterns of words in a corpus.
Distributional semantics: An approach to word meaning that defines semantics based on the contexts in which a word appears.
Vector space model: A computational method of representing words as vectors based on the contexts in which they co-occur.
Word embedding: A method of representing words as dense numerical vectors that capture semantic and syntactic relationships.
Natural language processing: The field of computer science focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
Parsing: The process of analyzing a sentence to determine its grammatical structure and constituent relationships.
Morphological analysis: The process of segmenting a word into its constituent morphemes and identifying their grammatical roles.
Part-of-speech tagging: The computational process of assigning grammatical categories, such as noun, verb, or adjective, to words in a text.
Named entity recognition: The computational task of identifying and classifying proper names and other entities in text, such as persons, places, and organizations.
Discourse representation: A formal framework for representing the semantic content of a discourse, tracking entities, events, and their relations.
Model-theoretic semantics: An approach to formal semantics that interprets linguistic expressions in terms of mathematical models or possible worlds.
Possible worlds semantics: A framework in formal semantics that evaluates the truth of propositions across sets of possible worlds.
Intensional semantics: A semantic framework that treats meanings as functions from possible worlds to extensions, accounting for modal and intensional contexts.
Extensional semantics: A semantic framework in which the meaning of an expression is its referent or truth value in the actual world.
Montague semantics: A formal semantic framework developed by Richard Montague that treats natural language with the mathematical tools of formal logic.
Lambda calculus: A formal system of function application, variable binding, and substitution used in formal semantics and type theory.
Type theory: A formal system in which every expression has a type, used in semantics to ensure well-formedness of semantic combinations.
Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to meaning that defines the semantic content of an expression in terms of the conditions under which it is true.
Event semantics: An approach to semantics that represents the meaning of sentences in terms of structured events or situations.
Situation semantics: A framework in which the meaning of a sentence is evaluated relative to a set of possible situations rather than possible worlds.
Dynamic semantics: An approach to the semantics of discourse in which the meaning of an utterance updates a context or information state.
Discourse representation theory: A framework for representing the meaning of discourse through structured tables of events, entities, and their conditions.
Anaphoric binding: The syntactic and semantic relationship between a pronoun or anaphor and its antecedent.
Referential ambiguity: The uncertainty about which entity a referring expression points to in a given context.
Quantifier scope ambiguity: Ambiguity arising when a quantifier can take scope over or under another quantifier in a sentence.
Conditionality: The semantic and pragmatic study of conditional sentences, including their truth conditions and inference patterns.
Modality: The grammatical and semantic expression of possibility, necessity, permission, obligation, or desire.
Epistemic modality: Modality expressing the speaker's degree of certainty or evidence about a proposition, such as "might" or "must."
Deontic modality: Modality expressing obligation, permission, or prohibition, such as "should," "may," or "must."
Bouletic modality: Modality expressing desire, want, or intention, such as "I want to go."
Dynamic modality: Modality expressing physical or psychological ability, such as "can" in "I can lift that."
Subjunctive: A verb mood used to express hypothetical, desired, or non-actual situations.
Optative: A mood or construction expressing a wish or hope.
Imperative: A sentence mood used to issue commands, requests, or instructions.
Jussive: A grammatical mood expressing commands, requests, or wishes, particularly in African languages.
Cooperative principle: The assumed principle of conversation that participants will make their contributions appropriate to the purpose of the exchange.
Conversational implicature: An indirect meaning derived from a speaker's presumed adherence to conversational maxims.
Gricean flouting: The deliberate violation of a conversational maxim to generate an implicature, such as saying "What a calm sea!" during a storm.
Conversational implicature: A meaning that is not part of the literal content but is inferred from the conversational context and maxims.
Scalar implicature: An implicature arising from the use of a weaker term on a scale, such as "some" implying "not all."
Horn scale: A linguistic scale of strength, such as all > most > some > a few, used to generate scalar implicatures.
Reverse Horn scale: A scale of weakness, such as a few < some < most < all, used in negative contexts to generate implicatures.
Free choice: A property of certain quantifiers, such as "any," that can be interpreted in questions and negative contexts without specific reference.
Free variable: A pronoun or quantifier whose referent is not fixed by a specific antecedent, such as "any" in "Anyone can come."
Bounded quantifier: A quantifier whose scope is limited by the domain of discourse or a specific context.
Maximizing: The process of assigning the most specific or informative interpretation to a quantifier or expression in context.
Minimizing: The process of assigning the least specific or least informative interpretation, often in negative or restrictive contexts.
Sensitivity: The property of a linguistic expression whose interpretation is affected by the syntactic or semantic environment.
Context sensitivity: The dependence of an expression's interpretation on the surrounding discourse or situational context.
Indexical context: The set of parameters, such as speaker, time, and location, that determine the interpretation of indexical expressions.
Salience: The degree to which an entity or concept is prominent in a discourse or the cognitive context.
Accessibility: The ease with which a referent can be identified or brought to mind in a given discourse context.
Given: Information in a discourse that is assumed to be known or recoverable by the listener.
New: Information in a discourse that is not previously established and is being introduced to the listener.
Focus marking: The linguistic means, such as intonation, particles, or word order, used to signal the focus of an utterance.
Contrastive focus: A focus that highlights a difference between the focused element and a set of alternatives.
Information-focus: A focus that signals new information being added to the discourse.
Corpus-based: An approach to linguistics that relies on the analysis of large collections of naturally occurring texts.
Experimental: An approach to linguistics that uses controlled experiments to test hypotheses about language processing, acquisition, or use.
Judgment: A speaker's or researcher's assessment of the grammaticality, acceptability, or meaning of a linguistic example.
Paraphrase test: A method of testing synonymy or entailment by checking whether two sentences can be restated in each other's terms.
Substitution test: A method of testing whether two expressions are interchangeable in a given context without changing meaning.
Deletion test: A method of identifying syntactic constituents by checking whether they can be omitted from a sentence.
Clefting test: A syntactic test for constituenthood that involves moving a constituent into a cleft construction.
Fronting: A syntactic test or operation in which a constituent is moved to the beginning of a sentence.
Coordination test: A syntactic test for constituency that checks whether two elements can be joined by a coordinating conjunction.
Movement: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from one position in the structure to another.
Head movement: A type of syntactic movement in which a head element is moved, as in verb movement in French questions.
Feature checking: A theoretical mechanism in which syntactic features are matched and validated during the derivation of a structure.
Agreement: The process by which morphological features on one element are matched with features on another, such as number and person.
Merging: A fundamental operation in minimalist syntax in which two syntactic objects are combined into a single structure.
Move: A fundamental operation in minimalist syntax in which a syntactic object is copied from one position and inserted in another.
Derivation: The process by which a syntactic structure is built step by step through the application of operations like Merge and Move.
Convergent derivation: A syntactic derivation in which the target structure is built through a sequence of operations, each of which yields a well-formed intermediate structure.
Late insertion: A theoretical approach in which morphemes are inserted into a syntactic structure after it has been built, rather than being part of the initial structure.
Late insertion: A view in which morphological structure is determined after syntactic structure has been assembled.
Morphological insertion: The process of selecting and inserting the appropriate morphemes into a syntactic structure to satisfy their features.
Exponence: The overt phonological realization of a grammatical morpheme.
Zero morpheme: The absence of any overt phonological material where a morpheme is theoretically required.
Suppletive: A morphological relationship in which different roots are used to express a grammatical or derivational connection.
Productivity: The extent to which a grammatical pattern is actively extended to new forms by speakers.
Neologism: A newly coined word or a word assigned a new meaning, entering the lexicon through creative use.
Loan translation: A calque in which a foreign word or phrase is translated word by word into the target language.
Semantic shift: A historical change in the meaning of a word, such as broadening, narrowing, or metaphorical extension.
Semantic broadening: A change in which a word's meaning becomes more general over time, such as "bird" from "young bird" to any bird.
Semantic narrowing: A change in which a word's meaning becomes more specific over time, such as "meat" from any food to animal flesh.
Metaphorical extension: A semantic change in which a word's meaning expands to a new domain based on perceived similarity.
Pejoration: A semantic change in which a word's connotation becomes more negative over time.
Amelioration: A semantic change in which a word's connotation becomes more positive over time.
Taboo: A social prohibition against using a particular word, often replaced by euphemisms.
Euphemism replacement: The cyclical process by which a euphemism becomes the standard term and then itself requires a new euphemism.
Register variation: Differences in language use corresponding to different social or communicative situations.
Formality: The degree to which language conforms to the conventions of a particular social or communicative setting.
Colloquialism: A word or expression used in informal, everyday speech rather than in formal or literary language.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession, group, or community.
Slang: Informal, often nonstandard vocabulary that is characteristic of a particular group, era, or subculture.
Argot: A specialized, often secretive vocabulary used by a particular group, historically associated with criminal or underworld speech.
Cant: A form of argot or coded speech used to maintain secrecy within a group.
Pigeon English: An informal term for a simplified or pidginized form of English used in contact situations.
Broken language: An informal term for a non-native speaker's imperfect use of a language, though linguistically it is a valid variety.
Idiolect: The unique language variety of an individual speaker, incorporating their personal grammatical, lexical, and phonological choices.
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects across a region where neighboring dialects are mutually intelligible but extreme ends may not be.
Standard language: A variety of a language that has been codified and is used in education, media, and formal institutions.
High variety: In a diglossic situation, the prestige variety used in formal, literary, and educational contexts.
Low variety: In a diglossic situation, the colloquial variety used in everyday, informal communication.
Lingua franca: A language used as a common means of communication between groups that speak different native languages.
Esperanto: A constructed international auxiliary language designed in the 19th century to facilitate communication among speakers of different native languages.
Constructed language: A language deliberately designed and created by individuals or groups, as opposed to a naturally evolved language.
Artificial language: A language invented for specific purposes, such as literary works (Klingon, Elvish) or communication (Esperanto).
Planned language: A constructed language designed to serve as a means of communication, such as Esperanto or Interlingua.
Auxiliary language: A constructed language designed to supplement or facilitate communication between speakers of different native languages.
International auxiliary language: A language created to serve as a common means of communication in international contexts.
Sign language: A natural language that uses manual gestures, facial expressions, and body movements as its primary mode of communication.
Manualism: The view that sign languages are natural languages with their own grammatical structure, independent of spoken language.
Phonology of sign language: The study of the distinctive manual, spatial, and non-manual parameters that serve as the building blocks of sign language.
Morphology of sign language: The study of how meaning is built through combinations of handshapes, locations, movements, and non-manual markers.
Syntax of sign language: The study of the rules governing the combination of signs into phrases and sentences in sign languages.
Bimodal: Pertaining to languages that use both a manual (visual-spatial) and an oral (auditory) modality, such as the interaction of sign and spoken language.
Code-blending: The process of combining elements from two or more languages within a single utterance, often by bilingual speakers.
Intralingual code-switching: Switching between different varieties or registers of the same language within a conversation.
Intersentential switching: Code-switching that occurs at sentence boundaries, with each sentence in a different language.
Intrasentential switching: Code-switching that occurs within a single sentence, mixing elements from different languages.
Tag-switching: The insertion of a short phrase or tag from one language into a sentence in another, such as "No mames."
Language mixing: The broader phenomenon of combining linguistic elements from two or more languages in the speech of bilingual or multilingual speakers.
L1: The first language, or native language, acquired by a speaker in early childhood.
L2: The second language, acquired after the first language, which may be a foreign or additional language.
L3: A third language acquired by a speaker who is already bilingual or multilingual.
Interlanguage: The developing linguistic system of a second language learner, which is neither the L1 nor the target L2 but an evolving system.
Fossilization: The process by which certain errors or features in a learner's interlanguage become fixed and resistant to further development.
Overgeneralization: A language acquisition process in which a regular rule is applied too broadly, such as "goed" for "went."
Undergeneralization: A language acquisition process in which a rule is applied too narrowly, such as using "man" instead of "people."
Nativization: The process by which a learner's interlanguage becomes increasingly similar to the target language through overgeneralization of target rules.
Overtransfer: The application of L1 rules to L2 production, leading to errors in the second language.
Undertransfer: The failure to apply a rule that exists in both L1 and L2, often because the learner has not yet identified the rule.
Native speaker: A speaker who acquired a language as their first language in early childhood and uses it as their primary means of communication.
Fluent speaker: A speaker who can use a language with considerable ease and proficiency, regardless of whether it is their L1 or L2.
Bilingual: A person who can use two languages, either simultaneously or in alternation, to a functional degree.
Balanced bilingual: A speaker who has roughly equal proficiency in both of their languages.
Dominant bilingual: A speaker who has significantly greater proficiency in one of their two languages.
Additive bilingualism: The acquisition of a second language that adds to and does not replace the first language.
Subtractive bilingualism: The acquisition of a second language that comes at the expense of the first language, leading to L1 attrition.
Language attrition: The gradual loss or weakening of a language, typically the L1, due to reduced exposure and use.
Reactivation: The process of regaining proficiency in a previously acquired but dormant language.
Cognitive load: The mental effort required to process and produce language, which increases with complexity and unfamiliarity.
Processing: The real-time mental operations involved in comprehending and producing language.
Parsing: The online, real-time process of analyzing the syntactic structure of an utterance as it is heard or read.
Comprehension: The process of understanding the meaning of a spoken or written language.
Production: The process of planning, encoding, and articulating a spoken or written utterance.
Fluency: The smoothness, speed, and ease of language production without excessive pauses or breakdowns.
Accuracy: The degree to which a speaker's or writer's output conforms to the grammatical and lexical norms of the target language.
Proficiency: The overall level of skill and competence a speaker has in a language, encompassing accuracy, fluency, complexity, and range.
Complexity: The range and sophistication of grammatical structures, vocabulary, and discourse patterns used by a speaker.
Range: The variety and breadth of linguistic forms and functions a speaker can produce.
Communicative competence: The ability to use language appropriately and effectively in real communicative situations, beyond mere grammatical correctness.
Linguistic competence: The underlying knowledge of the rules, patterns, and structures of a language that a speaker possesses.
Performance: The actual use of language in real situations, which may be affected by factors such as anxiety, fatigue, or memory.
Competence-performance distinction: The theoretical distinction between a speaker's knowledge of language (competence) and its actual use (performance).
I-language: In Chomskyan theory, the internal, individual language system of a particular speaker.
E-language: In Chomskyan theory, the external, observable data or language of a speech community.
Universal Grammar: The innate, biologically endowed set of principles and parameters that constrain the possible human languages.
Parameters: The specific settings or choices that vary across languages within the space of Universal Grammar, such as the head-direction of phrases.
Principles: The invariant, universal properties of human language that do not vary across languages.
Language acquisition device: The hypothetical innate mechanism in the human brain that enables children to acquire language.
Critical period hypothesis: The theory that there is a biologically determined window during which language acquisition proceeds most effectively.
Language deprivation: The failure of a child to receive adequate linguistic input during the critical period, as illustrated by cases of feral children.
Genetic predisposition: The inherited biological factors that make humans capable of acquiring language.
Nature-nurture: The debate over the relative contributions of innate biological factors and environmental input to language acquisition.
Input: The linguistic data that a language learner is exposed to, such as the speech directed at a child.
Comprehensible input: Linguistic input that a learner can understand, slightly above their current level of competence.
Output: The linguistic data that a learner produces in speech or writing.
Negotiation of meaning: The process by which communication partners work together to resolve misunderstandings and clarify meaning.
Recasts: A type of implicit correction in which a learner's error is reformulated correctly in the response.
Scaffolding: The support provided by a more knowledgeable speaker to help a learner accomplish a communicative task.
Zone of proximal development: The range of tasks a learner can accomplish with assistance but not yet independently.
Longitudinal study: A research design that tracks language development or change over an extended period of time.
Cross-sectional study: A research design that examines language at a single point in time across different age groups or populations.
Diachronic: Pertaining to the study of language change over historical time.
Synchronic: Pertaining to the study of a language at a single point in time, without regard to its history.
Historical linguistics: The branch of linguistics that studies language change and reconstructs the history of languages.
Comparative method: The systematic comparison of related languages to identify regular sound correspondences and reconstruct proto-languages.
Sound correspondences: Systematic similarities in pronunciation between related words in different languages that indicate common descent.
Regular sound change: A sound shift that applies uniformly to all eligible words in a language, as opposed to irregular or analogical changes.
Analogy: A linguistic process in which a form is changed to match the pattern of other related forms, rather than following a regular sound change.
Analogical leveling: The process by which irregular alternations in a paradigm are smoothed out by analogy with regular patterns.
Lexical diffusion: The process by which a sound change spreads gradually through the vocabulary of a language, word by word.
Dialectal diffusion: The spread of a linguistic feature across dialect boundaries over time.
Isogloss: A geographic line separating areas where different linguistic features are used.
Linguistic geography: The study of the spatial distribution of linguistic features and their relationship to the physical and social environment.
Dialectology: The branch of linguistics that studies the geographic and social distribution of language variation.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and social factors such as class, gender, ethnicity, and region.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language using large, systematic collections of real-world texts.
Corpus-based: An approach to linguistic analysis that is grounded in the empirical data of a corpus.
Corpus-driven: An approach to linguistic analysis in which patterns are discovered inductively from corpus data rather than deduced from theory.
Concordance: A display of all occurrences of a word or phrase in a corpus, showing the surrounding context for each instance.
Collocates: Words that frequently co-occur with a given word or phrase in a corpus.
Keyword: A word or phrase that occurs significantly more frequently in one text or corpus than in a reference corpus.
Collocation profile: A list of the most frequently co-occurring words with a given target word in a corpus.
Semantic profiling: The analysis of the different meanings or uses of a word as revealed by its distributional patterns in a corpus.
Functional load: The number of distinct functions or categories that a single linguistic form is required to express.
Functional equivalence: The principle that when a form in one language is borrowed into another, the borrower may adjust the form to fit its own phonological system.
Phonological adaptation: The process by which a borrowed word is modified to conform to the phonological constraints of the borrowing language.
Morphological adaptation: The process by which a borrowed word is modified to conform to the morphological patterns of the borrowing language.
Semantic adaptation: The process by which the meaning of a borrowed word is adjusted to fit the conceptual categories of the borrowing language.
Cognate: A word in two or more languages that is derived from a common ancestral word in a proto-language.
False cognate: A pair of words in two languages that look or sound similar but have different meanings and do not share a common etymological origin.
Doublet: Two words in the same language that derive from the same ancestral root through different paths of borrowing or change.
Etymological doublet: A pair of words in the same language that descend from the same root but entered the language through different routes.
Loan translation: A calque in which a foreign word or expression is translated into the target language using native morphemes.
Borrowing: The process by which a language takes in words, morphemes, or grammatical structures from another language.
Lexical borrowing: The adoption of individual words from one language into another.
Grammatical borrowing: The adoption of grammatical patterns, such as case markers or word order, from one language to another.
Structural borrowing: The adoption of syntactic or phonological patterns from a language in prolonged contact.
Language contact: The situation in which speakers of two or more languages interact and influence each other's linguistic systems.
Contact language: A language that has developed as a result of prolonged contact between speakers of different languages, such as pidgins and creoles.
Pidginization: The process by which a simplified contact language, or pidgin, develops between groups with no shared language.
Creolization: The process by which a pidgin becomes the native language of a community and develops a full grammatical system, becoming a creole.
Post-creole: A stage in the development of a creole language after it has been established as a native language and is undergoing further change.
Relexification: A process in which a new lexicon is mapped onto an existing grammatical system, often proposed in the development of some creole languages.
Nativization: The process by which a contact or pidgin language develops native speakers and a full, complex grammatical system.
Intelligibility: The degree to which a speech variety can be understood by listeners, a key factor in distinguishing dialects from separate languages.
Mutual intelligibility: The degree to which speakers of two language varieties can understand each other, often used as a criterion for distinguishing languages from dialects.
Language: A system of communication used by a community, characterized by shared grammatical rules, vocabulary, and conventions.
Dialect: A regional or social variety of a language that is mutually intelligible with other varieties of the same language.
Idiolect: The unique linguistic system of an individual speaker, reflecting personal choices and idiosyncrasies.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular communicative situation, defined by context, audience, and purpose.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, such as a profession, class, or age group.
Ethnolect: A variety of language associated with a particular ethnic or cultural group.
Jargon: Specialized technical vocabulary used within a particular profession, field, or group.
Slang: Informal, often nonstandard vocabulary associated with a particular social group, subculture, or era.
Gamboling: A nonstandard or archaic term; in linguistics, not a standard term.

Morpho-semantic: Relating to the relationship between morphological structure and semantic content.
Morphophonological: Relating to the interaction between morphological and phonological processes.
Morphophonemic: Pertaining to the study of how morphemes affect and are affected by phonological processes.
Allophonic: Pertaining to or involving allophones, the phonetic variants of phonemes.
Phonemic: Pertaining to phonemes, the abstract contrastive units of sound in a language.

Phonological: Relating to the abstract, systematic patterns of sound in a language, as opposed to their physical properties.
Articulatory: Relating to the production of speech sounds by the organs of speech, such as the tongue, lips, and vocal folds.
Acoustic: Relating to the physical sound waves produced in speech and their measurable properties.
Perceptual: Relating to the human perception and interpretation of speech sounds.
