Sagittal: Describing the front-to-back plane of the mouth, used to describe tongue position for vowel and consonant articulation.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: The theory that the language one speaks shapes or constrains one's thought and perception of reality.
Sandbox: Not a standard linguistics term; included only to illustrate the format. (See "morpheme sandbox" in some language pedagogy contexts.)
Sibilant: A type of fricative or affricate produced with a high degree of noise at a high frequency (e.g., /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/).
Simplification: A phonological process in which a complex segment or sequence is replaced by a simpler one (e.g., cluster reduction).
Singulative: A grammatical number form that refers to one individual as part of a larger group, the opposite of the plural (used in some Bantu and other languages).
Slang: Informal, often fleeting vocabulary used by a particular social group, subculture, or profession.
Sound change: A systematic shift in the pronunciation of a language over time (e.g., the Great Vowel Shift in English).
Spondee: A metrical foot consisting of two stressed syllables (e.g., "fighting," "truth tell").
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached; it may consist of a root plus derivational affixes.
Stratum: A layer of vocabulary in a language derived from a particular source or period (e.g., the Latin stratum, the French stratum, the Anglo-Saxon stratum in English).
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or phrase, marked by greater loudness, length, or pitch.
Subjunctive: A verb mood used to express hypothetical situations, wishes, commands, or uncertainty (e.g., "I wish I were rich").
Suffix: A morpheme attached after the base or root of a word (e.g., "-ing," "-ness," "-tion").
Syllable: The basic unit of phonological structure, typically consisting of an onset, a nucleus (usually a vowel), and an optional coda.
Synchronic: The study of a language at a single point in time, as opposed to diachronic (historical) study.
Syntactic tree: A diagrammatic representation of the hierarchical structure of a sentence, showing constituent relationships.
Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the rules and principles governing the arrangement of words and phrases to form well-structured sentences.
Tactile: Relating to the sense of touch; in linguistics, sometimes used in discussions of Braille and haptic communication.
Tautology: The unnecessary repetition of meaning in different words (e.g., "free gift," "ATM machine").
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speaking (e.g., past, present, future).
Thematic: Pertaining to the topic or subject matter of discourse; in morphology, a thematic vowel (thematic morpheme) that links a verb root to its inflectional endings.
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object (e.g., "eat" in "She ate an apple").
Transliteration: The systematic conversion of text from one writing system to another, preserving phonetic values as closely as possible.
Truncation: The shortening of a word by removing part of it (e.g., "fridge" from "refrigerator").
Turkish: The language of Turkey, a Turkic language with a rich agglutinative morphology and vowel harmony.
Typology: The classification of languages according to shared structural features, regardless of genetic relationship.
Umlaut: A historical or synchronic vowel mutation triggered by a following front vowel or consonant (e.g., German "Maus" → "Mäuse").
Unaspirated: A consonant produced without a puff of air at release, contrasted with aspirated (e.g., /b/ vs. /pʰ/).
Underlying form: The abstract, pre-phonological representation of a word or morpheme before phonological rules are applied.
Underived: A word that is not derived from any other word within the same language, often considered a root.
Underspecification: The representation of a phonological or morphological element with fewer features than are needed for its full realization.
Vernacular: The everyday spoken language of a community, as opposed to a formal, literary, or liturgical register.
Vellum: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example. (More commonly a bookbinding term.)
Velar: A consonant articulated with the back of the tongue against the soft palate (velum), such as /k/, /g/, /ŋ/.
Ventriloquism: The art of making it appear that sound originates from a direction other than the speaker's mouth; tangentially related to phonetic perception.
Vernacular: The native or everyday language of a region or community, as distinct from a second language or formal register.
Verb: A word that expresses an action, state, or occurrence and serves as the predicate of a clause.
Vernacular language: The common, everyday language used in a particular community, as opposed to a learned, liturgical, or foreign language.
Vernacular: The ordinary language of a particular region or group, as opposed to a formal or standard variety.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a speech sound, distinguishing voiced from voiceless segments.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract, without significant constriction (e.g., /a/, /i/, /u/).
Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which all vowels in a word or phrase share a particular feature, such as frontness or rounding (common in Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian).
Vulgar: Pertaining to the speech of ordinary people, often with a pejorative connotation; in historical linguistics, "vulgar Latin" refers to the spoken Latin that evolved into the Romance languages.
Zero morpheme: A grammatical category marked by the absence of any overt affix (e.g., the English plural in "sheep," or the present tense in "I walk").
Zombie: Not a standard linguistics term; included only to illustrate the format of this glossary.
Zwicky: Relating to the morphological theory proposed by Arnold Zwicky and others concerning complex predicate structures.
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes, each carrying a single grammatical meaning (e.g., Turkish, Japanese, Swahili).
Analytic: A language or grammatical strategy that relies on separate words and word order rather than inflection to express grammatical relationships (e.g., Modern English, Mandarin).
Apocryphal: In historical linguistics, a form or word of uncertain or dubious authenticity, not reliably attested in the historical record.
Areal linguistics: The study of linguistic features shared by languages in geographical proximity, regardless of genetic relationship (e.g., the Balkan sprachbund).
Archaic: A word, form, or feature that belonged to an earlier period of a language and is now obsolete or restricted to formal/literary use.
Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal flow of an event (e.g., perfective, imperfective, progressive, habitual).
Aspiration: The burst of air accompanying the release of certain stops, distinguishing /pʰ/ from /p/ in languages like Hindi or Korean.
Assimilative: Describing a process or relationship in which one sound or form becomes more like another.
Attic: Pertaining to the dialect of ancient Greek spoken in Athens, considered the classical standard of the Greek language.
Austrian school: The Vienna School of linguistics (Hjelmslev, etc.) that emphasized the structural and formal aspects of language, also known as glossematics.
Auxiliary: A verb that supports the main verb to express tense, mood, voice, or aspect (e.g., "have" in "have eaten," "will" in "will go").
Balto-Slavic: The proposed common ancestral stage of the Baltic and Slavic branches of Indo-European.
Bantu: A large group of related Niger-Congo languages spoken across sub-Saharan Africa, characterized by complex noun class systems.
Bar: A symbol (|) used in prosodic phonology to mark a major prosodic boundary.
Base: The form to which an affix is attached in a derivational or inflectional process; the underlying lexical item.
Bath rule: A principle in historical linguistics (after William S. Allen) stating that a later sound change will not affect older loanwords that have already entered the language.
Bilabial: A consonant produced with both lips (e.g., /p/, /b/, /m/, /w/).
Bipolar: Describing a grammatical category with two contrasting values (e.g., the transitive/intransitive distinction).
Bivalent: Having two arguments or valency of two (e.g., a transitive verb).
Borrowing: The process by which a language takes in a word or grammatical feature from another language.
Bricolage: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example. (More commonly an art/design term.)
Broad transcription: The phonetic transcription that captures the most salient and distinctive features of speech, using fewer diacritics than narrow transcription.
Bylaw: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Calque: A loan translation in which the meaning of a foreign word or phrase is rendered element by element in the target language (e.g., "telephone" from French "téléphone").
Cangue: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Canonical: In phonology, the prototypical or unmarked form of a pattern, as contrasted with marked or exceptional forms.
Catenative: Describing a verb construction in which one verb takes another as its complement (e.g., "begin to sleep," "try to leave").
Celtic: The branch of Indo-European languages including Irish, Welsh, Breton, Scottish Gaelic, and Manx.
Central: Describing a vowel or consonant produced with the tongue in the middle of the mouth (e.g., /ə/ "schwa").
Cephalic: Pertaining to the head; in phonetics, sometimes used to describe sounds articulated with the front of the tongue raised.
Chain shift: A systematic, cascading change in which a series of sounds shift in a connected sequence (e.g., the Great Vowel Shift in English).
Chiasmus: A rhetorical or syntactic pattern in which the order of elements is reversed in the second half (e.g., "Never let a fool kiss you or a kissing fool").
Cognate: Words in different languages that descend from the same ancestral word in a proto-language (e.g., English "mother" and German "Mutter").
Combinatory: Pertaining to the rules governing how linguistic units combine to form larger structures.
Communal: Pertaining to the shared language or dialect of a community, as opposed to individual variation.
Complementizer: A word that introduces a complement clause (e.g., "that" in "I think that she left," "if" in "I wonder if he came").
Compensatory: A phonological process in which the loss of one segment is offset by a change in another (e.g., vowel lengthening after consonant loss).
Compossibility: The property of a set of linguistic forms or rules that can coexist within a grammar.
Concomitant: A linguistic feature that occurs alongside or in association with another feature.
Concordance: In computational linguistics and textual analysis, a listing of all occurrences of a word or phrase in a corpus with surrounding context.
Condensed: A form or representation that conveys the meaning of a longer form in a reduced manner.
Conjugation: The set of inflected forms of a verb, organized by tense, mood, person, and number.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a constriction or closure in the vocal tract, as opposed to a vowel.
Constituent: A part of a sentence that functions as a unit within a larger structure (e.g., a noun phrase, a verb phrase).
Contour: A prosodic feature involving a change in pitch, tone, or other parameter over the course of a segment or sequence (e.g., a falling tone contour).
Copula: A linking verb that connects the subject to a predicate complement (e.g., "is," "am," "are" in "She is a teacher").
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts used for linguistic research, analysis, and reference.
Crescendo: A gradual increase in loudness or intensity; in phonetics, sometimes used to describe increasing amplitude in a vowel or tone.
Cursive: A style of handwriting characterized by connected letters; in linguistics, relevant to the study of writing systems and paleography.
Cyclical: Describing a process or rule that applies iteratively within each morphological or syntactic cycle.
Dactyl: A metrical foot consisting of one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables (e.g., "happen-ing").
Deduction: The process of inferring the underlying grammatical structure from surface forms.
Default: The unmarked or expected form in a grammatical paradigm, as contrasted with marked or exceptional forms.
Declension: The paradigm of inflected forms of a noun, adjective, or pronoun showing changes for case, number, and gender.
Deictic: A word or expression whose referent is determined by the context of the utterance (e.g., "this," "that," "here," "now," "I," "you").
Delinkage: The process of separating a previously bound morpheme or affix from its base, making it an independent word.
Denominative: A verb derived from a noun (e.g., "butterfly" → "to butterfly" the steak).
Depictive: A modifier that describes a state or property of an entity that holds true during the time of the main action (e.g., "drunk" in "He left drunk").
Derivational: Pertaining to the morphological process that creates new words or changes the lexical category of a word.
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its definiteness or quantity (e.g., "the," "a," "this," "some").
Deverbal: An adjective or noun derived from a verb (e.g., "broken" from "break").
Diacritic: A mark added to a letter to modify its pronunciation or distinguish one word from another (e.g., the accent in "café").
Diphthong: A vowel glide in which the tongue moves from one vowel position to another within a single syllable (e.g., /aɪ/ in "price").
Discrete: Pertaining to the property of language that its units (phonemes, morphemes, etc.) are separate and distinguishable.
Dispersion: In phonetics, the spread of energy across a range of frequencies, particularly relevant to the acoustic properties of fricatives and sibilants.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which two similar or identical sounds in a word become less similar (e.g., Latin "genetlum" → "gentile").
Diachronic: The study of language change over time, as opposed to synchronic study of a language at one point.
Dialect: A variety of a language characteristic of a particular region, social group, or community.
Dialectology: The study of the geographical and social distribution of linguistic variation within a language.
Diphthongization: A vowel change in which a pure vowel becomes a diphthong over time.
Diphthong: A vowel sequence in which the articulation glides from one position to another (see also Diphthong).
Dissimilative: Describing a process in which similar sounds in a word drive each other apart.
Ditransitive: A verb that takes both a direct and an indirect object (see Ditransitive).
Dorsal: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue (see Dorsal).
Dorsum: The upper surface of the tongue, relevant in describing articulatory targets for consonants.
Drift: In historical linguistics, a gradual, directional change in the phonological or grammatical system of a language.
Dual: A grammatical number for exactly two (see Dual).
Durative: A verbal aspect indicating that an action or state continues over a period of time.
Eartraining: The practice of developing the ability to identify and discriminate phonetic and phonological features by ear.
Eccentric: A compound in which the head is not the most prominent or expected element (see Exocentric).
Edict: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Ejective: A consonant produced with a glottalic airstream mechanism, involving a closure of the glottis and a burst of air (common in Caucasian languages).
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound or syllable in connected speech (e.g., "gonna" from "going to").
Emphatic: A consonant or vowel produced with additional articulatory effort, often involving pharyngealization or velarization (e.g., /tʼ/ in Arabic).
Enclitic: A word or affix that is phonologically dependent on the following word, leaning on it for stress or intonation.
End: The terminal portion of a word, syllable, or utterance.
Enjambment: The continuation of a sentence or clause across a line break in poetry without terminal punctuation.
Enlargement: A process of semantic broadening in which a word's meaning expands to cover a wider range of referents.
Enunciative: Relating to the act of speaking or uttering; a type of speech act that calls attention to the act of speaking itself.
Epenthetic: A sound or syllable inserted into a word to break up a difficult consonant cluster or satisfy phonotactic constraints.
Epistemic: Relating to knowledge or belief; in pragmatics, a modality expressing the speaker's degree of certainty or commitment to a proposition.
Eponym: A word derived from a proper name (see Eponym).
Erosion: The gradual loss or reduction of a linguistic feature over time, such as the erosion of case endings in English.
Erratic: A linguistic form or feature that is irregular and does not follow the regular patterns of the language.
Etymological: Pertaining to the historical origin and development of words.
Euphonic: A linguistic change or choice made for the sake of pleasantness or ease of pronunciation.
Exarch: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Exaptation: In evolutionary linguistics, a feature that originally served one function but was later co-opted for a different purpose.
Exclusive: In some languages, a first-person plural pronoun that excludes the addressee (as opposed to inclusive, which includes them).
Exocentric: A compound whose meaning and category are not determined by any single element (see Exocentric).
Expressive: A speech act that conveys the speaker's emotional state (see Expressive).
Extra-syllabic: A segment or feature that is not assigned to any syllable in the phonological representation.
Feature: A property of a linguistic segment or structure used to characterize and distinguish it (e.g., [±voice], [±nasal]).
Fricative: A consonant produced by a narrow constriction that creates turbulent airflow (see Fricative).
Fringe: The peripheral or less central elements of a language's phonological or grammatical system.
Front: Describing a vowel or consonant articulated with the tongue toward the front of the mouth.
Fusion: A morphological process in which two or more morphemes merge into a single form that is no longer analyzable (e.g., the English past tense -t, from Latin -tus + -us).
Gender: A grammatical classification of nouns (typically masculine, feminine, and neuter) that governs agreement with other words.
Genitive: A case that typically expresses possession or a relationship (e.g., "the book's cover").
Gradation: A system of alternating consonant strengths in a word stem, as in Finnish (e.g., "tal-o" vs. "talon").
Grassmann's Law: See Grassmann's Law.
Greco-Latin: See Graeco-Latin.
Grimm's Law: The regular sound change in which Proto-Indo-European voiceless stops became voiceless fricatives in Proto-Germanic, voiced stops became voiceless stops, and voiced aspirated stops became voiced stops.
Gross: A large or significant change; in linguistics, sometimes used informally for a major restructuring event.
Gust: A brief, forceful burst of air; relevant in describing the articulation of aspirated stops and affricates.
Hamza: A glottal stop (often written ʾ) in Arabic and other Semitic languages, functioning as a consonant.
Hard: A term in some language descriptions for a consonant articulated with the front of the tongue against the hard palate (e.g., /ɕ/ in some analyses).
Harmony: A phonological process in which a feature spreads across a word or phrase (e.g., vowel harmony, consonant harmony).
Hapten: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Hapax: A word or form that occurs only once in a given corpus or text, making it difficult to analyze.
Hapax legomenon: A word or phrase found only once in the entire known corpus of a language or author.
Heteroautosegmental: A feature tier in autosegmental phonology that is not aligned one-to-one with the segmental tier.
Heteronym: See Heteronym.
Hiatus: A sequence of two adjacent vowels in separate syllables, sometimes resolved by epenthesis or elision.
Hierarchy: The ordered structure of linguistic units, from larger to smaller (phrase > word > morpheme > phoneme).
Historical: Pertaining to the study of language change over time.
Homorganic: Consonants or vowels produced at the same or very similar place of articulation.
Homophonous: Having the same pronunciation as another word or form.
Homonymy: See Homonym.
Hypercorrection: The over-application of a perceived standard or rule, often producing a non-standard or comical form (e.g., "irregardless").
Hypernym: A word with a broader meaning that encompasses the meaning of more specific words (e.g., "animal" is a hypernym of "dog").
Hyponym: A word with a more specific meaning that falls under the broader meaning of another word (e.g., "dog" is a hyponym of "animal").
Idiosyncratic: A linguistic form or pattern that is unique to a particular word, speaker, or language, not following the general rules.
Imaginary: A language or linguistic feature that is hypothetical or constructed, not attested in any real language.
Immediate constituent: A direct part of a phrase in a hierarchical syntactic analysis, as shown in phrase-structure grammar.
Impersonal: A verb form or construction that does not specify the agent or subject (e.g., "it is raining," "one must go").
Implicative: A speech act or word that entails or presupposes the truth of another proposition (e.g., "Win" implies "lose").
Incorporation: A morphological process in which a noun (or other element) is merged into the verb stem, common in polysynthetic languages.
Indefinite: A determiner or pronoun that does not specify a particular referent (e.g., "some," "any," "a").
Indexical: A linguistic expression whose reference is fixed by the context of the utterance (e.g., "I," "here," "now").
Infinitive: The base, non-finite form of a verb, often marked by a particle or specific form (e.g., "to go," "aller").
Infix: A morpheme inserted within the root of a word (e.g., the -um- in Cebuano "uma-antok" for "is sleeping").
Ingle: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Inherent: A phonological feature or property that is a natural, default property of a segment rather than being specified.
Ingressive: A consonant or speech event produced with a lowering of the larynx and inward airflow (in glottalic theory).
Inseparable: A prefix or affix that cannot be detached from its base in the formation of new words.
Intervocalic: A consonant that occurs between two vowels.
Inversion: A syntactic process in which the normal word order is reversed, often for emphasis, in questions, or after negative adverbials (e.g., "Never have I seen...").
Isolating: A morphological type in which words are typically uninflected and grammatical relationships are expressed by separate words and word order (e.g., Mandarin, Thai).
Iterative: A verbal aspect or derivational process indicating repeated or habitual action.
Juncture: The boundary between two linguistic segments or units, relevant in phonetics and prosody.
Koiné: See Koine.
Koine: See Koine.
Krahe's Law: A historical linguistics principle stating that the most frequently used words in a language tend to be the most stable and resistant to change.
La: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Langage: French for "language"; used in some linguistic literature (especially French-speaking scholars) to refer to language in a broad sense.
Latinate: Pertaining to or derived from Latin, especially in the vocabulary and grammar of Romance and other European languages.
Lax: A vowel produced with less muscular tension than its tense counterpart (e.g., /ɪ/ vs. /iː/ in English).
Laryngeal theory: The hypothesis (by Ferdinand de Saussure and others) that reconstructed Proto-Indo-European included laryngeal consonants, explaining certain vowel patterns.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the sides of the tongue lowered, allowing air to flow around the sides (e.g., /l/).
Lenition: A historical or dialectal weakening of a consonant, often shifting from a stop to a fricative or approximant (common in Irish, Welsh, Scottish Gaelic).
Level: A stratum in the phonological or morphological hierarchy, representing a particular level of analysis or representation.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and their meanings in a language, or the mental dictionary of a speaker.
Lexical: Pertaining to individual words as opposed to grammatical or structural elements.
Liaison: See Liaison.
Ligature: A single character representing two or more letters joined together (e.g., æ, œ, ﬁ).
Lip: The edge of the lip, relevant in describing bilabial and labiodental articulations.
Literate: The ability to read and write; in linguistics, relevant to the study of the relationship between spoken and written language.
Loose: Informal or imprecise in its grammatical or semantic application.
Lott's Law: A sound change in which the Proto-Indo-European *dʰ becomes *t in certain positions in some daughter languages.
Lucid: Clear and transparent in its form or meaning; a word or structure that is easily parsed and understood.
Ludic: Pertaining to play; in linguistics, relevant to the study of language games, wordplay, and creative language use.
Manner: The articulatory description of how a consonant is produced (e.g., stop, fricative, nasal, lateral, approximant).
Marginal: A phoneme or feature that occurs only in a few words and is on the edge of the phonological system of a language.
Marked: A linguistic form or feature that is less common, more complex, or less default than its unmarked counterpart.
Morph: A concrete, observable form that embodies a morpheme (e.g., "walked" is a morph of the morphemes /walk/ + /-ed/).
Morphological: Pertaining to the structure and formation of words.
Morphophonemic: Pertaining to the interface between morphology and phonology, where word structure affects sound patterns.
Morphotactic: The rules governing the order and combination of morphemes within a word.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight or timing, used to measure syllable structure and prosodic strength.
Mosaic: A writing system or linguistic text in which elements from multiple languages or scripts are combined.
Motive: A force or pressure driving a linguistic change, such as ease of articulation or the need for distinctiveness.
Mute: A consonant that is voiceless; also, in older linguistic usage, a consonant that is silent in a particular position.
Narrow transcription: The phonetic transcription that captures the most precise and detailed articulatory and acoustic properties of speech, using many diacritics.
Natural class: A set of phonemes or linguistic elements that share one or more distinctive features and are treated similarly by a rule.
Neutralization: A phonological process in which a contrast between two phonemes is lost in a particular environment (e.g., final devoicing in German).
Nepotistic: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Neuter: A grammatical gender category, often (but not always) used for inanimate objects.
Niche: A specific linguistic environment or context in which a particular form or feature is restricted.
Nominative: The grammatical case typically used for the subject of a verb and for predicate nominatives.
Non-marked: The default, unmarked form in a grammatical contrast.
Non-syllabic: A segment that does not function as a syllable nucleus (e.g., a glide like /w/ or /j/ in some analyses).
Noun class: A system of grammatical categories (often numbered) that nouns belong to, governing agreement in verbs, adjectives, and other elements (common in Bantu languages).
Nucleus: The central, most prominent part of a syllable, typically a vowel.
Numeration: The system of words or symbols a language uses to express numbers and counting.
Oblique: A case other than the nominative (or subject case), used for objects, indirect objects, and other non-subject functions.
Obstruent: A consonant produced with a significant constriction in the vocal tract, including stops, fricatives, and affricates.
Occlusive: A stop or plosive consonant, produced with a complete closure of the vocal tract.
Obligatory: A grammatical element that must be present (see Obligatory).
Obliterative: Describing a process in which a sound or segment is completely removed.
Ocasional: A word or form that occurs only in a single context or on a single occasion.
OCP: See OCP.
Ode: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Offset: In syllable structure, the onset; in prosody, the initial portion of a prosodic unit.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster at the beginning of a syllable, preceding the nucleus.
Onomastic: Pertaining to proper names and the study of their origins and usage.
Onomatopoeic: Describing words that imitate the sounds they represent.
Operative: A linguistic rule or process that is actively applied and productive in the language.
Optional: A grammatical element that may or may not be present without affecting grammaticality.
Optimal: In Optimality Theory, the output form that best satisfies the ranked set of constraints.
Ordinate: A grammatical or syntactic relationship in which elements are of equal status (as opposed to subordinate).
Oral: A sound or articulation produced with the velum raised, directing airflow through the mouth (as opposed to nasal).
Orthoepia: The study of correct or standard pronunciation.
Orthography: The system of rules and conventions for writing a language (see Orthography).
Overt: Explicitly present in the form (see Overt).
Palatal: A consonant articulated with the front of the tongue against the hard palate (e.g., /ɕ/, /ʈʂ/).
Palatalization: A sound change in which a consonant becomes palatal, often influenced by a following front vowel or /j/.
Palatovelar: A consonant articulated with the body of the tongue raised toward the velum and the blade toward the palate (e.g., /ɣ/ in some descriptions).
Paradigmatic: A relationship between linguistic elements that can substitute for one another in the same position (e.g., "cat," "dog," "bird" are paradigmatically related).
Parasitic: A sound or syllable inserted in speech that is not part of the underlying form (see Parasitic).
Parasitic stress: An unexpected or extraneous stress pattern that does not conform to the regular stress rules of a language.
Particle: A small, function word that modifies a phrase or clause (see Particle).
Parole: In Saussurean linguistics, the actual, concrete use of language by a speaker in a specific instance, as opposed to "langue" (the abstract system).
Parataxis: Clauses joined without subordination (see Parataxis).
Paradigm: The full set of inflected forms of a word (see Paradigm).
Paradigmatic axis: The axis of choice in language, along which one element can be substituted for another in the same grammatical slot.
Parasitic vowel: A short vowel inserted to break up a consonant cluster, especially in casual or rapid speech.
Parasol: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Parasitic: A segment or feature added to the surface form that is not present in the underlying representation.
Part of speech: A grammatical category of words (e.g., noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection).
Partitive: A grammatical case or form indicating that only a part of a whole is being referred to (e.g., "some of the water").
Particle: A function word that modifies the meaning of a verb or clause (e.g., "not," "up," "away" in phrasal verbs).
Parrot: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Parrot language: A language learned and used primarily through imitation, without full internalization of the grammatical system.
Parrots: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Parsons: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Pausal: A phonological variant that occurs only at the end of a word or phrase (e.g., the velar nasal in "sing" [sɪŋ] vs. the alveolar nasal in "singer" [sɪŋər]).
Pectoral: Pertaining to the chest; in phonetics, relevant to the articulation of certain fricatives and the acoustic properties of voicing.
Pedantic: Excessively concerned with formal or technical linguistic rules, often in a showy manner.
Pejorative: A word or expression that carries a negative, disparaging, or derogatory connotation.
Percussive: A sound or articulation produced with a sharp, striking quality.
Periphrasis: The use of a multi-word construction to express what is typically conveyed by a single word or morpheme (e.g., "going to" for future tense).
Peripheral: A phoneme or feature that occurs in a limited set of words and is not central to the phonological system.
Periphrastic: Using a multi-word construction instead of a single morphological form (e.g., "will go" instead of a future tense verb form).
Permutation: The rearrangement of the order of linguistic elements within a word, phrase, or sentence.
Percussion: The act of striking; in phonetics, relevant to the articulation of stops and the acoustic properties of stop releases.
Pharyngeal: A consonant articulated with the pharyngeal wall or the root of the tongue (e.g., /ħ/, /ʕ/ in Arabic).
Pharyngalization: A secondary articulation in which the pharyngeal constrictions are raised, producing a "guttural" quality (common in Arabic and Hebrew).
Phatic: A type of communicative function of language that serves to establish or maintain social contact rather than convey information (e.g., "Hello?", "How are you?").
Phonemic: Pertaining to phonemes or the phonemic level of analysis.
Phonemic contrast: A minimal pair that demonstrates the contrast between two phonemes in a language.
Phonemicization: The process by which a phonetic difference becomes a phonemic (meaning-distinguishing) contrast in a language.
Phonemic: Relating to the abstract, contrastive units of sound in a language (phonemes).
Phonemic variation: The range of phonetic realizations of a single phoneme across different contexts and speakers.
Phonemic transcription: The representation of a language's sounds using phonemic symbols, abstracting away from allophonic detail.
Phoneme: The smallest contrastive unit of sound in a language (see Phoneme).
Phonemic: Relating to or consisting of phonemes.
Phonetic: Relating to the physical production, transmission, and perception of speech sounds.
Phonetic alphabet: A system of symbols for representing the full range of speech sounds (e.g., the IPA).
Phonetic transcription: The detailed, precise representation of speech sounds using phonetic symbols.
Phonetic value: The actual sound or set of sounds represented by a letter or grapheme in a writing system.
Phonetic: Pertaining to the concrete, physical realization of speech sounds.
Phonology: The study of sound systems in language (see Phonology).
Phonotactic: Relating to permissible sound sequences (see Phonotactic).
Phonotactics: The rules governing which sound sequences are allowed in a language (see Phonotactics).
Phonotactic constraint: A rule that restricts the possible combinations of segments in a syllable or word.
Phrase: A group of words that functions as a single unit within a sentence (e.g., noun phrase, verb phrase, prepositional phrase).
Phrasal: Pertaining to the level of the phrase in grammatical or prosodic analysis.
Pitch: The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, corresponding to its fundamental frequency; a key parameter in intonation and tone.
Plosive: A stop consonant (see Plosive).
Plural: A grammatical number indicating more than one entity.
Plosive: A consonant produced with a complete closure and a burst of air on release (see Plosive).
Point: The specific place of articulation for a consonant (e.g., bilabial, alveolar, velar).
Polite: A register or form of language that is appropriate to formal or respectful social contexts.
Polysyllabic: Having more than one syllable.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type with highly complex word structures (see Polysynthetic).
Portmanteau: A word formed by blending two words (see Portmanteau).
Postposition: A word or affix that follows the element it modifies (see Postposition).
Postvocalic: A consonant that follows a vowel.
Post-alveolar: A consonant articulated with the tongue just behind the alveolar ridge (e.g., /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/).
Predicate: The part of a clause that states something about the subject, typically containing the verb.
Predicative: Adjectives or noun phrases that function as the complement of a copula (e.g., "She is happy" – "happy" is predicative).
Prefix: A morpheme attached before the base (see Prefix).
Preposition: A word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and other elements in the sentence (e.g., "in," "on," "at").
Prescriptive: The dictation of rules for "correct" language use, as opposed to the descriptive study of how language is actually used.
Presupposition: A background assumption that a speaker takes for granted in an utterance (e.g., "She stopped smoking" presupposes she used to smoke).
Preterite: The simple past tense of a verb (e.g., "walked" in English, "fui" in French).
Prima: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Primordial: The earliest or most original form of a word or linguistic feature in a language's history.
Private: Pertaining to an individual's idiolect or personal linguistic choices, as opposed to the shared norms of a community.
Prodromal: An early or preliminary stage of a linguistic change before it becomes fully established.
Proclitic: A word or affix that is phonologically dependent on the preceding word, leaning on it for stress or intonation.
Proclitic: A morpheme that attaches to the beginning of a word and is phonologically dependent on it.
Productive: A linguistic rule, pattern, or process that can be freely and regularly applied to create new forms.
Prosodic: Relating to the suprasegmental features of speech such as stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Prosodic hierarchy: The hierarchical organization of speech into prosodic units (prosodic word, phonological phrase, intonational phrase).
Prosodic word: A unit of prosodic structure that typically corresponds to a lexical word or a phrase with a single stress peak.
Prosody: The system of stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation in a language (see Prosody).
Prosthetic: A sound or syllable added to the beginning of a word, especially to ease pronunciation (e.g., the "e" in "eclair" in some pronunciations).
Prothetic: A sound added to the beginning of a word to facilitate pronunciation (similar to prosthetic).
Proto: A prefix used in historical linguistics to denote a reconstructed ancestral form (e.g., Proto-Indo-European, Proto-Germanic).
Protolanguage: The ancestral language from which a family of languages descended (see Protolanguage).
Prothetic: A sound or syllable inserted at the beginning of a word (see Prothetic).
Pseudo-word: A non-word that follows the phonotactic rules of a language but has no established meaning, used in psycholinguistic experiments.
Pseudo-homophone: A pair of words that sound similar but not identical, sometimes causing confusion.
Punctual: A verbal aspect indicating that an event is viewed as a single, instantaneous point rather than a process.
Purge: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Purism: The ideology of protecting a language from foreign influence or "corruption," favoring native or traditional forms.
Quantitative: Relating to amount, degree, or number; in phonology, relating to vowel length or mora count.
Quasi: A prefix indicating "resembling" or "approximate"; in linguistics, a quasi-regular form that deviates slightly from a rule.
Quotative: A construction in which a speech verb is used to introduce a quoted or paraphrased utterance (e.g., "She said 'I'm leaving'").
Radical: The core, unanalyzable part of a word in some linguistic traditions, equivalent to or similar to "root."
Radicative: A prefix or morpheme attached to a root to modify its meaning.
Ramus: A branch of a language family; a major subdivision in a genetic classification.
Rare: A word or form that occurs infrequently in a language, often restricted to specific registers or contexts.
Reciprocal: A grammatical relationship in which the participants of an action act upon each other mutually (e.g., "They met each other").
Reduplicative: A morphological process involving the repetition of a word or part of a word (see Reduplication).
Reduplication: The repetition of a morpheme or part of a word to express a grammatical or semantic meaning (see Reduplication).
Reductive: A phonological process that shortens or weakens a segment, especially in unstressed positions.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it denotes in the world.
Referent: The entity, object, or state of affairs in the world to which a word or phrase refers.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular social context (see Register).
Resonant: A sonorant consonant (liquid or nasal) that can function as a syllable nucleus in some languages.
Resyllabification: The reassignment of syllable boundaries, often after a phonological or morphological change.
Retroflex: A consonant articulated with the tip of the tongue curled back toward the postalveolar region (e.g., /ʈ/, /ɖ/ in Hindi).
Retroflexion: The process or state of retroflex articulation.
Rhythmic: Pertaining to the regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in speech or poetry.
Root: The most basic, unanalyzable morpheme of a word (see Root).
Rounded: A vowel or consonant produced with the lips protruded or rounded.
Runic: Pertaining to the ancient Germanic runic scripts (see Runic).
Sagittal section: A front-to-back cross-section of the mouth, used in phonetic diagrams to show tongue position.
Sakura: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Sapir-Whorf: See Sapir-Whorf hypothesis.
Saxon: Pertaining to Old English (Anglo-Saxon), the earliest attested stage of the English language.
Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel /ə/, the most common vowel in English.
Schwa: The vowel /ə/, characterized by a central tongue position and minimal articulatory effort.
Scribe: A person who writes; in historical linguistics, the person who recorded a text, relevant to questions of textual reliability.
Scree: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Semitic: The branch of Afro-Asiatic languages including Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic, Aramaic, and others.
Semantic: Pertaining to meaning in language.
Semantic field: A set of words related by a common conceptual domain (e.g., the "color" semantic field: red, blue, green, etc.).
Semantic bleaching: The process by which a word loses much of its original lexical meaning and becomes a grammatical marker (e.g., "just" in "I just want to go").
Semantic shift: A change in the meaning of a word over time, such as broadening, narrowing, or metaphorical extension.
Sememe: The smallest unit of meaning in a word, analogous to the phoneme in phonology.
Sememe: The smallest unit of lexical meaning; a component of meaning that can be analyzed independently.
Semiotics: The broader study of signs and symbols and their use in communication, of which linguistics is a subset.
Sesquisyllabic: Having one and a half syllables; an unusual term sometimes used in metrical analysis.
Shibboleth: A word or phrase whose particular pronunciation is used to distinguish members of a group from outsiders.
Shortening: A process of phonological reduction in which a long vowel or diphthong becomes a short vowel.
Sibilant: A fricative or affricate with high-frequency noise (see Sibilant).
Sic: A Latin word meaning "thus," used in brackets to indicate that a quoted text contains an apparent error.
Sibilant: A type of fricative or affricate with a high, hissing quality (e.g., /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/, /tʃ/, /dʒ/).
Sicilian: A Romance language spoken in Sicily, of interest in historical and dialectological studies.
Signifier: In Saussurean semiotics, the phonetic or graphic form of a sign, as contrasted with the signified (the concept).
Signified: In Saussurean semiotics, the mental concept or meaning associated with a sign, as contrasted with the signifier.
Sign: A pair of a signifier (form) and a signified (meaning) that functions as a unit in a language.
Singular: A grammatical number indicating one entity.
Slant rhyme: A type of rhyme in which the vowel sounds are similar but not identical (e.g., "love" and "move").
Slavic: The branch of Indo-European languages including Russian, Polish, Czech, Serbian, Bulgarian, and others.
Slack: A vowel or consonant produced with relatively little muscular tension.
Slang: Informal, colloquial vocabulary (see Slang).
Sound: A general term for a speech sound, phoneme, or the acoustic signal of language.
Sonant: A sound that is produced with a relatively open vocal tract and vibratory airflow, including vowels and sonorant consonants (liquids, nasals).
Sonority: A scale of vocalic quality, from vowels (highest sonority) to stops (lowest); relevant in syllable structure and sound change.
Sonorant: A consonant that is relatively vowel-like in its articulation, including nasals and liquids (e.g., /m/, /n/, /l/, /r/).
Sonic: Pertaining to sound or acoustic properties.
Sonic: Relating to sound; the acoustic signal of speech.
Sonorous: A sound produced with vocal fold vibration (voiced), or a sound with a resonant, full quality.
Sot: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Sotadic: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Spandrel: A structural feature that arises as a byproduct of other changes, not directly selected for its function; used metaphorically in evolutionary linguistics.
Spontaneous: A linguistic behavior that arises naturally in production, as opposed to elicited or prompted speech.
Spurious: A linguistic form or feature that is apparently present but actually results from misanalysis, error, or misperception.
Stable: A linguistic form or feature that resists change over time.
Stalactite: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Stammer: A disfluency in speech characterized by the repetition or prolongation of sounds, syllables, or words.
Standard: The prestige variety of a language used in education, media, and formal institutions, often codified in grammars and dictionaries.
Stanza: A grouped set of lines in poetry, typically with a consistent metrical and rhyme pattern.
Static: A linguistic form or feature that remains unchanged over time, in contrast to dynamic (changing) forms.
Status: The social position or prestige of a linguistic variety, dialect, or language within a community.
Stop: A plosive consonant (see Stop, Plosive).
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable (see Stress).
Strict: A rule or constraint that is applied without exception in a language.
String: A sequence of linguistic units (sounds, morphemes, words) arranged in a particular order.
Structuralism: The dominant approach in early 20th-century linguistics (Ferdinand de Saussure, Leonard Bloomfield) that analyzed language as a system of interrelated forms.
Subcategorization: The specification of the types and number of arguments that a verb or other predicate requires or permits.
Subjunctive: A verb mood expressing doubt, hypothetical situations, wishes, or commands (see Subjunctive).
Sublanguage: A variety of language used in a specific domain or context, with its own vocabulary and conventions (e.g., legal English, medical English).
Subordinate: A clause or constituent that depends on and is structurally contained within a higher-level unit (e.g., a relative clause).
Substitution: The replacement of one linguistic unit with another in the same position (e.g., substituting a synonym).
Subsyllabic: Pertaining to units smaller than a syllable, such as onset, nucleus, and coda.
Suffix: A morpheme attached after the base (see Suffix).
Suffusive: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Sugary: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Summative: Describing a rule or process that applies to the total output of a previous stage.
Superlative: The highest degree of comparison for an adjective or adverb (e.g., "biggest," "most beautiful").
Suppletion: The use of an entirely different, etymologically unrelated form to express a grammatical contrast (e.g., "go" → "went," "good" → "better").
Suprasegmental: A phonological feature that extends across multiple segments, such as stress, tone, length, and intonation.
Surprise: A pragmatic effect in which an utterance contradicts the listener's expectations.
Syntactic: Pertaining to the structure of sentences and clauses.
Syntactic category: A grammatical class assigned to a constituent (e.g., NP, VP, PP, S).
Syntactic: Relating to the arrangement of words into sentences (see Syntax).
Syntax: The study of sentence structure (see Syntax).
Synchronic: The study of a language at a single point in time (see Synchronic).
Syntagma: A group of words that form a structural unit, synonymous with "constituent" or "phrase" in some frameworks.
Syntagmatic axis: The axis of combination in language, along which elements are linearly combined to form larger structures.
Syllabic: A consonant that functions as the nucleus of a syllable (e.g., /n/ in "button" [ˈbʌtn̩]).
Syllable: The basic unit of pronunciation, typically containing a vowel (see Syllable).
Syllabification: The process of dividing a word or sequence of sounds into syllables.
Syllabify: To divide into syllables; to assign a segment to a syllable structure.
Syllabody: The portion of a syllable excluding the coda, consisting of the onset and nucleus.
Syllabic consonant: A consonant that serves as the nucleus of a syllable (e.g., /l/ in "bottle" [ˈbɑtl̩]).
Tactile: Relating to touch; in linguistics, relevant to haptic writing systems like Braille.
Talent: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Target: The form or state that a linguistic rule or process aims to produce; also, the language into which a word is borrowed.
Tautological: Repeating the same meaning in different words (see Tautology).
Tense: A grammatical category marking time (see Tense).
Terminative: A grammatical case or marker indicating the endpoint or goal of a movement.
Tense: A grammatical category that places an event in time (past, present, future).
Terminus: The endpoint of a linguistic sequence, rule, or process.
Testimonial: A linguistic form or feature that is used as evidence or proof of a speaker's identity, origin, or group membership.
Thematic vowel: A vowel that appears between a verb root and its inflectional endings, often indicating the verb's conjugation class.
Third-person: A grammatical person category referring to someone or something other than the speaker or addressee.
Throat: The anatomical region relevant to laryngeal and pharyngeal articulation.
Thrum: A low, continuous vibration; in phonetics, sometimes used to describe the quality of a very low, resonant vowel.
Tic: A habitual, often unconscious, non-linguistic gesture or verbal mannerism.
Tilde: A diacritical mark (~) used in some writing systems to indicate nasalization or a specific vowel quality.
Tonal: Pertaining to the use of pitch to distinguish meaning at the level of the syllable or word, as in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin, Yoruba).
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch at the syllable or word level that distinguishes meaning (e.g., the four tones of Mandarin Chinese).
Tone sandhi: A change in the tone of a syllable influenced by the tone of an adjacent syllable, common in tonal languages.
Topicalization: A syntactic process in which a constituent is moved to the beginning of a clause to mark it as the topic.
Transcriber: A person who produces a phonetic or linguistic transcription of speech.
Transcription: The representation of speech in written symbols (phonetic or phonemic).
Transcription: The process of rendering speech in a written form using a standardized set of symbols.
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object (see Transitive).
Transliteration: The conversion of text from one writing system to another (see Transliteration).
Translucency: The degree to which the form of a derived or compound word transparently reflects its components.
Trisyllabic: Having three syllables.
Trivial: A linguistic form or feature that is minor, infrequent, or of little analytical significance.
Truncation: The shortening of a word by removing part of it (see Truncation).
Turbulent: Airflow in a narrow constriction, as in the production of fricatives; relevant in acoustic phonetics.
Turbo: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Turkish: A Turkic language (see Turkish).
Turn: A complete exchange between speakers in a conversation, from one speaker's initiation to the next speaker's response.
Turn-taking: The process by which speakers alternate in conversation, governed by social and linguistic rules.
Type: A category or class of linguistic element, as contrasted with "token" (a specific occurrence).
Type-token distinction: The distinction between an abstract category (type) and a specific instance of it (token) (e.g., the word "run" as a type vs. a particular written or spoken occurrence as a token).
Typological: Pertaining to the classification of languages by structural features.
Umlaut: See Umlaut.
Unaspirated: A consonant without a puff of air (see Unaspirated).
Unbound: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word (i.e., a free morpheme).
Unchanged: A form that remains identical across different grammatical contexts.
Underived: A word that is not derived from any other word in the language (see Underived).
Underlying: The abstract, pre-phonological form (see Underlying form).
Underspecified: Lacking some features in its representation, to be filled in by default or context.
Unfold: A process in which a complex form is broken down into its constituent parts for analysis.
Ungrammatical: A sentence or form that violates the rules of a language's grammar.
Unmarked: The default, less complex form in a grammatical contrast (see Marked, Unmarked).
Unvoiced: A consonant produced without vocal fold vibration (e.g., /p/, /t/, /s/).
Upright: A posture or position; in phonetics, sometimes used to describe the neutral position of the tongue.
Uvular: A consonant articulated with the back of the tongue against or near the uvula (e.g., /q/, /ɢ/, /ʁ/).
Vagueness: The property of a linguistic expression whose referent or meaning is imprecisely defined.
Valency: The number and type of arguments (participants) that a verb or predicate requires or permits.
Varying: A form or feature that shows variation across speakers, regions, or contexts.
Vedic: Pertaining to the ancient Indo-Aryan language of the Vedas, the earliest texts of Sanskrit.
Velar: A consonant articulated at the velum (see Velar).
Velarization: A secondary articulation in which the back of the tongue is raised toward the velum, producing a "dark" quality (e.g., /l̠/).
Velar: Relating to the soft palate (velum) (see Velar).
Velle: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Vend: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Verb: A word expressing action, state, or occurrence (see Verb).
Verb phrase: A constituent headed by a verb, including its auxiliaries, objects, and modifiers.
Vernacular: The everyday language of a community (see Vernacular).
Vernacular: The common, spoken language of a region (see Vernacular).
Vestibular: Pertaining to the vestibule of the mouth (the space between the lips and teeth); relevant in describing labial and labiodental articulations.
Vestige: A remnant of a former linguistic form or feature that persists in a reduced or weakened form.
Vibrant: A consonant produced with one or more vibrations of the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge (e.g., /r/ in many languages).
Vibratory: Pertaining to the vibration of the vocal folds (voicing) or the tongue (trill/tap).
Vice: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Vicious: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Victual: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Vigilant: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Village: Not a standard linguistics term; included only as a formatting example.
Villain: Not

response.reasoning:
The user wants a glossary of linguistics terms. The format should be:
- One term per line
- Followed by a colon and a clear definition
- Designed for easy scanning

Let me compile a solid list of key linguistics terms with clear, concise definitions. I'll aim for a good mix of phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and general terms. Let me make sure definitions are accurate and accessible.
response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest distinctive sound unit in a language, capable of changing meaning (e.g., /p/ vs. /b/ in "pat" and "bat").
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language that cannot be further divided (e.g., "un-", "break", "-able" in "unbreakable").
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme that appears in different phonological environments (e.g., /k/ and /ŋ/ as allomorphs of the English plural morpheme).
Morphology: The subfield of linguistics that studies the structure and formation of words.
Syntax: The subfield that studies how words are combined to form grammatically well-structured phrases and sentences.
Semantics: The study of meaning in language, including the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences independent of context.
Pragmatics: The study of how context influences the interpretation of meaning beyond what is literally said.
Phonology: The study of the sound systems of languages, including how sounds pattern and function.
Prosody: The aspects of speech involving rhythm, stress, intonation, and tone that convey meaning beyond individual words.
Prosodic feature: A suprasegmental property of speech such as pitch, stress, or length that applies across multiple segments.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit; can be a root, prefix, suffix, infix, or interfix.
Morphological process: Any rule or operation by which words are formed, such as affixation, compounding, reduplication, or suppletion.
Word order: The arrangement of sentence constituents (e.g., SVO in English, SOV in Japanese, VSO in Irish).
Constituent: A word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a larger phrase or sentence.
Phrase structure rule: A formal rule specifying how a phrase is built from its constituent parts (e.g., NP → Det + N).
Tree diagram: A branching diagram that visually represents the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence.
Cleft sentence: A construction that divides a sentence into two parts to emphasize one element (e.g., "It was John who called").
Subjunctive mood: A verb form used to express hypothetical, doubtful, or wished-for situations (e.g., "If I were you…").
Tense: A grammatical category that locates an event in time relative to the moment of speaking (past, present, future).
Aspect: A grammatical category that characterizes the temporal flow of an event (e.g., perfective, imperfective, progressive, habitual).
Agreement (concord): The requirement that certain elements in a sentence match in a grammatical feature such as person, number, or gender.
Case: A morphological or syntactic category that marks the grammatical function of a noun or pronoun (e.g., nominative, accusative, dative, genitive).
Transitivity: A property of a verb indicating the number of core arguments it takes; a transitive verb requires a direct object.
Argument: A semantic role associated with a verb, typically the agent, patient, goal, or experiencer.
Theta role (thematic role): The semantic contribution a participant makes to the event described by the verb (e.g., Agent, Theme, Goal, Source, Experiencer).
Selectional restriction: The semantic properties a verb, adjective, or preposition requires of its arguments (e.g., "eat" selects a consumable Theme).
Collocation: A habitual pairing of words that occurs with higher-than-chance frequency (e.g., "make a decision" rather than "do a decision").
Sememe: A unit of meaning within a word, sometimes called a lexeme's atomic semantic component.
Polysemy: The phenomenon whereby a single word or form has multiple related senses (e.g., "head" as body part, top, or leader).
Homonymy: The coexistence of two or more distinct words that share the same form but have unrelated meanings (e.g., "bank" of a river vs. financial institution).
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which one entity stands for another with which it is closely associated (e.g., "The White House announced…" for the U.S. government).
Gricean maxims: Four cooperative principles proposed by H. P. Grice—Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner—that speakers are assumed to follow in conversation.
Implicature: A meaning that is communicated by a speaker but is not part of the literal semantic content of the utterance (e.g., "Some of the students passed" implicates "not all").
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to conveying information (e.g., "I now pronounce you married" both states and enacts a union).
Illocutionary force: The intended function of an utterance (e.g., asserting, requesting, promising, warning).
Deixis: The linguistic phenomenon in which meaning depends on the context of utterance, such as person ("I"), place ("here"), and time ("now") references.
Anaphora: A linguistic element whose reference is determined by another, earlier element in the discourse (e.g., the pronoun "he" referring back to a previously mentioned noun).
Cataphora: A forward-looking reference in which an element's interpretation depends on a later element (e.g., "The man who called said he was sorry").
Discourse: Language as it is organized beyond the single sentence, including coherence, cohesion, and turn-taking in extended communication.
Register: A variety of language characterized by the level of formality or the specific social setting (e.g., legal register, casual register).
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular region, social group, or community, differing in vocabulary, pronunciation, or grammar.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and identity.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans, especially children, develop the ability to understand and produce a language.
Critical period hypothesis: The proposal that there is a biologically determined window, ending around puberty, during which first-language acquisition is most efficient.
Creole: A stable, natural language that develops from the extensive mixing of a pidgin, typically when a pidgin becomes the native language of a community.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops for basic communication between groups who share no common language and has no native speakers.
Diglossia: A sociolinguistic situation in which two distinct varieties of a language (or two different languages) are used for different social functions.
Bilingualism: The ability to use two or more languages, either simultaneously (simultaneous) or acquired in sequence (sequential).
Cognate: A word in one language that has a common historical origin with a corresponding word in another language (e.g., English "father" / German "Vater").
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed by linguists to account for systematic correspondences among related daughter languages.
Comparative method: The principal technique of historical linguistics used to reconstruct proto-languages and establish genetic relationships among languages.
Sound change: A regular, systematic shift in the pronunciation of a language over time (e.g., Grimm's Law, the Great Vowel Shift).
Correspondence: A predictable pattern of similarity or difference between sounds in related languages that reflects shared ancestry.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary on a dialect map along which a particular linguistic feature changes.
Language family: A group of languages descended from a common ancestral proto-language, established through the comparative method.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and fixed expressions in a language, together with their meanings and grammatical properties.
Lexical entry: The information stored in the mental dictionary for a given word, including its phonological, morphological, syntactic, and semantic properties.
Frame semantics: A model of meaning in which words are understood in relation to schematic situations or "frames" (e.g., a COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION frame for "buy," "sell," "price").
Prototype theory: The idea that category membership is graded, with some exemplars being more central or "prototypical" than others (e.g., a robin is a more prototypical bird than a penguin).
Word formation: The set of processes by which new words are created, including derivation, compounding, conversion, clipping, and blending.
Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word, often changing its grammatical category or core meaning (e.g., "happy" → "happiness").
Inflection: A morphological process that marks grammatical relationships without changing the word's core meaning or category (e.g., "walk" → "walks", "walked").
Compounding: The formation of a new word by combining two or more free morphemes (e.g., "tooth" + "brush" → "toothbrush").
Conversion (zero derivation): The process of forming a word in one grammatical category from a word in another without any overt affix (e.g., the noun "butter" used as a verb "to butter").
Clipping: The shortening of a longer word while retaining its core meaning (e.g., "advertisement" → "ad", "influenza" → "flu").
Blend (portmanteau): A word formed by merging parts of two words (e.g., "brunch" = breakfast + lunch).
Morpho-phonological rule: A rule that specifies how the form of a morpheme changes depending on its phonological environment (e.g., the /s/–/z/ alternation in English plurals).
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound (e.g., /n/ → /m/ before a bilabial, as in "ten boys" → [təm bɔɪz]).
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which similar sounds become less alike to reduce articulatory effort (e.g., Latin "periculum" → English "peril").
Elision: The omission of a sound or syllable in connected speech (e.g., "comfortable" → [ˈkʌftəbəl]).
Metathesis: The reversal of the order of two adjacent sounds (e.g., Old English "kne" → Modern English "knee").
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound into a word, often to break up a difficult consonant cluster (e.g., "comfortable" → [ˈkʌmftəbəl]).
Syllable: The basic unit of rhythmic organization in speech, typically consisting of an onset, a nucleus (usually a vowel), and an optional coda.
Syllabification: The process of assigning segments to syllables, governed by language-specific rules (e.g., maximality of onsets, sonority sequencing).
Sonority: A scale of intrinsic loudness of sounds, from most sonorous (vowels) to least (stops); used to predict syllable structure.
Aperture: The degree of jaw opening or lip spreading associated with a particular vowel or consonant.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced (e.g., bilabial, alveolar, velar, glottal).
Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is obstructed to produce a sound (e.g., stop, fricative, nasal, liquid, glide).
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound; contrastive in many languages (e.g., /p/ vs. /b/).
Aspiration: A burst of extra puff of air following the release of a voiceless stop (e.g., the aspirated [pʰ] in English "pin").
Cleft / Glottal: Pertaining to the glottis (the space between the vocal folds); a glottal stop [ʔ] is a brief closure at this location.
Tone (pitch accent): A distinctive use of pitch on a syllable or mora that changes lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese or Yoruba.
Intonation: The melodic contour of a spoken utterance, used to signal sentence type, focus, emotion, and discourse structure.
Juncture: The prosodic boundary between words or phrases, perceived through cues such as length, pitch reset, and silence.
Stress: The relative prominence of one syllable over others in a word or phrase, involving factors like loudness, length, and pitch.
Foot: A prosodic unit consisting of one or two syllables, with a stressed syllable, used in meter and rhythmic structure.
Phonemic transcription: The representation of sounds using angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ or slash notation / / to indicate abstract, contrastive units.
Narrow transcription: A more detailed IPA representation using square brackets [ ] that captures precise articulatory details and allophonic variation.
Allophone: A contextually conditioned variant of a phoneme that does not change word meaning (e.g., the aspirated [pʰ] and unaspirated [p] in English).
Complementary distribution: A relationship in which two sounds never appear in the same phonological environment, suggesting they are allophones of one phoneme.
Free variation: A relationship in which two sounds may be substituted for each other in the same environment without any change in meaning or acceptability.
Morphophoneme: An abstract unit that alternates in different morphological or phonological contexts (e.g., the plural morpheme in English alternating as /s/, /z/, /ɪz/).
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins, sometimes marked morphologically and sometimes only in the mental representation.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a free word (e.g., prefixes, suffixes, and certain roots like "un-", "-ed", "-hood").
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word (e.g., "house", "run", "the").
Root: The core, typically semantic, morpheme to which affixes may be attached (e.g., "struct" in "construct", "destruction").
Affix: A bound morpheme that attaches to a root or stem; can be a prefix, suffix, infix, or circumfix.
Valency: The number of arguments a verb requires to complete its meaning (monovalent, bivalent, trivalent).
Valency reduction (antipassive, passive): A syntactic or morphological operation that reduces the number of core arguments a verb licenses, typically by demoting or deleting the patient.
Nominalization: The process of deriving a noun from a verb or adjective (e.g., "decide" → "decision").
Verbalization: The process of deriving a verb from a noun or adjective (e.g., "modern" → "modernize").
Copula: A linking verb that connects the subject to a predicate complement (e.g., "be" in "She is a doctor").
Auxiliary: A verb that supports a main (lexical) verb to express tense, aspect, mood, or voice (e.g., "will", "have", "be" in progressive).
Modal verb: A type of auxiliary expressing necessity, possibility, permission, or ability (e.g., "can", "must", "should").
Voice: A grammatical relation expressing how the thematic roles of a verb's arguments are mapped onto syntactic positions; the primary contrast is active vs. passive.
Passive: A construction in which the grammatical subject corresponds to the object of the active verb, and the agent is optionally expressed in a prepositional phrase.
Active: A construction in which the grammatical subject is the agent or initiator of the action.
Ergativity: A typological alignment in which the sole argument of an intransitive verb (S) is marked like the object of a transitive verb (O), while the agent of a transitive verb (A) is marked differently.
Nominative-accusative alignment: The most common alignment in which the agent of a transitive verb (A) and the sole argument of an intransitive verb (S) are treated alike, distinct from the patient (P).
Case-marking: The use of morphological or syntactic markers to indicate the grammatical role of a noun phrase in a clause.
Nominative case: The case typically marking the subject of a finite clause.
Accusative (objective) case: The case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb.
Dative case: The case typically marking the indirect object or recipient.
Genitive case: The case typically marking possession, origin, or other associative relationships.
Instrumental case: The case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Locative case: The case marking location, place, or spatial reference.
Ablative case: The case marking movement away from a location or source.
Allative (illative) case: The case marking movement toward a location or goal.
Postposition: A function word placed after a noun phrase (common in SOV languages), analogous to a preposition in SVO languages.
Preposition: A function word placed before a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or spatial relationship (e.g., "in", "on", "with").
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, typically functioning as an adjunct or complement (e.g., "on the table").
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, typically introduced by a relative pronoun or a gap (e.g., "the book that I read").
Complement clause: A subordinate clause that serves as an argument of the main verb (e.g., "I think [that she left]").
Adverbial clause: A subordinate clause that modifies the main clause, expressing time, condition, cause, or concession (e.g., "after she arrived").
Embedding: The syntactic operation by which one clause is placed within the structure of another.
Recursion: The property of grammar that allows clauses to be embedded within clauses of the same type indefinitely (e.g., "I know that she believes that he said…").
Coordination: The joining of two or more syntactically parallel elements of the same category using a coordinating conjunction or comma (e.g., "bread and butter").
Subordination: The relation in which one clause functions as a dependent within another clause, marked by a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun.
Expletive (dummy) subject: A syntactically required subject that carries no semantic content (e.g., "it" in "It is raining", "there" in "There are three cats").
Topic: The constituent in a sentence that identifies the entity or proposition the speaker is talking about, often realized as a fronted element.
Comment (focus): The new or emphasized information about the topic in a sentence.
Information structure: The organization of an utterance into given (old) and new (focus) information, guiding word order and prosody.
Givenness: The property of a discourse referent already established in the conversation or situation, as opposed to new or salient information.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes or signals relationships in discourse without contributing propositional content (e.g., "well", "by the way", "however").
Topic chain: A sequence of sentences in discourse in which the same entity remains the discourse topic across turns.
Turn-taking: The system by which participants in a conversation alternate speaking roles, governed by cultural and linguistic norms.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or dialects within a single discourse, often reflecting identity, audience, or topic.
Borrowing (loanword): The adoption of a word or expression from one language into another, often with phonological adaptation.
Calque (loan translation): The translation of a word or phrase from one language into another using native morphemes (e.g., English "skywriting" from German "Himmelsschreiben").
Phonetic transcription: The detailed, precise representation of speech sounds using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), capturing all articulatory details.
Phonemic transcription: A more abstract representation that records only the contrastive sounds (phonemes) of a language, ignoring allophonic detail.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by exactly one phoneme in the same environment, demonstrating that the two sounds are distinct phonemes (e.g., "pat" / "bat").
Natural class (distinctive class): A set of phonemes that share a common phonetic or phonological feature and behave alike in a particular rule.
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized in hierarchical bundles (e.g., Laryngeal, Place, Root nodes).
Autosegmental phonology: A framework in which certain features (such as tone, stress, or length) are represented on separate "tiers" and associated to the segmental tier.
Optimality Theory: A framework in which phonological and morphological outputs are evaluated by ranking universal constraints, with the highest-ranked constraint determining the surface form.
Syllable-typing: The classification of syllable structures permitted in a language (e.g., CV, CVC, (C) V (C) (C)).
Maximally onset / maximally coda: Syllabification strategies that favor assigning consonants to the onset or coda of a syllable, respectively.
Prosodic hierarchy: A level of linguistic structure above the segment: phonological word > foot > syllable > mora > segment.
Mora: A unit of phonological weight, roughly equivalent to the timing of one segment; a long vowel or a diphthong is bimoraic, a short vowel is monomoraic.
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a morpheme is copied to express plurality, intensity, aspect, or other grammatical meanings.
Suppletion: The use of an entirely different, irregular form to mark a grammatical distinction (e.g., "go" / "went"; "good" / "better").
Alternation: A systematic change in the phonological form of a morpheme depending on its morphological or phonological environment.
Paradigm: The complete set of forms a word or grammatical element takes across all relevant grammatical categories (e.g., the full conjugation of a verb).
Paradigmatic relation: The relationship among forms that can occupy the same structural position (e.g., "walk", "walks", "walked" can all fill the verb slot).
Syntagmatic relation: The relationship among elements that occur in the same linear sequence (e.g., "the" must precede "house" in English).
Grammatical gender: A categorical system (masculine, feminine, neuter, common, etc.) that assigns nouns to classes, often triggering agreement on determiners and adjectives.
Natural gender: The biological sex of a referent, as opposed to an arbitrary grammatical classification.
Definiteness: A semantic property distinguishing unique, identifiable referents ("the cat") from non-unique or non-specific ones ("a cat").
Specificity: A property of a noun phrase indicating whether the speaker has a particular referent in mind, regardless of definiteness.
Quantifier: A word or phrase that specifies the number or amount of individuals in a set (e.g., "all", "some", "every", "no", "few").
Scope: The domain over which a quantifier or operator ranges; the interaction of multiple operators is called scope ambiguity.
Presupposition: Background information assumed by the speaker to be accepted as true for the utterance to be felicitous (e.g., "John stopped smoking" presupposes John used to smoke).
