Entailment: A logical relation in which the truth of one proposition guarantees the truth of another (e.g., "She is a doctor" entails "She is a professional").
Implicature (Gricean): A non-literal, context-dependent meaning inferred by the hearer based on the assumption of cooperative communication.
Scalar implicature: An implicature arising from a scale of alternatives (e.g., using "some" implicates "not all"; "a" implicates "not a unique").
Horn scale: A semantic scale ordered by informativeness (e.g., all > most > some > none) that underlies scalar implicature.
Lachlan scale / reverse scale: A scale in which the stronger term does not entail the weaker (e.g., "kill" > "hurt" > "touch"), relevant to strengthening implicatures.
Conversational implicature: A non-conventional, context-sensitive meaning derived from the maxims of cooperation.
Conventional implicature: A meaning attached to a word or expression regardless of context (e.g., "but" signals contrast, "also" signals addition).
Entailment cancelability: A test distinguishing entailment (uncancelable) from implicature (cancelable without contradiction).
Speech act theory: A framework in which utterances are analyzed as actions performed by speakers (locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts).
Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful string of words with a particular sense and reference.
Perlocutionary effect: The effect an utterance has on the hearer (e.g., persuading, frightening, informing).
Performatives: Utterances that, by being spoken under the right conditions, perform the action they describe (e.g., "I promise", "I name this ship…").
Felicity conditions: The contextual requirements that must be met for a performative utterance to be successfully enacted.
Deictic: Pertaining to linguistic elements whose reference depends on the situational context of the utterance (speaker, hearer, time, place).
Indexical: A deictic expression whose reference is determined by parameters of the speech situation (e.g., "I", "you", "here", "now", "this").
Anaphoric: Pertaining to a linguistic element whose referent is found in a preceding element in the same discourse.
Cataphoric: Pertaining to a linguistic element whose referent is found in a following element in the discourse.
Coreference: The relationship between two or more expressions that refer to the same entity (e.g., "John" and "he").
Binding: A principle governing the interpretation of pronouns and reflexives relative to their antecedents (Binding Principles A, B, and C in Government and Binding / Minimalist Theory).
Binding Principle A: A reflexive must be bound (have a co-argument antecedent) in its local domain.
Binding Principle B: A pronoun must be free (not bound) in its local domain.
Binding Principle C: An R-expression (e.g., a full name) must be free in all domains.
Thematic role (theta role): The semantic role an argument plays in the event denoted by the predicate (Agent, Patient, Theme, Goal, Source, Experiencer, Instrument, etc.).
Argument structure: The set of thematic roles a predicate licenses and how they are mapped onto syntactic positions.
Unaccusative verb: An intransitive verb whose sole argument is semantically a Theme or Patient rather than an Agent (e.g., "arrive", "fall", "die").
Unergative verb: An intransitive verb whose sole argument is semantically an Agent (e.g., "run", "sneeze", "laugh").
Causative: A construction or derivation in which an external Agent is added to a change-of-state predicate (e.g., "The storm broke the window" from "The window broke").
Antipassive: A construction that reduces the valency of a transitive verb by demoting the patient to an oblique or omitting it.
Middle voice: A verbal construction in which the subject is neither the agent nor the patient but is affected by the action (e.g., "The book sells well").
Applicative: A construction that promotes a peripheral participant (often a beneficiary or recipient) to the status of a core object.
Nominalization / verbalization: See above under word formation.
Lexical gap: A slot in a language's vocabulary that has no single-word expression, requiring a periphrastic or multi-word workaround (e.g., English lacks a single word for "to undress a shirt").
Folk etymology: A folk reinterpretation of a word's form based on similarity to a more familiar word (e.g., "crispin" for "crimson").
Taboo / euphemism: A culturally motivated avoidance of a word, often replaced by a milder or indirect expression (e.g., "passed away" for "died").
Slang: Informal, often innovative vocabulary associated with particular social groups, subcultures, or periods.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used by a professional or occupational community.
Neologism: A newly coined word or expression entering a language's vocabulary.
Dead word / obsolescence: A word or form that has fallen out of active use (e.g., "whom" in casual spoken English, though not fully dead).
Archaism: A word or form that belongs to an earlier period of the language and is now rare or obsolete (e.g., "thou", "whence").
Denotation: The literal, dictionary-defined meaning of a word or expression.
Connotation: The associative, emotional, or cultural meanings that accompany a word beyond its literal definition.
Pejorative / laudatory: Terms that carry a negative or positive evaluative coloring, respectively.
Semantic field: A set of lexemes that are related by meaning and belong to the same conceptual domain (e.g., "buy", "sell", "price", "market", "vendor").
Hyponym / hypernym: A hierarchical semantic relation in which the meaning of one term (hyponym, e.g., "robin") is included within that of a broader term (hypernym, e.g., "bird").
Antonym: A word whose meaning is the opposite of another in a particular dimension (e.g., "hot" / "cold", "borrow" / "lend").
Gradable antonym: An antonym pair on a continuous scale where the midpoint is possible (e.g., "tall" / "short").
Complementary antonym: A binary antonym pair with no middle ground (e.g., "alive" / "dead", "male" / "female").
Complementary / conversive antonym: Pairs that describe the same relation from opposite perspectives (e.g., "buy" / "sell", "husband" / "wife").
Near-synonym: Words that overlap substantially in meaning but differ in register, connotation, collocational preferences, or semantic range.
Semantic shift (semantic change): A change in the meaning of a word over time, including broadening, narrowing, amelioration, and pejoration.
Polysemy vs. homonymy: Polysemy involves related senses of one lexical item; homonymy involves unrelated meanings that share form by coincidence.
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the rules used to combine them.
Non-compositional (idiomatic) expression: A multi-word unit whose meaning cannot be predicted from the meanings of its individual words (e.g., "kick the bucket" = "die").
Idiom: A fixed, conventionalized multi-word expression with a figurative or opaque meaning.
Collocation: See above.
Phraseology: The study of fixed and semi-fixed multi-word expressions, including collocations, idioms, phrasal verbs, and proverbs.
Phrasal verb: A multi-word predicate formed from a verb plus one or more particles, often with a non-compositional meaning (e.g., "give up", "look after").
Prepositional verb: A verb that takes a prepositional phrase as an integral complement (e.g., "depend on", "look into").
Light verb: A verb that carries little semantic content and relies on its nominal complement for meaning (e.g., "make a decision", "take a walk").
Copular construction: A construction in which a copula links the subject to a predicate adjective, noun, or prepositional phrase (e.g., "She is tall", "He became a teacher").
Predicate: The part of a sentence that says something about the subject, typically containing the verb and its complements.
Subject: The syntactic element that typically agrees with the verb in person and number and, in active clauses, corresponds to the Agent.
Object (direct / indirect): The syntactic element corresponding to the Theme/Patient (direct) or Recipient/Goal (indirect) of a transitive verb.
Adjunct: An optional, typically peripheral modifier in a clause (e.g., an adverbial phrase of time, place, or manner).
Complement: An obligatory argument required by a predicate to complete its meaning (e.g., the direct object of a transitive verb, the clause after "think").
Modifier: An element that restricts or adds descriptive information to a head (e.g., an adjective modifying a noun, a relative clause modifying a noun).
Head: The central word of a phrase that determines its category and core meaning (e.g., the noun in a noun phrase, the verb in a verb phrase).
Specified head: The element that projects the syntactic and semantic properties of a phrase.
Phrase vs. clause: A phrase is a constituent headed by a lexical category; a clause contains a subject-verb predicate structure.
Clause: The smallest grammatical unit containing a finite verb and its arguments, able to express a proposition.
Subordinate (dependent) clause: A clause that cannot stand alone and functions as a constituent within a larger clause.
Main (matrix / independent) clause: A clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence.
Embedded clause: A clause that appears within the syntactic structure of another clause.
Finite verb: A verb that is marked for tense, person, and number and can serve as the main predicate of an independent clause.
Non-finite verb: A verb form that is not marked for finite tense and cannot serve as the main predicate alone (infinitive, participle, gerund).
Participle: A non-finite verb form used adjectivally or in progressive/passive constructions (e.g., "running", "broken").
Gerund: A verbal noun formed with the -ing form, functioning as a noun (e.g., "Running is fun").
Infinitive: The base, non-finite form of a verb, often preceded by "to" (e.g., "to run", "run" after "make").
Aspectual auxiliary: A verb that combines with a lexical verb to express aspect (e.g., "be + V-ing" for progressive, "have + V-en" for perfect).
Perfect aspect: An aspect that relates an event to a reference time, often indicating anteriority or completion (e.g., "has gone", "had finished").
Progressive (continuous) aspect: An aspect that presents an event as ongoing or in progress at a reference time (e.g., "is sleeping").
Habitual aspect: An aspect that indicates a repeated or customary action (e.g., "She walks to work" in the present simple).
Perfective aspect: An aspect presenting an event as a complete whole, without internal structure.
Imperfective aspect: An aspect presenting an event as ongoing, habitual, or incomplete.
Durative / punctual: A distinction between events that extend over time (durative: "build") and events that occur at a point (punctual: "arrive").
Punctual / ingressive: A further distinction between a state or change (ingressive: "break") and a sustained state.
Aktionsart: The intrinsic aspect or internal temporal structure of a verb (state, semelpunctual, durative, punctual, iterative, etc.), as described by Vendler and others.
Vendler's classification: A taxonomy of verb classes based on internal temporal structure: states, achievements, semelpunctual actions, activities, and Accomplishments.
State: A verb denoting a static condition with no internal change (e.g., "know", "love", "belong").
Achievement: A verb denoting a punctual change of state (e.g., "recognize", "find", "arrive").
Accomplishment: A verb denoting a bounded, durative process with an endpoint (e.g., "build a house", "run a mile").
Activity: A verb denoting an unbounded, durative process (e.g., "run", "swim", "walk").
Semelpunctual: A verb denoting a single, instantaneous action (e.g., "knock once", "sneeze").
Iterative: A verb or construction denoting repeated or habitual action (e.g., "used to run", "keep knocking").
Resultative: A predicate or complement that describes the state resulting from an event (e.g., "She slept the baby to death" – resultative "to death").
Causative-stative: A construction in which a causative verb takes a stative complement (e.g., "The movie bored me" vs. "I was bored by the movie").
Change-of-state predicate: A predicate that entails a transition from one state to another (e.g., "break", "melt", "die").
Stative predicate: A predicate that describes a condition without change (e.g., "know", "own", "be tall").
Agentivity: The degree to which the subject of a predicate is a volitional, animate initiator of the event.
Patienthood: The degree to which the object of a predicate is affected, undergoes change, or is controlled by the action.
Transitivity hierarchy: A ranked list of features (number of arguments, agentivity, specificity, volitionality, duration, etc.) that predict a language's transitivity-marking patterns.
Alignment: The system by which a language groups and marks grammatical roles (nominative-accusative, ergative-absolutive, tripartite, etc.).
Split ergativity: A system in which the alignment varies according to some grammatical or semantic condition, such as tense, animacy, or definiteness.
Nominative-accusative alignment: See above.
Ergative-absolutive alignment: See above.
Tripartite alignment: A system in which S, A, and O are each marked differently, with no pairing.
Actor-patient alignment: An alignment in which the choice of marking depends on the semantic roles (actor vs. patient) rather than syntactic positions.
Person hierarchy: A ranking of person pronouns (typically 1st > 2nd > 3rd) that affects agreement, cliticization, and other morphological processes.
Agreement (concord): See above.
Government: A syntactic or morphological relation in which one element determines the form of another (e.g., a preposition governing the case of its complement).
Control: A syntactic relation in which the subject or object of a main clause is co-referential with the subject of an embedded non-finite clause (e.g., "John tried [to leave]").
Raising: A syntactic relation in which a subject of an embedded clause appears in the matrix clause, often in a non-finite or "seem/appear" construction (e.g., "John seems [to be tall]").
Passivization: See voice above.
Nominalization: See word formation above.
Apposition: The placement of two noun phrases side by side where one renames or specifies the other (e.g., "Paris, the capital of France, is beautiful").
Appositive: The noun phrase that renames or specifies another noun phrase.
Genitive / possessive: A construction expressing possession, association, or attribution (e.g., "John's book", "the book of John").
Genitive chain: A sequence of possessive or genitive phrases (e.g., "the brother of the king of France").
Dative shift: An alternation between a double-object construction and a prepositional dative (e.g., "give her a book" / "give a book to her").
Double object construction: A transitive clause with two objects, a direct and an indirect (e.g., "I gave her a book").
Prepositional dative: A construction in which the indirect object is introduced by a preposition (e.g., "I gave a book to her").
Dative alternation: The systematic variation between double-object and prepositional-dative constructions for certain verbs.
Causative alternation: The variation between a causative transitive and an intransitive form of the same predicate (e.g., "The heat melted the ice" / "The ice melted").
Middle alternation: The variation between an agentive transitive and a middle (intransitive with affected subject) form (e.g., "The book sells" / "They sell the book").
Unaccusative hypothesis: The claim that the sole argument of an unaccusative verb is base-generated as an object and raises to subject position.
A-movement / A'-movement: A distinction in syntactic theory; A-movement targets argument positions (subject, object), while A'-movement targets non-argument positions (wh-words, topicalization).
Wh-movement: The displacement of a wh-word (who, what, where, when, why, how) from its base position to a clause-initial or C-position, forming a question or relative clause.
Subject–verb inversion: The reversal of the expected subject-verb order, often triggered by a fronted negative or focus element (e.g., "Never have I seen…").
Clefting: See cleft sentence above.
Pseudo-cleft: A cleft construction using a "what"-clause (e.g., "What I need is a break").
Heavy NP shift: The tendency to place a long or complex noun phrase later in the clause, often after the verb, to ease processing.
Left dislocation: Fronting of a topic with a resumptive pronoun in the comment (e.g., "John, I think he's great").
Right dislocation: Placement of a topic-like element after the clause, separated by a comma (e.g., "He's great, John").
Topic-comment structure: A discourse-level organization in which the topic is presented first and the comment adds new information.
Given-new chain: A discourse principle stating that sentences begin with given (old) information and end with new information.
Thematic progression: The pattern by which themes (topics) of successive sentences are linked, either repeated, advanced, or derived.
Cohesion: The use of linguistic devices (reference, conjunction, lexical repetition, ellipsis) to link parts of a text.
Reference: The use of pronouns, demonstratives, or definite descriptions to link to previously or subsequently mentioned entities.
Conjunction: The use of connective words or phrases (and, but, because, however, therefore) to express logical or temporal relations between clauses or sentences.
Ellipsis: The omission of a word or phrase that is recoverable from context (e.g., "I like tea, and she likes coffee" – the verb "likes" is understood in the second clause if omitted).
Lexical substitution: The replacement of a word with a synonym, pronoun, or other expression to maintain cohesion.
Hallidayan cohesion: M. A. K. Halliday and J. R. Hasan's classification of cohesive devices into reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, and lexical cohesion.
Discourse analysis: The study of language as it is used in extended texts, conversations, and social interactions, going beyond the single sentence.
Text linguistics: A subfield focused on the structure, coherence, and composition of written and spoken texts.
Conversation analysis: An ethnomethodological approach to the study of talk-in-interaction, focusing on turn-taking, repair, and sequencing.
Pragmatic inference: The process by which a hearer goes beyond the literal meaning of an utterance to derive its intended meaning in context.
Speech act: See above.
Illocutionary force: See above.
Perlocutionary force: See above.
Performative verb: A verb that, when used in the first person present, performs the action it describes (e.g., "promise", "declare", "apologize").
Indirect speech act: An utterance whose form (e.g., a question or statement) differs from its illocutionary force (e.g., "Could you pass the salt?" is a request, not a question about ability).
Deixis: See above.
Demonstrative: A determiner or pronoun that points to entities relative to the speaker's spatial or discourse context (e.g., "this", "that", "these", "those").
Deictic pronoun: A pronoun whose reference depends on the speech situation (e.g., "I", "you").
Deictic adverb: An adverb that references the speech situation (e.g., "here", "there", "now", "then").
Indexical shift: A change in the reference parameters of an indexical (e.g., in reported speech, "I" in the original becomes "he" in the report).
Quotation: The reproduction of another's utterance, either directly (verbatim, in quotes) or indirectly (paraphrased).
Reported speech: The indirect reporting of another's utterance, typically involving changes in person, tense, and deixis.
Free direct speech: A narrative technique in which a character's thoughts or speech are presented without quotation marks or reporting clauses.
Free indirect speech: A narrative technique that blends the narrator's voice with a character's perspective, typically without quotation marks.
Discourse marker: See above.
Hesitation marker: A word or sound that signals a pause or difficulty in producing the next segment (e.g., "um", "uh", "well").
Repair: A sequence in conversation in which a speaker or hearer identifies and corrects a problem in prior talk (e.g., "I was going to say the other thing…").
Self-repair / other-repair: Repair initiated by the speaker of the trouble source vs. repair initiated by the hearer.
Turn constructional unit (TCU): The smallest unit of talk that can constitute a complete turn in conversation, identified by its projected end.
Completion: The point at which a speaker has reached the projected end of a TCU, making it available for the next speaker to take a turn.
Adjacency pair: A pair of turns in which the second turn is strongly conditioned by the first (e.g., question–answer, greeting–greeting, request–accept/refuse).
Preference organization: The tendency in conversation to treat "preferred" responses (e.g., acceptance, agreement) as quicker and less marked than "dispreferred" responses (e.g., refusal, disagreement).
Face (facework): Goffman's concept; the public self-image a person claims in social interaction, which speakers manage through polite or mitigating strategies.
Positive face: The desire to be liked, approved of, and included.
Negative face: The desire to be unimposed upon and to have freedom of action.
Politeness strategy: A linguistic choice that mitigates a face-threatening act (e.g., using a question form to make a request, hedging, indirectness).
Mitigation: The use of linguistic devices (hedges, understatement, softening particles) to reduce the force of a statement or request.
Hedge: A word or phrase that reduces the commitment of a speaker (e.g., "sort of", "I think", "maybe", "somewhat").
Scalar hedge: A hedge that places a statement on a scale of intensity (e.g., "somewhat", "rather", "pretty").
Epistemic hedge: A hedge that signals uncertainty or limited knowledge (e.g., "I believe", "as far as I know", "apparently").
Appositive: See above.
Nominal clause: A clause whose predicate is a noun phrase, adjective, or prepositional phrase linked by a copula (e.g., "She is a teacher").
Verbal clause: A clause whose predicate is a verb phrase (e.g., "She reads books").
Small clause: A predicateless phrase combining a noun phrase and an adjective, noun, or prepositional phrase (e.g., [the movie boring]).
Predicate nominative: The noun phrase that follows a copula and identifies or classifies the subject (e.g., "She is [a teacher]").
Predicate adjective: The adjective that follows a copula and describes the subject (e.g., "The soup is [hot]").
Extraposition: The movement of a heavy constituent (often a clause) to a later position, replacing it with a placeholder (e.g., "It is clear [that she left]" from "[That she left] is clear").
Heavy constituent: A long or syntactically complex phrase that tends to be placed later in a clause for ease of processing.
Information-structural inversion: Subject-verb inversion triggered by the fronting of a focus or topic element.
V2 (verb-second) constraint: A word-order constraint in which the finite verb occupies the second position in a main clause, as in German, Dutch, and Scandinavian languages.
Head-final / head-initial: A typological parameter describing whether the head of a phrase (verb, preposition, postposition) precedes or follows its complements.
SOV / SVO / VSO: The basic canonical word order of a language, described by the order of Subject, Object, and Verb.
Postmodifier / premodifier: A modifier placed after (postmodifier) or before (prefilter) the head noun, typical of relative clauses and pre/postpositional phrases, respectively.
Modifier: See above.
Specifier: In phrase-structure and X-bar theory, the element preceding the head within a phrase (e.g., the determiner in a noun phrase).
Complement: See above.
Adjunct: See above.
X-bar scheme: A model of phrase structure in which every phrase has a head (X), an intermediate projection (X'), and a maximal projection (XP).
Maximal projection: The largest node in a phrase (XP), corresponding to a full phrase.
Intermediate projection (X'): The node below the maximal projection, typically containing the head and its complement (X + Complement → X').
Projection principle: The principle that the syntactic structure of a phrase mirrors the subcategorization and selectional properties of its lexical head.
Subcategorization: The specification of the types and number of complements a verb, adjective, or preposition requires.
Selectional restriction: See above.
Idiosyncratic: Pertaining to properties of a particular lexeme that are not predictable from general rules (e.g., irregular verb forms, idiom meaning).
Productive: A rule or process that can be applied to novel or unlimited inputs (e.g., regular -ed past tense).
Unproductive (dead) process: A morphological rule that is no longer applied to new forms (e.g., the -en past in "dreamt" vs. "dreamed", or the "old English" -eth third person).
Suppletion: See above.
Allomorphy: The existence of multiple phonological forms for the same morpheme, conditioned by context or history.
Morphophonology: The subfield dealing with the interaction of morphological structure and phonological form.
Morphotactics: The rules governing the order and combination of morphemes within a word.
Stem: The morpheme (or morpheme sequence) to which inflectional affixes are attached; may consist of a root plus derivational affixes.
Base: The form to which a morpheme is attached in a particular derivation or inflection; may be a root, stem, or full word.
Morpheme: See above.
Morphological typology: The classification of languages by the degree of morphological fusion (isolating, agglutinative, fusional, polysynthetic).
Isolating (analytic) language: A language with little or no inflectional morphology, relying on word order and function words (e.g., Mandarin Chinese, Vietnamese).
Agglutinative language: A language in which morphemes are concatenated with relatively consistent boundaries, each morpheme carrying a single grammatical meaning (e.g., Turkish, Finnish, Japanese).
Fusional (synthetic) language: A language in which a single affix may encode multiple grammatical features simultaneously (e.g., Latin -ō, English -s for third-person singular).
Polysynthetic language: A language in which a single word can contain an entire clause's worth of morphemes, incorporating arguments and other constituents (e.g., many Native American languages).
Morpheme density: A measure of the average number of morphemes per word, used to characterize a language's morphological typology.
Morpheme inventory: The set of morphemes available in a language.
Morphological paradigm: The full set of inflected forms a word takes across grammatical categories.
Paradigmatic economy: The tendency of a language to minimize the number of distinct forms in a paradigm by using zero forms, allomorphy, or suppletion.
Morphological default: A form that is used in the absence of specific agreement or inflectional marking (e.g., the third-person singular or the unmarked case).
Zero morpheme: The absence of overt morphological marking where a grammatical feature is understood from context (e.g., the English third-person plural -∅).
Portmanteau morpheme: A single morpheme that fuses the functions of what would otherwise be two or more morphemes (e.g., the French -ent in "parlent" encoding both 3rd person and plural).
Bound root: A root morpheme that cannot appear as a standalone word but can serve as the base for derivation (e.g., English "-struct" in "construct").
Free root: A root that can appear as a standalone word (e.g., English "book", "run").
Derivational affix: An affix that creates a new word, often changing the grammatical category (e.g., "-ness", "un-", "able").
Inflectional affix: An affix that marks grammatical relationships within a phrase or clause without changing the word's category (e.g., "-s", "-ed", "-ing").
Morphological derivation: The process of creating a new lexeme by adding a derivational affix or using conversion.
Morphological inflection: The process of marking a word for tense, number, case, person, etc.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a host word but syntactically behaves like a free word (e.g., English "'s" in "John's", French "-en" in "il les a vus").
Enclitic: A clitic that attaches to the end of its host (e.g., English "'s", Spanish "-se").
Proclitic: A clitic that attaches to the beginning of its host (e.g., English "n't", French "je", "tu" before a vowel).
Semi-affix: A morpheme that shows properties intermediate between a clitic and an affix.
Morpheme order: The linear sequence of morphemes within a word, which is language-specific (e.g., English: root + derivational + inflectional).
Affix order: The hierarchical or linear order in which multiple affixes attach to a root.
Morphological hierarchy: The layering of affixes on a root, with derivational affixes closer to the root and inflectional affixes on the outside (in English).
Morphological blocking: The prevention of a regular form by the existence of an irregular or more frequent form (e.g., "men" blocks "**mans" in some contexts).
Morphological analogization: The extension of a regular pattern to an irregular form, often as a step in language change (e.g., "goed" for "went").
Morphological productivity: The degree to which a particular affix or process is actively used to form new words.
Derivational class: A set of words that share a common derivational base and affix pattern.
Lexicalization: The process by which a multi-word phrase or a formerly productive form becomes a fixed, stored lexical item.
Morphological irregularity: A form that deviates from the regular morphological patterns of a language (e.g., "foot/feet", "go/went").
Morphological change: Diachronic shifts in the morphological system of a language (e.g., the loss of case endings in English, the rise of periphrastic forms).
Morphosyntax: The interface between morphology and syntax, studying how morphological form and syntactic structure interact.
Morpho-phonology: See morphophonology above.
Lexicon (mental dictionary): The abstract inventory of stored words and their properties in a speaker's mind.
Lexical entry: See above.
Lexical semantics: The study of word meaning, including sense relations, semantic features, and the structure of the lexicon.
Semantic feature analysis: A method of representing word meanings as sets of binary or gradable features (e.g., [+human], [+animate], [±adult]).
Componential analysis: A type of semantic feature analysis that breaks down word meanings into a small number of distinguishing features.
Feature matrix: A table in which words or concepts are arranged as rows and semantic features as columns, marked for presence or absence.
Semantic prototype: The most central, typical member of a lexical category or concept, around which other members are organized radially.
Radial category: A conceptual category organized around a central prototype with extensions connected by metaphor, metonymy, or other links.
Metaphor: A figurative mapping from a source domain to a target domain that allows one to be understood in terms of the other (e.g., "argument" mapped from "war": "attack a point", "defend a position").
Metaphorical extension: The process by which a word's meaning spreads to a new domain via metaphor.
Metonymic extension: The process by which a word's meaning spreads to a related entity via contiguity or association.
Conceptual metaphor: A systematic, recurring mapping between conceptual domains that structures thought and language (e.g., TIME IS MONEY: "spend time", "waste time").
Image schema: A basic, recurrent pattern of perceptual or motor experience (e.g., container, path, force, balance) that structures metaphorical and figurative language.
Force dynamic: A conceptual schema describing how forces (or tendencies) act on, resist, or enable the motion or state of an entity.
Container schema: The image schema in which a bounded region (container) has an interior, exterior, and boundary, underlying spatial, grammatical, and figurative language.
Path-goal schema: The image schema of an entity moving along a path toward a goal, underlying narrative structure, case marking, and aspect.
Semantic map: A network of related senses or meanings for a lexeme, showing the paths of semantic extension.
Lexical field / semantic domain: A set of words related by a shared topic or conceptual area.
Antonymy: See above.
Synonymy: The relation between words that have the same or very similar meanings, though differing in connotation, register, or collocation.
Tautology: The use of two or more words with the same or overlapping meaning, often for emphasis or by convention (e.g., "free gift", "ATM machine").
Plurality / number: A grammatical category distinguishing singular, dual, tria, plural, and sometimes paucal forms.
Dual: A grammatical number category for exactly two (present in Arabic, Slovene, Hindi, and others).
Tria: A grammatical number category for exactly three (present in a few languages, e.g., some Australian languages).
Paucal: A grammatical number category for a small, indefinite number (more than dual, fewer than full plural).
Singularia tantum: Nouns that occur only in the singular form (e.g., English "sheep", "cattle" in some uses; German "das Geld").
Pluralia tantum: Nouns that occur only in the plural form (e.g., English "scissors", "trousers"; Latin "menstrua").
Suppletive plural: A plural form built from an entirely different root than the singular (e.g., English "man/men", "goose/geese", "child/children").
Irregular plural: A plural form that does not follow the regular -s/-es pattern (e.g., "mouse/mice", "tooth/teeth").
Regular plural: A plural formed by the standard, productive affix (e.g., English -s, -es).
Plural agreement: The requirement that verb, determiner, or adjective forms agree in number with the subject or noun.
Collective noun: A noun that denotes a group or collection of individuals (e.g., "flock", "herd", "committee").
Mass noun (uncountable noun): A noun that refers to a substance, material, or abstract entity not naturally divided into discrete units (e.g., "water", "advice", "furniture").
Count noun: A noun that refers to discrete, countable entities (e.g., "book", "cat", "idea").
Partitive: A construction expressing a portion of a mass or collective (e.g., "a cup of tea", "a piece of advice", "a group of students").
Partitive case: A case marking a part of a whole (e.g., Finnish -a/-ä: "kirjaa" = "of a book").
Distributive: A grammatical or semantic property indicating that an action applies to individual members of a group (e.g., "The children each received a gift").
Distributive number: A grammatical marker indicating that an action or property applies to one member at a time within a group.
Singular (absolutum): A form used without a determiner or other specifier, often for generic reference.
Generic reference: The use of a singular or plural noun without a determiner to refer to the class as a whole (e.g., "Dogs are loyal" = dogs in general).
Bare noun: A noun phrase without a determiner, used for generic reference in some languages or in fixed expressions.
Article: A determiner that marks definiteness (definite article: "the") or indefiniteness (indefinite article: "a/an").
Demonstrative determiner: A determiner that points to a specific referent relative to the speaker or discourse context (e.g., "this", "that").
Possessive determiner: A determiner expressing ownership or association (e.g., "my", "your", "John's").
Quantifier: See above.
Numeral: A word expressing a number; can be cardinal (one, two, three) or ordinal (first, second, third).
Cardinal number: A numeral expressing quantity (one, two, three).
Ordinal number: A numeral expressing position in a sequence (first, second, third).
Fractional number: A numeral expressing a part of a whole (half, quarter, third).
Multiplier: A word expressing a multiple of a quantity (double, triple, quadruple).
Distributive numeral: A word expressing a number of times or per individual (each, every, both).
Collective numeral: A word expressing a group of a specific size (dozen, hundred, thousand, pair).
Measure phrase: A noun phrase expressing a quantity or amount (e.g., "a pound of sugar", "two meters of rope", "a cup of coffee").
Measure word (classifier): A word used in some languages to classify count nouns when a numeral is involved (e.g., Mandarin "yī gè rén" = "one [CL-person] person"; Japanese "san-biki no inu").
Classifier system: A grammatical system in which count nouns must be combined with a classifier in the presence of numerals, quantifiers, or definite articles.
Noun class system: A grammatical system (common in Bantu and other African languages) in which nouns are assigned to classes, each with its own set of agreement markers.
Gender (grammatical): See grammatical gender above.
Animacy hierarchy: A ranking of noun classes by perceived animacy (1st person > 2nd person > human > animal > inanimate) that influences case marking, agreement, and word order.
Definiteness marking: The morphological or syntactic means by which a language distinguishes definite from indefinite noun phrases.
Articleless language: A language that lacks a dedicated definite/indefinite article system (e.g., Russian, German uses articles but not for all cases; Japanese has no articles).
Specificity: See above.
Uniqueness: The property of a referent being the only one of its kind in the discourse or situation.
Situational uniqueness: A referent that is unique in the immediate context but not globally (e.g., "the coffee" in a room where there is only one cup).
Inherent uniqueness: A referent that is unique by nature (e.g., "the sun", "the moon", "my mother").
Anaphoric reference: Reference to a previously mentioned or salient entity.
Cataphoric reference: Reference to a subsequently mentioned entity.
Deictic reference: Reference to an entity identified by the physical or situational context.
Exophoric: Reference to an entity in the external, non-linguistic context (e.g., "Look at that bird!" while pointing).
Endophoric: Reference to an entity within the discourse itself (anaphoric or cataphoric).
Coreference: See above.
Co-reference: Same as coreference.
Anaphor: A referring expression whose interpretation depends on an antecedent (pronoun, reflexive).
Antecedent: The expression to which an anaphor refers.
Reflexive: A pronoun that refers back to its own subject (e.g., "himself", "herself", "itself").
Reciprocal: A pronoun expressing a mutual or reciprocal relationship (e.g., "each other", "one another", "mutually").
Reflexive binding: The syntactic and semantic constraint that a reflexive must be bound by a subject in the same clause (Binding Principle A).
Pronoun: A word that stands in for a noun or noun phrase, avoiding repetition (e.g., "he", "she", "it", "they", "who", "which").
Personal pronoun: A pronoun referring to the speaker, addressee, or a third party (e.g., I, you, he, she, we, they).
Demonstrative pronoun: A pronoun that points to a specific entity (e.g., this, that).
Relative pronoun: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause (e.g., who, whom, which, that).
Interrogative pronoun: A pronoun used to ask questions (e.g., who, what, which, whose).
Indefinite pronoun: A pronoun referring to a non-specific entity (e.g., someone, nothing, everything, anyone).
Reciprocal pronoun: See reciprocal above.
Intensive pronoun: A pronoun used for emphasis rather than coreference (e.g., "I myself did it" vs. "I did it myself" where "myself" is intensive).
Reflexive vs. intensive: A reflexive is bound by its antecedent; an intensive is a free appositive for emphasis.
Pronominalization: The replacement of a noun phrase with a pronoun to avoid repetition and maintain discourse flow.
Pronominal case: The case form of a pronoun (e.g., English "I/me/my/mine"; Latin "ego/mei/mihi/me/me").
Pronoun case system: The set of case forms a pronoun takes in a language.
Pronominal agreement: The matching of a pronoun's person, number, and gender to its antecedent.
Gender agreement with pronouns: The requirement that a pronoun's gender form match the semantic or grammatical gender of its antecedent.
Neuter pronoun: A pronoun form used for inanimate or abstract referents (e.g., English "it", German "es", French "ce").
Third-person pronoun: A pronoun referring to a person or entity other than the speaker or addressee (e.g., he, she, it, they).
Third-person plural "they": The English pronoun used both for known plural antecedents and, increasingly, as a singular gender-neutral pronoun.
Gender-neutral pronoun: A pronoun form not marked for natural gender (e.g., English "they" in singular use, Scandinavian "hen", English "ze/zir").
Bound pronoun: A pronoun that is syntactically bound (coreferential) to an antecedent within a specific domain.
Free pronoun: A pronoun that is not syntactically bound and can refer to any appropriate antecedent.
Pronominal anaphor: A pronoun that functions as an anaphor (e.g., "himself" in "John criticized himself").
Pronominal reference: The use of a pronoun to refer to a discourse entity.
Pronoun resolution: The process by which a hearer determines the referent of an ambiguous pronoun.
Pronoun ambiguity: The situation in which a pronoun could refer to more than one antecedent.
Weak pronoun: A clitic or unstressed pronoun form (e.g., French "le", "la", "lui").
Strong pronoun: A full, stressed pronoun form (e.g., French "lui", "elle", "eux").
Stressless / unstressed pronoun: A pronoun form that is phonologically reduced or unstressed.
Stressed / emphatic pronoun: A pronoun form used for emphasis or contrast (e.g., French "moi" vs. "me"; English "I" vs. "me" in certain emphatic contexts).
Pronominalization constraint: A syntactic or semantic restriction on the use of pronouns (e.g., Binding Principles, the that-t effect).
Pronoun case alternation: The variation between nominative and accusative forms of pronouns in different syntactic positions.
Reflexive pronoun: See reflexive above.
Reflexive binding domain: The local syntactic domain within which a reflexive must find its antecedent (typically the closest subject or clause).
Local binding: Binding within the same clause or a locally defined domain.
Long-distance binding: Binding that crosses clause boundaries, typical of some anaphors in certain languages (e.g., Japanese "zisin").
Anaphoric binding: The general relation of coreference between an anaphor and its antecedent.
A-bound: An expression that is bound (coreferential) within a specific syntactic domain.
A-free: An expression that is not bound within a specific syntactic domain.
C-command: A structural relation in which one node dominates another and the first branching node above both; essential for Binding Theory.
Binding domain: The minimal syntactic domain (usually a clause or phrase) within which binding must or must not occur.
Governing category: The minimal phrase containing a subject and a verb that governs (theta-marks or selects) the anaphor or pronoun.
Minimal governing category: The smallest phrase that contains the anaphor, a subject, and a potential binder.
Binding Principle A: See above.
Binding Principle B: See above.
Binding Principle C: See above.
Binding Theory: The set of principles (A, B, C) governing the distribution of anaphors, pronouns, and R-expressions.
Government: A relation in which a head (typically a verb or preposition) theta-marks or selects the complement or trace of an anaphor.
Theta-marks: A verb or preposition assigns a thematic role to its argument.
Trace: The empty category left in the base position of a moved element (e.g., the trace of a wh-moved element).
R-expression: A referring expression that is not a pronoun or anaphor (e.g., a proper name, a definite description, a complex NP).
Anaphor: See above.
Pronoun: See above.
Coreferential: Two or more expressions referring to the same entity.
Non-coreferential: Expressions that do not refer to the same entity.
Co-argument: Two arguments of the same predicate that can be in a binding relationship.
Anti-command: The structural relation in which a node is dominated by another without a branching node in between, the inverse of c-command.
C-command: See above.
Government (syntactic): A relation in which a head selects or theta-marks a complement within its immediate dominance.
Licensing: The requirement that certain elements (anaphors, pronouns, expletives) must be in a specific structural configuration to be grammatical.
Licensing domain: The syntactic domain within which a licensing relation must hold.
Minimal link condition: A condition requiring that the closest potential antecedent or binder be the actual one.
Locality: The general principle that syntactic and binding relations are restricted to a local domain.
Island: A syntactic domain from which extraction (movement) is blocked (e.g., complex noun phrases, subject islands, adjunct islands).
Complex NP island: A noun phrase containing an embedded clause that blocks extraction of an element from within it.
Subject island: A clause in which extraction of a subject is blocked.
Adjunct island: A syntactic adjunct (adverbial clause or phrase) from which extraction is blocked.
Wh-island: An embedded wh-question that blocks extraction of a second wh-element.
Superiority effect: The preference in multiple wh-questions for the higher-ranked wh-phrase to be fronted first.
Wh-agreement: The requirement that wh-movement and the C-position (complementizer) agree in features.
Wh-scope: The domain over which a wh-quantifier ranges in a question or relative clause.
Wh-movement: See above.
Wh-in-situ: A wh-element that remains in its base position, as in English yes-no questions with a wh-word ("What did you say?") or in many non-English languages.
Wh-feature: The set of features (wh, q, focus) that trigger movement to the C-position.
Q (question) feature: The feature on the complementizer that triggers question interpretation and wh-movement.
Echo question: A question formed by repeating or partially repeating a previous utterance, often with rising intonation, to express surprise or request clarification.
Polarity question: A yes/no question that can be answered with "yes" or "no" (as opposed to a wh-question).
Wh-question: A question containing a wh-word that asks for specific information (who, what, where, when, why, how).
Alternative question: A question that presents two or more alternatives (e.g., "Do you want tea or coffee?").
Tag question: A short interrogative tag appended to a declarative sentence, seeking confirmation (e.g., "It's cold, isn't it?").
Polar tag: A tag that matches the polarity of the main clause ("It's cold, isn't it?").
Reversed-polarity tag: A tag that contrasts with the polarity of the main clause ("It isn't cold, is it?").
Tag agreement: The matching of person, number, and tense between the tag and the main clause.
Rhetorical question: A question asked for effect rather than to elicit an answer.
Tagless question: A question without an overt question word or intonation marking, relying on context (e.g., "You're coming, right?").
Question intonation: The pitch contour (typically rising for polar questions, falling for wh-questions in English) that signals interrogative force.
Question word: A wh-word or other interrogative element (who, what, where, when, why, how, which).
Question complementizer: The C-head that bears the question feature (e.g., "that" in embedded questions, or a zero complementizer in main questions).
Embedded question (indirect question): A question embedded within a larger clause (e.g., "I wonder [what she said]").
Direct question: A question that stands as a main clause.
Indirect question: See embedded question.
Question embedding: The process of embedding a question clause as a complement or adjunct within a larger clause.
Question scope: The domain over which the question operator ranges, determining which element is questioned.
Question focus: The element in a question that carries the primary interrogative intonation and is the target of the answer.
Answer: The utterance that addresses the information sought by a question.
Answer focus: The element in an answer that corresponds to the question focus.
Given-focus: The element in a question or answer that is presupposed or already established.
New-focus: The element in a question or answer that provides new, requested information.
Focus: The element in a sentence that is new, emphasized, or contrastive, often marked by prosodic stress or clefting.
Information focus: The primary new information in a sentence.
Contrastive focus: The element that is contrasted with an implicit or explicit alternative.
Topic focus: The element that identifies the domain of the sentence.
Focus marking: The linguistic means (prosodic, morphological, syntactic) by which focus is indicated.
Cleft focus: Focus expressed through a cleft construction ("It was John who…").
Scrambling: The free or flexible word order in which arguments and adjuncts can appear in various positions, common in Japanese, Korean, and German.
Word order freedom: The degree of syntactic flexibility in the linear ordering of sentence constituents.
Fixed word order: A language in which constituents must appear in a specific, rigid order (e.g., English SVO).
Free word order: A language in which constituents can appear in multiple orders without changing grammaticality (e.g., Latin, Russian to a degree).
Movable word order: A language in which some constituents can be repositioned for focus, topic, or emphasis (e.g., German V2, English fronting).
Word order typology: The classification of languages by their canonical and flexible word orders.
SOV languages: Languages with Subject-Object-Verb order (e.g., Japanese, Turkish, Latin, Hindi).
SVO languages: Languages with Subject-Verb-Object order (e.g., English, Mandarin, French, Arabic).
VSO languages: Languages with Verb-Subject-Object order (e.g., Irish, Welsh, Classical Arabic, Basque).
V2 languages: Languages with a verb-second constraint in main clauses (e.g., German, Dutch, Scandinavian languages, Yiddish).
OVS / OSV / VOS: Rare word orders where the object precedes the verb or subject in non-canonical patterns.
Basic word order: The most frequent or canonical word order of a language.
Harmonic word order: A language in which the word order is consistent across different syntactic contexts (e.g., consistently SOV or consistently SVO).
Scrambling: See above.
Topicalization: The fronting of a topic to the left periphery of a clause, often with a resumptive pronoun or gap.
Focalization: The fronting of a focus element to the left periphery, often with contrastive intonation.
Left periphery: The clause-initial position(s) in a sentence where topics, foci, and other discourse elements can be fronted.
Right periphery: The clause-final position(s) where dislocated topics, sentence-final particles, or other elements can appear.
Discourse position: The syntactic position in a clause that is motivated by discourse needs (topic, focus) rather than by thematic role.
A-position / A'-position: Argument vs. non-argument positions in the syntactic tree.
Move: The operation of copying an element from one position to another, leaving a trace or copy in the base position.
Copy theory of movement: The proposal that movement leaves a full copy in the base position, and the interpretation depends on whether the higher or lower copy is pronounced.
Trace: See above.
Copy: A full duplicate of a moved element left in the base position under the copy theory of movement.
Chain: The sequence of positions (trace/copy + moved element) created by a movement operation.
Movement: The syntactic operation by which an element is displaced from its base position to a higher position.
Raising: See above.
Control: See above.
Passive: See above.
Causative: See above.
Application: See applicative above.
Nominalization: See above.
Verbalization: See above.
Derivation: See above.
Inflection: See above.
Compounding: See above.
Conversion: See above.
Borrowing: See above.
Calque: See above.
Clipping: See above.
Blending: See above.
Reduplication: See above.
Suppletion: See above.
Portmanteau: See above.
Zero derivation: Same as conversion.
Affixation: The addition of a bound morpheme (prefix, suffix, infix, circumfix) to a root or stem.
Infix: A morpheme inserted within a root (e.g., English "ab-sole-ute", Malagasy "man-" → "man-").
Circumfix: A morpheme that surrounds a root (e.g., German "be-…-en", Indonesian "me-…-kan").
Overtness: The property of a morpheme being phonologically realized (overt) vs. absent (zero).
Zero morpheme: See above.
Allomorph: See above.
Morphophonemic alternation: The systematic variation in the phonological form of a morpheme depending on its phonological environment.
Morphotactic: Pertaining to the ordering of morphemes within a word.
Morphosyntactic: Pertaining to the interaction between morphological and syntactic structure.
Morpho-semantic: Pertaining to the relation between morphological form and semantic content.
Lexical morphology: The study of word formation and the structure of the lexicon.
Inflectional morphology: The study of grammatical inflection (tense, case, number, agreement).
Derivational morphology: The study of word-formation processes that create new lexemes.
Paradigmatic morphology: The study of morphological paradigms (sets of related forms).
Morphological typology: See above.
Historical morphology: The study of the diachronic development of morphological systems.
Synchronic morphology: The study of the morphological system of a language at a single point in time.
Diachronic: Pertaining to the study of language change over time.
Synchronic: Pertaining to the study of a language at a single point in time.
Language change: The diachronic process by which languages evolve over generations.
Sound change: See above.
Analogical change: Language change driven by the extension of regular patterns to irregular forms.
Semantic change: See semantic shift above.
Grammaticalization: The process by which lexical items or constructions develop into grammatical markers (e.g., "going to" → "gonna"; "have" + verb → perfect aspect).
Grammaticalized: A lexical item that has become a grammatical marker.
Cliticization: The process by which a free word becomes phonologically dependent on a host (clitic).
Reanalysis: The re-interpretation of a linguistic structure, often leading to grammaticalization or morphological change.
Morpholog
