Allomorph: A variant phonetic form of a morpheme (e.g., /s/ and /z/ in English plural).
Allophone: A context-dependent phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not distinguish meaning.
Amalgamation: The blending of two or more words into a single new word (e.g., "brunch" from "breakfast" and "lunch").
Antecedent: A word or phrase that a pronoun or other anaphoric expression refers back to.
Apocope: The omission of a sound or syllable at the end of a word.
Aphaeresis: The omission of a sound or syllable at the beginning of a word.
Archiphoneme: A phoneme that is not contrastive in all phonological environments and represents a set of merged contrasts.
Assimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes more similar to an adjacent sound.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which a sound becomes less similar to a nearby sound.
Metathesis: The transposition of two adjacent sounds within a word (e.g., "ask" from an earlier "aks").
Lenition: A sound change in which a consonant becomes weaker or softer over time.
Fortition: A sound change in which a consonant becomes stronger or more articulatorily complex.
Epenthesis: The insertion of an extra sound into a word, typically to break up a cluster.
Elision: The deletion of a sound or syllable from a word, especially in rapid speech.
Sandhi: A set of phonological rules that describe how sounds change at morpheme or word boundaries.
Aspiration: A burst of breath accompanying the release of certain stop consonants, such as the [h] in English "pit."
Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins at one position of articulation and glides to another within a single syllable.
Triphthong: A vowel sequence of three phonemes that function together as a single syllable nucleus.
Monophthong: A pure vowel sound that does not change in quality during its articulation.
Glottal stop: A consonant produced by complete closure of the vocal folds, transcribed as [ʔ].
Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel to create turbulent noise (e.g., /f/, /s/).
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure followed by a sudden release of air (e.g., /p/, /t/, /k/).
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing airflow through the nasal cavity (e.g., /m/, /n/, /ŋ/).
Lateral: A consonant in which airflow is directed around the sides of the tongue (e.g., /l/).
Trill: A consonant produced by rapid, repeated contacts of an articulator (e.g., the Spanish /r/).
Tap: A consonant produced by a single rapid contact of an articulator, also called a flap (e.g., the American English /ɾ/ in "butter").
Semivowel: A sound with phonetic properties of a vowel that functions syllabically as a consonant (e.g., /w/, /j/).
Suprasegmental: A prosodic feature of speech that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Tone: A contrastive use of pitch on a syllable or word that distinguishes lexical or grammatical meaning.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable within a word or utterance, typically marked by greater loudness, length, or pitch.
Intonation: The variation of pitch across a phrase or sentence that conveys grammatical, pragmatic, or emotional meaning.
Pitch: The perceptual correlate of frequency in the human voice, perceived as how high or low a sound is.
Formant: A peak in the amplitude spectrum of a vowel or voiced consonant produced by the resonances of the vocal tract.
Alveolar: A place of articulation where the tongue tip contacts the alveolar ridge behind the upper front teeth.
Bilabial: A place of articulation involving both lips (e.g., /p/, /b/, /m/).
Dental: A place of articulation in which the tongue tip contacts the upper teeth.
Labiodental: A place of articulation in which the lower lip contacts the upper teeth (e.g., /f/, /v/).
Palatal: A place of articulation in which the body of the tongue raises toward the hard palate.
Velar: A place of articulation in which the back of the tongue contacts the soft palate (e.g., /k/, /g/).
Uvular: A place of articulation in which the back of the tongue contacts the uvula.
Pharyngeal: A place of articulation in which the back of the tongue or the pharyngeal wall is raised.
Voiced: A segment produced with regular vibration of the vocal folds.
Voiceless: A segment produced without vibration of the vocal folds.
Syllable: The basic unit of organization in a spoken language, typically consisting of a vowel (nucleus) optionally surrounded by consonants.
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable preceding the nucleus.
Nucleus: The core vowel or syllabic consonant of a syllable.
Coda: The final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable following the nucleus.
Rhyme: The portion of a syllable consisting of the nucleus and any following coda.
Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning (e.g., /p/ vs. /b/ in "pat" vs. "bat").
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in only one phonological segment and have different meanings, used to establish phonemic contrast.
Complementary distribution: A situation in which two sounds never occur in the same phonological environment and are therefore allophones of a single phoneme.
Free variation: A situation in which two or more phonetic forms can be used interchangeably in the same environment without a change in meaning.
Phonotactics: The set of constraints governing permissible sound sequences and syllable structures within a particular language.
Distinctive feature: A binary or multi-valued property used to describe and contrast phonological segments (e.g., [+voice], [±nasal]).
Feature geometry: A theoretical framework organizing distinctive features into hierarchical tiers to explain the structure of segments.
Underlying form: The abstract, pre-surface representation of a word in phonological theory before phonological rules are applied.
Surface form: The final, realized phonetic or phonemic output of a word after all phonological rules have been applied.
Neutralization: A phonological process in which a contrast between two phonemes is lost in a particular environment.
Mora: A unit of syllable weight or timing used in metrical and prosodic phonology.
Syllable weight: A measure of the complexity or duration of a syllable, often based on the number of morae it contains.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or a grammatical function.
Morph: The smallest observable linguistic unit, a concrete phonological or orthographic realization of a morpheme.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning and to which other morphemes may attach.
Stem: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached, often consisting of a root plus derivational morphemes.
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Prefix: An affix that is attached before a root or stem.
Suffix: An affix that is attached after a root or stem.
Infix: An affix that is inserted within the root or stem of a word.
Circumfix: A morpheme that surrounds a root or stem with two parts, one prefixal and one suffixal.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to another morpheme.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word (e.g., "book," "run").
Inflection: A morphological process that modifies a word to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or aspect without changing its lexical category.
Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word, often in a different lexical category, by adding an affix or other process.
Compounding: The formation of a new lexical item by combining two or more free morphemes or roots.
Conjugation: The paradigm of inflected forms of a verb.
Declension: The paradigm of inflected forms of a noun, adjective, or pronoun.
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a particular word in a language.
Allomorphy: The phenomenon in which a single morpheme has two or more phonetic or orthographic variants.
Zero morph: An absence of a phonological segment that nonetheless marks a grammatical function (e.g., the absence of a plural suffix in "sheep").
Portmanteau: A single morpheme that simultaneously encodes two or more grammatical meanings (e.g., English "-ings" in "walkings" encoding plural and gerund).
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a morpheme is repeated to express grammatical meaning.
Suppletion: A morphological process in which an entirely different root is used to express a grammatical contrast (e.g., "go" / "went").
Agglutination: A morphological strategy in which morphemes are concatenated with relatively transparent boundaries, each expressing a single grammatical meaning.
Fusion: A morphological strategy in which multiple grammatical meanings are expressed by a single affix that cannot be cleanly decomposed.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words are typically monomorphemic and grammatical relations are expressed by word order or particles.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which a single word can encode the content of what would be an entire clause in other languages.
Grammaticalization: The process by which lexical items or phrases develop into grammatical markers over time.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of the lexicon representing a set of inflectional forms sharing a common meaning (e.g., the lexeme "run" includes "runs," "running," "ran").
Lexicalization: The process by which a phrase or expression becomes fixed in the lexicon as a single unit.
Clause: A grammatical unit containing a subject and a predicate (a verb phrase), which may be independent or subordinate.
Phrase: A group of words headed by a single constituent of a particular category (e.g., a noun phrase, verb phrase).
Sentence: A grammatical unit consisting of one or more clauses that can stand alone as a complete utterance.
Constituent: A word or group of words that functions as a single unit within a hierarchical syntactic structure.
Subcategorization: The property of a verb or preposition specifying what types of arguments (complements) it requires or permits.
Theta role: A semantic relation assigned by a predicate to its arguments, such as Agent, Patient, Goal, or Theme.
Case: A grammatical category expressed by inflection or word order that indicates the syntactic role of a noun phrase.
Ergative: A case marking system in which the agent of a transitive verb is marked differently from the single argument of an intransitive verb and the patient of a transitive verb.
Accusative: A case marking system in which the object of a transitive verb is marked distinctly from the subject.
Split ergativity: A case marking system in which the language uses ergative alignment in some constructions and accusative alignment in others, often conditioned by tense, aspect, or animacy.
Agreement: The requirement that certain elements in a sentence share grammatical features such as person, number, gender, or case.
Binding: A set of principles governing the co-reference between pronouns, anaphors, and noun phrases in a sentence.
A-movement: Syntactic movement that preserves the theta-role assignment of the moved element (e.g., passivization, raising).
A-bar movement: Syntactic movement that changes the theta-role assignment of the moved element (e.g., wh-movement, topicalization).
Wh-movement: The movement of an interrogative or relative pronoun from its original position to the edge of a clause.
Passive: A syntactic construction in which the patient or theme of a transitive verb becomes the grammatical subject.
Voice: A grammatical category expressing the relationship between the verb and its arguments, most commonly active and passive.
Complementizer: A functional word that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "that," "if," or "whether" in English.
Determiner: A word that precedes a noun and limits its reference, such as "the," "a," "this," or "every."
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, typically including determiners, adjectives, and other modifiers.
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its complements, objects, and adjuncts.
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition, typically including a noun phrase complement.
Coordination: A syntactic process in which two or more constituents of the same category are linked by a conjunction (e.g., "and," "or," "but").
Subordination: A syntactic process in which one clause is embedded within or attached to another as a dependent element.
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is typically introduced by a relative pronoun such as "who," "which," or "that."
Finite verb: A verb form that is inflected for person, number, and tense and can serve as the main verb of an independent clause.
Non-finite verb: A verb form that lacks tense and person marking, such as an infinitive, gerund, or participle.
Auxiliary: A verb that combines with a main verb to express grammatical categories such as tense, aspect, modality, or voice.
Modal: A type of auxiliary verb expressing notions of possibility, necessity, permission, or obligation (e.g., "can," "must," "should").
Negation: A grammatical element that inverts or denies the truth value of a proposition, typically expressed by a particle such as "not."
Topicalization: The movement of a constituent to the beginning of a sentence to mark it as the discourse topic.
Focus: The element in a sentence that carries new or emphasized information, often marked prosodically or syntactically.
Cleft sentence: A syntactic construction that splits a clause into two parts to emphasize a particular constituent, as in "It was John who called."
Extraposition: The movement of a heavy or long constituent (such as a clause) to the end of a sentence for ease of processing.
Raising: A syntactic process in which a subject or object of an embedded clause becomes the subject or object of the matrix clause.
Control: A syntactic relationship in which the subject or object of a matrix clause determines the reference of an argument in a non-finite clause.
Pro: An unpronouned element (empty category) that serves as the subject or object of a non-finite clause in control constructions.
Prole: An unpronounced subject of a finite clause, found in languages with null-subject properties.
Specifier: The position in a phrase structure that precedes the head and typically contains a determiner, quantifier, or topic.
Head: The central, category-determining element of a phrase (e.g., the noun in a noun phrase).
Complement: An obligatory element required by a head to complete its subcategorization frame.
Adjunct: An optional modifier that can be added to or removed from a phrase without affecting its grammaticality.
X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure in which every phrase consists of a specifier, a head, and a complement, with an intermediate X-bar projection.
Phrase structure grammar: A type of grammar that uses hierarchical rewrite rules to generate the constituent structure of sentences.
Dependency grammar: A syntactic theory in which word structure is represented by direct dependency relations between words rather than constituent groupings.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of syntactic structure in which nodes are joined by branches showing hierarchical relations.
Deep structure: In generative grammar, the underlying hierarchical representation of a sentence before transformational rules are applied.
Surface structure: In generative grammar, the final representation of a sentence after all transformations have been applied.
Transformation: A rule in generative grammar that maps a deep structure to a surface structure by moving, deleting, or inserting elements.
Universal Grammar: The hypothesized innate, language-specific component of the human mind that provides the structural framework for all natural languages.
Principles and parameters: A framework in which Universal Grammar consists of invariant principles and language-specific binary or multi-valued parameters.
Complementizer phrase (CP): The maximal projection headed by a complementizer, dominating a sentence in phrase structure grammar.
Inflection phrase (IP) / Tense phrase (TP): The projection dominated by an inflection or tense head, governing the assignment of tense and agreement features.
Verb phrase (VP): The projection dominated by a verb, governing its complements and adjuncts.
Noun phrase (NP): The projection dominated by a noun, governing its determiner, modifiers, and complements.
C-command: A structural relation in which a node governs every node that is not its ancestor or descendant, central to binding and movement theories.
Government: A structural relation in which a head directly dominates a complement or adjacent element, central to case assignment and binding.
Extended Projection Principle (EPP): A principle of Universal Grammar requiring that every finite clause have an overt or covert subject.
Anaphor: A reflexive or reciprocal element that must be bound within a local domain (e.g., "himself," "each other").
Reciprocal: A pronoun expressing a mutual relationship between two or more participants (e.g., "each other," "one another").
R-expression: A referring expression such as a proper noun or definite description that is not subject to anaphoric binding.
Subjacency: A locality condition on movement in generative grammar, restricting movement to cross at most one bounding node at a time.
Trace: An empty element left in the original position of a moved constituent, marking the gap in the sentence.
Empty category: A position in a sentence that is syntactically occupied but phonetically unrealized, such as a trace or pro.
Subcategorization frame: The set of arguments and adjuncts that a particular verb or preposition selects or permits.
Selectional restriction: A semantic constraint on the types of arguments a predicate can take (e.g., "drink" requires a liquid theme).
Compositionality: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined.
Entailment: A semantic relation in which the truth of one proposition logically guarantees the truth of another.
Presupposition: A background assumption made by a speaker that is taken for granted in an utterance and survives under negation.
Conversational implicature: An implicit meaning inferred by the hearer based on the assumption that the speaker is following the Cooperative Principle.
Gricean maxims: Four conversational principles (Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner) proposed by H.P. Grice to explain how speakers and hearers generate and interpret implicatures.
Cooperative Principle: Grice's general maxim that participants in a conversation are expected to make contributions appropriate to the purpose of the exchange.
Politeness: A set of linguistic strategies speakers use to minimize face-threatening acts and maintain social harmony.
Face: The public self-image a person claims in social interaction; divided into positive face (desire for approval) and negative face (desire for autonomy).
Face-threatening act (FTA): A speech act that endangers the positive or negative face of the hearer or the speaker.
Locution: The literal, propositional content of an utterance.
Illocution: The speaker's intended force or function in performing a speech act (e.g., asserting, requesting, promising).
Perlocution: The effect a speech act has on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Speech act: An utterance viewed as an action performed by the speaker, characterized by its locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary dimensions.
Performative: A sentence that explicitly names the speech act it performs (e.g., "I hereby declare you married").
Direct speech act: A speech act in which the illocutionary force matches the propositional content (e.g., a question that is literally a question).
Indirect speech act: A speech act in which the illocutionary force differs from the literal propositional content (e.g., "Can you pass the salt?" as a request).
Deixis: The dependence of the interpretation of certain words or expressions on the context of their use, such as "here," "now," "I," and "this."
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers to an element occurring earlier in a discourse or sentence.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers to an element occurring later in a discourse or sentence.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it designates in the world.
Denotation: The set of entities in the world to which a word or expression applies.
Connotation: The additional associative or emotional meaning a word carries beyond its literal denotation.
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word or expression has multiple related senses.
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two or more distinct words share the same form but have unrelated meanings.
Synonymy: The relation between words or expressions that have the same or very similar meanings.
Antonymy: The relation between words that have opposite meanings (e.g., "hot" and "cold," "big" and "small").
Hyponymy: A semantic relation in which the meaning of one word is included in the meaning of another (e.g., "rose" is a hyponym of "flower").
Meronymy: A semantic relation expressing a part-to-whole relationship (e.g., "wheel" is a meronym of "car").
Metonymy: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase is used to refer to something closely associated with it (e.g., "the White House said…").
Metaphor: A figure of speech in which one entity is described in terms of another based on a perceived similarity.
Semantic role: The role a participant plays in the event described by a predicate (e.g., Agent, Patient, Instrument, Goal).
Agent: The semantic role of the entity that performs or causes an action.
Patient: The semantic role of the entity that is affected by or undergoes an action.
Theme: The semantic role of the entity that is moved, transferred, or presented.
Goal: The semantic role of the destination or endpoint of a motion or transfer.
Source: The semantic role of the origin or starting point of a motion or transfer.
Recipient: The semantic role of the entity that receives something.
Instrument: The semantic role of the tool or means by which an action is carried out.
Location: The semantic role of the place where an event occurs.
Cause: The semantic role of the entity or event that brings about another event.
Beneficiary: The semantic role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed.
Truth value: The logical property of a proposition being either true or false.
Tautology: A statement that is true by virtue of its logical form alone (e.g., "All bachelors are unmarried").
Contradiction: A pair of propositions that cannot both be true at the same time.
Semantic change: The process by which the meaning of a word shifts over time.
Broadening: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more general (e.g., "bird" from "young bird" to all birds).
Narrowing: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more specific (e.g., "meat" from "food" to "animal flesh").
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more negative or derogatory connotation.
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more positive or respectful connotation.
Semantic bleaching: A process in which a word loses much of its original lexical meaning and becomes a grammatical marker.
Neologism: A newly coined or newly adopted word or expression in a language.
Archaism: A word, phrase, or form that has fallen out of common use and is considered outdated.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words and their meanings.
Cognate: A word in one language that is derived from the same proto-language root as a word in another language.
Swadesh list: A standardized list of approximately 200 basic vocabulary items used in lexicostatistics for estimating the age of language divergence.
Glottochronology: A method for estimating the time since two languages diverged by comparing the percentage of shared basic vocabulary.
Lexicostatistics: A quantitative method for classifying languages based on the percentage of shared cognates in a basic vocabulary list.
Comparative method: A method of historical linguistics that reconstructs proto-languages by systematically comparing regular sound correspondences across related languages.
Internal reconstruction: A method of historical linguistics that infers earlier stages of a single language from its internal morphophonological alternations.
Sound change: A systematic, regular shift in the pronunciation of one or more sounds within a language over time.
Regular sound change: A sound change that applies uniformly across all applicable linguistic environments, as described by Grimm's Law or Verner's Law.
Irregular sound change: A sound change that is conditioned by morphological, phonological, or sociolinguistic factors and does not apply uniformly.
Analogy: A linguistic change in which a form is altered to conform to the pattern of other forms in the language.
Calque: A loan translation in which a word or phrase from one language is translated component by component into another language.
Loanword: A word borrowed directly from another language, sometimes with phonological adaptation.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages that can lead to mutual influence, borrowing, or the creation of new languages.
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that evolves from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Diglossia: A sociolinguistic situation in which two distinct varieties of a language are used for different social functions (e.g., formal and informal).
Polyglossia: A situation in which more than two language varieties coexist in a speech community for different functions.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be used.
Language endangerment: A situation in which a language is at risk of losing its remaining speakers and becoming extinct.
Language revitalization: Efforts to increase the number of speakers of an endangered or dormant language and restore its vitality.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually abandons its native language in favor of another.
Dialect: A variety of a language characteristic of a particular region, social group, or community.
Sociolect: A variety of language associated with a particular social group, class, or community.
Idiolect: The unique set of linguistic features (vocabulary, pronunciation, grammar) characteristic of an individual speaker.
Ethnolect: A variety of language associated with a particular ethnic or cultural group.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular context, purpose, or audience (e.g., formal, informal, academic).
Jargon: The specialized terminology used by a particular profession, trade, or group.
Argot: A specialized vocabulary or dialect used by a social group, often to exclude outsiders.
Slang: Informal, often playful or irreverent vocabulary used within a particular social group or community.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsh, blunt, or offensive one.
Dysphemism: A harsh, offensive, or deliberately unpleasant term used in place of a neutral or polite one.
Taboo: A socially or culturally prohibited word or expression that is avoided in polite or formal speech.
Vernacular: The everyday, unmarked variety of a language used in ordinary, informal communication.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The interleaving of elements from two or more languages within a single clause or sentence.
Interlanguage: The evolving linguistic system developed by a second language learner, distinct from both the L1 and the target L2.
Fossilization: The permanent stabilization of errors or non-target features in a second language learner's interlanguage.
L1 transfer: The influence of a speaker's first language on their production or comprehension of a second language.
Language socialization: The process by which individuals learn the norms, practices, and values of a speech community through participation.
Critical period hypothesis: The proposed existence of a biologically determined window during which language acquisition occurs most easily and completely.
Sensitive period: A period of heightened receptivity to a particular type of learning, including language, after which acquisition becomes more difficult.
Universal Grammar (UG): The theoretical innate endowment of the human mind that provides the initial structural conditions and constraints for language acquisition.
Nativism: The theoretical position that language acquisition is primarily driven by innate, biologically endowed linguistic capacity.
Empiricism: The theoretical position that language acquisition is primarily driven by general cognitive mechanisms, experience, and environmental input.
Usage-based approach: A theoretical framework in which linguistic knowledge is constructed from patterns of language use rather than an innate grammar.
Zone of proximal development: A concept from Vygotsky's theory referring to the gap between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance.
Scaffolding: The temporary support provided by a more knowledgeable other that helps a learner accomplish a task and is gradually withdrawn.
Speech act theory: A framework in pragmatics that analyzes utterances as actions performed by speakers, distinguishing locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic framework developed by Sperber and Wilson that explains communication in terms of the cognitive principle of seeking optimal relevance.
Discourse: Language extended beyond the sentence, organized into coherent and cohesive stretches of text or talk.
Cohesion: The set of grammatical and lexical links that create surface connections between elements in a text.
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of ideas in a text, ensuring that the discourse makes sense as a whole.
Theme: The given or starting point of a sentence, the information about which the speaker is saying something new.
Rheme: The new or focal information in a sentence, what is being said about the theme.
Given: Information that is already established or accessible in the discourse context.
New: Information that is being introduced for the first time in the discourse.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse, signals a shift in topic, or marks a speaker's stance (e.g., "well," "meanwhile," "however").
Intertextuality: The relationship between a text and other texts, involving reference, quotation, allusion, or transformation.
Genre: A category of discourse characterized by a conventional structure, purpose, and audience (e.g., news report, argumentative essay, recipe).
Turn-taking: The system of organization in conversation by which speakers alternately produce and receive contributions.
Adjacency pair: A pair of consecutive turns in conversation in which the second turn is a relevant response to the first (e.g., question–answer, greeting–greeting).
Repair: A mechanism in conversation by which speakers detect and fix problems in production, formulation, or understanding.
Corpus: A systematically collected and organized body of texts, either written or transcribed from speech, used for linguistic analysis.
Corpus linguistics: A branch of linguistics that uses large collections of authentic language data to study linguistic patterns.
Collocation: A statistically significant or conventional co-occurrence of words (e.g., "strong tea" rather than "powerful tea").
N-gram: A sequence of N adjacent words (or tokens) in a text, used in statistical language models and corpus analysis.
Token: An individual occurrence of a word or form in a text or corpus.
Type: A unique word form in a text or corpus, as distinct from its multiple occurrences as tokens.
Part-of-speech tagging: The automated assignment of grammatical categories (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) to words in a text.
Named entity recognition: The identification and classification of proper names and other named entities (persons, places, organizations) in text.
Dependency parsing: The automatic determination of the syntactic head-dependency relations among words in a sentence.
Constituent parsing: The automatic determination of the hierarchical phrase structure of a sentence, identifying its constituent parts.
Word segmentation: The process of identifying word boundaries in a string of characters, especially important for languages with unspaced writing systems.
Tokenization: The process of breaking a stream of text into individual tokens (words, punctuation, etc.) for computational processing.
Stemming: A rule-based or algorithmic process of reducing inflected or derived words to their root or stem form.
Lemmatization: A process of reducing words to their dictionary form (lemma) using morphological analysis, as distinct from simple stemming.
Treebank: A corpus of text that has been annotated with syntactic structure, typically in the form of parse trees.
WordNet: A lexical database that organizes English nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs into sets of cognitive synonyms (synsets) and records various lexical relations.
FrameNet: A lexical semantic database that organizes words into frames, specifying the roles and participants associated with each concept.
Semantic role labeling: The task of identifying the semantic roles (Agent, Patient, Theme, etc.) of arguments associated with a predicate in a sentence.
Natural language processing (NLP): The field of computer science and linguistics concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
Machine translation: The automatic conversion of text from one natural language into another using computational algorithms.
Speech recognition: The computational process of converting spoken language into written or symbolic form.
Speech synthesis: The computational generation of artificial speech from text, also known as text-to-speech conversion.
Language model: A statistical or neural model that assigns probabilities to sequences of words, used in speech recognition, machine translation, and text generation.
Perplexity: A measure of how well a language model predicts a sample of text, expressed as the geometric mean of the inverse probability assigned to each word.
BLEU score: A metric for evaluating the quality of machine translation output by comparing it to one or more reference translations.
ROUGE score: A set of metrics for evaluating automatic summarization by measuring the overlap between generated and reference summaries.
Precision: The proportion of retrieved items that are relevant, a key measure in information retrieval and text classification.
Recall: The proportion of all relevant items that have been retrieved, a key measure in information retrieval and text classification.
F-score: A harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a single measure that balances both.
Embedding: A dense vector representation of a word, phrase, or sentence that captures its semantic properties in a continuous space.
Contextual embedding: A word representation that varies depending on the surrounding context, as produced by models like BERT or GPT.
Transfer learning: A machine learning technique in which a model pre-trained on one task or dataset is adapted for a related task or domain.
Supervised learning: A machine learning paradigm in which a model is trained on labeled input-output pairs.
Unsupervised learning: A machine learning paradigm in which a model finds patterns in data without explicit labels.
Recurrent neural network (RNN): A type of neural network designed to process sequential data by maintaining a hidden state across time steps.
Transformer: A neural network architecture based on self-attention mechanisms that has become dominant in natural language processing.
Attention mechanism: A method in neural networks that allows the model to focus on different parts of the input when producing each part of the output.
Pre-training: The process of training a large language model on a vast corpus of unlabeled data before fine-tuning on a specific task.
Fine-tuning: The process of further training a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to improve performance.
Broca's area: A region in the left inferior frontal gyrus of the brain involved in speech production and syntactic processing.
Wernicke's area: A region in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus of the brain involved in language comprehension.
Aphasia: A language disorder resulting from brain damage, characterized by impairments in language production, comprehension, or both.
Broca's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech production with relatively preserved comprehension.
Wernicke's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by fluent but often meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.
Conduction aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by impaired repetition with relatively preserved speech production and comprehension.
Global aphasia: A severe type of aphasia involving substantial impairment in both speech production and comprehension.
Anomia: A language disorder characterized by difficulty in word retrieval and naming.
Agrammatism: A severe impairment in the production of grammatical structure, often associated with Broca's aphasia.
Scanning speech: A disfluent pattern of speech production in which words are uttered slowly and with little or no grammatical function words, typical of severe Broca's aphasia.
Hemispheric lateralization: The specialization of the left and right cerebral hemispheres for different functions, with the left hemisphere typically dominant for language.
Corpus callosum: The bundle of nerve fibers connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, involved in interhemispheric communication.
Arcuate fasciculus: A white matter tract connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas, implicated in speech production and repetition.
fMRI: Functional magnetic resonance imaging, a technique that measures brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow.
PET scan: Positron emission tomography, a neuroimaging technique that measures metabolic activity in the brain.
EEG: Electroencephalography, a technique that records electrical activity of the brain from the scalp.
MEG: Magnetoencephalography, a technique that measures the magnetic fields produced by electrical activity in the brain.
TMS: Transcranial magnetic stimulation, a non-invasive technique that uses magnetic fields to stimulate or inhibit specific brain regions.
Split-brain: A condition resulting from surgical severing of the corpus callosum, studied to investigate hemispheric specialization for language.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn and develop language, from infant language learning to second language acquisition.
Language development: The progressive unfolding of linguistic competence in children from infancy through adolescence.
Lexical access: The cognitive process by which a listener or reader retrieves the meaning of a word from the mental lexicon.
Word recognition: The process of identifying a written word and accessing its form, meaning, and other properties.
Parsing: The process of assigning a syntactic structure to a sentence during real-time language comprehension.
Chunking: The process of grouping individual words into larger meaningful units to facilitate processing and memory.
Working memory: A limited-capacity system for temporarily holding and manipulating information, crucial for language processing.
Long-term memory: A relatively permanent storage system for linguistic knowledge, including the mental lexicon, grammar, and discourse knowledge.
Priming: A phenomenon in which exposure to a stimulus influences the processing of a subsequent related stimulus, used to study semantic and lexical networks.
Spreading activation: A model of semantic memory in which activation spreads from a processed concept to related concepts in a network.
Semantic network: A cognitive model in which concepts are represented as nodes linked by relations, explaining how meaning is organized and accessed.
Lexical decision task: An experimental paradigm in which participants determine as quickly as possible whether a string of letters is a real word or a non-word.
Word association: The process of linking a stimulus word to one or more associated words, used to study semantic relations and memory.
Naming: The cognitive process of retrieving and producing the appropriate label for a perceived object or concept.
Lexical retrieval: The process of accessing a word's phonological, orthographic, and semantic properties from the mental lexicon.
Phonological loop: A component of Baddeley's working memory model responsible for holding and rehearsing verbal and auditory information.
Central executive: A component of working memory responsible for coordinating attention, integrating information, and managing cognitive resources.
Language production: The cognitive and neurolinguistic process of generating and articulating a spoken or written message.
Language comprehension: The cognitive and neurolinguistic process of perceiving, interpreting, and understanding spoken or written language.
Sentence processing: The real-time cognitive process of constructing a representation of a sentence's meaning and structure during comprehension.
Readability: The degree to which a text is easy to understand, often measured by formulas based on word and sentence length.
Dyslexia: A specific learning disability characterized by difficulty in accurate and fluent word recognition and poor spelling.
Aphasology: The study of language disorders resulting from brain damage.
Neurolinguistics: The interdisciplinary study of the neural and cognitive basis of language.
Cognitive linguistics: A theoretical framework that views language as grounded in general cognitive processes such as perception, memory, and categorization.
Prototype theory: A cognitive linguistic model in which categories are organized around central, prototypical members rather than by strict necessary and sufficient conditions.
Fuzzy logic: A mathematical framework for reasoning with partial truth values, applied to the grad

Boundary: A morpheme or word limit that marks the division between two linguistic units.
Morpheme boundary: The point at which one morpheme ends and another begins within a word.
Lexical entry: The representation of a word in the mental lexicon or a dictionary, including its form, meaning, and grammatical properties.
Mental lexicon: The hypothetical store in the mind containing all of a speaker's knowledge of words, including their forms, meanings, and grammatical properties.
Lexicology: The study of the vocabulary, word structure, and word formation of a language.
Lexicography: The practice of compiling dictionaries and organizing lexical information.
Orthography: The system of conventions for writing a language, including letters, diacritics, and punctuation.
Morphology: The study of the internal structure of words and the rules governing word formation.
Syntax: The study of the structure of sentences and the rules governing the combination of words into phrases and clauses.
Semantics: The study of meaning in language, including the meaning of words, sentences, and the logical relations between them.
Pragmatics: The study of how context contributes to meaning in language, including speaker intent, implicature, and speech acts.
Phonetics: The study of the physical production, transmission, and perception of speech sounds.
Phonology: The study of the sound systems of languages and the abstract rules governing the organization of sounds.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and the social factors influencing language use.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neural processes underlying language acquisition, production, comprehension, and storage.
Historical linguistics: The study of language change over time and the reconstruction of earlier stages of languages.
Computational linguistics: The application of computer science methods to the analysis and processing of natural language.
Theoretical linguistics: The branch of linguistics concerned with developing formal models and theories of the structure of language.
Applied linguistics: The branch of linguistics that applies linguistic theory and methods to practical problems, especially language teaching, translation, and language policy.
Descriptive linguistics: The objective, empirical description of a language as it is actually used by its speakers.
Prescriptive linguistics: The practice of dictating how language should be used, often based on traditional or perceived standards of correctness.
Synchronic analysis: The study of a language at a single point in time, abstracting away from historical change.
Diachronic analysis: The study of a language's development and change over time.
Morphosyntax: The interface between morphology and syntax, studying how word structure and sentence structure interact.
Phonosemantic: The study of the association between sound and meaning, including sound symbolism.
Sound symbolism: The phenomenon in which specific phonetic features are associated with particular semantic content (e.g., "gl-" in English suggesting light or smoothness).
Phonosemantics: The study of the relationship between phonological form and semantic content.
Onomatopoeia: A word that phonetically imitates or suggests the sound it denotes (e.g., "buzz," "bang," "splash").
Mimicry: The use of sound patterns in language that imitate or evoke sensory experiences, broader than onomatopoeia.
Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which vowels within a word or phrase must share a particular feature such as backness or roundedness.
Consonant harmony: A phonological process in which consonants within a word or phrase share a particular articulatory feature.
Prosody: The suprasegmental features of speech, including stress, rhythm, intonation, and tone, that contribute to the expression of meaning.
Rhythm: The patterned alternation of stressed and unstressed syllables or short and long units in speech or poetry.
Isogloss: A geographical boundary line on a map separating areas where a particular linguistic feature is used.
Dialect continuum: A chain of dialects in which neighboring varieties are mutually intelligible but distant varieties may not be.
Sprachbund: A group of geographically proximate languages that share structural features as a result of prolonged contact rather than genetic relationship.
Language isolate: A language with no known genetic relationship to any other living or extinct language.
Language family: A group of languages that share a common ancestor, related through genetic descent.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of modern languages is believed to have descended.
Genetic relationship: A relationship between languages established through regular sound correspondences indicating common descent.
Areal relationship: A relationship between languages in a geographical area sharing structural features due to contact rather than common ancestry.
Substrate: The language of an earlier inhabitants of a region that exerts influence on the vocabulary and structure of a subsequently dominant language.
Superstrate: A language imposed on a community that influences the vocabulary and structure of the previously dominant language.
Adstrate: A language that influences another language through prolonged contact, without a clear dominance relationship.
Language drift: The gradual, often unconscious shift in a language's phonology, vocabulary, or grammar over time.
Language isolation: The process by which a community's language becomes isolated from contact with other languages, potentially leading to unique developments.
Convergence: The process by which unrelated or distantly related languages in contact begin to share structural features.
Divergence: The process by which related languages or dialects become increasingly different over time, potentially leading to mutual unintelligibility.
Language split: The process by which a single language or dialect splits into two or more distinct varieties.
Reanalysis: A change in the grammatical interpretation of a form without an immediate change in its phonetic or orthographic shape.
Morphological erosion: The process by which morphological distinctions are lost or simplified over time.
Morphological leveling: The process by which irregular alternations in a paradigm are regularized.
Paradigmatic leveling: The reduction of irregularity within a single morphological paradigm.
Analogical change: A linguistic change in which a form is altered to match the pattern of other, similar forms.
Neologism: A newly created or newly adopted word or expression in a language.
Coinage: The deliberate creation of a new word or expression.
Back-formation: The creation of a new word by removing an apparent affix from an existing word (e.g., "edit" from "editor").
Blending: The creation of a new word by combining parts of two existing words (e.g., "motel" from "motor" + "hotel").
Clipping: The shortening of a word without changing its meaning or part of speech (e.g., "ads" from "advertisements").
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced as a word (e.g., "NASA," "laser").
Initialism: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced letter by letter (e.g., "FBI," "UNESCO").
Eponym: A word derived from a proper name, especially the name of a person or place (e.g., "sandwich," "guinness").
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more negative or derogatory connotation over time.
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more positive or honorable connotation over time.
Semantic shift: The process by which the meaning of a word changes over time in a particular direction.
Semantic drift: The gradual, often uncontrolled shift in the meaning of a word over time.
Taboo replacement: A type of semantic change in which a word associated with a taboo topic is replaced by a euphemism.
Euphemistic chain: A cycle of semantic change in which euphemisms progressively lose their positive connotation and become new taboos, requiring replacement.
Register: A variety of language characterized by its use in a particular social setting, domain, or for a particular communicative purpose.
Situation: The social, cultural, and physical context in which a communicative event takes place, influencing language choice.
Field: The subject matter or topic of a communicative event, influencing the vocabulary and register used.
Tenor: The social relationship between the participants in a communicative event, influencing formality and politeness strategies.
Mode: The channel of communication (spoken or written) and its structural characteristics, influencing linguistic form.
Multimodality: The simultaneous use of multiple semiotic modes (verbal, visual, gestural, spatial) in communication.
Paralinguistics: Non-verbal vocal elements that accompany speech, such as pitch, volume, rate, pauses, and laughter.
Gesture: Bodily movements, particularly of the hands and arms, that accompany or substitute for verbal communication.
Proximity: The physical distance between speakers, which influences and is influenced by communicative behavior.
Gaze: The direction and duration of eye contact in conversation, which plays a role in turn-taking, attention, and social dynamics.
Posture: The physical positioning and orientation of the body in interaction, conveying attitudes, emotions, and social relations.
Affect: The emotional component of a speaker's or listener's response to communication, expressed through verbal and non-verbal cues.
Body language: The collective term for non-verbal signals conveyed through the body, including gestures, posture, facial expressions, and eye contact.
Conversational analysis: A method of studying the organization of talk in interaction, focusing on turn-taking, sequence, repair, and other micro-structures.
Interactional sociolinguistics: The study of how social factors such as identity, power, and solidarity are constructed and negotiated through language in interaction.
Discourse marker: A word or phrase that organizes discourse, signals shifts in topic or stance, or manages the flow of conversation.
Metadiscourse: Language that refers to or comments on the discourse itself, such as "as I said earlier" or "to put it simply."
Topicalization: The syntactic or pragmatic process of marking a constituent as the discourse topic, often by moving it to the beginning of a sentence.
Focus: The element in a sentence or discourse that carries the primary new or contrastive information.
Given-new structure: The discourse-pragmatic principle that sentences typically present given (already established) information before new information.
Old-new structure: A discourse principle in which the old or presupposed information precedes the new or assertive information in a clause.
Information structure: The organization of discourse into topic and focus, given and new, and related pragmatic categories.
Rhetoric: The art of effective persuasion through the use of language, involving the strategic use of style, argument, and appeal.
Argumentation: The process of presenting reasons, evidence, and logical structures to support or refute a claim.
Persuasion: The use of language and discourse strategies to influence the beliefs, attitudes, or actions of an audience.
Narration: A genre of discourse that tells a story, presenting a sequence of events in a temporal or causal structure.
Exposition: A mode of discourse that explains, describes, or informs the audience about a topic.
Description: A mode of discourse that presents the characteristics, features, or state of a person, place, or thing.
Dialogue: A form of discourse consisting of an exchange of turns between two or more participants.
Monologue: A form of discourse consisting of a continuous speech production by a single speaker.
Adjacency: The property of two discourse or conversation elements being produced consecutively and forming a functional pair.
Sequence organization: The structuring of conversational turns into sequences, including openings, closings, and topic transitions.
Repair: A mechanism in conversation by which a problem in production, formulation, or understanding is detected and resolved.
Self-repair: A repair in which the speaker who produced the problem initiates the correction.
Other-repair: A repair in which a listener or another participant initiates or provides the correction for a speaker's problem.
Preferential structure: The tendency in conversation for certain responses (agreement, acceptance) to be produced more readily and with less elaboration than others (disagreement, rejection).
Conversation analysis: A qualitative method of studying the detailed organization of spoken interaction, including turn-taking, sequence, and repair.
Discourse strategy: The deliberate or habitual choices a speaker makes regarding the organization, structure, and content of their discourse.
Face work: The linguistic strategies speakers use to protect, enhance, or manage their own and others' face in interaction.
Positive politeness: Strategies that emphasize solidarity, closeness, and the speaker's respect for the hearer's positive face (e.g., compliments, in-group markers).
Negative politeness: Strategies that emphasize deference, respect for the hearer's autonomy, and minimization of imposition (e.g., hedging, apologies).
Bald on-record: A direct, unmitigated speech act with no politeness strategy, used when face concerns are minimal.
Off-record: An indirect speech act in which the speaker implies rather than explicitly states the illocutionary force, making denial possible.
Face-threatening act: A speech act that poses a threat to the positive or negative face of the hearer or the speaker.
Mitigation: The use of linguistic strategies to reduce the face-threatening potential of a speech act.
Hedging: The use of words or phrases that express uncertainty, softening, or qualification (e.g., "perhaps," "I think," "somewhat").
Approximator: A word or phrase that indicates imprecision or approximation (e.g., "about," "roughly," "a few").
Booster: A word or phrase that reinforces the speaker's commitment to the truth of a proposition (e.g., "certainly," "absolutely").
Shield: A linguistic device that allows the speaker to distance themselves from the force or responsibility of an utterance (e.g., "it's not me, but…").
Politeness theory: A framework in pragmatics and sociolinguistics, developed by Brown and Levinson, explaining how speakers manage face in interaction.
Goffman: Erving Goffman, a sociologist who introduced the concept of "face" and frame analysis, foundational to pragmatics and discourse studies.
Grice: H.P. Grice, a philosopher who formulated the Cooperative Principle and the maxims of conversation, foundational to pragmatics.
Austin: J.L. Austin, a philosopher who introduced the theory of speech acts and the distinction between perlocutionary and illocutionary acts.
Searle: John Searle, a philosopher who extended speech act theory and developed a classification of illocutionary acts.
Sperber and Wilson: Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson, who developed Relevance Theory as a cognitive account of pragmatic inference.
Vygotsky: Lev Vygotsky, a developmental psychologist whose work on the Zone of Proximal Development and social interaction influenced language acquisition theory.
Chomsky: Noam Chomsky, a linguist who founded the generative grammar tradition and proposed the theory of Universal Grammar.
Skinner: B.F. Skinner, a behaviorist psychologist who argued that language is learned through reinforcement and conditioning.
Piaget: Jean Piaget, a developmental psychologist whose theory of cognitive stages influenced early accounts of language development.
Bruner: Jerome Bruner, a cognitive psychologist who studied the role of language in cognitive development and introduced the concept of scaffolding.
Firth: J.R. Firth, a British linguist who emphasized the importance of language in context and developed the framework of systemic linguistics.
Halliday: M.A.K. Halliday, a linguist who developed Systemic Functional Linguistics, emphasizing the functional and social dimensions of language.
Saussure: Ferdinand de Saussure, the founder of structural linguistics, who distinguished between langue and parole, and signifier and signified.
Trubetzkoy: Nikolai Trubetzkoy, a Prague School linguist who made foundational contributions to phonology and the distinction between phonemic and phonetic analysis.
Hjelmslev: Louis Hjelmslev, a Danish linguist who developed glossematics, a formal approach to the structuralist analysis of language.
Bloomfield: Leonard Bloomfield, an American structuralist who defined a morpheme as a minimal significant form and emphasized the behavioral definition of language.
Bally: Charles Bally, a Swiss linguist who contributed to lexicology, stylistics, and the study of language and thought.
Ladefoged: Peter Ladefoged, a British phonetician who made extensive contributions to the description of the world's speech sounds.
Wells: John Wells, a British phonetician known for his work on English phonology and the creation of the IPA chart.
Catford: John Catford, a British linguist who made significant contributions to linguistic theory, translation studies, and structuralism.
Leech: George Leech, a British linguist who developed the semantic theory of meaning and contributed to pragmatics and stylistics.
Quirk: Randolph Quirk, a British linguist known for his work on English grammar, particularly the multi-word verb and the noun phrase.
Greenbaum: Sidney Greenbaum, a British linguist known for his work on English grammar, corpus linguistics, and the Oxford English Grammar.
Huddleston: Rodney Huddleston, a British linguist known for his work on English grammar, particularly the multi-volume Cambridge Grammar of the English Language.
Carnie: Andrew Carnie, an American linguist known for his work on syntax, particularly the Minimalist Program and English syntax.
Rothstein: Beth Rothstein, a linguist known for her work in formal semantics and pragmatics.
Karttunen: Lauri Karttunen, a Finnish-American linguist known for his work on intonation, meaning, and the semantics of questions.
Montague: Richard Montague, a logician and philosopher who founded formal semantics with his program of translating natural language into a formal logical language.
Dowty: David Dowty, a linguist known for his work in formal semantics, particularly the semantics of verbal aspect and the argument structure of predicates.
Simpson: Jane Simpson, a linguist known for her work on semantics, particularly the semantics of focus and information structure.
Jackendoff: Raymond Jackendoff, a linguist who developed the theory of Conceptual Semantics and contributed to the interface between syntax and semantics.
Pinker: Steven Pinker, a cognitive psychologist and linguist known for his work on language evolution, the language instinct, and cognitive grammar.
Newmeyer: Fred Newmeyer, a linguist known for his work in syntax, particularly the theory of Case and binding.

Partee: Barbara Partee, a linguist known for her work in formal semantics, particularly the lambda calculus and the semantics of quantification.
Steedman: Mark Steedman, a linguist known for his work on the syntax and semantics of coordination, subcategorization, and phrase structure.
Hirst: Greville Hirst, a linguist known for his work in discourse analysis, semantics, and computational linguistics.

Fillmore: Charles Fillmore, a linguist who developed Case Grammar and Frame Semantics, and contributed to the development of cognitive approaches to grammar.

Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.

Aspiration: The release of a puff of air during the articulation of a consonant.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during speech production.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where a consonant is produced.
Manner of articulation: The manner in which airflow is obstructed or modified to produce a sound.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract and no significant constriction.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a constriction or closure in the vocal tract.
Suprasegmental: A phonetic property that extends over more than one segment, such as stress or tone.
Stress: The relative emphasis or prominence given to a syllable within a word or phrase.
Tone: The contrastive use of pitch on a syllable to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning.
Intonation: The pattern of pitch rise and fall across a phrase or sentence.
Mora: A unit of metrical weight in phonological representation.
Distinctive feature: A binary or scalar property used to characterize and distinguish phonemes.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a word consisting of a peak (nucleus) optionally surrounded by consonants.
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable.
Nucleus: The most sonorous part of a syllable, typically a vowel.
Coda: The final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing permissible sound combinations in a language.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ in exactly one phoneme and have different meanings.
Complementary distribution: A situation where two sounds never occur in the same phonetic environment.
Contrastive distribution: A situation where two sounds can occur in the same environment and produce different meanings.
Archiphoneme: An abstract phoneme representing a set of distinct phonemes that share a common environment.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable.
Monophthong: A single steady vowel sound without an internal glide.
Schwa: The mid-central vowel, often the most common or default vowel in many languages.
Glottal: Relating to the glottis, the space between the vocal folds.
Fricative: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract to create turbulent airflow.
Plosive: A consonant produced by completely blocking and then suddenly releasing airflow.
Stop: A type of plosive consonant produced by a complete closure of the vocal tract.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the tongue tip raised but the sides lowered, allowing air to flow around the tongue.
Approximant: A consonant produced by narrowing the vocal tract without creating turbulent airflow.
Trill: A consonant produced by rapid vibration of one articulator against another.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single brief contact of one articulator against another.
Semivowel: A sound with vowel-like acoustic qualities but functioning as a consonant in the syllable structure.
Laryngeal: Relating to the larynx or produced with articulation in the laryngeal region.
Pharyngeal: Relating to the pharynx or produced with articulation in the pharyngeal region.
Uvular: Produced with the back of the tongue against or near the uvula.
Velar: Produced with the back of the tongue against or near the soft palate.
Palatal: Produced with the middle of the tongue raised toward the hard palate.
Alveolar: Produced with the tongue tip or blade against the alveolar ridge.
Dental: Produced with the tongue tip or blade against the upper teeth.
Labiodental: Produced with the lower lip against the upper teeth.
Bilabial: Produced with both lips brought together.
Labiovelar: A velar consonant produced with simultaneous lip rounding.
Palatalization: The addition of a palatal quality to a consonant, often represented as a secondary articulation.
Labialization: The addition of lip rounding to a consonant or vowel as a secondary articulation.
Velarization: The addition of a velar quality to a consonant or vowel as a secondary articulation.
Rhotacization: The historical or dialectal change of a sound into a rhotic (r-like) sound.
Devoicing: The loss of voicing in a sound, often in syllable-final position.
Spirantization: The change of a stop consonant into a corresponding fricative.
Nasalization: The addition of nasal airflow to a vowel or consonant.
Fronting: The forward movement of a vowel in the oral cavity.
Backing: The backward movement of a vowel in the oral cavity.
Raising: The upward movement of the tongue body during vowel articulation.
Lowering: The downward movement of the tongue body during vowel articulation.
Sandhi: The set of sound changes that occur at morpheme or word boundaries.
Assimilation: The process by which one sound becomes more similar to a neighboring sound.
Dissimilation: The process by which similar sounds become less alike within a word.
Elision: The omission of a sound or syllable in connected speech.
Metathesis: The transposition or swapping of two sounds or segments within a word.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound between two existing sounds to ease pronunciation.
Gemination: The lengthening or doubling of a consonant.
Lenition: The weakening of a consonant's articulation, often due to its position in a word.
Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant's articulation, often due to its position in a word.
Creaky voice: A register of phonation characterized by irregular, low-frequency vocal fold vibration.
Breathy voice: A phonation type in which the vocal folds do not close completely, allowing turbulent airflow.
Whistled vowel: A vowel produced with a small, whistle-like opening of the lips.
Click: A consonant produced by creating and releasing a pressure differential in the mouth cavity.
Ejective: A consonant produced by closing the glottis and using the compressed air in the oral cavity for release.
Implosive: A consonant produced by lowering the larynx during the closure phase.
Flapped: A type of tap consonant produced with a quick, single movement of the tongue.
Long: A phonological category indicating extended duration of a segment relative to a short counterpart.
Short: A phonological category indicating reduced duration of a segment relative to a long counterpart.
Quantity: The relative length or duration of a segment, used as a phonological contrast.
Syllabic: Capable of serving as the nucleus of a syllable.
Nonsyllabic: Not capable of serving as the nucleus of a syllable.
Release: The articulatory movement that opens the closure at the end of a plosive.
Closure: The complete obstruction of the vocal tract during the hold phase of a plosive.
Phonation: The manner of vibration or non-vibration of the vocal folds during speech.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or grammatical function.
Allomorph: A variant phonological form of a morpheme.
Morph: A concrete phonological realization of a morpheme.
Root: The core, typically unanalyzable morpheme that carries the primary lexical meaning of a word.
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a root or stem.
Prefix: An affix placed before the root or stem.
Suffix: An affix placed after the root or stem.
Infix: An affix inserted within the root or stem.
Circumfix: A bound morpheme that surrounds the root, consisting of both a prefix and suffix component.
Interfix: An affix used to join two or more roots or morphemes within a compound.
Derivational morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new word or changes the word class of a stem.
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that marks grammatical relationships such as tense, number, or case.
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which morphemes are attached as transparent, one-to-one segments.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single morpheme may express multiple grammatical categories simultaneously.
Isolating: A morphological type in which each morpheme corresponds to a single word, with little or no affixation.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which many morphemes, often representing whole clauses, are combined into single words.
Noun: A word that typically refers to an entity, person, or concept and can function as a subject or object.
Verb: A word that expresses an action, state, or event and serves as the predicate of a clause.
Adjective: A word that modifies a noun and typically expresses a property or quality.
Adverb: A word that modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb, often expressing manner, time, or degree.
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and typically expresses definiteness or quantity.
Article: A type of determiner that indicates definiteness or indefiniteness of a noun phrase.
Pronoun: A word that stands in for a noun or noun phrase and refers to a participant in the discourse.
Preposition: A word placed before a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or semantic relation.
Postposition: A word placed after a noun phrase to indicate a grammatical or semantic relation.
Conjunction: A word that connects clauses, phrases, or words.
Interjection: A word or phrase expressing a sudden emotion or reaction, syntactically independent of the sentence.
Complement: A constituent that completes the subcategorization frame of a head.
Specifier: A constituent that specifies or restricts the referent of a phrase.
Head: The central, categorially determining constituent of a phrase.
Complementizer: A word or morpheme that introduces a complement clause.
Subcategorization: The specification of the arguments and complements that a predicate requires.
Valency: The number of arguments a predicate requires or can take.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent or Patient.
Case: A grammatical category expressed by inflection or word order that marks the syntactic or semantic role of a noun.
