response.text:
Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning, such as /p/ and /b/ in English "pat" and "bat."
Allophone: A phonetic variant of a phoneme that occurs in a predictable phonological environment, such as the aspirated and unaspirated [p] in English "pin" and "spin."
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by only one phoneme and have distinct meanings, such as "cat" and "bat," used to identify phonemic contrasts.
Phonotactics: The set of rules in a language that govern which sequences of sounds are permitted in syllables and words.
Syllable: The basic unit of rhythmic organization in speech, typically containing a vowel nucleus and optional consonantal onset and coda.
Onset: The consonant or consonant cluster that precedes the vowel nucleus in a syllable, as in /b/ in "bat."
Coda: The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the vowel nucleus in a syllable, as in /t/ in "bat."
Nucleus: The vowel or sonorant at the center of a syllable, around which the other consonantal elements are organized.
Voicing: The vibration of the vocal folds during phonation, distinguishing voiced sounds like /b/ from voiceless sounds like /p/.
Place of articulation: The location in the vocal tract where an obstruction is created to produce a consonant, such as bilabial, alveolar, or velar.
Manner of articulation: The manner in which the airflow is obstructed or modified during consonant production, such as stop, fricative, or nasal.
Aspiration: A burst of strong airflow that follows the release of a stop consonant, as in English "pin" [pʰɪn] versus "spin" [spɪn].
Nasality: The production of sound with the velum lowered, allowing air to flow through the nasal cavity, as in /m/, /n/, and /ŋ/.
Vowel: A speech sound produced with an open vocal tract configuration, without significant constriction, characterized by tongue height, backness, and lip rounding.
Consonant: A speech sound produced with a significant constriction or complete closure somewhere in the vocal tract.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that begins with one vowel quality and glides into another within a single syllable, as in /aɪ/ in "time."
Monophthong: A single, steady vowel sound produced without a glide or change in quality, as in /iː/ in "see."
Phonemic contrast: A pair of sounds that distinguish word meanings in a particular language, such as /l/ and /r/ in English.
Phonemic neutralization: The phenomenon whereby two or more phonemes become indistinguishable in certain phonological environments, as in English final-obstruent devoicing.
Suprasegmental: A phonological property that extends over more than one segment, including stress, tone, intonation, and rhythm.
Stress: The relative prominence of a syllable in a word or phrase, typically realized through increased loudness, pitch, and duration.
Tone: The use of pitch variation at the syllable or word level to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Intonation: The variation of pitch across an utterance or phrase, used to convey grammatical structure, speaker attitude, or discourse function.
Prosody: The study of the suprasegmental properties of speech, including stress, tone, intonation, rhythm, and timing.
Phonological rule: A formal statement in a phonological grammar that describes a regular alternation between sounds in specific contexts.
Distinctive feature: A binary property of speech sounds (such as [+voice], [-nasal], [+continuant]) used to characterize and contrast phonemes.
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation that organizes distinctive features into a hierarchical structure of feature classes and nodes.
Optimality Theory: A theoretical framework in phonology that explains sound patterns through a set of ranked, violable constraints rather than ordered rules.
Autosegmental phonology: A phonological framework that represents certain features (like tone or nasality) on separate tiers from the segmental tier.
Morpheme: The smallest grammatical unit in a language that carries meaning or grammatical function, such as "un-" in "unhappy."
Allomorph: A variant form of a morpheme that occurs in different phonological or morphological environments, such as /w/ and /j/ for English plural genitive.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "un-" or "-ed."
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can function as a standalone word, such as "cat," "run," or "happy."
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries its primary lexical meaning and to which affixes may be added.
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify meaning or grammatical category, including prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
Prefix: An affix that is attached to the beginning of a root or stem, such as "un-" in "undo" or "re-" in "rewrite."
Suffix: An affix that is attached to the end of a root or stem, such as "-ed" in "walked" or "-ness" in "happiness."
Infix: An affix that is inserted within the root of a word, as in some forms of emphasis in Indonesian or historical English "ab-so-lutely."
Circumfix: An affix that surrounds a root, consisting of two parts, such as German "be-...-en" in "begehen."
Derivational morpheme: A morpheme that creates a new word, often changing the lexical category or core meaning, such as "-ness" in "happiness."
Inflectional morpheme: A morpheme that marks grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person without changing the word's core lexical meaning.
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which words are formed by concatenating distinct morphemes, each typically representing one grammatical category, as in Turkish.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single affix simultaneously encodes multiple grammatical categories, as in Latin or Spanish verb endings.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words consist of single morphemes and grammatical relationships are expressed through word order and particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which a single word can encode what other languages express as an entire clause, as in many Native American languages.
Morphological alternation: A systematic change in the form of a morpheme or root depending on its morphological or phonological environment.
Suppletion: The phenomenon in which the inflected forms of a word are built on entirely different roots, as in English "go/went/gone."
Paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word that shows its morphological patterns across all grammatical categories.
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on a neighboring word but syntactically independent, such as English "-s" in "doesn't."
Compounding: A morphological process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to form a new word, such as "blackboard" or "toothbrush."
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to express grammatical or lexical meaning, as in "copycat" or many Austronesian languages.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that is expressed with no phonological material, as in the absence of an inflectional ending to mark plural in English "sheep."
Portmanteau morpheme: A single morpheme that encodes the meaning of two or more separate morphemes, as in the Latin suffix "-ant" (present + active + indicative).
Morphological process: Any rule-governed operation that changes the form of a word, including affixation, compounding, reduplication, and suppletion.
Grammar: The systematic set of rules, principles, and patterns that govern the structure of a language, encompassing phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics.
Syntax: The subfield of linguistics that studies the rules and principles governing the arrangement of words and phrases to form grammatically well-formed sentences.
Phrase structure grammar: A model of syntactic description that uses rules to specify how phrases are built from smaller constituents, without transformational operations.
Constituency: The property of a string of words or morphemes forming a single syntactic unit that can be moved, substituted, or tested as a group.
Head: The central or most important word in a phrase that determines the phrase's syntactic and semantic category, such as the noun in a noun phrase.
Complement: A constituent that is required by a head to complete its meaning or subcategorization frame, such as "the door" in "open the door."
Specifier: A constituent that precedes the head of a phrase and typically provides information about its reference, such as the determiner in a noun phrase.
Adjunct: An optional modifier in a phrase or clause that adds descriptive or circumstantial information but is not required by the head, such as "in the park" in "walk in the park."
Phrase: A syntactic unit headed by a word of a particular category, such as a noun phrase, verb phrase, or adjective phrase.
Clause: A syntactic unit containing at least a subject and a predicate, capable of expressing a complete or incomplete proposition.
Sentence: A complete grammatical unit that expresses a full proposition, typically consisting of at least one clause and marked by final intonation or punctuation.
Tree diagram: A hierarchical graphical representation of syntactic structure showing how words and phrases combine into larger constituents.
Binary branching: The syntactic principle that each node in a phrase structure tree branches into exactly two daughters.
X-bar theory: A generalization in generative syntax that posits three levels of structure (X, X', X'') for every phrasal category in a language.
Government and Binding: A framework in generative grammar (1980s) that organizes syntactic principles into modules: X-bar theory, Case theory, Binding theory, and Binding (Theta) theory.
Minimalist Program: The most recent framework in generative grammar, seeking to reduce the range of syntactic operations to the single operation of Merge.
Case: A grammatical category that indicates the syntactic or semantic role of a noun phrase in a clause, marked by morphological endings or position.
Nominative case: The grammatical case typically marking the subject of a transitive verb in nominative-accusative languages.
Accusative case: The grammatical case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb in nominative-accusative languages.
Dative case: The grammatical case marking the indirect object or recipient in many languages, as in German or Latin.
Genitive case: The grammatical case expressing possession, origin, or other relationships, as in "the book's cover" or Russian case endings.
Ergative case: The grammatical case marking the subject of an intransitive verb in an ergative-absolutive alignment system.
Absolutive case: The grammatical case marking the patient of a transitive verb and the sole argument of an intransitive verb in ergative-absolutive systems.
Transitive: A verb that takes a direct object in addition to a subject, such as "eat" in "She eats an apple."
Intransitive: A verb that takes no object and only a single argument (subject), such as "sleep" in "She sleeps."
Valency: The number and type of arguments a verb requires or can take, such as one for intransitive verbs and two for transitive verbs.
Argument: A constituent in a clause that is semantically selected by a predicate, such as the subject and object of a transitive verb.
Theta role: A semantic role assigned to an argument by a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, Experiencer, or Goal.
Agent: The theta role denoting the volitional initiator of an action, typically realized as the subject of an active transitive verb.
Patient: The theta role denoting the entity that undergoes the action or is affected by it, typically realized as the direct object.
Experiencer: The theta role denoting a sentient entity that undergoes a psychological or physical state, as in "She felt sad."
Goal: The theta role denoting the endpoint or recipient of a directed action or motion.
Source: The theta role denoting the origin or starting point of a directed action or motion.
Subject: The grammatical argument that typically agrees with the verb and occupies the preverbal position in many languages.
Object: The grammatical argument that is the target or patient of an action, typically occupying the postverbal position.
Indirect object: The grammatical argument that denotes the recipient or beneficiary of an action, as in "She gave him a book."
Passive voice: A verbal construction in which the patient of an active sentence becomes the subject, and the agent is optionally expressed in a prepositional phrase.
Active voice: A verbal construction in which the agent of an action is the subject of the sentence.
Voice: A grammatical category relating the semantic roles of arguments to the morphosyntactic structure of a clause, primarily active and passive.
Cleft sentence: A construction that divides a clause into two parts to place focus on a particular constituent, as in "It was John who broke the vase."
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and is introduced by a relative pronoun or complementizer, as in "the book that I read."
Subordinate clause: A clause that cannot stand as a complete sentence and depends on a main clause for its interpretation.
Coordinate clause: A clause that is joined to another clause of equal status by a coordinating conjunction, such as "and," "but," or "or."
Complement clause: A clause that functions as the complement of a verb, adjective, or noun, such as "that she left" in "I know that she left."
Noun phrase: A phrase headed by a noun or pronoun, including its determiners, modifiers, and complements.
Verb phrase: A phrase headed by a verb, including its auxiliaries, complements, and adjuncts.
Adjective phrase: A phrase headed by an adjective, including its modifiers and complements.
Adverb phrase: A phrase headed by an adverb, used to modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, or entire clauses.
Prepositional phrase: A phrase headed by a preposition and including its object, such as "in the garden."
Determiner: A word that introduces a noun phrase and specifies its reference, such as articles, demonstratives, or quantifiers.
Article: A type of determiner that marks definiteness or indefiniteness, such as "the" and "a" in English.
Pronoun: A word that functions as a substitute for a noun or noun phrase, such as "he," "she," or "it."
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned entity in discourse.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an entity that will be mentioned later in discourse.
Binding: The syntactic relationship in which one expression (the binder) determines the referent of another (the variable), governed by Binding Theory.
Coreference: The relationship between two expressions in a discourse that refer to the same entity.
Binding Theory: A set of syntactic principles (A, B, and C conditions) that govern the distribution of anaphors, pronouns, and referential expressions.
C-command: A structural relationship in a syntactic tree in which a node X commands a node Y if the first branching node above X also dominates Y.
Government: A structural relationship in syntax in which a head governs its complement, licensing case assignment and anaphoric binding.
Subcategorization: The property of a lexical item specifying the types and number of complements it can take, such as transitive verbs requiring an object.
Theta criterion: The principle that each argument receives exactly one theta role and each theta role is assigned to exactly one argument.
Trace: An empty syntactic element left behind at the original position of a moved constituent.
Movement: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from its base-generated position to a new structural position.
A-movement: Movement of a constituent to a position that bears Case and theta roles, such as passive or raising movement.
A-bar movement: Movement of a constituent to a position that does not bear a theta role, such as wh-movement to clause-initial position.
Wh-movement: The movement of an interrogative or relative wh-word to the clause-initial position, as in "What did you eat?"
Topicalization: A syntactic operation that moves a constituent to the beginning of a sentence for discourse purposes, as in "That book, I really enjoyed."
Raising: A syntactic movement in which a subject is moved from an embedded clause to the subject position of a higher clause, as in "She seems to be happy."
Control: A syntactic relationship in which the subject of a non-finite clause is co-indexed with an argument in the matrix clause, as in "John tried to leave."
PRO: The unpronounced subject of non-finite clauses in control and exceptional case-marking constructions.
Pro: The unpronounced subject in languages that permit null subjects in finite clauses, as in Italian or Spanish.
Pro-drop: The phenomenon in which subjects can be omitted (or are null) in clauses where their identity is recoverable from context.
Word order: The sequence in which constituents appear in a language, which can be fixed (as in English SVO) or flexible (as in Latin or Hindi).
SVO: A word order in which the Subject precedes the Verb, which precedes the Object, typical of English.
SOV: A word order in which the Subject precedes the Object, which precedes the Verb, typical of Japanese and Turkish.
VSO: A word order in which the Verb precedes the Subject, which precedes the Object, typical of classical Arabic and Welsh.
V2: The grammatical constraint in which the finite verb appears in the second position of a clause, characteristic of German, Dutch, and Scandinavian languages.
Scrambling: The syntactic phenomenon in which the linear order of arguments is freely permutable, as in Japanese and Hindi.
Topic: A discourse constituent that establishes the frame of reference for an utterance, often marked by word order, particles, or prosody.
Focus: The discourse constituent that presents new or contrastive information, typically marked by stress, clefting, or word order.
Information structure: The organization of an utterance into given (old) and new (information) components for discourse purposes.
Given: Information in a discourse that is already known or established to the participants.
New: Information in a discourse that is being introduced or is not yet established to the participants.
Discourse: The study of language use beyond the sentence level, including the organization of connected utterances in conversation or text.
Coherence: The logical and thematic connectedness of ideas within a discourse, independent of grammatical linking.
Cohesion: The use of grammatical and lexical devices (such as reference, conjunction, and substitution) to link elements in a text.
Semantics: The subfield of linguistics concerned with the meaning of words, phrases, sentences, and larger units of language.
Meaning: The interpretive content or significance conveyed by linguistic expressions.
Sense: The particular meaning or interpretation of a lexical item in a specific context.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity, event, or state in the world it denotes.
Denotation: The literal, dictionary-like meaning of a word or expression, as opposed to its connotative or pragmatic meaning.
Connotation: The additional cultural, emotional, or associative meaning that a word carries beyond its literal denotation.
Polysemy: The phenomenon in which a single word has multiple related senses, such as "head" (body part, top, leader).
Homonymy: The phenomenon in which two or more unrelated words share the same form, such as "bank" (financial institution) and "bank" (river edge).
Synonymy: The relationship between two or more words that have the same or very similar meanings, such as "big" and "large."
Antonymy: The relationship between words with opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold" or "buy" and "sell."
Hyponymy: A semantic relationship in which the meaning of one word (hyponym) is included within the meaning of another (hypernym), as in "rose" and "flower."
Hypernymy: The semantic relationship in which a more general term (hypernym) encompasses the meaning of a more specific term (hyponym).
Meronymy: A semantic relationship in which one entity is a part of another, as in "finger" and "hand."
Holonymy: The whole entity in a part-whole relationship, as in "hand" in "finger is a part of a hand."
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition logically guarantees the truth of another, as in "She is a bachelor" entails "She is male."
Presupposition: A background assumption made by a speaker that is taken for granted in an utterance, surviving under negation, as in "She stopped smoking" presupposes she used to smoke.
Implicature: A meaning that is not explicitly stated but is inferred by the hearer based on context and conversational principles, as in Grice's theory.
Scalar implicature: An implicature derived from the use of a weaker element on a semantic scale, such as "some" implicating "not all."
Truth-conditional semantics: An approach to semantics that defines the meaning of an expression in terms of the conditions under which it is true.
Compositional semantics: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and their mode of combination.
Lexical semantics: The study of the meaning of words, including word sense, semantic relations, and the organization of lexical knowledge.
Word sense: A distinct meaning of a polysemous or homonymous word, as in "bank" (financial) versus "bank" (river).
Frame: A structured set of related concepts and roles that organizes the interpretation of a word or event, as in "buy" involving a Buyer, Seller, Goods, and Money.
Prototype: A central or most typical exemplar of a category to which other members are related by varying degrees of similarity.
Metaphor: A figurative language device in which meaning is transferred from one conceptual domain to another, as in "time is money."
Metonymy: A figurative language device in which one entity is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it, as in "The White House issued a statement."
Semantic role: The thematic or logical function that a noun phrase fulfills in relation to a predicate, such as Agent, Patient, or Instrument.
Semantic field: A set of words related to a particular concept or domain of meaning, such as the semantic field of "color" or "kinship."
Semantic change: The diachronic process by which the meaning of a word shifts over time.
Semantic bleaching: The gradual loss of specific lexical meaning by a word, as it becomes a grammaticalized or function word.
Semantic shift: A systematic change in the meaning of a word over time, including narrowing, broadening, amelioration, or pejoration.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression used in place of one considered harsh, blunt, or unpleasant.
Dysphemism: An expression that is deliberately harsh, offensive, or unpleasant in connotation.
Neologism: A newly coined or recently introduced word, expression, or meaning.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of vocabulary representing the set of inflected forms of a word, such as the lexeme RUN encompassing "run, runs, running, ran."
Lemma: The citation form or dictionary entry of a word, typically the base or infinitive form, such as "run" as the lemma of "runs."
Lexicon: The inventory of words and expressions in a language, or the mental lexicon of a speaker.
Vocabulary: The set of words known or used by a particular person, group, or language.
Lexical entry: The complete set of information about a word stored in a dictionary or mental lexicon, including form, meaning, and grammar.
Collocation: A sequence of words that frequently co-occur and sound natural together, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Semantic ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from a single word or expression having multiple meanings, as in "I saw the man with the telescope."
Structural ambiguity: Ambiguity arising from more than one possible syntactic parse of a sentence, as in "The old man the boats."
Syntactic ambiguity: Ambiguity caused by a sentence having more than one possible grammatical structure.
Lexical ambiguity: Ambiguity caused by a word having more than one lexical sense in a given context.
Vagueness: The property of an expression whose meaning lacks precise boundaries, such as "tall" or "heap."
Pragmatics: The subfield of linguistics concerned with how context influences the interpretation of meaning in language use.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to conveying information, such as promising, ordering, or questioning.
Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful utterance with a specific propositional content.
Illocutionary act: The intended force or function of an utterance, such as asserting, requesting, or warning.
Perlocutionary act: The effect an utterance has on the hearer, such as persuading, frightening, or informing.
Performative: An utterance that brings about the very state of affairs it describes, such as "I promise" or "I name this ship."
Deixis: The linguistic phenomenon in which the interpretation of an expression depends on the context of utterance, such as "here," "now," and "I."
Gricean maxims: The four conversational principles proposed by H.P. Grice: Quality, Quantity, Relation (Relevance), and Manner.
Maxim of Quality: The conversational principle to say what one believes to be true and do not assert what lacks adequate evidence.
Maxim of Quantity: The conversational principle to make one's contribution as informative as required, but not more than required.
Maxim of Relation: The conversational principle to be relevant to the ongoing topic of conversation.
Maxim of Manner: The conversational principle to be clear, brief, and orderly, avoiding ambiguity and obscurity.
Cooperative principle: Grice's general principle that participants in a conversation are expected to make contributions appropriate to the accepted purpose of the exchange.
Conversational implicature: A meaning inferred by the hearer from the assumption that the speaker is adhering to the maxims of conversation.
Utterance: A single instance of language in use, as opposed to an abstract sentence or linguistic expression.
Discourse marker: A word or expression that signals the speaker's management of the discourse, such as "well," "anyway," or "by the way."
Turn-taking: The system by which participants in a conversation alternate in speaking, governed by social and linguistic conventions.
Adjacency pair: A pair of sequentially related utterances in conversation, such as question-answer, greeting-greeting, or offer-acceptance.
Repair: The process by which speakers identify and correct miscommunication or errors in conversation.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or varieties within a single conversation or utterance.
Code-mixing: The interweaving of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance, often at the word or morpheme level.
Register: A variety of language characterized by a particular style or level of formality appropriate to a specific communicative context.
Dialect: A variety of a language characterized by distinctive phonological, lexical, and grammatical features associated with a region or social group.
Sociolect: A dialect or variety of language associated with a particular social group, such as class, profession, or age cohort.
Idiolect: The unique language variety used by an individual speaker, incorporating personal features and choices.
Language contact: The interaction between speakers of different languages, which can result in borrowing, interference, or the development of pidgins and creoles.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word, morpheme, or structural pattern from one language into another.
Calque: A word or phrase formed by translating another language's word or expression element by element, as in "skyscraper" for French "gratte-ciel."
Pidgin: A simplified contact language that develops as a means of communication between groups with no common language, lacking native speakers.
Creole: A natural language that develops from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community, with full grammatical complexity.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be actively used.
Language endangerment: The condition in which a language is at risk of falling out of use as its speaker base declines or shifts.
Language revitalization: Efforts to increase the number of speakers of a language and restore its use in education, media, and daily life.
Multilingualism: The use or knowledge of more than one language by an individual or a speech community.
Bilingualism: The use or knowledge of two languages by an individual or a speech community.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn to perceive, produce, and understand language, including first and second language learning.
First language: The primary language acquired in early childhood, also called the native language or L1.
Second language: A language acquired after the first language, either in a formal setting or through immersion.
Universal Grammar: The innate, biologically determined system of principles and parameters that underlies all human languages, as proposed in generative linguistics.
Critical period: The hypothesized window of time in early development during which language acquisition occurs most naturally and completely.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurological processes underlying language acquisition, comprehension, and production.
Language processing: The cognitive mechanisms by which speakers comprehend and produce language, including parsing and sentence formulation.
Parsing: The real-time process by which a language processor constructs a syntactic structure from a sequence of words.
Comprehension: The process of understanding and interpreting linguistic input, whether spoken or written.
Production: The process of formulating and articulating linguistic output, from conceptualization to phonetic realization.
Agrammatism: A language impairment, often resulting from brain damage, characterized by the omission of functional morphemes and simplified sentence structure.
Aphasia: A language disorder resulting from brain damage, affecting various aspects of language production and/or comprehension.
Broca's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension, associated with damage to Broca's area.
Wernicke's aphasia: A type of aphasia characterized by fluent but meaningless or paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension, associated with damage to Wernicke's area.
Stuttering: A fluency disorder characterized by repetitions, prolongations, or blocks in the flow of speech.
Dyslexia: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by difficulty in reading, decoding words, and spelling, despite normal intelligence and education.
Computational linguistics: The field that applies computational methods to the analysis, processing, and generation of natural language.
Natural language processing: The subfield of computer science and linguistics concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
Machine translation: The automated conversion of text or speech from one natural language to another.
Named entity recognition: The task of identifying and classifying proper nouns and other named entities in text into predefined categories.
Part-of-speech tagging: The process of assigning grammatical category labels (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) to each word in a text.
Dependency parsing: The construction of a directed graph representing the syntactic relationships between words in a sentence, with dependencies between heads and dependents.
Corpus linguistics: The study of language based on large, structured collections of text or spoken data (corpora).
Corpus: A large, structured collection of text or spoken data used for linguistic analysis, research, or language technology.
Frequency: The number of times a linguistic item (word, morpheme, construction) occurs in a text or corpus.
Concordance: A display of all occurrences of a word or phrase in a corpus, showing the surrounding context for each instance.
Zipf's law: The empirical observation that the frequency of a word in a text is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency table.
Entropy: A measure from information theory quantifying the unpredictability or average information content of a message source.
Redundancy: The proportion of a message that is predictable or can be recovered in the presence of noise or damage.
Language model: A statistical or computational model that assigns probabilities to sequences of words, used in speech recognition and machine translation.
N-gram: A sequence of n contiguous words used as a unit in statistical language modeling, such as bigrams (2-grams) or trigrams (3-grams).
Tokenization: The process of splitting a stream of text into discrete units (tokens) such as words, punctuation, and subword pieces.
Stemming: A morphological process in computational linguistics that reduces words to their root form by stripping affixes, as in "running" → "run."
Lemmatization: A morphological process that reduces words to their dictionary form (lemma) using linguistic rules, as in "better" → "good."
Historical linguistics: The subfield of linguistics that studies the origin, development, and changes of languages over time.
Comparative method: The systematic procedure used to establish genetic relationships between languages by comparing regular sound correspondences.
Sound change: A regular, systematic shift in the phonological system of a language over time, such as the Great Vowel Shift in English.
Sound law: A regular, rule-governed pattern of sound change that applies across all appropriate contexts in a language.
Analogy: A morphological or phonological change in which a form is modeled on another, more regular or more frequent form.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language reconstructed by linguists to account for the regular correspondences among its descendant languages.
Reconstruction: The method of inferring the phonological, morphological, and lexical features of an unattested proto-language.
Cognate: A word in one language that is historically related to a word in another language through common descent from a proto-form.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words, including their form, meaning, and usage.
Language family: A group of languages that are descended from a common ancestral proto-language, such as the Indo-European family.
Language isolate: A language with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other living or extinct language, such as Basque.
Language area: A geographical region in which unrelated languages share structural features due to prolonged contact.
Sprachbund: A group of geographically adjacent languages that share features through areal diffusion rather than genetic relatedness.
Diffusion: The borrowing of linguistic features (phonological, lexical, grammatical) across language boundaries through contact.
Substrate: A language spoken by the original inhabitants of a region whose features are transferred to a later, dominant superstrate language.
Superstrate: A language imposed by a politically or culturally dominant group onto the substrate language of a region.
Adstrate: A language spoken by a neighboring group that influences another language through prolonged contact without dominance.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually abandons its original language in favor of another.
Dialect chain: A series of neighboring dialects that gradually change from one to another, with adjacent dialects being mutually intelligible but distant ones not.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line on a map that separates areas where a particular linguistic feature is found from areas where it is not.
Dialectology: The branch of linguistics that studies the geographic distribution and variation of dialects within a language.
Prescriptivism: The approach to language that advocates for adherence to established norms and "correct" usage rules.
Descriptivism: The approach to language that documents and analyzes language as it is actually used by speakers, without imposing value judgments.
Standard language: A variety of a language that has been codified and is used in education, media, and formal institutions.
Prestige: The social value or positive evaluation attached to a particular language variety, speaker, or linguistic feature.
Stigma: The negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety, accent, or speaker.
Language attitude: The beliefs, values, and feelings that individuals or communities hold about languages, dialects, and their speakers.
Linguistic determinism: The strong version of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis claiming that language determines the structure of thought and perception.
Linguistic relativity: The weak version of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis suggesting that language influences but does not strictly determine thought.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: The hypothesis that the structure of a language affects its speakers' worldview and cognitive processes.
Universal: A property or feature that is common to all human languages, either in form or in the range of possible values.
Parameter: A binary or limited-choice setting in Universal Grammar that varies across languages, such as the head-direction parameter.
Language typology: The classification of languages into types based on shared structural features, independent of genetic relationship.
Parameter setting: The process by which the values of parameters in Universal Grammar are fixed for a particular language during acquisition.
Syntagmatic: Relating to the horizontal, linear combination of elements in a sequence, as opposed to the vertical paradigmatic relation.
Paradigmatic: Relating to the vertical relationship between elements that can occupy the same position in a structure, as in the set of nouns.
Signifier: In Saussurean linguistics, the physical form of a linguistic sign, such as the sound pattern or written shape of a word.
Signified: In Saussurean linguistics, the conceptual content or meaning associated with a signifier.
Arbitrariness: The principle that the relationship between a signifier and its signified is conventional and not motivated by any inherent connection.
Linearity: The property of language by which signs are arranged in a sequence over time (speech) or space (writing), one after another.
Langue: In Saussurean linguistics, the abstract, shared system of language rules and conventions of a speech community.
Parole: In Saussurean linguistics, the concrete, individual act of speaking or an actual utterance.
Synchronic: The study of a language at a single point in time, as a self-contained system, as opposed to diachronic study.
Diachronic: The study of language change and development over historical time periods.
Structuralism: A linguistic approach emphasizing the analysis of language as a system of interrelated elements defined by their differences.
Generative grammar: The approach to syntax, initiated by Chomsky, that seeks to characterize the set of all grammatical sentences of a language using a finite set of rules.
Transformational grammar: A model of syntax in which deep structures are converted to surface structures through a series of transformational rules.
Deep structure: The underlying syntactic representation of a sentence that encodes its thematic and semantic relationships before surface transformations.
Surface structure: The final, phonetically interpretable form of a sentence after all syntactic transformations have been applied.
Recursion: The syntactic property that allows phrases to be embedded within phrases of the same type indefinitely, as in "the book that the man that I saw read."
Embedding: The syntactic process by which one clause is incorporated within another, as in "I think that she said that he left."
Hierarchy: The tiered, branching organizational structure of a syntactic representation, from phrase to word to morpheme.
Recursion: The ability of a grammatical rule to apply within its own output, generating potentially unbounded complexity.
Locality: The syntactic principle that certain operations, such as movement and binding, are constrained to apply within limited structural distances.
Economy: A theoretical principle in minimalist syntax that prefers derivations with fewer steps, operations, or elements.
Neurolinguistics: The study of the neural basis of language, investigating how the brain organizes and processes linguistic information.
Broca's area: A region of the left frontal lobe (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) associated with speech production and syntactic processing.
Wernicke's area: A region of the left temporal lobe (Brodmann area 22) associated with language comprehension and semantic processing.
Lateralization: The tendency for language processing to be predominantly localized in the left hemisphere of the brain.
Speech motor control: The neural mechanisms that coordinate the articulatory organs (larynx, tongue, lips, jaw) for precise speech production.
Phonological loop: A component of working memory model that holds and rehearses verbal and auditory information.
Lexical access: The cognitive process of retrieving a word's meaning, form, and grammatical information from the mental lexicon.
Retrieval: The process of accessing stored linguistic knowledge, such as word meanings, syntactic constructions, or phonological forms, from long-term memory.
Morphological analysis: The process of decomposing a word into its constituent morphemes and identifying their grammatical and semantic functions.
Corpus: A systematically collected and annotated body of language data used for linguistic research or language technology.
Frequency: The count of occurrences of a linguistic item within a defined text or corpus.
Collocational: Pertaining to the tendency of words to co-occur with specific partners, such as the collocation "strong tea" rather than "powerful tea."
Semantic bleaching: The diachronic process in which a lexical item loses its specific content meaning and becomes a grammatical or functional marker.
Morpheme boundary: The position within a word where one morpheme ends and another begins.
Morphological well-formedness: The property of a word form that conforms to the morphological rules of a language.
Allomorphy: The phenomenon in which a single morpheme has multiple phonological realizations depending on context.
Morphophonology: The interface between morphology and phonology, studying how morphological structure influences phonological processes and vice versa.
Vowel harmony: A phonological process in which vowels in a word or morpheme sequence agree in a feature such as backness or roundedness.
Tone sandhi: The modification of a tonal pattern when tones interact across syllable or morpheme boundaries.
Consonant cluster: A sequence of two or more consonants that occur together within a syllable, such as /str/ in "strength."
Syllable weight: The phonological property of a syllable being "light" or "heavy" based on its consonantal structure, affecting stress and meter.
Iamb: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable, as in "a-LICE."
Trochee: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable, as in "HAP-py."
Foot: The basic unit of metrical structure in prosody, grouping syllables into stressed and unstressed patterns.
Meter: The rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of poetry.
Rhythm: The patterned alternation of strong and weak beats in speech or poetry.
Prosodic word: The largest unit of prosodic structure that projects from a morphologically bounded unit, often corresponding to a phonological word.
Intonational phrase: A prosodic unit that carries a single intonational contour, often corresponding to a clause or clause group.
Prominence: The degree to which a syllable is perceptually salient relative to its neighbors, realized through pitch, duration, and intensity.
Accent: A particular pattern of stress, tone, or intonation characteristic of a region, social group, or individual.
Pitch accent: A prosodic system in which the placement of a high or low pitch on a syllable distinguishes words, as in Japanese.
Tone: A prosodic feature in which pitch variation at the syllable level carries lexical or grammatical meaning.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source of information for a proposition, such as direct observation, hearsay, or inference.
Person: A grammatical category that distinguishes the speaker (first person), the addressee (second person), and others (third person).
Number: A grammatical category that distinguishes singular, dual, trial, plural, or other quantity-based noun categories.
Gender: A grammatical category that classifies nouns into sets (often masculine, feminine, neuter) governing agreement patterns.
Class: A grammatical category in some languages that groups nouns into sets based on shape, animacy, or semantic properties, governing agreement.
Definiteness: A grammatical or semantic property indicating that a noun phrase refers to a specific, identifiable entity.
Animacy: A grammatical or semantic hierarchy ranking nouns by the degree of their aliveness, affecting case, agreement, and word order in many languages.
Natural class: A set of linguistic elements that share one or more phonological, morphological, or semantic features and undergo the same rules.
Morph: A realized phonological form of a morpheme in a specific context.
Stem: The part of a word to which affixes are attached, consisting of a root plus any derivational morphemes.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, as opposed to a bound morpheme that requires attachment.
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that must be attached to a stem and cannot appear as an independent word.
Inflection: The modification of a word's form to express grammatical categories such as tense, number, case, or person.
Derivation: The morphological process of forming new words from existing ones by adding derivational affixes or other processes.
Paradigm: The full set of inflected forms of a word across all grammatical categories, organized in a tabular display.
Morphological type: The classification of languages according to the degree of morphological complexity, such as isolating, agglutinative, fusional, or polysynthetic.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language, such as "un-" in "unhappy" or "cat" in "cats."
Morphology: The subfield of linguistics that studies the internal structure of words and the rules governing their formation.
Phonology: The subfield of linguistics that studies the systematic organization of sounds in a language, including phonemes, syllable structure, and phonological processes.
Phonetics: The subfield of linguistics that studies the physical properties of speech sounds, including their articulation, acoustic characteristics, and perception.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of the movements and positions of the articulators (tongue, lips, velum, larynx).
Acoustic phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of their measurable physical properties, such as frequency, amplitude, and duration.
Auditory phonetics: The study of how speech sounds are perceived by the human auditory system.
Spectrogram: A visual representation of the acoustic properties of speech, showing frequency intensity over time.
Formant: A band of frequencies of enhanced energy in the vocal tract resonance, used to characterize vowel quality.
F0: The fundamental frequency of the vocal fold vibration, perceived as pitch.
Glottal stop: A consonant produced by complete closure of the vocal folds, as in the [ʔ] in some varieties of English "uh-oh."
Fricative: A consonant produced by creating a narrow channel that causes turbulent airflow, as in /s/, /f/, or /ʃ/.
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure followed by a sudden release of air, as in /p/, /t/, or /k/.
Approximant: A consonant produced by bringing articulators close together without creating turbulent airflow, as in /l/, /r/, or /w/.
Lateral: A consonant in which air flows around the sides of the tongue, as in /l/.
Rhotic: A consonant associated with the /r/ sound, which varies cross-linguistically as trill, tap, fricative, or approximant.
Velarized: A consonant or vowel produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the soft palate, as in some English /l/ sounds.
Palatal: A consonant or vowel produced with the front of the tongue raised toward the hard palate, as in /ʃ/ or /j/.
Retroflex: A consonant produced with the tip of the tongue curled back toward the middle of the palate, as in the /r/ of Indian English.
Uvular: A consonant produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the uvula, as in French /ʀ/ or German /x/.
Pharyngeal: A consonant produced with the constriction in the pharyngeal cavity, as in Arabic /ʕ/ and /ħ/.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word to break up a phonotactically disallowed sequence, as in "quartet" pronounced [kwɑːrtˈɛt].
Elision: The deletion of a sound or syllable in a word, as in the loss of /r/ in "car" in some English dialects.
Assimilation: The phonological process in which one sound changes to become more like a neighboring sound, as in "input" → [ɪmpʊt].
Dissimilation: The phonological process in which a sound changes to become less like a neighboring sound, as in Latin "vīs" → "vīs" with dissimilation.
Metathesis: The phonological or morphological process in which two sounds swap positions, as in "ask" historically from /eks/.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a segment to ease pronunciation, such as the /t/ in "water" [wɔːtər] in some dialects.
Devoicing: The phonological process in which a voiced sound becomes voiceless, as in German final-obstruent devoicing.
Lenition: The weakening or softening of a consonant, such as the change of /p/ to /f/ in Celtic languages.
Fortition: The strengthening or hardening of a consonant, the opposite of lenition.
Phonological alternation: A regular pattern in which two or more phonological forms of a morpheme or root alternate in different contexts.
Syllable: The basic unit of rhythm in a language, typically organized around a vowel nucleus with optional consonantal onset and coda.
Coda: The consonant or consonants following the vowel nucleus in a syllable.
Onset: The consonant or consonants preceding the vowel nucleus in a syllable.
Peak: The most sonorous point of a syllable, usually the vowel or a sonorant consonant.
Margin: The consonantal onsets and codas that surround the syllable peak.
Sonority: The relative loudness or strength of a speech sound, used to describe the internal structure of syllables.
Syllable well-formedness: The set of constraints governing which combinations of onset, nucleus, and coda are permitted in a language.
CV: A syllable structure consisting of a single consonant followed by a single vowel.
CVC: A syllable structure consisting of a consonant, vowel, and consonant.
CCV: A syllable structure with a consonant cluster onset followed by a vowel.
VCC: A syllable structure with a vowel followed by a consonant cluster coda.
Morphological process: Any rule-governed operation that modifies the form of a word, including affixation, compounding, reduplication, and internal vowel change.
Suppletion: The use of unrelated morphological forms for different grammatical paradigms of the same lexeme, as in "go/went/gone."
Zero derivation: The formation of a new word from an existing one without any overt morphological change, as in "butter" (noun) from "butter" (verb).
Conversion: A morphological process in which a word changes grammatical category without any overt affixation, as in "to email" (verb) from "email" (noun).
Compounding: A word-formation process in which two or more free morphemes are combined to create a new lexical item.
Blending: A word-formation process that combines parts of two words into a new word, as in "brunch" (breakfast + lunch).
Clipping: A word-formation process that shortens a word by removing one or more syllables, as in "phone" from "telephone."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced as a word, as in "laser" or "radar."
Initialism: A word formed from the initial letters of a phrase, pronounced letter by letter, as in "FBI" or "NASA."
Back-formation: A word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing an apparent affix, as in "edit" from "editor."
Coinage: The creation of a wholly new word not derived from existing linguistic material.
Borrowing: The adoption of a word or expression from one language into another, as in "café" from French into English.
Loan translation: A calque, in which the meaning of a foreign word is translated element by element into the target language.
Semantic narrowing: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more specific over time, as in "meat" from "food" to "animal flesh."
Semantic broadening: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more general over time, as in "bird" from "young bird" to any bird.
Amelioration: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more positive or favorable over time.
Pejoration: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more negative or derogatory over time.
Taboo: A cultural prohibition against using certain words or expressions, leading to euphemistic replacement or avoidance.
Euphemistic: Pertaining to the use of mild or indirect expressions in place of blunt or offensive ones.
Slang: Informal, often transient vocabulary used by particular social groups, often considered non-standard.
Jargon: The specialized technical vocabulary of a particular profession, field, or community.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its individual components, as in "kick the bucket."
Phrasal verb: A verb combined with a particle (adverb or preposition) to create a meaning different from the verb alone, as in "give up."
Particle: A small, often uninflected word that modifies a verb or other expression, such as "up" in "give up."
Preposition: A word that typically precedes a noun phrase to indicate its grammatical or semantic relationship to other elements, as in "in," "on," "by."
Postposition: A word that follows a noun phrase to indicate its relationship to other elements, as in Japanese "de" or "ni."
Conjunction: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses, such as "and," "but," or "because."
Subordinating conjunction: A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause, such as "because," "although," or "if."
Coordinating conjunction: A conjunction that joins elements of equal grammatical rank, such as "and," "or," and "but."
Interjection: A word or expression that expresses a sudden emotion or reaction, such as "oh," "wow," or "ouch."
Quantifier: A word or expression that specifies the quantity or degree of something, such as "all," "some," "many," or "few."
Negation: A grammatical category expressing the denial or opposite of a proposition, marked by words like "not," "never," or "no."
Auxiliary: A verb that supports the main verb in expressing tense, aspect, mood, or voice, such as "have," "be," and "will."
Modal: A type of auxiliary verb expressing concepts like possibility, necessity, or permission, such as "can," "must," or "should."
Copula: A verb that links the subject to a predicate complement, such as "be" in English or "ser/estar" in Spanish.
Tense: A grammatical category that locates a situation in time relative to the moment of speaking (past, present, future).
Aspect: A grammatical category that describes the temporal structure of a situation, such as perfective, imperfective, or progressive.
Mood: A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the proposition, such as indicative, subjunctive, or imperative.
Evidentiality: A grammatical category that encodes the source or type of evidence for a statement, such as witnessed, reported, or inferred.
Valency: The number of arguments a verb lexically requires, as in zero-valency (intransitive), one-valency, or two-valency (transitive).
Government: A syntactic relationship in which a head selects and licenses its complements, often involving case assignment.
Case assignment: The process by which a syntactic head (typically a verb or preposition) assigns a grammatical case to its complement.
Theta role: The semantic role assigned to an argument by a verb, such as Agent, Theme, Goal, or Source.
Assignment of theta roles: The process by which a predicate assigns thematic roles to its arguments according to its subcategorization frame.
Subjacency: A constraint in Government and Binding theory that limits the distance and complexity of constituent movement.
Subgovernment: A syntactic relationship in which certain elements (like prepositions) govern their complements with restricted movement possibilities.
Island: A syntactic construction from which extraction (movement) is ungrammatical, such as complex noun phrases or relative clauses.
Complex NP constraint: A syntactic constraint that prohibits extraction from within a complex noun phrase.
Wh-island: A syntactic constraint that prohibits the extraction of a second wh-element from within a wh-interrogative clause.
Empty category: A phonologically null element in a syntactic structure that occupies a position and bears grammatical features.
PRO: The null subject of non-finite clauses in control constructions and exceptional case-marking environments.
pro: The null subject in finite clauses of pro-drop languages, licensed by agreement morphology.
Null object: The absence of an overt object in a clause where one is syntactically required, as in some pro-drop languages.
Null subject: The absence of an overt subject in a finite clause, as in Italian or Spanish sentences.
Agreement: The morphological process by which one word changes form to match grammatical features (person, number, gender, case) of another.
Concord: The systematic matching of grammatical features between related elements in a clause, such as subject-verb agreement.
Government: The structural relationship in which a head determines the form or properties of its dependents.
Dependency: A syntactic or morphological relationship in which one element (dependent) relies on another (head) for its grammatical interpretation.
Head: The central element in a syntactic or morphological structure that determines the category and many properties of the whole.
Head-dependent: A relationship in which the dependent element's form or position is governed by the head.
Head-initial: A structural property in which the head precedes its dependents, as in English noun phrases ("the big house").
Head-final: A structural property in which the head follows its dependents, as in Japanese noun phrases.
Specifier: The element that immediately precedes the head of a phrase and typically restricts or specifies its reference.
Complement: The element that immediately follows the head of a phrase and completes its subcategorization frame.
Adjunct: An optional modifier that can be iterated and is not required by the head, such as adverbial phrases.
Recursion: The property of grammar that allows structures to be embedded within structures of the same type without limit.
Unboundedness: The theoretical property of human language that permits the generation of an infinite number of sentences from a finite set of rules.
Productivity: The property of a linguistic construction or pattern that allows it to be applied to new or novel elements.
Idiomaticity: The property of an expression whose meaning is non-compositional and fixed, resistant to modification or extension.
