Phoneme: The smallest unit of sound in a language that can distinguish meaning between words.
Allophone: A variant form of a phoneme that does not change the meaning of a word.
Phonetics: The branch of linguistics that studies the physical properties and production of speech sounds.
Phonology: The study of the systematic organization and patterning of sounds in a language.
Consonant: A speech sound produced by a partial or complete closure of the vocal tract, as opposed to a vowel.
Vowel: A speech sound produced without significant obstruction of the airflow through the vocal tract.
Plosive: A consonant produced by a complete closure of the vocal tract followed by a sudden release of air, such as /p/, /t/, /k/.
Fricative: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow channel, creating friction, such as /s/, /f/, /ʃ/.
Nasal: A consonant produced with the oral cavity closed and airflow directed through the nasal cavity, such as /m/, /n/, /ŋ/.
Affricate: A consonant that begins as a plosive and releases into a fricative, such as /tʃ/ or /dʒ/.
Approximant: A consonant produced by bringing one articulator close to another without creating turbulent airflow, such as /l/, /r/, /w/, /j/.
Lateral: A consonant produced with the center of the tongue raised while air flows around the sides, such as /l/.
Rhotic: A consonant associated with the /r/ sound, produced with the tongue curled or bunched.
Velar: A sound of articulation produced with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, such as /k/, /g/, /ŋ/.
Palatal: A sound produced with the body of the tongue raised toward the hard palate, such as /j/.
Alveolar: A sound produced with the tongue tip or blade at or near the alveolar ridge, such as /t/, /d/, /s/, /n/.
Dental: A sound produced with the tongue tip against the upper teeth, such as the /θ/ and /ð/ in English.
Labial: A sound produced with one or both lips as the primary articulator, such as /p/, /b/, /m/, /f/.
Glottal: A sound produced at or near the glottis, such as the glottal stop /ʔ/.
Aspirate: A consonant followed by a strong puff of air at release, as in the /p/ in English "pin."
Voiced: A sound produced with the vocal folds vibrating, as in /b/, /d/, /z/, and /a/.
Voiceless: A sound produced without vocal fold vibration, as in /p/, /t/, /s/, and /i/.
Suprasegmental: A phonological feature that extends over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, or intonation.
Tone: A variation in pitch that distinguishes meaning in tonal languages, such as in Mandarin Chinese.
Stress: The relative emphasis placed on a particular syllable in a word or utterance, often marked by greater loudness, length, or pitch.
Intonation: The rise and fall of pitch across a phrase or sentence, conveying attitude, grammatical function, or discourse meaning.
Syllable: A unit of organization in a word, typically consisting of a vowel nucleus possibly preceded and/or followed by consonants.
Mora: A unit of prosodic weight used in syllable structure, roughly equivalent to the length of a short vowel.
Syllabification: The process of dividing a word or sequence of sounds into syllables.
Phonotactics: The set of rules governing permissible sound sequences in a language.
Distinctive feature: A binary or gradational property of a sound (such as [±voice] or [±nasal]) used to characterize and contrast phonemes.
Feature matrix: A table listing the distinctive features of a set of sounds to show their phonological contrasts.
Minimal pair: A pair of words that differ by only one phoneme in the same position, demonstrating that the two sounds are distinct phonemes.
Complementary distribution: The situation in which two sounds never appear in the same phonological environment, suggesting they are allophones of a single phoneme.
Free variation: The interchangeable use of two or more sounds or forms in the same phonological environment without a change in meaning.
Phonemic contrast: The opposition between two phonemes that can distinguish word meanings in a given language.
Coda: The final consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, following the nucleus.
Onset: The initial consonant or consonant cluster of a syllable, preceding the nucleus.
Nucleus: The central vowel or sonorant of a syllable around which the syllable is organized.
Epenthesis: The insertion of a sound into a word, often to break up an illicit consonant cluster.
Elision: The omission or deletion of a sound from a word, as in "gonna" for "going to."
Assimilation: A phonological process in which one sound changes to become more like a neighboring sound.
Dissimilation: A phonological process in which two similar sounds become less alike to avoid adjacency.
Metathesis: The transposition of two sounds or segments within a word, as in "ask" from earlier "aks."
Apocope: The loss of a sound or syllable at the end of a word, as in "ad" for "adverb."
Apheresis: The loss of a sound or syllable at the beginning of a word, as in "uitar" for "guitar."
Prosthesis: The addition of a sound at the beginning of a word, as in "umpire" from "arbitre."
Lenition: A cline of sound change from stronger to weaker articulation, such as a stop becoming a fricative or approximant.
Fortition: A cline of sound change from weaker to stronger articulation, such as a fricative becoming a stop.
Vowel harmony: A phonological rule requiring vowels within a word to agree in some feature, such as backness or height.
Sandhi: The set of phonological changes that occur at morpheme, word, or phrase boundaries.
Devoicing: A phonological process in which a voiced sound becomes voiceless, as in final /b/ becoming [p] in some languages.
Nasalization: A phonological process in which a sound acquires nasal airflow, often when adjacent to a nasal consonant.
Palatalization: A phonological process in which a consonant becomes more palatal, often before front vowels, as in /k/ → /tʃ/.
Velarization: A phonological process in which a consonant is articulated with secondary velar contact, as in the "dark l" [ɫ] in English.
Uvular: A sound produced with the back of the tongue raised toward the uvula, such as /q/ or /ʁ/.
Pharyngeal: A sound produced with the pharyngeal wall constricted, such as the Arabic /ħ/ and /ʕ/.
Creaky voice: A vocal register in which the vocal folds vibrate with a stiff, irregular cycle, producing a creaky or "laryngeal" sound.
Whispered voice: A vocal register in which air passes through the glottis without vocal fold vibration, producing an unvoiced, breathy sound.
Formant: A concentration of acoustic energy in the frequency spectrum of a vowel, determined by the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract.
Fundamental frequency: The lowest frequency in a complex sound, corresponding to the rate of vocal fold vibration and perceived as pitch.
Amplitude: The magnitude of a sound wave, perceived as loudness or volume.
Duration: The length of time a sound is held, which can be phonemically relevant in some languages.
Manner of articulation: A phonetic classification of consonants based on how the airstream is obstructed, such as plosive, fricative, nasal, or approximant.
Place of articulation: A phonetic classification of consonants based on where the primary constriction occurs in the vocal tract.
Acoustic phonetics: The study of speech sounds as physical sound waves, analyzing their frequency, amplitude, and spectral properties.
Articulatory phonetics: The study of speech sounds in terms of the movements and positions of the articulators in the vocal tract.
Auditory phonetics: The study of the perception and auditory processing of speech sounds.
Spectrogram: A visual display of the frequency content of a sound over time, used extensively in phonetic analysis.
Prosody: The aspects of speech that go beyond individual segmental sounds, including stress, rhythm, intonation, and phrase-level pitch patterns.
Rhythm: The patterning of stressed and unstressed syllables in speech, varying by language as stress-timed, syllable-timed, or mora-timed.
Stress accent: A type of prosodic accent in which stress falls on a fixed syllable relative to the end of the word, as in German or Russian.
Pitch accent: A type of prosodic accent in which a high pitch is assigned to a specific syllable in a word, as in Japanese.
Contour tone: A tone in a tonal language in which pitch moves upward, downward, or in a curve over the duration of the syllable.
Level tone: A tone in which pitch remains at a constant level over the duration of the syllable.
Rising tone: A tone in which pitch increases over the duration of the syllable.
Falling tone: A tone in which pitch decreases over the duration of the syllable.
Morpheme: The smallest meaningful unit of language, such as "un-" in "unhappy" or "s" in "cats."
Morphology: The branch of linguistics that studies the structure and formation of words.
Root: The core morpheme of a word that carries the primary lexical meaning, such as "act" in "action" or "react."
Affix: A bound morpheme attached to a root or stem to modify its meaning or grammatical function.
Prefix: An affix that precedes the root or stem, such as "un-" in "undo" or "pre-" in "preview."
Suffix: An affix that follows the root or stem, such as "-ness" in "happiness" or "-ed" in "walked."
Infix: An affix that is inserted within a root or stem, as in the Tagalog -um- in "gumawa."
Circumfix: A bound morpheme that consists of two parts, one at the beginning and one at the end of the stem, such as German ge-…-en in "gesprochen."
Clitic: A morpheme that is phonologically dependent on an adjacent word but syntactically independent, such as the English contraction "don't" or French "l'" before a vowel.
Free morpheme: A morpheme that can stand alone as a word, such as "dog" or "run."
Bound morpheme: A morpheme that cannot stand alone as a word and must be attached to another morpheme, such as "-s" or "un-."
Inflection: A morphological process that marks grammatical relations such as tense, number, case, or person without changing the basic meaning or word class.
Derivation: A morphological process that creates a new word or changes the word class of a morpheme, such as "happy" to "happiness."
Agglutinative: A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together distinct morphemes, each expressing a single grammatical category, as in Turkish or Finnish.
Fusional: A morphological type in which a single morpheme can express multiple grammatical categories simultaneously, as in Latin or Spanish verb endings.
Isolating: A morphological type in which words typically consist of a single morpheme, with grammatical relations expressed by word order or particles, as in Mandarin Chinese.
Polysynthetic: A morphological type in which words can incorporate multiple morphemes, including arguments, into a single complex verb, as in many Native American languages.
Allomorph: A variant phonological form of a morpheme, such as the plural /s/, /z/, and /ɪz/ in English.
Morphological paradigm: The complete set of inflected forms of a word or word class in a language.
Lexeme: An abstract unit of lexical meaning, encompassing all its inflected forms, such as the lexeme RUN covering "run," "runs," "ran," and "running."
Allomorphy: The phenomenon whereby a single morpheme has two or more phonological forms.
Zero morpheme: A morpheme that has no phonological content, such as the plural marking on the word "sheep."
Compounding: A derivational process in which two or more free morphemes or stems are combined to form a new word, such as "blackboard."
Reduplication: A morphological process in which all or part of a word is repeated to express grammatical or semantic effects, as in "tiki-taka" or "makan-makan."
Suppletion: A morphological process in which a form is borrowed from an entirely different root, as in "go/went" or "man/men."
Portmanteau: A word formed by blending two or more words, combining their sounds and meanings, such as "brunch" (breakfast + lunch) or "smog" (smoke + fog).
Bound root: A root morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word but can serve as the base for derivation, such as "-ceive" in "receive."
Productive morpheme: An affix that is actively used by speakers to form new words, such as English "-ness."
Unproductive morpheme: An affix that is no longer used productively but survives in existing words, such as the "-hood" in "knighthood."
Syntax: The branch of linguistics that studies the rules and principles governing the structure of sentences.
Sentence: A grammatical unit consisting of a clause or sequence of clauses expressing a complete thought.
Clause: A grammatical unit containing a subject and a predicate, which may be independent or dependent.
Phrase: A group of words that functions as a single constituent in a syntactic structure, such as "the old house."
Constituent: A part of a sentence that functions as a single unit in syntactic analysis, such as a noun phrase or verb phrase.
Phrase structure rule: A rule in a generative grammar that specifies how constituents are combined to form larger constituents.
Tree diagram: A visual representation of the hierarchical syntactic structure of a sentence, showing constituent relationships.
Dependency grammar: A model of syntactic structure in which words are linked to a head word through direct dependency relations rather than constituent nesting.
Head: The central or governing word in a phrase or clause to which other elements are subordinated.
Complement: An obligatory constituent that completes the meaning of a head, such as the object in a transitive verb phrase.
Specifier: A constituent that precedes the head of a phrase in X-bar theory, such as a determiner in a noun phrase.
Adjunct: An optional constituent that modifies a phrase or clause but is not required for its grammaticality.
Trace: A theoretical element left in a syntactic structure at the original position of a moved constituent.
Movement: A syntactic operation in which a constituent is displaced from one position to another in the structure.
A-movement: Movement that preserves the θ-role of the element, as in subject raising or passive.
A-bar movement: Movement that changes or assigns a new thematic role, as in wh-movement or topicalization.
Binding theory: A component of syntax that governs the distribution of anaphoric expressions, pronouns, and names relative to their antecedents.
C-command: A structural relation in which one node dominates another and all sisters of the first node dominate the second.
θ-role: A thematic or semantic role assigned to an argument at the level of logical form, such as Agent, Patient, or Goal.
Case: A grammatical category marked on nouns, pronouns, or adjectives that indicates their syntactic function in a clause.
Agreement: A grammatical process in which one element takes on the features (such as number, gender, or person) of another element.
Government: A syntactic relation in which a head governs the case or form of a dependent element.
X-bar theory: A model of phrase structure in which every phrase is built around a central head of type X, with intermediate X' levels.
Tree-adjoining grammar: A formal grammar formalism that uses substitution and adjunction operations in addition to standard phrase structure rules.
Context-free grammar: A type of formal grammar in which the left-hand side of each production rule is a single nonterminal symbol.
Context-sensitive grammar: A type of formal grammar in which the left-hand side of a production rule may include context symbols.
Generative grammar: A theoretical framework, associated with Noam Chomsky, that aims to describe the innate capacity of humans to generate and understand sentences.
Transformational grammar: An earlier model of generative grammar in which deep structures are transformed into surface structures.
Universal Grammar: The hypothesized set of innate linguistic principles and parameters shared by all human languages.
Parameter: A binary or restricted choice in Universal Grammar that accounts for cross-linguistic variation, such as head-initial vs. head-final order.
Principle: A universal, unvarying component of Universal Grammar that is shared by all human languages.
Government and Binding: A major version of generative grammar developed in the 1980s, organizing syntax into modules including binding, case, government, and binding.
Minimalist Program: The most recent version of generative grammar, seeking to reduce the syntactic machinery to a single core operation, Merge.
Merge: The core operation in the Minimalist Program that combines two syntactic objects into a larger structure.
Move: The operation in the Minimalist Program that applies to a previously merged element, creating a copy in a new position.
Feature checking: A process in which a head checks whether its complement or specifier bears the appropriate uninterpretable features, triggering movement or agreement.
EPP: The Extended Projection Principle, a syntactic requirement that every clause must have a subject.
Anaphor: A linguistic expression that must have an antecedent within a certain domain, such as a reflexive pronoun.
Reflexive: A pronoun that refers back to the subject of the clause, such as "himself" or "herself."
Reciprocal: A pronoun expressing a mutual relationship between participants, such as "each other" or "one another."
Pronominal: A category of expression referring to a pronominal form, as opposed to a full noun phrase or anaphor.
Antecedent: The expression to which a pronoun or anaphor refers, providing its referent.
Case filter: A syntactic principle requiring that every overt noun phrase must bear overt Case.
Control: A syntactic relationship in which the subject of an embedded non-finite clause is determined by an element in the main clause, as in "John tried to leave."
Raising: A syntactic process in which a subject or object of an embedded clause appears in a higher position, as in "John seems to be happy."
Passivization: A syntactic process in which the object of a transitive verb becomes the subject, and the original subject is demoted or omitted.
Dative: A grammatical case or syntactic role typically marking the indirect object or recipient of an action.
Ergative: A grammatical case or alignment system in which the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb share the same marking.
Absolutive: The case in an ergative system marking the subject of an intransitive verb and the object of a transitive verb.
Nominative: The grammatical case typically marking the subject of a transitive verb.
Accusative: The grammatical case typically marking the direct object of a transitive verb.
Genitive: The grammatical case marking possession or association, such as "John's book."
Instrumental: The grammatical case marking the means or instrument by which an action is performed.
Semantics: The branch of linguistics that studies meaning in language, particularly the meaning of words, phrases, and sentences.
Pragmatics: The branch of linguistics that studies how context influences the interpretation of meaning in language use.
Denotation: The literal, dictionary-defined meaning of a word or expression, as opposed to its connotation.
Connotation: The associated, emotional, or cultural meaning of a word beyond its literal denotation.
Sense: A particular meaning or interpretation of a word or expression, one of potentially several in a polysemous lexeme.
Reference: The relationship between a linguistic expression and the entity or state of affairs it refers to in the world.
Referent: The entity, object, or state of affairs in the world to which a linguistic expression refers.
Synonymy: The relationship between words or expressions that have the same or very similar meaning.
Antonymy: The relationship between words that have opposite meanings, such as "hot" and "cold."
Hyponymy: A semantic relation in which the meaning of one term is included within the meaning of another, as in "rose" and "flower."
Hypernymy: The inverse of hyponymy, where the more general term is the hypernym, as in "flower" for "rose."
Meronimy: A semantic relation expressing a part-whole relationship, as in "wheel" and "car."
Holonymy: The inverse of meronymy, expressing the whole in a part-whole relationship, as in "car" for "wheel."
Tautology: A logical or semantic relationship in which one expression necessarily follows from another without adding new information.
Contradiction: A semantic relationship in which two propositions cannot both be true at the same time.
Entailment: A semantic relationship in which the truth of one proposition necessarily implies the truth of another.
Presupposition: A background assumption or condition that must be true for an utterance to be meaningful or felicitous.
Implicature: A meaning that is conveyed by an utterance but is not part of its literal semantic content, inferred from context and conversational principles.
Gricean maxims: The set of conversational principles proposed by H.P. Grice, including the maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner.
Relevance theory: A pragmatic framework developed by Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson that explains how listeners interpret utterances by seeking optimal relevance.
Speech act: An utterance that performs an action in addition to conveying a propositional content, such as promising, ordering, or thanking.
Illocutionary act: The intended function of an utterance, such as asserting, requesting, or warning.
Perlocutionary act: The effect of an utterance on the hearer, such as persuading, alarming, or amusing.
Locutionary act: The act of producing a meaningful utterance with a specific propositional content.
Deixis: The phenomenon whereby the meaning of a word depends on the context of its utterance, such as person, time, and place expressions.
Indexical: A linguistic expression whose referent depends on the context of the utterance, such as "I," "here," or "now."
Demonstrative: A word or expression used to point to or identify a specific entity, such as "this," "that," or "these."
Tense: A grammatical category that locates a situation in time relative to the moment of utterance, such as past, present, or future.
Aspect: A grammatical category that expresses the temporal structure or internal temporal profile of an event, such as perfective or progressive.
Modality: A grammatical category expressing the speaker's attitude toward the truth or likelihood of a proposition, such as obligation, possibility, or permission.
Scope: The domain over which a quantifier, operator, or adverb applies, which can be ambiguous in natural language.
Focus: The element in an utterance that carries new or contrastive information, often marked prosodically.
Topic: The element in an utterance about which something is asserted, typically the given or background information.
Information structure: The organization of a discourse into given and new, topical and focal elements.
Contrast: A pragmatic or prosodic marking that highlights a difference between the focused element and an implied alternative.
Scalar implicature: An implicature derived from the assumption that a speaker uses the strongest term on a scale appropriate to the situation, as in "some" implicating "not all."
Presupposition accommodation: The process by which a listener accepts a presupposition as true in order to make sense of an utterance.
Lexicon: The inventory of words and fixed expressions in a language.
Lexeme: An abstract entry in the lexicon representing a word and all its inflected forms.
Lemma: The citation form of a word, typically the base or dictionary headword, such as "run" for "runs," "ran," and "running."
Headword: The word under which an entry appears in a dictionary.
Polysemy: The phenomenon whereby a single word or expression has multiple related meanings.
Homonymy: The phenomenon whereby two or more distinct words share the same form but have unrelated meanings.
Homophone: Two or more words that are pronounced the same but differ in meaning and often spelling, such as "flour" and "flower."
Homograph: Two or more words that are spelled the same but differ in pronunciation and meaning, such as "lead" (verb) and "lead" (noun).
Neologism: A newly coined or recently adopted word or expression in a language.
Archaism: A word or expression that is no longer in current use but appears in older texts.
Jargon: Specialized vocabulary used by a particular profession, group, or community.
Slang: Informal, colloquial language that may be specific to a social group, age group, or time period.
Euphemism: A mild or indirect word or expression used in place of one that is considered harsh, blunt, or offensive.
Dysphemism: A deliberately harsh, derogatory, or offensive word or expression used where a neutral or mild one would suffice.
Register: A variety of language appropriate to a particular social or communicative context, such as formal, informal, or technical.
Dialect: A variety of a language associated with a particular geographic region, social group, or community.
Idiom: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of its individual words, such as "kick the bucket."
Phraseology: The study of fixed and semi-fixed expressions and their usage in a language.
Collocation: A statistically significant or conventionally expected combination of words, such as "make a decision" rather than "do a decision."
Borrowing: The adoption of a word or expression from one language into another.
Calque: A word or expression formed by translating the components of a foreign expression into the native language, such as "skyscraper" for French "gratte-ciel."
Loanword: A word adopted directly from another language, often with some phonological adaptation.
Loan translation: A translation of a foreign word or expression into the native language using native morphemes, equivalent to a calque.
Internationalism: A word or expression found in many languages with similar form and meaning, often from a common source such as Latin.
Etymology: The study of the origin and historical development of words and their meanings.
Sociolinguistics: The study of the relationship between language and society, including variation, change, and the social functions of language.
Dialectology: The study of dialects and regional or social variation in language.
Linguistic variation: The existence of different forms of a linguistic element within a speech community, correlated with social, regional, or stylistic factors.
Code-switching: The alternation between two or more languages or dialects within a single conversation or discourse.
Code-mixing: The interleaving of elements from two or more languages within a single utterance or sentence.
Pidgin: A simplified language that develops as a means of communication between groups that do not share a common language, typically with a reduced grammar and vocabulary.
Creole: A fully developed natural language that arises from a pidgin when it becomes the native language of a community.
Lingua franca: A language used as a common means of communication between speakers of different native languages.
Language death: The process by which a language loses its last native speaker and ceases to be used.
Language shift: The process by which a speech community gradually abandons its native language in favor of another.
Language vitality: The degree to which a language is actively used and transmitted to new generations within a community.
Language planning: The deliberate effort by governments, institutions, or communities to influence the development, status, or use of a language.
Language policy: The official or informal set of decisions and regulations governing the use, status, and teaching of languages.
Standard language: A codified variety of a language that is used in formal education, media, and government, often held up as the normative model.
Vernacular: The native, everyday language of a community, as opposed to a standard or prestige variety.
Prestige: The social value or status associated with a particular language variety, often linked to socioeconomic class or education.
Stigma: Negative social evaluation attached to a particular language variety, speaker, or linguistic feature.
Superstrate: A language that dominates a subordinate language in a contact situation, typically that of a politically or socially dominant group.
Substrate: A language that is replaced or suppressed by another but may leave traces in the dominant language.
Adstrate: A language that coexists with another on roughly equal terms and influences it through prolonged contact.
Isogloss: A geographic boundary line on a map marking the area of use of a particular linguistic feature.
Linguistic landscape: The visible linguistic elements in a public environment, such as signs, advertisements, and official notices.
Language ideology: The beliefs and attitudes a community holds about language and its varieties, which influence language use and change.
Linguistic relativity: The hypothesis that the structure of a language influences or determines the way its speakers perceive and think about the world.
Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: The linguistic relativity hypothesis associated with Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, proposing that language shapes thought.
Contact linguistics: The study of linguistic phenomena that arise when speakers of different languages interact.
Multilingualism: The use or knowledge of two or more languages by an individual or a speech community.
Bilingualism: The use or knowledge of two languages by an individual or a speech community.
Trilingualism: The use or knowledge of three languages by an individual or a speech community.
Historical linguistics: The study of language change over time and the reconstruction of earlier language states.
Comparative method: A systematic procedure for establishing genetic relationships between languages and reconstructing proto-languages by comparing cognate forms.
Reconstructive method: A method in historical linguistics for hypothesizing the forms of a proto-language based on systematic sound correspondences among descendant languages.
Proto-language: A hypothetical ancestral language from which a family of related languages is reconstructed through the comparative method.
Language family: A group of languages that are descended from a common ancestral proto-language.
Language tree: A branching diagram representing the genealogical relationships among languages within a family.
Cognate: A word in one language that has a common etymological origin with a word in another related language, such as English "father" and Latin "pater."
Sound change: A systematic shift in the pronunciation of a sound in a language over time, such as the Great Vowel Shift in English.
Sound law: A regular, exceptionless phonological change that operates within a language over a given period.
Regular change: A sound change that applies uniformly across all words in which the relevant phonological environment is present.
Irregular change: A sound change that does not apply uniformly, often due to analogy, borrowing, or lexical diffusion.
Analogical change: A linguistic change driven by the influence of similar or related forms, such as "mouses" being corrected to "mice."
Divergence: The process by which related languages or dialects become increasingly different over time.
Convergence: The process by which unrelated or previously divergent languages or dialects become more similar through contact.
Split: A sound change in which a single phoneme develops into two or more distinct outcomes in different environments.
Merger: A sound change in which two or more previously distinct phonemes become phonologically identical.
Chain shift: A series of linked sound changes in which the output of one change triggers the next, as in the Great Vowel Shift.
Semantic shift: A change in the meaning of a word or expression over time.
Broadening: A semantic change in which the meaning of a word becomes more general, as in "meat" from "flesh" to "animal flesh."
Narrowing: A semantic change in which the meaning of a word becomes more specific, as in "deer" from "any wild animal" to a specific species.
Pejoration: A semantic change in which a word acquires a negative or derogatory connotation, as in "silly" shifting from "happy" to "foolish."
Amelioration: A semantic change in which a word acquires a more positive or favorable connotation, as in "nice" shifting from "foolish" to "pleasant."
Metonymy: A semantic or rhetorical process in which a word is used to refer to something associated with its literal meaning, such as "the Crown" for the monarchy.
Metaphor: A semantic or rhetorical process in which a word is used to refer to something based on perceived similarity, such as "the leg of a table."
Taboo replacement: A semantic or lexical change in which a word is replaced due to cultural taboos, such as the replacement of direct references to death.
Archaism: A word or expression that has fallen out of everyday use but survives in literary, legal, or formal registers.
Psycholinguistics: The study of the psychological and neurological processes underlying language production, comprehension, and acquisition.
Language acquisition: The process by which humans learn to use language, whether as a first or second language.
First language acquisition: The process by which children acquire their native language from infancy to early childhood.
Second language acquisition: The process by which an individual learns a language other than their native language.
Critical period: A hypothesized window of developmental time during which language acquisition occurs most easily and fully.
Language delay: A developmental condition in which a child acquires language later than the typical age range.
Aphasia: The loss or impairment of language abilities due to brain damage, such as stroke or injury.
Dyslexia: A neurodevelopmental condition characterized by difficulty in reading and decoding written language.
Word order: The arrangement of sentence elements such as subject, object, and verb in a clause.
Parsing: The process by which a speaker or listener analyzes a string of words into a structured syntactic representation.
Chunking: The cognitive process of grouping individual elements into larger units to reduce processing load in working memory.
Working memory: The cognitive system responsible for temporarily holding and manipulating information during language processing.
Long-term memory: The cognitive system responsible for the durable storage of linguistic knowledge, including vocabulary, grammar, and discourse structures.
Priming: A cognitive phenomenon in which exposure to a stimulus influences the processing of a subsequent related stimulus.
Lexical access: The cognitive process of retrieving a word's form and meaning from the mental lexicon during comprehension or production.
Lexicalization: The process by which a multi-word expression or a morphological pattern becomes a single lexical item in the vocabulary.
Linguistic typology: The comparative study of the structural features of the world's languages, classifying and generalizing over patterns of grammatical variation.
SVO: A word order in which the subject precedes the verb, which precedes the object, as in English "I see her."
SOV: A word order in which the subject precedes the object, which precedes the verb, as in Japanese or Turkish.
VSO: A word order in which the verb precedes the subject, which precedes the object, as in classical Arabic or Modern Irish.
VOS: A word order in which the verb precedes the object, which precedes the subject, as in Malagasy.
OVS: A word order in which the object precedes the verb, which precedes the subject, as in some Mayan languages.
OSV: A word order in which the object precedes the subject, which precedes the verb, as in some Native American languages.
Split ergativity: An alignment system in which ergative marking applies in some clause types (often past or perfective) and nominative-accusative marking in others.
Incorporation: A morphological process in which a noun or noun phrase is merged into a verb to form a single complex word.
Serial verb construction: A construction in which two or more verb forms appear in sequence without conjunction or subordinate marking to express a complex event.
Cleft: A syntactic construction that highlights a particular constituent, such as "It was John who broke the window."
Relative clause: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun and provides additional information about it, such as "the man who called."
Subordinate clause: A clause that is syntactically dependent on another clause and cannot stand alone as a sentence.
Embedded clause: A clause that is syntactically contained within another clause, such as the complement in "I think that she is right."
Main clause: The primary or matrix clause in a sentence, to which other clauses may be subordinated.
Coordination: A syntactic process that joins two or more elements of the same rank, such as "bread and butter" or "He came and she left."
Discourse: Extended language beyond the individual sentence, including conversation, narrative, and written texts.
Discourse analysis: The study of language use in extended contexts, examining how meaning is constructed across sentences, turns, and texts.
Text linguistics: The study of the linguistic properties that make a sequence of sentences a coherent and cohesive text.
Coherence: The logical and semantic connectedness of ideas within a text or discourse, allowing the reader to follow the argument or narrative.
Cohesion: The formal, linguistic links between elements in a text, such as reference, substitution, and conjunction.
Anaphora: A linguistic expression that refers back to a previously mentioned antecedent in the discourse, such as a pronoun referring to a prior noun phrase.
Cataphora: A linguistic expression that refers forward to an antecedent that appears later in the discourse, such as "As I mentioned, this is a complex topic."
Ellipsis: The omission of a word or phrase that is recoverable from context, such as "She can too" for "She can do it too."
Substitution: The replacement of a word or phrase with a pro-form such as "do so" or "one" to avoid repetition.
Conjunction: A cohesive device that links sentences or clauses through connective words such as "however," "therefore," or "meanwhile."
Lexical cohesion: A cohesive device in which related or identical lexical items are repeated or used synonymously across a text.
Referential cohesion: A cohesive device in which pronouns, determiners, or other pro-forms refer back to previously mentioned entities.
Discourse marker: A word or expression that signals a discourse function, such as turning the topic, indicating a speaker's stance, or managing turn-taking, e.g., "well," "anyway," "I mean."
Topic shift: A change in the subject of discussion within a discourse.
Topic continuity: The maintenance of a single topic or subject throughout a stretch of discourse.
Given-new: A discourse principle distinguishing information the listener already knows from information that is new.
Old-new: A synonym for the given-new distinction, describing the progression from known to unknown information in discourse.
Background-foreground: A discourse distinction between the assumed, given context (background) and the new, asserted information (foreground).
Neurolinguistics: The study of the neural basis of language, examining how language is processed, represented, and produced in the brain.
Brain lateralization: The tendency for certain cognitive functions, including language, to be dominant in one cerebral hemisphere over the other.
Broca's area: A region in the left frontal lobe (roughly Brodmann areas 44 and 45) associated with speech production and syntactic processing.
Wernicke's area: A region in the left temporal-parietal lobe (roughly Brodmann areas 21 and 22) associated with language comprehension.
Angular gyrus: A region at the junction of the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes involved in integrating visual, auditory, and linguistic information.
Arcuate fasciculus: A bundle of white matter fibers connecting Broca's area and Wernicke's area, traditionally associated with speech and language processing.
Hemispheric specialization: The phenomenon in which the two cerebral hemispheres take on specialized roles, with language typically dominant in the left hemisphere.
Split-brain: A condition resulting from severing the corpus callosum, studied to investigate the functional roles of each cerebral hemisphere.
fMRI: Functional magnetic resonance imaging, a technique that maps brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow related to neural activity.
EEG: Electroencephalography, a technique that records electrical activity from the scalp to study brain processes including language.
ERP: Event-related potential, a component of EEG that averages brain responses time-locked to specific stimuli, used in psycholinguistic research.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation: A non-invasive technique that uses magnetic fields to temporarily disrupt neural activity in a targeted brain region, used to study language processing.
Broca's aphasia: A language disorder characterized by non-fluent, effortful speech production with relatively preserved comprehension, resulting from damage to the left frontal lobe.
Wernicke's aphasia: A language disorder characterized by fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension, resulting from damage to the left temporal-parietal region.
Conduction aphasia: A language disorder characterized by impaired repetition despite relatively preserved comprehension and production, associated with damage to the arcuate fasciculus.
Anomic aphasia: A language disorder primarily characterized by word-finding difficulty and naming impairments, with relatively preserved grammar and comprehension.
Global aphasia: A severe language disorder involving profound impairment in both comprehension and production, typically resulting from extensive left-hemisphere damage.
Transcortical aphasia: A language disorder in which repetition is preserved despite impairments in comprehension and/or production, distinguishing it from Broca's or Wernicke's aphasia.
Language network: The set of interconnected brain regions involved in language processing, including but not limited to Broca's area, Wernicke's area, and the inferior parietal region.
Sign language: A natural language expressed primarily through manual gestures, facial expressions, and body movement, used as the primary language of deaf communities.
Manual alphabet: A system of handshapes representing individual letters of a writing system, used in sign language to spell out words.
Fingerspelling: The act of representing individual letters using handshapes in a manual alphabet, common in sign languages.
Non-manual marking: The use of facial expressions, head movements, and body orientation in sign language to convey grammatical information such as questions, negation, or topic.
Spatial grammar: The use of spatial locations in the signing space to encode grammatical relations, such as referents, agreement, or direction.
Orthography: The conventional system of writing a language, including the rules for spelling and the use of letters, symbols, and diacritics.
Alphabet: A writing system in which individual symbols (letters) represent individual phonemes, such as the Latin or Greek alphabets.
Syllabary: A writing system in which each symbol represents a syllable, such as Japanese hiragana or katakana.
Abjad: A writing system in which symbols primarily represent consonants, with vowels indicated optionally or not at all, such as Arabic or Hebrew.
Abugida: A writing system in which each symbol represents a consonant-vowel combination, with diacritics or modifications for different vowels, such as Devanagari.
Logography: A writing system in which each symbol represents a word or morpheme, such as Chinese characters.
Grapheme: The smallest unit of a writing system that carries meaning, such as a letter or a cluster of letters representing a single phoneme.
Digraph: A pair of letters representing a single phoneme, such as "sh" in English or "ch" in Spanish.
Trigraph: A sequence of three letters representing a single phoneme, such as "tch" in "beach."
Diacritic: A mark added to a base letter to modify its pronunciation or meaning, such as the acute accent in French "café" or the umlaut in German "Mädchen."
Accent mark: A diacritic that indicates the position of primary stress or a particular vowel quality, such as the acute accent in Spanish "sí."
Punctuation: The system of symbols used to divide a text into sentences, clauses, and phrases, including periods, commas, question marks, and exclamation points.
Spelling: The conventional way of representing the sounds of a word using letters in a particular orthography.
Etymological spelling: A spelling convention that reflects the historical origin of a word rather than its current pronunciation, as in "knight" or "debt."
Corpus: A large, structured collection of texts in digital form, used for linguistic research and analysis.
Corpus linguistics: A research methodology that uses large corpora of natural language data to study linguistic patterns, frequency, and usage.
N-gram: A sequence of N consecutive words, tokens, or characters in a text, used in computational linguistics and corpus analysis.
Concordance: A list of all instances of a particular word or phrase in a corpus, with surrounding context, used for usage analysis.
Collocational analysis: The study of the statistical co-occurrence patterns of words in a corpus to identify typical and preferred combinations.
Computational linguistics: The interdisciplinary field that applies computational methods to the study and modeling of natural language.
Natural language processing: The field of computer science and linguistics concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
Speech recognition: The technological process of converting spoken language into written text.
Machine translation: The use of software to automatically translate text from one natural language to another.
Sentiment analysis: A subfield of NLP that identifies and categorizes the emotional polarity (positive, negative, neutral) in a text.
Part-of-speech tagging: The computational process of assigning a grammatical category (such as noun, verb, adjective) to each word in a text.
Named entity recognition: The computational task of identifying and classifying proper noun mentions in text into categories such as person, organization, location, and date.
Dependency parsing: A computational method of syntactic analysis that identifies the head-dependent relations between words in a sentence.
Constituent parsing: A computational method of syntactic analysis that identifies the phrase-level structure of a sentence.
Semantic parsing: The computational process of converting a natural language sentence into a formal logical or semantic representation.
Dialogue system: A computer program that interacts with users through natural language conversation, such as a chatbot or virtual assistant.
Chatbot: A software application designed to simulate human conversation through text or voice, often using rule-based or machine-learning approaches.
Morphophonology: The interface between morphology and phonology, studying how morphological structure affects phonological processes and vice versa.
Alternation: A phonological or morphophonological process in which a single underlying form surfaces in more than one phonological shape.
Neutralization: A phonological environment in which a contrast between two or more phonemes is lost, such as final devoicing in Russian.
Binary feature: A distinctive feature that takes one of two values, typically + or −, such as [±voice].
Privative feature: A distinctive feature that marks the presence of a property without specifying its value, as opposed to a binary feature.
Gradual feature: A distinctive feature that takes values on a continuum rather than in discrete binary categories, such as [high].
Feature geometry: A model of phonological representation in which distinctive features are organized into a hierarchical structure of natural classes.
Autosegment: A phonological element (such as tone or register) that is represented on a separate tier from the segmental consonant and vowel tiers.
Tier: A parallel line of representation in autosegmental phonology, each tracking a different set of phonological features or elements.
Association line: A line in an autosegmental diagram that links elements on one tier to their corresponding positions on another tier.
Spread: A delinked autosegment that associates to two or more segmental positions, extending a feature across a domain.
Delinking: The removal of the association between an autosegment and a segmental position, leaving the segment without that feature.
Floating: An autosegment that is not linked to any segmental position, available for later association.
Underlying form: The abstract, pre-phonological representation of a word or morpheme before any phonological rules are applied.
Surface form: The phonological output of a word after all phonological rules have been applied, corresponding to the actual pronunciation.
Rule ordering: The sequential arrangement in which phonological or morphological rules apply to a representation.
Strict cycle: The principle that phonological rules apply cyclically to each morpheme and then to the entire word.
Post-lexical rule: A phonological rule that applies after all lexical (word-internal) processes have been completed, often affecting prosodic or intonational structure.
Lexical rule: A phonological rule that applies within the lexicon, i.e., to the internal structure of words.
Strict cycle: The principle that phonological rules apply in a cyclic fashion to each morpheme and then to the whole word.
Post-cyclic: A rule that applies after the cycle of lexical phonological rules has completed, affecting the entire word or phrase.
Pre-cyclic: A rule that applies before the standard cycle of lexical phonological rules, affecting the underlying form.
Lexical rule: A phonological rule that is associated with specific lexical entries and is not productive across the language.
Post-lexical rule: A phonological rule that applies to the entire word or phrase after lexical rules have been processed, such as intonational rules.
Morphophonological alternation: A change in the phonological form of a morpheme triggered by its morphological or phonological environment.
Nativism: The theoretical position in language acquisition that the ability to acquire language is largely innate and biologically programmed.
Empiricism: The theoretical position in language acquisition that language is learned through general cognitive mechanisms, experience, and input.
Usage-based: A theoretical framework in language acquisition that emphasizes the role of frequent, repeated language use and general learning mechanisms over innate grammar-specific modules.
Construction grammar: A linguistic framework that models language as a collection of learned pairings of form and meaning (constructions) rather than a set of abstract generative rules.
Cognitive grammar: A linguistic framework developed by Ronald Langacker that analyzes grammatical structure in terms of cognitive processes such as image schemas, force dynamics, and conceptualization.
Functional grammar: A linguistic framework that analyzes grammatical structure in terms of communicative functions and the roles that language plays in interaction.
Language faculty: The hypothesized innate cognitive system that enables humans to acquire and use language.
Innateness: The hypothesis that certain aspects of linguistic knowledge are biologically predetermined and present at birth.
Language universal: A structural or functional property shared by all or nearly all human languages, proposed as evidence for Universal Grammar.
Language acquisition device: Chomsky's term for the innate biological mechanism that enables children to acquire the grammar of their native language.
Interlanguage: The developing linguistic system of a second language learner, which is a unique and evolving system distinct from both the L1 and the target L2.
Fossilization: The process in which a second language learner's interlanguage stabilizes and errors persist despite continued exposure and instruction.
Transfer: The influence of a speaker's first language on the learning or production of a second language, including both positive and negative transfer.
Proficiency: The overall competence of a speaker in using a language, encompassing accuracy, fluency, and appropriateness.
Fluency: The smoothness, speed, and ease with which a speaker produces language, without excessive pauses or breakdowns.
Accuracy: The degree to which a speaker's language output conforms to the grammatical norms of the target language.
Competence: A speaker's underlying knowledge of the rules, structures, and patterns of a language, as distinguished from actual performance.
Performance: The actual use of language in real communicative situations, which may deviate from competence due to memory limitations, errors, or external factors.
Contrastive analysis: A method of second language teaching and research that compares the L1 and L2 to predict areas of difficulty for learners.
Error analysis: The systematic study of errors made by second language learners to understand the interlanguage system and inform pedagogy.
L1: The first language, or native language, acquired by a speaker.
L2: The second language, learned after the first language, which may be a foreign or additional language.
Phonemic contrast: The functional opposition between two sounds in a language, demonstrated by minimal pairs.
Tonal language: A language in which pitch differences on syllables serve to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning, as in Mandarin Chinese or Yoruba.
Level tone: A tone in which the pitch remains constant over the duration of the syllable.
Rising tone: A tone in which the pitch contour moves from low to high over the syllable.
Falling tone: A tone in which the pitch contour moves from high to low over the syllable.
Register: A variety of language used in a particular social or professional context, as in formal, legal, or technical register.
Prosodic: Pertaining to the features of speech that extend beyond individual segments, such as stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Syllable-timed: A rhythm type in which each syllable is given approximately equal duration, as in French or Spanish.
Stress-timed: A rhythm type in which stressed syllables occur at roughly equal intervals, with unstressed syllables compressed, as in English.
Mora-timed: A rhythm type in which each mora is given approximately equal duration, as in Japanese.
Isochrony: The property of a speech rhythm in which a particular unit (beat, syllable, or mora) occurs at equal time intervals.
Creaky voice: A vocal register characterized by low-frequency, irregular vibration of the vocal folds, producing a rough or "laryngeal" quality.
Whispered voice: A vocal register in which air flows through a constricted glottis without vocal fold vibration, producing a breathy, unvoiced sound.
Laryngealization: A phonetic or phonological process involving constriction of the larynx, including creaky voice, whisper, and glottal stop.
Glottalization: The addition of a glottal stop or glottal constriction to a segment or syllable.
Pharyngealization: A phonetic or phonological process involving constriction of the pharyngeal wall, as in the pharyngealized consonants of Arabic.
Lip rounding: A feature of vowel production in which the lips are rounded, affecting the formant structure of the vowel.
Lip spreading: A feature of vowel production in which the lips are spread horizontally, as in front vowels like /i/ and /e/.
Tongue root: A distinctive feature of vowels indicating whether the tongue root is advanced or retracted, affecting vowel space.
Vowel space: The acoustic or articulatory space in which vowels are distributed, typically represented by height and backness coordinates.
Vowel length: A phonemic or phonological contrast in the duration of a vowel, as in the distinction between short and long vowels in many languages.
Diphthong: A vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable, such as /aɪ/ in "price."
Centring diphthong: A diphthong in which the second element is a central vowel, such as /ɪə/ in "near."
Offglide: The second element of a diphthong, the vowel quality toward which the first element glides.
Onset glide: A glide consonant that serves as the onset of a syllable, such as /w/ or /j/.
Glottal stop: A consonant produced by a complete closure of the vocal folds, as in the "uh-oh" of English or the /ʔ/ in Arabic.
Trill: A consonant produced by the vibration of an articulator, such as the tongue tip for /r/ in Spanish.
Tap: A consonant produced by a single, brief contact of an articulator, such as the /ɾ/ in many varieties of Spanish "pero."
Lateral tap: A lateral consonant produced with a brief tap, such as the /l/ in some Australian English dialects.
Tense consonant: A consonant articulated with greater muscular tension, as in the voiceless stops of English.
Lax consonant: A consonant articulated with less muscular tension, as in the voiced stops of English.
Tense vowel: A vowel articulated with greater muscular tension, often shorter and more peripheral in the vowel space.
Lax vowel: A vowel articulated with less muscular tension, often longer and more central in the vowel space.
Peripheral vowel: A vowel articulated at the extremes of the vowel space, such as /i/, /u/, and /a/.
Central vowel: A vowel articulated near the center of the vowel space, such as /ə/.
Front vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue positioned toward the front of the mouth, such as /i/ and /e/.
Back vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue positioned toward the back of the mouth, such as /u/ and /o/.
High vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue raised high in the mouth, such as /i/ and /u/.
Low vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue lowered in the mouth, such as /a/ and /æ/.
Mid vowel: A vowel articulated with the tongue at a medium height, such as /e/, /o/, and /ə/.
Unrounded vowel: A vowel articulated without lip rounding, such as /i/ and /e/.
Rounded vowel: A vowel articulated with lip rounding, such as /u/ and /o/.
Vowel quality: The distinctive acoustic or articulatory properties that differentiate one vowel from another, independent of duration or intensity.
Vowel reduction: The process by which a vowel in an unstressed syllable is weakened, often toward a central schwa /ə/.
Schwa: The mid-central, unstressed vowel /ə/, the most common vowel sound in English and many other languages.
Diphthongization: A sound change in which a monophthong vowel becomes a diphthong.
Monophthongization: A sound change in which a diphthong becomes a monophthong.
Vowel shift: A systematic change in the quality of a set of vowels over time, as in the Great Vowel Shift in English.
Great Vowel Shift: The series of vowel quality changes in English between the 15th and 18th centuries that transformed the vowel system.
Truncation: A phonological process in which a diphthong or long vowel is shortened or reduced.
Diphthong reduction: The weakening or shortening of a diphthong in unstressed syllables.
Vowel centralization: A sound change or process in which a peripheral vowel moves toward the center of the vowel space.
Vowel fronting: A sound change in which a back vowel moves toward the front of the vowel space.
Vowel backing: A sound change in which a front vowel moves toward the back of the vowel space.
Vowel raising: A sound change in which a low or mid vowel moves toward a higher position in the vowel space.
Vowel lowering: A sound change in which a high or mid vowel moves toward a lower position in the vowel space.
Vowel merging: A sound change in which two or more distinct vowels become acoustically or phonologically identical.
Vowel splitting: A sound change in which a single vowel develops into two or more distinct outcomes in different environments.
Vowel breaking: A historical sound change in which a monophthong develops into a diphthong, as in Old English "ā" to Modern English /ei/ in "gate."
Umlaut: A historical sound change in which a vowel is modified to harmonize with a suffix vowel, as in the English plural "foot/feet."
Mutation: A phonological process, particularly in Celtic languages, in which the initial consonant of a word changes depending on its grammatical context.
Lenition: The weakening of a consonant, such as a stop becoming a fricative or approximant.
Fortition: The strengthening of a consonant, such as a fricative becoming a stop.
Assibilation: A sound change in which a sibilant fricative develops into an affricate, as in /s/ → /ʃ/ or /s/ → /tʃ/.
Deaffrication: A sound change in which an affricate is simplified to a fricative, as in /tʃ/ → /ʃ/.
Devoicing: A process in which a voiced consonant becomes voiceless, often in certain phonological environments.
Voicing: A process in which a voiceless consonant becomes voiced, often in intervocalic or post-nasal position.
Nasalization: The addition of nasal airflow to an oral sound, often before a nasal consonant or in certain dialects.
Rhotacism: A sound change in which a sound becomes a rhotic consonant, as in Latin /s/ → /r/ in "ros" (now "rose").
Palatalization: The process by which a consonant becomes more front or palatal, often before front vowels.
Velarization: The process by which a consonant is articulated with secondary velar contact, as in the "dark l" [ɫ].
Labialization: The process by which a consonant is articulated with secondary lip rounding, as in /w/ or labialized /f/.
Uvularization: The process by which a consonant is articulated with secondary uvular contact.
Pharyngealization: The process by which a consonant is articulated with secondary pharyngeal constriction.
Guttural: A consonant articulated in the pharynx, larynx, or glottis, such as /ħ/, /ʕ/, /ʔ/.
Sibilant: A fricative or affricate consonant with a high-pitched, hissing quality, such as /s/, /z/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/.
Non-sibilant: A fricative or affricate consonant that lacks the high-pitched hissing quality of sibilants, such as /f/, /v/, /θ/, /ð/.
Labiodental: A consonant articulated with the lower lip and upper teeth, such as /f/, /v/.
Dentoalveolar: A consonant articulated with the tongue at the alveolar ridge near the teeth, such as /θ/, /ð/.
Retroflex: A consonant articulated with the tongue tip curled back toward the middle of the palate, as in /ʈ/, /ɖ/, /ʂ/ in Indic languages.
Uvular: A consonant articulated with the back of the tongue against the uvula, such as /q/, /ʁ/, /ʀ/.
Epiglottal: A consonant articulated with the epiglottis, as in some Semitic languages.
Implosive: A plosive consonant produced with an ingressive (inward) airstream, common in African and Southeast Asian languages.
Ejective: A consonant produced with a glottalic egressive airstream, creating a burst of compressed air, common in Caucasian and some Native American languages.
Click: A consonant produced by creating a suction or pop in the mouth, as in the Khoisan languages of southern Africa.
Lateral fricative: A fricative consonant with lateral airflow, as in /ɬ/ in Welsh and some Native American languages.
Lateral approximant: A lateral consonant with approximant manner, such as /l/.
Lateral plosive: A plosive consonant with lateral release, found in some African and Native American languages.
Alveolar flap: A consonant produced by a single rapid contact of the tongue tip with the alveolar ridge, as in the /ɾ/ in "butter" in many American English dialects.
Alveolar trill: A consonant produced by repeated vibration of the tongue tip against the alveolar ridge, as in the /r/ of Spanish "perro."
Velar fricative: A fricative consonant articulated at the velum, such as /x/ in German "Bach" or /ɣ/ in some Spanish dialects.
Uvular fricative: A fricative consonant articulated at the uvula, such as /ʁ/ in French "rouge" or /h/ in some Arabic dialects.
Pharyngeal fricative: A fricative consonant articulated with pharyngeal constriction, such as /ħ/ and /ʕ/ in Arabic.
Laryngeal fricative: A fricative consonant articulated at the larynx, such as /h/ or /ɦ/.
Glottal fricative: A fricative produced at the glottis, such as /h/, which is the same as the laryngeal fricative /h/.
Phonemic: Pertaining to a phoneme, the smallest contrastive unit of sound in a language.
Phonetic: Pertaining to the physical articulation, acoustic properties, or perception of speech sounds, as opposed to abstract phonological categories.
Phonological: Pertaining to the abstract, mental organization of sounds in a language, as opposed to their physical or phonetic properties.
Segmental: Pertaining to individual consonants and vowels, as opposed to suprasegmental features like stress and tone.
Suprasegmental: Pertaining to features that extend over multiple segments, such as stress, tone, rhythm, and intonation.
Prosodic: Pertaining to the organization of speech into rhythmic and intonational units, including stress, tone, and phrase boundaries.
Prosodic word: A prosodic unit corresponding roughly to a word, containing one or more syllables and a single primary stress.
Prosodic phrase: A prosodic unit larger than a word, corresponding to a phrase or clause boundary.
Intonational phrase: The largest prosodic unit, typically corresponding to a sentence or clause, with a single intonational contour.
Accent: In prosody, a prominent syllable or stress peak in a prosodic phrase or word.
Nuclear stress: The primary stress or pitch peak in a phrase or intonational unit.
Phrase accent: The secondary stress or pitch peak on a non-nuclear syllable within a phrase.
Downstep: A lowering of the pitch register after a high pitch accent, as in some intonational systems.
Upstep: A raising of the pitch register, as in certain intonational systems.
Declination: A fall in pitch across an intonational phrase or sentence.
Pitch accent: A prosodic system in which a high pitch is assigned to a specific syllable, as in Japanese.
Stress accent: A prosodic system in which one syllable is marked by greater loudness, duration, or pitch relative to others.
Tone accent: A system in which a tone is used to mark a particular syllable, distinct from stress or pitch accent systems.
Accentual: Pertaining to a system in which a particular syllable is marked by a special prosodic feature.
Isochronous: Having equal time intervals between beats, syllables, or moras.
Stress maximum: A principle in some languages that stress falls on the heaviest syllable in a word.
Quantitative: Pertaining to duration or length, as in contrastive vowel or consonant length.
Qualitative: Pertaining to the quality or type of a sound, as in the difference between /p/ and /t/.
Distinctive: Serving to distinguish one linguistic form from another.
Contrastive: Serving to create a meaningful distinction between two or more linguistic forms.
Redundant: A phonological or grammatical feature that is predictable from the surrounding context and does not add new information.
Marked: A linguistic form or feature that is less common, less natural, or more complex than its counterpart.
Unmarked: A linguistic form or feature that is more common, more natural, or less complex than its counterpart.
Default: A form or feature that is used in the absence of specific specification, often the unmarked option.
Productive: A grammatical process or pattern that is actively used by speakers to form new words or constructions.
Unproductive: A grammatical process or pattern that is no longer actively used but survives in existing forms.
Frequent: A word, form, or construction that occurs with high regularity in a language.
Infrequent: A word, form, or construction that occurs rarely in a language.
Opaque: A word or form whose etymological origin is no longer transparent or analyzable by modern speakers.
Transparent: A word or form whose etymological origin and morphological structure are readily analyzable.
Compound: A word formed by combining two or more free morphemes, such as "toothbrush" or "sunflower."
Derivative: A word formed by adding an affix to a root or stem, such as "happiness" from "happy."
Conversion: A morphological process in which a word changes its word class without any change in form, such as "to email" from the noun "email."
Back-formation: A word created by removing an apparent affix from an existing word, such as "edit" from "editor."
Blend: A word formed by combining parts of two or more words, such as "motel" (motor + hotel) or "brunch" (breakfast + lunch).
Clipping: A word shortened from a longer form, such as "phone" from "telephone" or "gym" from "gymnasium."
Acronym: A word formed from the initial letters of a multi-word expression, such as "NASA" or "laser."
Initialism: A sequence of initial letters pronounced letter by letter, such as "FBI" or "CIA."
Neologism: A newly created word or expression.
Backronym: An acronym retrofitted to form a phrase, such as "RADAR" supposedly standing for "Radio Detection And Ranging."
Portmanteau: A word blending two or more words in both sound and meaning, such as "smog" (smoke + fog)
